stories.Headline: Trade groups urge Congress to extend cybersecurity information sharing law through 2035
stories.Summary:
Thirty-five trade associations and cybersecurity groups wrote on November 1 to the leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees. They asked the conference negotiation to keep Section 1706 of the House-passed defense authorization bill. That section would extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through 2035. The authority now in force lapses on December 11. The groups sent the letter as Congress returned the week of November 9 with about four weeks to settle the bill.

Section 1706 writes a definition of artificial intelligence into the statute, borrowed from the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020. It adds a definition of critical infrastructure beside it, which widens who the rest of the Act covers without touching what may be shared. It adds language making clear the Act cannot be read to forbid using AI for cybersecurity purposes, and it brings AI owners into the group that gets security read-ins. The short title is untouched, and the definition of a cyber threat indicator is not widened to cover AI. The Senate version contains no reauthorization at all and does contain Section 1636, which directs a strategy for AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and remediation.

The letter says the speed and breadth with which defenders share information decides whether they keep pace. Henry Young, senior director of policy at the Business Software Alliance, told Axios two weeks into the first lapse that it “has reinserted lawyers into the conversation, which is going to slow down information sharing.” A Center for a New American Security commentary last May put the result plainly, saying information sharing did not collapse during the uncertainty but slowed. Milton Mueller of Georgia Tech’s Internet Governance Project argued in January that the federal sharing hub has withered. Mueller said commercial intelligence and the sector ISACs deliver better context, and that renewal would reward inertia rather than security.

The original authorization ended on September 30, 2025. The protection lapsed outright for about six weeks, came back in November 2025 with a term good to January 30, lapsed a second time for several days at the start of February, and has run on two more short-term extensions since. The one in force now expires on the same December day the government runs out of money, because the same stopgap law set both dates. In September, Anthropic published a report on attackers misusing its models, describing one group running agents “designed to continue iterating on” their toolkit “until it was undetected.” The report says the actor “used Claude to systematically identify, modify and redeploy the detected artifacts,” and that AI “has inverted the cost back onto defenders.”

The Act already says that sharing done while it was in force stays protected, so on its face the exposure a lapse creates runs forward rather than back. The liability shield covers a bank telling another bank what it just saw, and it covers the sector groups that carry a great deal of the useful traffic. One way to build a control that decides on the machine works in memory, changing the arrangement each time an application loads so code written against the expected layout fails at the moment it runs. That approach needs no hash and no indicator at all, shared or otherwise. It is no replacement for intelligence but covers the gap between the hour an attack starts and the hour anybody can describe it.

Congress comes back the week of November 9 with about four weeks to settle this, and the article urges keeping Section 1706 with a term long enough that a general counsel stops reopening the question every few weeks. The article says December 11 will come and go without changing what your own defense does on the morning a warning turns out to be correct and twelve hours late. The articles leave open whether the conference negotiation will keep Section 1706. They leave open what the Senate will accept, given that its version contains no reauthorization. They leave open whether the authority lapses again on December 11.

stories.Headline: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
stories.Summary:
The Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported a critical inflection point in adversarial AI on November 16, 2026. Threat actors are now deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks to execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. These adversaries include cyber criminals, espionage groups, and those conducting information operations. They use generative AI to compress attack timelines and scale their operations. This shift moves beyond basic prompting to fully automated offensive workflows.

The report identifies open source frameworks called ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI used for automated intrusions. CAIRN targeted the US aerospace sector, while PentAGI scanned Asian organizations from August to October 2026. CyberStrikeAI uses a Go-based backend API, and HexStrike AI integrates with the Model Context Protocol. Other tools mentioned include ZeroHollow for exploit development and Agent Zero for autonomous code execution. These systems automate the reverse engineering of patches to weaponize n-day vulnerabilities.

Google stated they are committed to developing AI boldly and responsibly through a multifaceted defense strategy. They use a Google AI Threat Defense architecture and BeyondZero for continuous monitoring and responding at machine speed. The company hardens models against misuse and proactively disrupts the projects and accounts of bad actors. Mandiant Consulting released a hardening guide and architectural defense framework to counter LLM-enabled tooling. Google Security Operations also deployed specialized rulepacks to detect the use of ARTEX.

Financially motivated actors affect enterprises by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources through a process called LLMJacking. These criminals resell access to high-performance AI models using underground proxy services known as LLM Mixers. State-sponsored groups and commercial Influence-as-a-Service vendors affect the public by producing synthetic media and localized personas. Cyber espionage groups target supply chains by manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors. These activities create a new defensive challenge by exploiting known weaknesses at extreme speed.

The articles note that zero-day exploits averaged 8 per month in 2025 and rose to 11 in 2026. This number spiked to 22 in August 2026, while overall disclosures nearly doubled between January and August. Previous quarterly research had only documented nascent adversary interest in these agentic capabilities. LLMs now automate labor-intensive phases like differential patch examination and dynamic protocol fuzzing. This automation reduces the window between the disclosure of a patch and its weaponized exploitation.

Threat actors will likely continue using these frameworks in global campaigns due to a low barrier to entry. Future operations are expected to move further along the autonomous scale toward fully agentic intrusions. While current tools trade stealth for velocity, future versions will likely increase in sophistication and stealth. The articles leave open how defenders will manage the increase in fake LLM-generated exploits. It remains unclear how quickly the industry can close the shrinking patch window for organizations.

Articles.Title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold

stories.Headline: European leaders meet in Dublin to discuss coordinating US and EU AI safety efforts
stories.Summary:
European leaders including Prime Minister Micheal Martin, Antonio Costa, and Roberta Metsola met in Dublin, Ireland, on November 13, 2026, to discuss artificial intelligence. This gathering highlighted the need for the United States and the European Union to coordinate on AI safety to prevent catastrophic risks. While the Trump administration has shown little interest in this engagement, recent cybersecurity incidents from American frontier labs may encourage narrower cooperation. Progress is more likely to occur through legislatures, specifically by creating a joint AI safety working group within the Transatlantic Legislators’ Dialogue.

This proposed coordination would utilize the Transatlantic Legislators’ Dialogue, which has met twice a year since 1999 to discuss security and trade. The effort would focus on interoperable incident reporting and establishing designated points of contact within regulatory and law enforcement agencies. It would build upon the October 2026 White House Accord on Super Intelligence and the bipartisan FRONTIER Act currently in the United States. European efforts include the AI Act and the Digital Omnibus, which entered into force in July 2026 to adjust compliance requirements.

The European Parliament's steering committee and a bipartisan US delegation are responsible for managing these legislative exchanges. These officials suggest that focusing on cybersecurity measures first would avoid contentious issues like data privacy or content moderation. They argue that an early dialogue with the incoming Democratic majorities in Congress would ensure that new enforcement measures are compatible. This approach aims to avoid previous failures where dialogues were dismissed as talk shops or seen as attempts to export regulatory regimes.

The current US policy is a patchwork of state laws and voluntary commitments, while the EU uses a formal legal framework. Unresolved questions remain regarding the oversight of restricted models, such as the Mythos rollout by Anthropic through Project Glasswing. Legislators face pressure from constituents to deliver meaningful safety measures that address risks extending across international borders. Future efforts will seek common definitions for incident reporting, drawing on the NIS2 Directive and the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act.

stories.Headline: Flagstar Bank uses Windows 11 and Intune to secure devices and run AI agents
stories.Summary:
Flagstar Bank built a secure, manageable foundation for AI with Windows 11, Microsoft reported on November 16, 2026. The bank invested in Microsoft Surface devices to bring a more secure foundation to employees. Windows 11 anchors Flagstar’s modernization, with Microsoft Entra for identity, Intune for device management, and Windows Autopilot for setup. Flagstar needed to unify a fragmented technology environment, simplify employee access and device management, and protect customer information as it introduced AI. Headquartered in New York, Flagstar Bank serves consumers and business clients across the United States.

Following mergers that brought together three organizations and six data centers, Flagstar needed a more consistent approach to employee access, device management, and AI. Its starting point was a patchwork of on-premises Active Directory systems and a legacy domain-join model for deploying devices. The bank is consolidating its Active Directory systems, with the goal of using Microsoft Entra as the authoritative source for employee identities and group membership. With Windows Hello for Business, employees sign in with a PIN or biometrics instead of relying on passwords. Microsoft Intune gives IT a single place to govern, control, and secure devices across the environment.

Kevin Kilbride, engineering manager at Flagstar Bank, said the Windows environment consisted of different hardware models and software versions, and that joining that with a domain legacy deployment system made it difficult to manage. Kilbride said moving to Windows as the secure foundation takes the bank from a fragmented environment to a more manageable IT experience, which translates to teams, employees, and then customers. Jason Pope, Flagstar’s chief technology and data officer, said that in a highly regulated organization you need to be able to show who, what, where, when, and how a specific user accessed an application, and that Windows together with Microsoft Entra and Intune gives the bank that ability. Kilbride said getting new devices imaged and shipped to employees used to take days, and that now the bank ships new Surface devices directly to employees and, with Windows Autopilot, employees are online in less than 15 minutes. Pope said using agentic AI on the Windows platform has enabled the bank to spend more time with customers and remove repetitive sequences, specifically in banking where there is a lot of duplication of entry.

Under the legacy domain-join model, IT spent at least a day or two getting each device ready before shipping it out, and employees had to wait for equipment to arrive before they could start work. Now the end-user support team simply allocates a device and gets it to the employee, and when the employee signs in with company credentials, Windows Autopilot and Intune automate the remaining setup. Employees across the bank already use StarIQ, the bank’s AI tool built on Microsoft Copilot, which Flagstar CEO Joseph Otting says has an adoption rate of about 83 percent. Within its Windows 11 environment, Flagstar also runs a custom small language model on Microsoft Surface devices, and its purpose-built agent, BranchIQ, uses the device’s neural processing unit to help bankers perform know-your-customer activities and accelerate onboarding customers. Localizing the AI model on the device supports the bank’s security priorities and enables offline access to policies, procedures, and customer-onboarding assistance.

When onboarding a customer, bankers must verify identity as part of know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering checks, which in the past meant jotting down details from a driver’s license or passport or keying them into a legacy system over and over. With BranchIQ, a banker can instead take a photo of the ID that stays on the device, and the agent extracts the details and enters them automatically into the systems of record used to set up the new customer and account. Windows supplies the operating environment and guardrails for this agent workflow with Microsoft Execution Containers, while Surface provides the neural processing unit and mobile form factor that bring it to branch colleagues’ flow of work. Agents on Surface devices are given their own identity in the Entra Suite, which lets the bank track an agent’s actions apart from a person’s. Microsoft Execution Containers, built into Windows 11, add control over what each agent can access and do, and give the bank a way to account for those actions to regulators.

Pope said that with the bank’s agents using Microsoft Execution Containers on its Windows platform, the bank was able to ascertain how an agent is working and control it, then prove how and why it controlled it and produce that report for regulators. Flagstar is now exploring how to expand its use of the containers as part of its Windows 11 AI work. Pope said the principle behind the bank’s Windows modernization is making work easier while keeping it secure, manageable, and compliant, and that from how employees sign in and get their devices to running AI locally on Surface, Windows is the foundation, and it is the same foundation the bank will use as it brings governed agents into the bank. Centralized policy management helps IT identify settings that need attention, resolve issues, and keep devices aligned as the bank’s security and compliance standards evolve. Together, these modern identity and device management tools help Flagstar document application access and demonstrate policy enforcement to auditors.

Articles.Title: Flagstar Bank builds a secure, manageable foundation for AI with Windows 11

stories.Headline: Fed governor Barr warns AI borrowing boom poses ten risks to financial stability
stories.Summary:
Fed Governor Michael Barr gave a long speech on November 16, 2026, regarding AI investment risks. He detailed ten big, complex, and opaque threats to financial stability. These risks stem from a borrowing boom, circular financing, and high equity prices. The Federal Reserve also warned about these stability aspects in its latest Financial Stability Report. This report was released on the Friday preceding the governor's speech.

On-balance-sheet debt for the seven largest AI firms may exceed 800 billion dollars by year end 2026. Off-balance-sheet liabilities, including lease commitments and energy contracts, are estimated to exceed 3 trillion dollars. Smaller firms have over 100 billion dollars in circular financing from hyperscalers and GPU producers. These arrangements involve equity investments used to rent or purchase compute from the investors. Some firms also use collateral guarantees for asset-based financings to support their credit.

Governor Barr stated that investment losses could lower output growth through direct drops in investment. He noted that a significant repricing of AI investments could be amplified by complex financing. Barr warned that rapid deleveraging and self-reinforcing fire sales could occur due to high risk appetite. He mentioned that counterparty exposures could rise during periods of equity market volatility. The governor also cautioned that AI trading models might autonomously develop collusive behavior.

Unsophisticated investors are affected because financial complexity makes it hard to know where risk resides. Lower-credit-quality firms are impacted as their cost of capital has risen significantly in recent months. Hedge funds are mentioned as having high leverage that could lead to rapid deleveraging. Large dealers are involved because they provide leverage via prime brokerage services. The broader economy could suffer if wealth losses lower consumer and business spending.

The current boom is compared to the telecom investment cycle of the late 1990s and early 2000s. This earlier period was characterized by a similar boom and bust cycle of investment. The articles mention dark fiber as an example of excess capacity that took years to become useful. Some theoretical research shows that Q-learning trading algorithms can learn to manipulate markets through spoofing. These algorithms can create and exploit bubbles, which then destabilize the markets.

Specialized chips may depreciate quickly as newer technologies overtake them, making current capacity useless. It remains unclear if electrical infrastructure like substations and grid connections will find other uses. The Federal Reserve will continue monitoring exposures to counterparties with large positions in AI. The articles leave open whether smaller firms can replace supplier funding with revenue from customers. It is also unknown if the current debt levels will surpass those of the telecom boom.

stories.Headline: Study finds AI-generated ad labels reveal only that AI played some role
stories.Summary:
A study published on November 16, 2026, in a TechXplore article republished from The Conversation examines what an "AI-generated" label in advertising actually communicates to consumers, concluding that such a label reveals only that artificial intelligence played some role without clarifying how large or small that role was. The article explains that AI might have served as one tool in a largely human-led creative process, perhaps editing an image or refining text, or it might have generated much of the finished advertisement with limited human input, and a single label can cover both extremes and everything in between. The authors note that advertising has long used disclosures, such as the "#ad" tag influencers place on social media or labels marking sponsored content, which help consumers recognize the commercial side of what they are watching or reading. Their research indicates that AI disclosures serve a different purpose, because traditional disclosures tell consumers why content is being shown to them while AI labels draw attention to how it was produced without revealing the respective roles of humans and machines.

The article reports that the distinction matters because evidence suggests disclosing AI involvement can reduce levels of trust, and other research points to overall consumer resistance to AI, although reactions vary considerably depending on what the technology is used to create. It notes that AI blurs the line between editing existing content and creating new content, since a person may still develop the idea and refine the result while the balance between human and machine contribution varies considerably, and disclosing AI involvement can invite judgments about who or what created the content, how much human input was involved and whether the use of AI was appropriate. The article says this may help explain criticism of AI-led campaigns by brands such as Coca-Cola and Gucci, and it describes how governments and platforms are beginning to address these questions through new approaches to AI transparency. The EU wants providers of certain generative AI systems subjected to strict disclosure requirements, and technology is emerging that allows digital content, including ads, to carry accessible information about its provenance and editing history.

The article reports that Meta acknowledged its "Made with AI" label appeared on content involving only minor AI modifications and did not provide sufficient context, and the company replaced that wording with "AI info" before later making the label less prominent when AI had been used to edit rather than generate content. It also describes the same ambiguity appearing in reverse, with labels reading "human-made" and "no AI" emerging to signal human authorship, and it asks whether these mean no AI whatsoever or a predominantly human process in which AI played a supporting role, since both kinds of label can obscure as much as they reveal. The authors advise consumers to take a little time to consider how they interpret AI labels, saying the term "AI-generated" tells us something but not everything about how content was produced and does not by itself mean the result is fake, poor quality or untrustworthy. They add that the label will not spell out the human role, including who developed the idea, selected and refined the output, checked its accuracy and decided what ultimately appeared, and they conclude that an AI label should be a starting point for evaluating content rather than the end.

Articles.Title: What does an 'AI‑generated' label in advertising actually tell us?

stories.Headline: Flagstar Bank deploys 4,000 Microsoft Surface devices to run its BranchIQ AI agent locally for employees
stories.Summary:
Flagstar Bank chose Microsoft Surface devices to bring hybrid AI and mobile banking to employees, Microsoft said in a customer story dated 11/16/2026. The bank’s own BranchIQ agent runs local AI on Surface, supported by Windows 11 and centralized device management. Flagstar is headquartered in New York and serves businesses, commercial real estate clients and consumers across America. The bank has 5,300 employees, according to chairman and CEO Joseph Otting. Flagstar’s planned rollout covers 4,000 Surface devices.

During rollout, Flagstar reduced initial Windows Autopilot setup from up to about an hour to 15 minutes. Surface devices are managed through Microsoft Intune, secured with Microsoft Entra and tied into the bank’s Microsoft 365 environment. Windows Hello for Business makes sign-in easier for employees. BranchIQ runs as part of a small language model locally on the Surface devices. Starting with a photo of an identification document, BranchIQ extracts required information locally and helps populate systems of record.

Otting said it was a moment when you start to see how everything links together and how the 5,300 employees could become more effective in the AI strategy. Otting said that when he saw what Surface could do and how AI could be used on the device, he was hooked. Jason Pope, chief technology and data officer, said Surface meets the bank’s needs by being rapid, quick and easy to use, and that speed matters because transaction per second in banking is important. Pope said BranchIQ lets branch colleagues perform know your customer activities, onboard individuals and access standards, policies and procedures directly on device, with or without an internet connection or Wi-Fi. Pope said Surface was the perfect blend from chip to cloud, not just hardware but hardware tied into Microsoft 365, managed by Intune and secured by Entra.

Christina Previti, head of tech product delivery, said employees are not sitting at a desk all day but are in front of clients, moving between buildings and meetings, and traveling. Previti said Surface lets them move across offices and states seamlessly, and that for a bank the security is critical. Previti said she lives in New York City and commutes on the subway every day, and the device fits in almost every bag she has. Pope said the bank was very deliberate with Surface pilots in branches, starting very small with one branch and taking a hands-on approach to change management. Pope said branch one loved it and started evangelizing it, and then branch two came on.

Flagstar has grown through mergers, and a unified employee experience is a priority, according to the story. Running Surface on Windows 11 gives employees the same seamless, secure experience wherever they work. Surface’s neural processing unit helped win Flagstar over and made hybrid intelligence a natural fit for a bank handling sensitive customer information. The bank considered the total cost of ownership, including its experience with older Surface devices still in use. Because Surface is designed by Microsoft to work with Microsoft software, Windows 11, Microsoft 365 and the tools that manage and secure them work as one experience.

Flagstar worked directly with Microsoft to cut initial Autopilot setup to 15 minutes, which Pope said meant less time waiting for a new device and more time getting back to work. As the rollout grows, the goal stays the same: better employee experiences that translate into more positive client interactions. The story directs readers to discover more about Flagstar Bank on LinkedIn and YouTube. The story lists the organization size as 1,000-9,999 employees and the country or region as the United States. The story does not say when the 4,000-device rollout will be completed.

This strategic move allows AMD to better compete with Nvidia, which currently holds a strong position through its open-weights models. The acquisition requires the integration of pioneering model research into the future hardware, software, and systems of the company. These new capabilities aim to help developers and researchers push the boundaries of what artificial intelligence can achieve. stories.Headline: Corporate leaders use vague language to hide AI-driven job losses
stories.Summary:
Corporate leaders are increasingly using vague euphemisms like delayering and efficiency to hide the impact of artificial intelligence on job losses during 2026. Companies such as Chime, Boston Scientific, and CRH have utilized this consultant-speak to describe transitioning to smaller teams or reducing expenses. These linguistic shifts occur as tech-enabled headcount reductions draw more public ire and political pushback from the general population. This trend masks the true scale of economic changes and makes it difficult to pinpoint which industries are hardest hit.

Better monitoring tools are required to avoid catastrophic disruption, including expanded funding for the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Census Bureau. According to Challenger, Gray & Christmas, companies cited AI in 121,400 job cut announcements in 2026, compared to 54,800 in 2025. The government must improve the frequency of the Displaced Worker Supplement report to better track these shifts. Such data is necessary to deploy retraining programs and relocation support for families affected by these technological changes.

Jonathan Levin argues that lawmakers must address these blind spots before a massive avalanche of job losses arrives. He suggests that the Trump administration and the newly elected Democrats should increase government budgets to improve labor data. Andy Challenger noted that companies will likely become even more careful with announcements, making the impact of AI more opaque. Meanwhile, executives like Charles Scharf of Wells Fargo and Brian Moynihan of Bank of America have emphasized using attrition and careful hiring instead of formal layoffs.

The current labor market remains stable, with unemployment dipping to 4.1 percent in October from 4.2 percent in September. However, Goldman Sachs economist Pierfrancesco Mei noted that workers displaced by AI often take longer to find new employment. If the government response is too slow, the United States risks a repeat of the China shock from the 2000s. Policymakers must now act to ensure the labor market is not automated into oblivion before the full impact is understood.

Articles.Title: Corporate-speak is masking the impact of AI on job losses—here's why that's a problem

stories.Summary:
Global manufacturing, utility and mining companies have shed $4.2tn in market value since June as the AI "picks and shovels" trade swings into reverse, according to a Financial Times analysis. The article, published on 16 November 2026 and written by Clara Murray, reports that data centre construction stocks have lost $4.2tn as the boom in the AI trade unravels. The report is an analysis piece, and the available text does not name the individual companies involved or give a precise date in June for the peak. The article as supplied is behind a subscription paywall, so the full details of the analysis are not available in the text provided.

The report places the losses at $4.2tn in market value across global manufacturing, utility and mining companies since June. It links the decline to the AI "picks and shovels" trade, the bet on the suppliers and builders behind the artificial intelligence boom, which the analysis says has swung into reverse. The text does not give a breakdown by sector or country, and it does not say what share of the $4.2tn falls on data centre construction stocks specifically. No further figures, dates or named companies appear in the article as supplied.

The article is attributed to Clara Murray of the Financial Times, and the available text does not include any direct comment from her or from the companies concerned. The report is presented as an analysis rather than a news report based on named sources, and the text provided does not say who supplied the figures behind the $4.2tn estimate. No executive, official or analyst is quoted in the material available, so no one's remarks can be paraphrased. The article's own framing is that the AI trade has unravelled, and that framing is the only characterisation the text supports.

The context given is the boom in the AI trade, which the article says has unravelled, and the "picks and shovels" label for the suppliers and builders that rose with it. The text does not say what happens next, whether the decline is expected to continue, or how the companies or investors have responded. Because the full article sits behind a paywall, the details that would normally follow, such as named stocks, regional splits and forward-looking comment, are not in the material provided. The available text supports only the scale and direction of the losses and the link to the reversing AI trade.

stories.Headline: Lawyers say generative AI gives narcissistic family litigants speed and false authority
stories.Summary:
A law.com expert opinion piece published on November 16, 2026, by Elisa Reiter of Calabrese Budner and Daniel Pollack of Yeshiva University's Wurzweiler School of Social Work describes how generative AI has affected narcissistic behavior in family litigation. The authors say that generative AI did not create narcissistic behavior in family litigation, but it has given that behavior speed, scale and a veneer of authority. They describe the litigant who treats the courthouse as a stage and files a dozen motions in a month. They describe the opposing party who rewrites the history of the marriage with unshakable confidence and frames every parenting exchange as proof of the other parent's unfitness. They describe the litigant who reacts to any adverse ruling as a personal insult.

The full text of the article sits behind a subscription paywall on Law.com, so the specific requirements, changes, numbers and dates it sets out are not available. The visible portion gives no figures, no court dates and no named cases beyond the authors themselves. The page does list related coverage, including a November 16, 2026, article by Laura Lorek reporting that court filings containing hallucinations have fallen for two straight quarters while subtler errors may be harder to catch. It also lists an October 22, 2026, report by Avalon Zoppo on the Fifth Circuit reassigning a case after a judge misused AI to draft a ruling, with Judge Jerry Smith writing for the appellate court. Those items are separate stories and are not part of the Reiter and Pollack piece.

The authors are responsible for the opinions in the article, and the visible text attributes the described litigation behavior to anonymous litigants rather than to any named person or firm. The article's own framing is that AI supplies speed, scale and a veneer of authority to behavior that already existed. Beyond that framing, the paywalled article does not disclose what the authors recommend or what they say should change. The surrounding coverage suggests that courts and practitioners are watching AI errors in filings, but the articles do not say what happens next in family law specifically. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Microsoft report guides workplace AI security priorities as IT teams face identity risks from agents and user-built apps
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Cybersecurity Insiders on November 16, 2026, sets out practical steps for containing and securing artificial intelligence in the workplace, and it draws heavily on Microsoft's yearly Digital Defense Report as a guiding priority list for the next twelve months. The author argues that the protection of AI use is not vastly different from the security work IT teams already do, despite the large amount of hysteria surrounding the technology. The piece notes that end users are increasingly building their own apps through vibe coding and then expecting IT to handle hosting, security and support. It also observes that attacks are often described as sophisticated when the root cause is simply someone misconfiguring a basic control that every product has. The article says identity is the surface that matters most, and that the core failure is too much standing access that is too loosely enforced, a weakness red teams have exploited for years.

It explains that AI agents operate like virtual users, with an identity, access to files and resources, and the ability to carry out digital tasks on a computer, so identity must remain a priority. The author advises against blocking all AI tools, because users have become very dependent on them, and instead recommends discovering what is being used, most easily through tools that inspect network traffic and show which domains and categories are visited. Presenting that data to business owners can shock them about where data is going, which typically convinces them that AI governance is not optional. The author, writing from an IT management perspective, says technology is the quicker and easier part of the job, while understanding and working with people is what separates one professional from the rest. The article asks whether the rest of the business received adequate training on approved AI tools and understands what not to do with business data, and whether some parts of the organization would be more productive with specialized tools routed through strong security controls.

It recommends asking people what business problem they are trying to solve, rather than accepting an answer that begins with a request for AI to do something. The author also sets out an order to follow, starting with identity and seeing how far an organization can get, because that path aligns with the failures that lead to most business compromises. The article notes that few IT staff have worked in environments where they are involved with all aspects of the cybersecurity strategy, and that starting at an MSP can make it difficult to know where to begin. It says all steps have their own merits, but some matter more than others, and it gives the example that starting with data governance while allowing all users to access stored data on any device has less impact than first preventing that action within the identity project. The conclusion states that the priority remains ensuring businesses implement the fundamental security controls long considered essential, since getting these basics right creates a stronger foundation and better prepares organizations for the risks of emerging technologies.

Articles.Title: Practical Strategies to Contain and Secure AI in the Workplace

stories.Headline: HPE builds ChatHPE on Azure to give 30,000 employees governed agentic AI
stories.Summary:
HPE built ChatHPE using Microsoft Azure capabilities to reduce the time employees spent searching a vast body of internal knowledge for information, according to a Microsoft customer story dated 11/16/2026. HPE needed enterprise AI that could provide trustworthy answers and support an evolution from answers to governed action. HPE is extending that foundation with HPE-developed AgentOps technology and agents developed using Microsoft Copilot Studio. HPE is advancing from trusted enterprise AI answers to governed agentic AI with HPE-developed AgentOps technology and Microsoft Azure capabilities. Approximately 30,000 employees use ChatHPE, and more than 300 applications consume ChatHPE capabilities.

The initial team started in October and released ChatHPE in February, with a working prototype in less than three months leveraging Azure capabilities, says Jose Mejias, Distinguished Technologist at HPE. Using Foundry IQ, ChatHPE retrieves relevant enterprise information and grounds responses only in sources employees are authorized to access, and citations help employees verify the underlying information. HPE applies enterprise identity and access, security and logging, auditability, tenant isolation, content safety, and API governance controls to help provide a secure and governed enterprise generative AI experience. HPE is evolving its architecture to enable agents developed with Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio, and other technologies to work together, including support for standards such as Agent2Agent (A2A). HPE-developed AgentOps technology supports hundreds of AI agents in production today and uses Microsoft Entra ID for identity and access management, along with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) for orchestration and Defender for Cloud for security.

Mejias says Azure has been an important technology environment supporting the development and scaling of ChatHPE and HPE's enterprise AI capabilities. Manmeet Dhillon, Head of Enterprise AI at HPE, says that as HPE continues to advance its enterprise AI strategy, Microsoft Azure will remain an important part of the technology ecosystem supporting this journey. Mejias says the team started in October and released in February, with a working prototype in less than three months leveraging Azure capabilities as part of the solution. HPE evaluates security, data sensitivity, performance, cost, capacity, and governance requirements case by case to determine where each workload should run, and Azure is often the first stop for new services. For workloads that require frontier models, Azure gives HPE access to the capabilities it needs to develop and scale new AI experiences.

Employees use ChatHPE to ask HR questions, understand technologies, locate hardware information, synthesize enterprise knowledge, and support other everyday work, with users reporting significant time savings. HPE created ChatHPE to help employees find and work with trusted information, as finding the right HR policy, technical documentation, or hardware information could be time-consuming. HPE began bringing together the conversational interface employees use, the grounding capabilities that connect responses to trusted enterprise information, and agents that can act on that information. This approach helps HPE extend AI across business use cases while maintaining consistent security, governance, and access controls, and the underlying authoritative systems remain the systems of record. Agents developed with Copilot Studio can participate alongside other agent technologies within HPE's broader agentic AI ecosystem.

HPE understands the challenge from both sides, building the compute, storage, networking, and cloud infrastructure that organizations use for AI while also addressing the same transformation internally. Most large enterprises can access powerful AI models, and the differentiator is how quickly they turn those models into experiences employees trust and use. A pilot can prove an idea works, but scaling it across tens of thousands of employees and hundreds of applications under enterprise security and governance requirements is the harder challenge. Access to capable models was only the beginning, and HPE expanded ChatHPE with an enterprise retrieval-augmented generation capability designed to ground responses in trusted enterprise content while respecting user access controls. Agents can interact with systems and take actions on a user's behalf, creating different operational and governance requirements than conversational AI alone.

HPE's experience with ChatHPE shows how enterprise AI can evolve from trusted conversational experiences to governed agentic capabilities at scale. Building on the adoption of ChatHPE, HPE is expanding its enterprise AI ecosystem through HPE-developed AgentOps technology, standards-based interoperability, and agents developed using technologies including Copilot Studio. As HPE extends those capabilities across more business processes, Azure remains part of the foundation supporting that evolution. HPE's enterprise AI architecture is designed to support different execution environments based on workload requirements. The articles do not say what specific business processes HPE will extend its agentic capabilities to next, nor which workloads HPE has chosen to run outside Azure.

Articles.Title: HPE moves from trusted AI answers to governed action with Azure

stories.Headline: Malaysia prepares AI governance framework to ensure human responsibility for system decisions
stories.Summary:
Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo told the Dewan Rakyat on October 5 that Malaysia is preparing a new AI governance framework. He stated that the Artificial Intelligence Governance Bill should be tabled in early 2027 to complement existing laws. This new legislation intends to take a risk-based approach across various sectors to enable benefits and build confidence. The framework follows a July consultation that proposed national governance principles, central oversight, and obligations proportionate to risk. These proposals aim to ensure that responsibility for AI remains with identifiable people rather than the systems.

The Bill will apply to companies using AI for credit, transaction flagging, and customer or patient communications. Directors must follow the Companies Act 2016, which requires duties of reasonable care, skill, and diligence. Section 216 of that Act suggests directors remain responsible for delegated powers unless they believe the delegate is competent. Section 17A of the MACC Act warns that directors are deemed to commit corruption offences unless they prove due diligence. The Securities Commission Malaysia also proposed clearer expectations for board oversight and listed companies' disclosures in July.

Tan Sri Abdul Rashid Hussain, founder of RHB Group, said boards must not delegate responsibility to an algorithm. He asked boards to identify where AI is used, who is accountable, and how failures are detected. He also questioned if boards could explain AI decisions to regulators, customers, or a court of law. Attorney General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar stressed that effective human oversight remains essential for AI output. Bank Negara Malaysia's governor stated on July 8 that AI belongs firmly on the board agenda.

Arup's Hong Kong office lost US$25 million in early 2024 due to deepfake video conference deception. A Canadian tribunal held Air Canada responsible for misleading bereavement fare information provided by its website chatbot. Small business owners may be affected if AI refuses financing without a practical way to test the decision. The broker Aon reported on October 5 that D&O cover for AI risks remains broadly available. Underwriters are now examining governance more closely as they evaluate policy wording, exclusions, and endorsements.

The articles cite a 64-page code of ethics from July 2000 that failed to prevent Enron's bankruptcy. This example illustrates that rules alone do not prevent failures in spaces where those rules do not reach. The prime minister emphasized on February 24 that ethical considerations would receive particular attention during the drafting process. The consultation paper's first principle focuses on human dignity and the need for human review of decisions. Traditional values like adab and amanah are mentioned as foundations for knowledge and trust.

The government will continue drafting the Bill before it is tabled in early 2027. Regulators will further define how the framework applies to AI used by public bodies in consequential decisions. The articles leave open the specific conditions and scope of a potential due-diligence defence within the Bill. It remains unclear how the relationship between regulatory fines and civil remedies for loss will be managed. The final text will determine how institutions give effect to the principle of identifiable human responsibility.

Articles.Title: My Say: The AI Bill and the boardroom: where responsibility lies

stories.headline_source: My Say: The AI Bill and the boardroom: where responsibility lies

stories.Headline: Law students sue Tribhuvan University over AI detection rules that reject theses
stories.Summary:
Law students including Vivek Chaudhary filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court of Nepal on 17 November 2026 against Tribhuvan University over its use of foreign AI-detection software. The petition challenges provisions of the university's Anti-Plagiarism Software Management and Operation Rules, 2080. Students say theses, seminar papers and clinical reports built over months of work were rejected on the estimated AI report shown by the private foreign software Turnitin. The petitioners named the Government of Nepal, the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, the Ministry of Education and Sports, the Ministry of Defense and Tribhuvan University as respondents. The students say they were punished without even the minimum opportunity to present their defense.

The complaint centres on clause 10(3) of the Tribhuvan University Rules 2080, under which theses, seminar papers and clinical reports are rejected solely on the estimated percentage shown by software such as Turnitin and iThenticate as likely AI-generated. The petition seeks an order of mandamus quashing the provision, plus an interim order and priority from the court to secure the students' academic future. It asks for a mandamus to repeal the controversial provision and to create scientific and transparent standards for the use and regulation of AI. The petition cites the Tribhuvan University Act, 2049, arguing the university exceeded its general rule-making authority by creating prohibitions and punitive consequences, including rejection of theses, not present in the act. It also cites Article 28 of the Nepal Constitution and the Personal Data Protection Act, 2075.

The petitioners argue that no prevailing law in Nepal defines AI plagiarism and that there is no official government standard or software to identify it. They say information from the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers clarified that no separate act or regulation specifically addressing AI has been issued in Nepal. Under the Nepal Government's Work Allocation Regulations, they say, jurisdiction to regulate AI lies with the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. They argue the regulation seriously violates the principles of natural justice because it gives no mandatory prior opportunity to present a defense, question the software's errors and conduct independent technical testing. They say the university council's regulation, made beyond the scope of the act, is entirely voidable.

The petition states that the software reports themselves admit that similarity does not mean plagiarism. Students say parts flagged as AI by Turnitin showed as human-written or zero percent AI on other detection software such as ZeroGPT and Grammarly. The petition says the software collects students' names, email addresses and thesis details, plus keystrokes, deleted parts, IP addresses and digital activities during writing, and stores them on external servers indefinitely. It says students face serious risk of phishing attacks, email spoofing and identity theft from sending sensitive personal information and intellectual property to foreign company servers without legal authority and explicit consent. As key evidence the petitioners presented the official stance of the University of Virginia in the United States and a 2026 study by researchers at the University of Florida concluding that commercial AI detectors are flawed and unsuitable for academic evaluation or action.

The petition cites general legal principles and precedents from the Supreme Courts of India and the Philippines stating that plagiarism requires malice, deliberate intent and the theft of another person's original creation. It argues that since artificial intelligence does not claim ownership or copyright, plagiarism in the traditional sense is not objectively applicable to the use of AI-generated content. It cites international judicial precedents and scientific studies confirming that AI detection tools cannot be considered conclusive evidence. The petition claims Tribhuvan University and other educational bodies made mandatory the use of private software like Turnitin and iThenticate to check the originality of students' theses, seminar papers and clinical reports. It argues these software give automated results as likely AI-generated based solely on probability, with high technical errors and false positive rates.

Tribhuvan University spokesperson Nabin Bhandari clarified that theses cannot be copied verbatim and that the software will automatically detect it if done so. He expressed the view that anti-plagiarism testing is essential to prevent one person from stealing another's thesis and to make research original. He said such a system is necessary to prevent thesis duplication. The petition requests an interim order, stating that depriving students of research or examinations based on results from flawed and unscientific technology will cause irreparable damage. The articles leave open the court's response to the petition and any hearing date.

stories.Headline: Nexus Legal Group launches simplified AI WebTracker plans for law firms
stories.Summary:
The Nexus Legal Group LLC announced on November 16, 2026, simplified plans for AI WebTracker, its AI-powered prospect intelligence platform that identifies people actively researching legal help in a firm's practice areas and markets, including people visiting competing law firm websites, and delivers them in a fresh feed every morning. The platform is now offered in two plans, Self-Serve and Done-For-You, and every plan includes lead scrubbing before a firm's team reaches out. The launch targets two of the largest drains on law firm marketing budgets, which are ad spend that reaches people who never call and per-lead fees paid to lead-generation companies for contacts that may be shared with other firms, outdated or unqualified. Each lead in the feed shows who the person is, why they entered the feed, which competing firms they viewed, and where and when they were active, down to the ZIP code, and firms export these audiences directly to their ad platforms and CRM.

The Self-Serve plan includes the daily prospect feed, audience exports to ad platforms and CRM, and built-in scrubbing, with the firm's own team running its ads, while the Done-For-You plan adds full Nexus Lead Validation and Database Scrubbing, audiences and Nexus-designed, firm-approved ad creatives uploaded to ad platforms the firm already owns, such as Google, Microsoft Bing and Meta, ongoing feed tuning, and a monthly report, review call and dedicated Nexus contact. Every plan includes TCPA Real-Time Scrubbing, Do Not Call Lookup, Phone List Scrubbing and the Name Recognition Algorithm, and the Done-For-You plan adds the Nexus Lead Validation and Database Scrubbing upgrade, which runs Scammer Scrub, TCPA Lookup and Scrubbing, and DNC Lookup and Scrubbing on a firm's monthly leads and uploaded lists, with each record marked Validated, Review or Do Not Contact and given a time-stamped Validation Record. AI WebTracker is a flat monthly subscription that is never tied to leads, cases or outcomes, there is no setup fee, and firms can cancel with 30 days' notice. Firms pay their ad platforms directly and keep ownership of their ad accounts and the audiences they build, and the ad budget is paid from the firm's own ad account, never handled by Nexus. An optional Nonprofit Outreach and Intake Support add-on is available with either plan and provided with Legal Support Cases, Inc. under a separate agreement.

Rob Parker, Managing Partner of The Nexus Legal Group, said firms are being squeezed from both sides, paying more every year to bid on the same keywords as every competitor in town and paying lead vendors for names that too often turn out to be wrong numbers, recycled lists or people who already hired someone. He said AI WebTracker lets a firm see who is actually researching its type of case, in its own markets, before that person picks up the phone. He also said a firm should not pay more because a vendor sent more names, and that with a flat subscription the feed grows the firm's own audience every day and the firm keeps what it builds.

AI WebTracker is designed for personal injury, mass tort, trucking and commercial vehicle, wrongful death and other practice areas where speed and geography decide which firm signs the case, and law firms can book a demo and receive pricing at WebTrackerLeads.ai. The company notes that AI WebTracker uses licensed data sources, that being identified in the feed is not consent to be contacted, and that scrubbing and Lead Validation reduce risk but do not guarantee compliance and are not legal advice. The Nexus Legal Group describes itself as a legal marketing and technology company that helps law firms find, reach and sign high-value cases, and its media contact is team@nexuslegal.group and 855-925-1035.

stories.Headline: BILL cuts 35 to 40 percent of staff and shifts focus to larger customers and AI
stories.Summary:
BILL cut its headcount by roughly 35% to 40% over the past year and is now shifting its focus toward revenue growth, Chief Financial Officer Rohini Jain said at a Citi financial technology event, according to TradingView. Jain said the company's priorities now include attracting larger customers, increasing revenue per customer and using artificial intelligence to improve retention and internal productivity. She expects growth to reach a low point in the second quarter before reaccelerating in the second half of the fiscal year. She described the simple algorithm for the business as getting more customers and monetizing them.

BILL's direct sales teams are concentrating on companies with approximately 20 to 250 employees, a group Jain said the platform serves well, and midmarket customers generate about four times as much total payment volume as the normal customer base. Average revenue per user rose about 4% year over year last quarter, while average revenue per new direct customer was 800 basis points higher sequentially, and Jain expects quarterly customer additions of roughly 2,500 to 3,000 for a short period. Despite a 30% to 35% reduction in engineering staff, merge requests rose about 10% year over year, and a majority of BILL's code is now written with AI. Jain said the company improved its margin profile by about 1,700 basis points in the first quarter, stock-based compensation has fallen to about 12% to 13% of net revenue from roughly 17% when she joined, and BILL had repurchased $600 million of stock under a $1 billion board authorization, leaving approximately $400 million available.

Jain said BILL has filled most sales positions that needed backfilling after the restructuring and quota coverage is nearly full, though new salespeople will need time to build relationships and pipelines, with benefits expected over the next quarter or two. The company consolidated product leadership under Chief Product Officer Mike Cieri, hired a chief revenue officer and put former CFO John Rettig in charge of its AI transformation, she said. Jain attributed the anticipated second-quarter growth trough partly to a strong comparison with the prior year, when Spend & Expense payment volume grew 26%, and to disruption from sales-team changes, and she declined to extrapolate a normalized Spend & Expense growth rate beyond the current year. BILL is also reducing its emphasis on custom-built solutions for smaller bank partners in favor of a standard Embed 2.0 platform, a shift Jain said would reduce customer count but have a less-than-one-percentage-point impact on total revenue for the year.

stories.Headline: Universal Music Group (ENXTAM:UMG) Stock Could Be 26% Above Fair Value As AI Lawsuit Pressure Builds
stories.Summary:
Bailey Pemberton wrote an article on November 15, 2026, about Universal Music Group. The company faces pressure from a lawsuit involving an AI music platform. This legal dispute may affect how the company monetizes its recordings. Investors are now questioning if the current market value matches expected cash. stories.Headline: Mayo researchers find AI EKG analysis flags hearts over 16 years older as a 65-year-old seeks the test
stories.Summary:
A 65-year-old man booked his Welcome to Medicare visit after reading about a Mayo Clinic discovery, according to 24/7 Wall St. Researchers found that an AI analysis of an electrocardiogram could identify patients whose hearts appeared more than 16 years older than their actual age. That warning was associated with increased cardiac risk in people with a particular inherited heart condition. He wants to know what his own EKG might reveal. The article was published on November 16, 2026, by Gerelyn Terzo.

Medicare covers a standard screening EKG once during the first 12 months of Part B if he receives a referral during his welcome visit. The visit costs nothing if the provider accepts assignment, and the deductible does not apply to it. The EKG works differently, with the patient paying 20% after the Part B deductible, which rose to $283 in 2026 from $257. If the visit comes early in the year before any deductible is paid, he may owe the entire approved charge for the EKG. At a hospital-owned clinic, he also owes the hospital a copayment.

Mayo cardiologist John Giudicessi said the technology could eventually help doctors recognize dangerous disease before conventional tests reveal obvious abnormalities. The findings were highlighted on October 23, 2026, and drew on a registry of 1,049 patients with genetic forms of cardiomyopathy. Researchers still need to validate the findings in another group of patients. The article states the findings do not mean an otherwise healthy 65-year-old whose EKG suggests an 81-year-old heart necessarily faces the same risks. The AI-estimated heart-age gap greater than 16 years was flagged in patients with LMNA-related cardiomyopathy, an inherited disease that can cause heart failure and dangerous arrhythmias.

Medigap Plan G pays the 20% coinsurance but leaves the Part B deductible to the patient. The AMA's temporary Category III codes for emerging technology include 0764T and 0765T, which describe AI-assisted EKG risk assessment for cardiac dysfunction such as low-ejection fraction, pulmonary hypertension and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Providers bill 0764T as an add-on to standard EKG codes 93000 and 93010. Since January 1, 2025, Medicare's hospital outpatient payment system has paid those codes as separate services, according to a 2026 vendor coding guide that cites CMS. The guide lists no physician-office rate.

The article says the codes do not establish how a clinic would bill for the Mayo-style heart-age estimate. It found no published Medicare price specifically for an AI heart-age estimate, nor confirmation that the cardiac-dysfunction codes apply to it. Medicare's Advance Beneficiary Notice, Form CMS-R-131, generally must be given before treatment when a provider expects Medicare to deny an otherwise covered service as medically unnecessary. An ABN is not required for services Medicare excludes altogether, so the absence of one does not mean nothing is owed. The article advises asking for an itemized estimate separating the standard EKG from any AI analysis.

The article advises getting the billing code and the price of each service before agreeing to the additional test. It says to ask directly whether the AI analysis is billed separately, and to whom. If an ABN is handed over, the article says to read which box is being checked before signing. A patient can turn down the AI portion and still get the covered screening EKG. The article advises booking the visit early, within the first 12 months of Part B, after which Medicare covers an EKG only as a diagnostic test requiring symptoms or a medical reason the doctor writes down.

stories.Headline: Bill Gates warns AI could erase many jobs forever and urges lawmakers to act
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates, the 71 year old cofounder of Microsoft, published a 6,000 word essay earlier this year titled “The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical,” in which he warned that artificial intelligence could wipe out careers over the course of a decade rather than a few generations. In the essay he called for certain jobs to be “human reserved” and said AI will take on work in law, customer service, medicine, software and manufacturing, adding that many jobs will disappear forever. He wrote that the transition to the AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history and that the world is not preparing adequately for that transition. He also said that if the world takes the right steps, AI will be a force for good and leave everyone better off.

The warning arrives alongside new figures on job losses, as Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported on November 5, 2026, that AI has been cited in 121,401 job cut announcements so far in 2026, which is approximately 20 percent of all cuts. Gates had already raised his concerns in September, when he appeared on NBC News’ Meet the Press with Kristen Welker and was asked whether AI is powerful enough to end all of humanity. He responded that AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths and that there has never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools. He added that self regulation is not enough and that legislation needs to be passed, with politicians and law enforcement offering safeguarding and monitoring.

The essay sets out Gates’ view that the coming shift will be turbulent and that choices made now are critical, and it calls for some roles to be set aside for humans rather than left to machines. His September remarks place the responsibility for safeguards on lawmakers and law enforcement rather than on the industry alone, since he said self regulation is not enough. The Challenger, Gray & Christmas count of 121,401 AI cited job cut announcements in 2026, about 20 percent of all cuts, gives a measure of how far the disruption has already gone. The articles do not say what steps, if any, governments or companies have taken in response to his call for legislation.

stories.Headline: Xero pushes AI tools for accountants as small business adoption lags
stories.Summary:
Xero, the financial software firm, is pushing AI offerings for accounting practices even though adoption among small businesses remains at an early stage. Xero estimates that across the UK, US, and Australia, some 77% of micro-businesses and 68% of small businesses are at an early stage or have not adopted AI. More than half of medium and large businesses actively use some form of AI, even something as basic as AI chat. CEO Sukhinder Cassidy said Xero has seen this sort of adoption curve before in the cloud space. The current nascent take-up is not slowing the firm's own push into AI offerings for when the customer base is more receptive.

Customer surveys show AI tools save the average accounting practice in the UK and Australia more than seven hours a week. More than 100 XeroForce workflows are already running day-to-day while the platform is still in alpha. More than 500 customers are on the waitlist for the data. One million customers have used Xero's generative AI features over the last 12 months, and monthly users are up ninefold year-on-year. Customers can adopt AI from Xero in two ways, by using packaged solutions on key Xero surfaces or by building their own workflows using the firm's infrastructure, data and tools.

Cassidy said that four to five years ago Xero was largely an accounting product, which gave fewer ways to deepen engagement and usage. He said the 3x3 strategy has helped Xero evolve into an AI-powered multi-product platform. He said Xero wants to deliver a category-defining experience for small businesses and accounting partners across accounting, payments and payroll. He said these higher-value jobs can expand average revenue per customer, absolute gross profit dollars and cash generation. He said Xero is delivering AI solutions designed around customer value and that adoption is growing.

Soon-Ee Cheah, Xero EGM of AI Products, said accountants and bookkeepers spend much of their time on tasks that live in between the software they use. He said this work, such as getting data out of Xero, combining spreadsheets, e-mailing a client and waiting for replies, is unbillable, manual and exhausting. He said XeroForce is a natural language agent builder that lets practices create agents without writing a single line of code. He said users can build an agent from scratch or use pre-made templates to get one running in just minutes. He said XeroForce looks at connected tools such as Xero, Office 365, Outlook and Calendly and works out how to put steps into a coherent workflow.

Sarah Lawrence, CEO of Australian accounting and advisory firm Hot Toast, said the firm has been Xero-only for over a decade. She said Xero was the first platform in the firm's technology stack and gave her flexibility and lifestyle as a business owner and for her team. She said team members are all up the East Coast of Australia with clients all across Australia, so they can service them instantly via the cloud platform. She said the Xero platform has been used as an all-inclusive workflow tool for everything from Accounts Payable to Receivable, to Payroll, to Reporting. She said AI will be another game changer and that accountants are naturally the trusted partner for clients and small businesses because they already sit in the data.

The article says each technology shift changes how small businesses, accountants and bookkeepers work, from desktops and the Internet to mobile, cloud and now AI. It says Xero has been at the forefront of these shifts and led customers through them. It says AI offers an even more transformative opportunity for Xero's customers. It says one of the more interesting user adoption curves to watch in the AI sector in 2026 has been the take-up in Finance. It says how Xero's pitch evolves in 2027 as XeroForce expands its footprint will be something to keep an eye on.

stories.Headline: Sound Ventures holds a $7 billion stake in Anthropic from a $435 million investment
stories.Summary:
Bloomberg reported on November 15, 2026, that Sound Ventures, the firm co-founded by music manager Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, holds a stake in Anthropic worth $7 billion based on private market valuations rather than any public share price. The relationship began in spring 2023, when Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei visited Oseary's Beverly Hills home and met with Oseary and Kutcher across the table. Sound Ventures made its first bet on Anthropic that spring with a $35 million investment in the company's Series C round, which valued the AI lab at roughly $4.6 billion before the new money arrived. Google and Spark Capital also participated in that round, giving the deal a mix of Big Tech strategic money and established venture backing.

Over several later rounds, Sound Ventures' total commitment to Anthropic grew to approximately $435 million, and the reported stake works out to roughly 16 times the total cash invested, though those are paper gains rather than realized returns. Sound Ventures was founded in 2015 out of A-Grade Investments, a collaboration between Oseary and Kutcher, and in 2023 it established a dedicated AI fund of nearly $240 million. Anthropic is preparing for an IPO anticipated for late 2026, which would give investors like Sound Ventures a public market for their shares and test the private valuations. Until then, the $7 billion figure is best read as a mark rather than a payout, since lockup periods, share price swings and the timing of any sales would all shape what the firm actually brings home.

The article attributes the reporting to Bloomberg and notes that the $7 billion figure rests on private market valuations, not on a public share price. It describes concentration as a quieter risk for Sound Ventures, because if one holding is worth far more than everything the firm put into it, a lot of the fund's results depend on that single company. The article says a few things are worth tracking from here, including whether Anthropic's IPO plans hold to the anticipated late 2026 timeline and how public markets value the company compared with its last private round. It adds that a third thing to watch is whether Sound Ventures decides to cut its position once there is a market to sell into.

The article notes that Anthropic was a young AI lab started by former OpenAI executives and was still proving it could compete with its old employer when Sound Ventures first invested. It observes that plenty of early backers make one bet and watch later rounds dilute them, while Sound Ventures kept investing, which helps explain how a $35 million opening check became a position measured in billions. It closes by noting that in 2023 Amodei may have been the least famous person in that Beverly Hills living room, and judging by the reported value of the stake, he may also have been the most consequential one for the people sitting across from him. The article carries a disclosure that it was edited by Diego Almada Lopez.

Articles.Title: Guy Oseary’s Sound Ventures reportedly holds a $7 billion stake in Anthropic

stories.Headline: Bill Gates warns AI could eliminate many jobs and urges safety nets and retraining
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates published a new essay warning that artificial intelligence could eliminate many jobs, and he expanded on the warning in an October 22 appearance on The Verge's Decoder podcast with host Nilay Patel. The essay and podcast remarks were reported by Laura Grande on November 16, 2026. Gates wrote that many jobs will disappear forever. He said entry- and mid-level positions face the greatest immediate danger. He expects disruption to spread across law, medicine, manufacturing, construction and hospitality.

Gates wrote that the change will hit these industries rapidly over the course of a decade rather than a few generations. He said the scarcity of white-collar skills will disappear and pointed to telesales, telesupport and accounting as jobs that could be heavily affected. He acknowledged new jobs will emerge but warned that without the right policies there could be far fewer than exist today. He wrote that there is no plan to ease the entry into the AI era. He said his big concern is a 20-year transition period with winners and losers and a lot of disruption.

Gates called for stronger safety nets and retraining programs, along with taxes on AI and robots. He proposed setting aside Human Reserved roles that society chooses to keep in human hands. He warned that waiting until people are already displaced or underemployed will be too late. He cited Stanford research finding workers ages 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations had a 16% relative employment decline after researchers controlled for firm-level shocks, while employment among more experienced workers remained stable. He wrote that the jobs at most risk are entry- and mid-level.

On Nov. 5, Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported that U.S. employers announced 43,994 job cuts in October. AI was blamed for 1,265 of them, bringing the year-to-date total to 121,401, second among reasons for job cuts behind economic conditions at 130,531. October's AI-related total was the lowest monthly figure recorded so far in 2026. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' November 6 report said employers added 165,000 jobs in October and unemployment held at 4.1%. The BLS found 2 million Americans had been unemployed for at least 27 weeks in October, accounting for 27.6% of everyone out of work.

Gates helped put a computer on nearly every desk as Microsoft co-founder. The warning comes as AI starts showing up more often in employers' layoff announcements, though it isn't the only reason companies are cutting jobs. Gates believes AI presents a different problem from downturns because a position automated out of existence may never come back. Once one business uses AI or robots to cut costs, competitors may feel pressure to adopt the same technology. Workers could then face retraining while trying to cover bills without their previous income.

Turning Gates's ideas into policy could take years. The article says workers can begin preparing sooner by calculating monthly household costs, including housing, groceries, utilities, insurance, transportation, minimum debt payments and essential medical expenses. It gives examples: costs of $4,000 per month would require $24,000 for six months, $36,000 for nine months and $48,000 for one year. It says saving $500 per month would produce $6,000 in one year before interest. The article leaves open whether Gates's timeline will hold and how his proposed policies would be enacted.

stories.Headline: Knit Health raises a $35 million Series A led by NEA to guide patient referrals with AI
stories.Summary:
Knit Health, a startup that uses an AI world model to predict patient care needs, forecast treatment impacts and optimize referrals, raised a $35 million Series A round led by NEA, CEO Jonathan Kolstad told Axios Pro exclusively. The round was reported by Will Maddox of Axios in a story published on November 16, 2026. The company's stated aim is to guide patient referrals with artificial intelligence. Investors are betting on AI that predicts patients' next health needs rather than simply documenting their current ones.

The $35 million Series A was led by NEA, according to the report, and the funding is intended to support Knit Health's work guiding patient referrals with AI. The company uses its AI world model for three stated purposes, which are predicting patient care needs, forecasting treatment impacts and optimizing referrals. The report frames the investment as a bet on prediction over documentation, meaning AI that anticipates what patients will need next instead of only recording what they currently need. The articles give no further terms of the deal, no total valuation and no list of other participating investors.

Jonathan Kolstad, the CEO of Knit Health, confirmed the $35 million Series A round to Axios Pro exclusively, and the report attributes the funding news to him. The articles do not include any further direct statements from Kolstad beyond his confirmation of the round and its amount. No other executives, investors or NEA representatives are named or quoted in the material provided. The report also does not say what Knit Health plans to do with the proceeds beyond its existing focus on AI-guided referrals.

The context given is that investors are placing bets on AI that predicts patients' next health needs rather than simply documenting their current ones, which is how the report describes the big picture behind the round. The articles do not say when the round closed, how the company will spend the money, or what happens next for Knit Health beyond the funding itself. No details are given about the company's customers, its market, or any prior funding. The report was published by Axios on November 16, 2026, with Will Maddox as the author.
