stories.Headline: Senator Elizabeth Warren urges Congress to restrict China's access to advanced AI technology
stories.Summary:
Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts used a post on X this past Sunday to call for new laws. She urged Congress to pass legislation that would restrict the access China has to advanced artificial intelligence technology. The Democratic senator argued that the financial interests of corporate executives could potentially undermine the national security of the United States. She questioned whether the leaders of major technology companies could be trusted to prioritize security over their own profits.

This legislative push comes as House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana notes a growing bipartisan consensus for tighter restrictions on Chinese access to advanced AI chips. President Donald Trump recently urged senators to pass the American Affordability and Jobs Act, also known as S. 5653, to lower energy costs. This act would require data centers to pay for their own electricity while speeding up general development. Meanwhile, Microsoft Corp. and various industry groups recently asked the Trump administration to drop a proposed ban on certain Chinese data center technology. These groups warned that such restrictions could disrupt construction and weaken the overall competitiveness of the United States.

Senator Warren stated that the American people cannot rely on Big Tech billionaire CEOs to put national security above their bottom line. Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp also emphasized that American technological leadership is critical because China is a formidable competitor. He argued that advanced defense technology is necessary to deter potential adversaries and help prevent future wars. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt warned last month that China could overtake the U.S. because its companies offer cheaper AI products. He noted that China's access to AI model distillation and advanced chips puts the American lead at risk.

The debate has intensified following reports that link former Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang to a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing. Because of this turmoil, Chinese AI firms are reportedly seeking Nvidia equipped data centers outside of China to secure computing resources. Scott Bessent has urged the U.S. and China to de-risk their relationship rather than decouple entirely amid these trade tensions. Beijing has warned of red lines regarding its national interests ahead of a meeting between President Trump and President Xi. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Experts warn banks may hold hung debt deals as AI infrastructure boom faces political uncertainty
stories.Summary:
Banks may be left holding debt deals tied to the AI infrastructure investment boom, experts warned, after a tech-led stock market rout wiped more than $3.2tn off US equities in a single day. The sell-off followed early November's Democratic wins in key states such as Texas, Georgia and Ohio, which account for around 38 per cent of planned US data centre capacity. OpenAI's Stargate data centre project, planned with a capacity of 1.2 gigawatts when fully built, faces growing political uncertainty. The Banker reported these developments on 16 November 2026, in an article by Anita Hawser.

The warning concerns so-called hung debt deals, which are loans banks have committed to provide but cannot sell on to investors. Banks may be insulated from direct losses, according to the article, but their links to private credit pose a less visible threat. The article gives no further figures on the size of the debt at risk or on which banks are exposed. It also does not say what happens next, beyond describing the political uncertainty facing the Stargate project.

The article attributes the warning to experts, who are not named, and it does not record any statement from a bank, a regulator or a government official. Responsibility for the debt deals is not assigned in the text, which describes the risk in general terms rather than naming the institutions involved. The only named project is OpenAI's Stargate data centre, which the article links to the political uncertainty rather than to the debt warning directly. No one quoted in the article responds to the experts' warning.

The context given is the recent tech-led stock market rout and the Democratic wins in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, states that account for around 38 per cent of planned US data centre capacity. The article presents these events as the backdrop to the warning about hung debt rather than as established causes of it. It does not say what happens next, and it gives no timetable for resolving the debt deals or for the Stargate project. The piece is an analysis of risk, not a report of losses already taken.

Articles.Title: Could banks be left holding the debt if the AI boom falters?

stories.Headline: New Jersey assembly members sponsor a bill to classify AI chatbots as consumer products
stories.Summary:
Assembly members Cody Miller, Marisa Sweeney, and Joe Danielsen sponsored a new bill in New Jersey. Anthony Angelozzi also co-sponsored the legislation. The bill was introduced in the General Assembly on October 5, 2026. It aims to hold AI chatbot providers to a higher standard of liability. The measure would classify AI chatbots as consumer products rather than services.

Assembly Bill A5607 would apply to developers and businesses that distribute chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude. It limits chat log retention to two years and restricts their use for advertising, training, and profiling. Providers cannot present outputs as professional advice or use children's personal data. Violations could result in civil penalties of 5,000 dollars per single violation. Users could sue for actual damages, court costs, and their attorneys' fees.

Kara Williams of EPIC testified that the bill would limit the exploitation of personal user data. The Consumer Federation of America stated the bill provides a straightforward approach to address chatbot harms. Ross Barnes of Galahad said treating chatbots as products is the right instinct for responsibility. EPIC argued that the legislature must act now to force tech companies to be more responsible. The CFA called the bill a crucial step forward for providing meaningful user protections.

The bill would affect New Jersey residents, 74 percent of whom used AI tools in 2025. This usage rate is higher than the 68 percent reported for the general U.S. population. EPIC warned of harms including suicide, financial scams, sexual exploitation, and AI psychosis. The legislation would cover general-purpose chatbots used for productivity and customer service. It would also prohibit discriminatory or retaliatory practices against the users of these AI tools.

The bill is based on a model developed by Fairplay, the CFA, and EPIC. It differs from New Jersey Bill A5090, introduced in May 2026, which targets specific harmful conduct. A5090 would impose civil penalties of 20,000 dollars per violation on generative AI platforms. California's SB 243 and New York's AI Companion Models Law focus only on companion chatbots. The Rutgers University study found 57 percent of New Jersey residents had used ChatGPT.

The bill moved to the Assembly Appropriations Committee on October 19 by a 5-1-1 vote. The committee must decide whether to advance the bill as written or with amendments. If the Assembly approves it, the bill will then proceed to the state Senate. Finally, Governor Mikie Sherrill would sign or veto the legislation if both chambers pass it. The articles leave open whether the committee will actually advance the bill for a vote.

Articles.Title: New Jersey Bill Aims to Hold AI Chatbots to a Higher Standard

stories.Headline: National Whistleblower Center hires Attention Studio to lobby for AI whistleblower protections
stories.Summary:
The National Whistleblower Center added Attention Studio as an outside lobbying firm in 2026 while it pushes the AI Whistleblower Protection Act, which remains in committee in both chambers of Congress. Attention Studio reported $100,000 for the third quarter in a filing signed on Nov. 9, and it is the only registrant on record for the center that quarter. Two lobbyists are named on the filing, Olivia Konar, a policy associate, and Ava Smithing, a founding partner, and both also appear on the firm's new client registration for the center. The bill would bar employers from retaliating against employees and independent contractors who report artificial intelligence security vulnerabilities or violations of AI-related laws.

The legislation would also bar contracts that waive those protections and give whistleblowers reinstatement and back pay. The filing lists S. 1792 and H.R. 3460 and says the lobbying urged Senate and House offices to cosponsor the bill and support committee action before the end of the 119th Congress. It names the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and the Commerce Committee. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA) sponsors S. 1792, which was introduced May 15, 2025, and referred to the HELP Committee, and Congress.gov shows 13 current cosponsors, five of them original, with no later committee or floor action. Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA-23) sponsors H.R. 3460, which was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day, and its cosponsor page shows 10 current cosponsors, one of them original.

A coalition letter dated June 10, 2025, backs S. 1792, and its 22 signers include Americans for Responsible Innovation, the Center for Democracy & Technology, the Government Accountability Project, Public Knowledge, and the National Whistleblower Center. The signers say fear of retaliation, including over confidentiality agreements, can deter insiders from disclosing AI risks, and they argue protections support transparency, accountability, public safety, and national security. The letter cites a June 2024 public statement by more than a dozen current and former employees of leading AI companies. Both bills wait in committee, S. 1792 in the Senate HELP Committee and H.R. 3460 in the House Education and Workforce Committee, and the filing's stated goal is committee action before the 119th Congress ends. Attention Studio is a new outside firm for the center, which makes the firm's work on this bill the change to track.

stories.Headline: AI helps pharmacovigilance teams detect safety signals earlier and reduce operational effort by 30-50%
stories.Summary:
A key message at this year’s World Patient Safety Congress was that pharmacovigilance is evolving from a reactive, compliance-driven function to a more predictive and science-led discipline, pharmaphorum reported on 16 November 2026. As therapies for chronic diseases expand globally, safety organisations face an unprecedented volume of evidence from ICSRs, clinical studies, scientific literature, electronic health records and real-world data. The challenge is no longer data collection but timely identification and interpretation of clinically meaningful safety signals within increasingly complex and heterogeneous datasets. Highly trained safety physicians and scientists often spend significant time aggregating and reviewing information rather than on signal evaluation, causality assessment and benefit-risk analysis. Artificial intelligence offers the potential to strengthen pharmacovigilance by accelerating evidence synthesis, supporting earlier signal detection and enhancing risk surveillance.

AI is not a replacement for medical judgement but enables a human-guided, scientifically grounded approach in which technology augments expert evaluation. The expansion of chronic disease therapies makes ongoing safety monitoring more demanding as medicines are used over longer periods by people with varying underlying health conditions and alongside other treatment. Diabetes patients are increasingly treated with combinations of glucose-lowering agents, cardiovascular therapies, obesity medicines and renal-protective treatments. Healthcare is becoming more connected through continuous glucose monitoring, digital health applications, wearable devices and remote patient monitoring. A potential safety concern may involve not only the medicine and an adverse event but patient characteristics, treatment duration, concomitant medications, disease progression, lifestyle factors and real-world treatment patterns.

The traditional process flows sequentially from collection of Individual Case Safety Reports to signal detection, signal validation, scientific assessment and regulatory action. AI is unlikely to replace pharmacovigilance processes but can enhance them as an additional analytical layer identifying weak signals and emerging patterns across multiple sources of evidence. The system ingests millions of data points, allowing AI to autonomously identify unusual patterns, which are escalated for medical safety review, signal validation, scientific assessment and risk-mitigation action. More advanced agentic AI coordinates tasks across connected workflows with clear escalation points for human review, and biopharma companies reduce operational effort by 30-50%, accelerate regulatory reporting, identify safety signals earlier and reduce the risk of inspection findings, product recalls and patient safety events. For larger safety reports, AI can pull together relevant evidence and draft sections while human experts review and sign off the conclusions.

AI does not establish causality, validate safety signals or make regulatory decisions, which remain the responsibility of qualified pharmacovigilance professionals, medical safety physicians, epidemiologists and regulatory authorities. The next opportunity is looking beyond individual reports to evidence in electronic health records, claims data, registries, clinical studies and scientific literature. If an older diabetic patient takes multiple treatments simultaneously, individual reports may not make the connection apparent, but AI-supported analysis across appropriate sources could bring that pattern to specialists’ attention sooner. Initiatives such as the FDA’s Sentinel programme and EMA’s DARWIN EU network demonstrate the importance of broader real-world evidence in safety assessment and highlight why AI is becoming critical. No pharmaceutical company has a complete view of patient experience, so collaboration is required, and underlying illnesses, concomitant medicines and reporting biases still require scientific assessment.

Sanjeev Sachdeva leads advisory and business process services globally for the life sciences unit at Tata Consultancy Services and is a member of the unit’s core leadership team. He drives strategic direction, business and IT advisory, thought leadership, industry collaboration and technology innovation, with more than 30 years of experience in business and technology transformation. He partners with customers across R&D, manufacturing, supply chain and commercial to adopt new technologies, processes and operating models. Sachdeva is a regular contributor to industry and academic forums including the Wharton Mack Institute for Innovation Management, DIA, PHUSE, PHORUM and IIT Delhi. He also speaks at industry roundtables and has authored white papers on AI enabled transformation in drug safety, clinical development, personalised medicine, digital health, quantum computing in life sciences, the future of the lab, blockchain, the metaverse and AI in regulated industries.

Governance by design requires defined responsibilities, quality standards, escalation routes and a traceable record of source information, AI outputs and human decisions that stands up to scrutiny. Validation before deployment is only the beginning, and teams must monitor whether systems continue to perform as intended and intervene when output becomes unreliable. This creates new skills requirements in data quality and AI oversight, and human expertise becomes more valuable as reviewers need the evidence, time and authority to challenge rather than simply approve outputs. As highlighted at the World Patient Safety Congress, AI’s greatest value lies in enabling safety organisations to shift from reactive reporting to predictive risk management, identifying emerging risks earlier so safety teams can intervene sooner and strengthen patient protection. The future is an AI-native safety enterprise where AI handles data-intensive processes and experts focus on critical medical decisions, enabling faster insights, earlier risk mitigation and greater confidence in patient safety.

Articles.Title: Catching the signals sooner: AI’s role in proactive pharmacovigilance

stories.Headline: UAE lawyer says companies face liability for harm from AI-generated advice under civil law
stories.Summary:
Under UAE law, liability for AI-generated advice or decisions that cause financial loss, legal violations or harm may be considered under general principles of civil liability, contractual obligations and any applicable sector-specific legislation, according to Ashish Mehta, founder and managing partner of Ashish Mehta & Associates, writing in Khaleej Times on 15 November 2026. The UAE Civil Transactions Law does not establish a separate liability regime specifically for AI-generated outputs or advice or work rendered on the basis of AI-generated advice, he wrote. Article 245(1) of Federal Decree-Law No. 25 of 2025 promulgating the Civil Transactions Law provides that, subject to special legislations, the chapter applies to liability arising from a harmful act committed by a natural or legal person. Article 246 provides that every act causing harm to another obligates its perpetrator to compensate for the damage, even if the perpetrator lacks discernment. Article 247 distinguishes harm caused directly, where a guarantee is due without any condition, from harm caused by causation, where no guarantee is due unless the perpetrator was a transgressor or acted intentionally, or the act led to the harm.

Liability may depend on the role each person played in the development, deployment or use of the AI system, the nature of the act or omission involved, and whether a sufficient connection can be established between that conduct and the damage suffered. Using AI as a tool would not by itself necessarily exclude liability on the part of the person or entity responsible for its use. A company may be liable where an AI system is used in its business operations and the resulting harm can be attributed to the company's acts or omissions, including inadequate assessment of the system, insufficient safeguards or a failure to appropriately monitor its use. Article 645 of the Civil Transactions Law defines a professional company as a company established by one or more persons licensed to practice a liberal profession, or thereby with others, whose purpose is to practice that profession, unless the law or the agreement provides otherwise. Article 651 provides that each partner is personally liable for their professional faults towards the professional company and the rest of the partners, and the professional company is liable for the faults of the partners vis-à-vis third parties.

Article 651 also provides that the professional company is liable for any act or conduct carried out by the manager or managers in the ordinary course of management, and for any act carried out by one of its employees or agents whenever such person has the authority to act on its behalf and the third party has relied on such authorization in dealing with it. Any provision in the articles of association of a professional company permitting approval of the exemption of any person from any personal liability borne thereby in their capacity as a current or former manager shall be void. Professional companies remain liable under UAE law for professional services they provide, regardless of whether rendered by a manager acting in the ordinary course of business or an authorised employee, and regardless of whether the service deliverables relied on advice generated by artificial intelligence. Such liability may not be expelled by the professional company's constitutional documents or other agreements. Article 3.2.1 of the AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (December 2022), issued by the UAE Ministry of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, provides that accountability for the outcomes of an AI system lies not with the system itself but is apportioned between those who design, develop and deploy it.

Article 3.2.2.1 of the AI Ethics Guidelines states that AI operators and AI developers should consider designating individuals to be responsible for investigating and rectifying the cause of loss or damage arising from the deployment of AI systems. Article 3.5.1 provides that AI developers should ensure AI systems will not cause any unintentional harm and adverse impacts. The AI Ethics Guidelines also provide procedures through which individuals affected by significant AI-assisted decisions may challenge those decisions and seek human review, but the Guidelines expressly describe themselves as non-binding and should be read as policy guidance rather than as a standalone basis for imposing legal liability. Where AI-generated advice or decisions by a company result in financial loss, legal violations or harm to an individual, the individual shall have a right of recourse against the company itself, and if the service was rendered by a partner, the partner remains personally liable to the company for any loss suffered as a result of such third-party claim or action.

As to a manager who was not acting in the ordinary course of business or an unauthorised employee acting in bad faith, the company may subsequently take action against such partner, manager or employee, including termination of employment. Article 614 clause 3 of the Civil Transactions Law provides that if the manager of the company exceeds the powers specified in the contract, he shall be liable for any damage that befalls the company as a result of such act. Clauses 2, 3, 4 and 9 of Article 44 of Decree Law No. 33 of 2021 on the Regulations of Employment Relations allow an employer to dismiss an employee without prior notice, after a written investigation and by a written and reasoned decision, in specified events. These include an employee committing an error resulting in gross material losses to the employer, or deliberately causing harm to the employer's property and admitting the same, provided the employer notifies the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation within 7 working days of being aware of the occurrence.

They also include violation of the establishment's bylaws on work and workers safety, where such instructions are in writing and posted in a visible place and the employee has been advised thereof, and failure to perform main duties under the employment contract despite a written investigation and two warnings of dismissal in case of recidivism. Clause 9 covers an employee abusing his position with the aim of obtaining personal gains and profits. Any claims by a company against an AI developer shall be subject to the contractual terms governing their relations. The applicable provisions cited are Federal Decree-Law No. 25 of 2025 promulgating the Civil Transactions Law and the AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (December 2022).

Ashish Mehta is qualified to practise law in Dubai, the United Kingdom and India, and full details of his firm are on www.amalawyers.com. Readers may e-mail their questions to news@khaleejtimes.com or send them to Legal View, Khaleej Times, PO Box 11243, Dubai. The article states that the information provided is intended for general guidance and does not constitute legal advice, and recommends seeking formal legal counsel. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Schneider Electric unveils Reference Design 115 for modular AI factories supporting 227 kW racks
stories.Summary:
Schneider Electric introduced its RapidScale Modular Data Center Reference Design 115 on October 21 at NVIDIA GTC Berlin, outlining a modular AI factory architecture engineered for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform. The design supports AI rack power reaching 227 kW, according to the company. A study conducted with Compass Datacenters documents an approximately 80% reduction in selected onsite installation activities through prefabricated white-space modules. Schneider describes the design as a 10, 20 MW, Tier III-targeted modular AI factory architecture developed to ANSI standards. The published example concentrates on one deployment unit containing four scalable units, designed around four NVIDIA Vera Rubin clusters with 1,008 GPUs each.

That translates to 4,032 GPUs distributed across 56 AI computing racks, supported by another 32 networking racks. The documented configurations support approximately 10.4 MW to 11.4 MW of active IT load, with total peak facility power of approximately 13.25 MW. The reference design assigns approximately 33,518 square feet to the deployment unit, divided between IT space and supporting utility infrastructure. Reference Design 115 uses four 3.75 MW RapidScale powertrains to serve the IT environment, providing a 3+1 distributed redundant UPS architecture. Each powertrain includes a 5,000-amp QED-2 switchboard, three parallel 1,250 kW Galaxy VXL UPS units, and associated distribution infrastructure, and the UPS systems provide five minutes of runtime at rated load.

Separate 2.5 MW powertrains provide 2N electrical infrastructure for the mechanical systems, with UPS support for critical coolant distribution units and pumps. The design continues to use 480V AC distribution for AI racks, with 415V distribution for networking equipment. At the Max-P operating point, each AI rack draws approximately 227 kW, while at Max-Q power consumption falls to approximately 188 kW per rack. In the tabulated Max-P configuration, 42 AI racks operate with approximately 10.4 MW of total IT demand, including networking equipment, and the Max-Q configuration supports all 56 AI racks with approximately 11.4 MW of aggregate IT demand. The Max-P configuration operates with three of the four IT electrical powertrains, while the full 56-rack Max-Q configuration uses all four.

Schneider's design assumes that liquid cooling removes approximately 96% of the heat generated by the liquid-cooled racks, with the balance handled by air-cooling infrastructure. Motivair liquid-to-liquid coolant distribution units connect the computing equipment to a high-temperature technology cooling loop designed for approximately 108°F supply and 126°F return temperatures. A separate chilled-water system supplies 64°F water to Uniflair fan walls, which manage residual rack heat and other air-cooled equipment. Schneider models annualized power usage effectiveness at approximately 1.1 under the San Francisco and Dallas conditions examined in the reference design. The companies first announced their jointly engineered EcoStruxure white-space module in September 2025, and their October 2026 White Paper 238 examines the installation sequence for integrated IT pods at a Compass hyperscale campus.

In the configuration studied, an approximately 1,000-square-foot pod accommodates up to 42 rack positions with a maximum electrical capacity of 1.2 MW. The study reports that selected onsite activities required 15 hours for the prefabricated pod, compared with 75.5 hours for the conventional approach. Compass also documented improvement through repetition, with one earlier installation requiring 18 hours compared with 15 hours for the later deployment examined in the study. In September, UL Solutions announced that Schneider had achieved the first certification under its UL 2140 program for specified prefabricated power distribution assemblies. The comparison excludes offsite manufacturing activities and does not measure total data center construction or commissioning time, and it also excludes certain conventional overhead-support installation work.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google launches Universal Cart while Nvidia unveils agent safety platform for banks
stories.Summary:
Google and Nvidia introduced new technologies in late 2024 to influence how consumers choose payment methods and how banks manage automated software. Google launched its Universal Cart service across Search and the Gemini app in the United States on October 15 to help shoppers track prices and select payment options. Meanwhile, Nvidia announced the Open Agent Safety Platform on September 28 to provide security frameworks that keep artificial intelligence agents within specific operational limits. These separate developments suggest that financial institutions must now compete for transactions while simultaneously governing software that acts on behalf of their customers.

The Universal Cart tool utilizes Google Wallet to recommend payment methods based on available benefits, which may change how card issuers compete for spending. Nvidia's safety platform combines activity restrictions with a monitoring system that intervenes when an agent exceeds its permitted boundaries. Citi and J.P. Morgan Chase are collaborating with Nvidia on this shared safety technology to ensure software does not move beyond established limits. Additionally, BBVA announced on October 21 that it would explore this approach to maintain oversight as the bank expands its use of complex AI agents.

Google stated that its new shopping tool keeps consumers in control by allowing them to complete purchases through Google Pay or merchant websites. The company clarified that retailers remain the sellers of record and continue to provide all necessary customer support and confirmations. Nvidia explained that its technology distinguishes between instructions telling an agent what to do and independent controls that enforce what it can actually do. These companies believe that their tools will help banks manage the risks associated with automated decisions and the visibility of card benefits.

These shifts require card teams to understand how shopping assistants present benefits and risk teams to establish strict permissions for autonomous software. Banks must now determine exactly when a human must intervene to prevent AI agents from operating outside of their authority. While it remains unclear if consumers are ready to delegate every financial decision, these tools identify the next operational priorities for the industry. Financial institutions must ensure their products remain competitive when software helps customers choose while maintaining rigorous internal security.

Articles.Title: Google and Nvidia Bring Banks to AI’s Checkout Test

stories.Headline: Barclays cuts 5,000 jobs as banks expand AI use across operations
stories.Summary:
Banks have been expanding their use of artificial intelligence across operations, customer service and compliance during the third quarter of 2026, while shifting some employees toward higher-value work, according to CNBC. Barclays unveiled layoffs in functions where AI is being deployed, and UniCredit and Santander said technology was freeing employees for more valuable tasks and improving processes. U.S. giants such as JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs are making similar changes in staffing and workflows. The moves came as lenders reported quarterly results that brought their use of AI into sharper focus. Barclays plans to cut 5,000 jobs, about 5% of its workforce, in 2026, with roughly 60% of the reductions affecting support functions including developer roles, though the bank said AI is not responsible for all the cuts.

Santander said its AI initiatives generated 194 million euros in business value in the first nine months of 2026, and UniCredit reported its best-ever quarterly profit of 3.3 billion euros. The Financial Times reported on Oct. 7 that HSBC could cut around half of management and specialist roles, and as many as 70% of financial adviser roles, in its U.K. wealth business. JPMorgan managers have been told to avoid hiring as the bank deploys AI, CFO Jeremy Barnum said on the third-quarter earnings call, and Goldman Sachs said it intends to constrain headcount growth. UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel called AI an opportunity to accelerate and a lever the bank did not anticipate it would have, saying on CNBC's Squawk Box Europe on Nov. 9 that it was working extremely well. Santander CFO José García Cantera told the same program on Oct. 28 that AI helps decrease low value-added processes so employees can focus on more valuable ones, affecting both revenue and costs, and that it is difficult to say how much comes from AI.

ABN AMRO CEO Marguerite Bérard said on Nov. 11 that AI supports anti-money-laundering checks and makes the bank easier to run and scale while preserving human judgement. KBW's Andrew Stimpson said the cuts are partly but not solely due to AI and have tended to come from back-office and support functions rather than the front office. A KBW study published in September found customer service was the most frequently cited use case for AI among European banks, followed by operations, identity checks and preventing financial crime, with just under half of tracked use cases aimed at cutting costs or improving efficiency. Analysts said wealth management and advisory are emerging as key tests of whether AI can boost revenues rather than only lower costs, with Ninety One's Sophia Whitbread saying the evidence is still strongest for improving service, engagement and employee productivity. Recruiter Mark Astbury of Morgan McKinley said demand is growing for specialists in AI, software engineering and data, and that banks will need to rethink how they develop the next generation of talent as entry-level positions become increasingly technical.

Articles.Title: AI is reshaping banking jobs – but its ability to drive profits remains unclear

stories.headline_source: AI is reshaping banking jobs – but its ability to drive profits remains unclear

stories.Headline: Researchers review how AI can cut emissions across iron and steelmaking
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive academic review published in Carbon Neutral Systems examines how artificial intelligence can accelerate decarbonization across the iron and steel industry by optimizing process efficiency, enabling feedstock substitution, and supporting carbon capture, utilization, and storage. The study was authored by Xidi Shang, Wuliang Yin, Jianxin Pan, Min Wang, Hua Wang, Kai Yang, and Qingtai Xiao. It synthesizes findings from 133 representative investigations identified through structured database searches covering research published between 2000 and 2025. The review was published on November 16, 2026, according to bioengineer.org. The article appeared under the site's Technology section with a reading time of five minutes.

The authors highlight that the global steel sector accounts for approximately 7 to 9 percent of direct industrial carbon dioxide emissions. Traditional blast furnace and basic oxygen furnace configurations generate roughly 70 percent of global crude steel output. Electric arc furnace operations currently produce approximately 41.5 percent of crude steel in the European Union and 68.0 percent in the United States. The review maps five technological pathways under evaluation across global producers, ranging from conventional coal-fed blast furnace systems paired with carbon capture to scrap-fed electric arc furnaces, hydrogen-based direct reduction, and electrolytic ironmaking. The article's subject of research is artificial intelligence applications in low-carbon iron and steel metallurgy.

The authors observe that current industrial applications remain predominantly confined to isolated processing units operating within narrow parameter boundaries. They state that most models lack comprehensive representations of dynamic cross-unit couplings among material, energy, and carbon flows, which restricts route-wide optimization across entire industrial complexes. They note that industrial datasets suffer from noise, missing values, regime drift, and a scarcity of validated operational logs for emerging hydrogen or electrolytic pilots. Because metallurgical operations depend strictly on thermodynamic conservation laws, the authors say unconstrained black-box learners risk outputting nonphysical predictions when extrapolating outside training domains. The review concludes that future progress depends on physics-informed, multi-scale gray-box architectures that embed conservation equations and transport kinetics directly into deep neural frameworks, supporting verifiable, plant-wide carbon reduction across the steel industry.

The authors highlight that broad deployment of newer hydrogen and electrolysis technologies faces substantial hurdles, including capital requirements, infrastructural bottlenecks, and high operational costs, requiring system-wide optimization within existing facilities while cleaner routes mature. They report that multimodal perception frameworks combining two-dimensional photographic images with three-dimensional point clouds have achieved material granularity recognition rates exceeding 90 percent. Vision-based monitoring tools detect bosh pressure channel anomalies eight to sixteen minutes prior to operational disruptions, according to the review. Digital-twin structures integrated with deep residual networks identify carbon emission deviations, categorizing operational anomaly severity with reported classification accuracies exceeding 97 percent. In electric arc furnaces, artificial neural networks estimate endpoint carbon concentrations, achieving reported hit rates of 96.67 percent within an error margin of 0.05 percent carbon.

The review delineates the baseline operating structure of integrated steelmaking, where raw-material preparation, blast furnace reduction, converter refining, and rolling units share significant energy flows and off-gas networks. Sintering, pelletizing, and coking supply the burden materials required for blast furnace operation, wherein fossil carbon acts simultaneously as a chemical reducing agent and an energy source. Conventional chemical analyses remain accurate but require offline sampling that cannot provide high-frequency process feedback. Echo state networks, variational mode decomposition, and swarm intelligence algorithms generate multi-step forecasts of blast furnace gas production and gasholder storage levels, driving root-mean-square errors below 0.05 across benchmark industrial datasets. The article's references cite Shang, X., Yin, W., Pan, J., Wang, M., Wang, H., Yang, K., & Xiao, Q. (2026), published in Carbon Neutral Systems, volume 2, issue 1.

The review states that future progress depends on physics-informed, multi-scale gray-box architectures that embed conservation equations and transport kinetics directly into deep neural frameworks. The authors observe that current industrial applications remain predominantly confined to isolated processing units operating within narrow parameter boundaries. The article does not state when or whether such plant-wide architectures will be deployed. It does not give a timeline for the five technological pathways it maps. The article does not report any response from steel producers or policymakers to the review. It does not state the review's conclusions on costs for the hydrogen and electrolysis routes beyond the hurdles it lists.

stories.Headline: Detectify launches Agentic Tooling to help AI agents verify software vulnerabilities in live applications
stories.Summary:
The Swedish application security firm Detectify AB launched its Agentic Tooling on November 16, 2026, to help organizations verify suspected software flaws. This new suite of tools allows artificial intelligence agents to test whether vulnerabilities in running applications can actually be exploited. The launch also includes a Security Ledger designed to record evidence for every test to ensure the results are authentic. These tools are specifically aimed at DevSecOps teams who struggle to trust the reports generated by their AI agents.

The system requires the use of loop engineering to run AI agents in automated workflows triggered by events like continuous integration runs. It integrates with the Model Context Protocol or a command-line interface to work with a customer's existing agents in their own environment. The tooling utilizes Alfred, an AI system launched in March 2025, along with attack surface data and payload assessments from ethical hackers. This setup creates a verification factory where agents read code and test live applications from an external perspective.

Chief Executive Rickard Carlsson explained that agents often fabricate proof to please users, making it impossible to know if code is truly secure. He stated that the company intends to build proof that an agent cannot fabricate by using an append-only ledger. This ledger is written by Detectify rather than the agent to separate actual test results from unsupported AI conclusions. Carlsson noted that the tools are available on request and build upon a server announced in May.

The release addresses a critical need because Detectify's H2 2026 Cyber Hygiene Index found that 90 percent of high-severity vulnerabilities remained exposed for over 90 days. Additionally, research from Tencent Holdings Ltd. and Fudan University showed that 76 percent of static-analysis alerts were false positives. The company is backed by investors including Balderton Capital (UK) LLP, Inventure, First Fellow Partners Oy, SquareOne App Ltd, and Insight Partners. Insight Partners took a majority stake in the company in October 2024.

stories.Headline: Congress seeks stricter AI chip export rules after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on November 12, 2026, after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang. U.S. Congress responded by seeking tighter AI chip export rules to China following this reported spy scandal. The resignation ended a 33-year tenure for the founder of the valuable technology giant. Authorities suspect Alice Huang acted as an intelligence asset for China's Ministry of State Security. This sequence of events triggered an immediate political push for stricter semiconductor legislation.

The AI Overwatch Act would require export licenses and 30 days' notice to Congress before the Commerce Department approves sales. The Chip Security Act proposes security mechanisms like on-site audits and ping-based location verification to detect chip diversion. The MATCH Act targets gaps in semiconductor manufacturing equipment controls by coordinating with allied supplier countries. These measures were included in a proposed manager's amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act. No physical location-tracking device is required for every chip under the proposed Chip Security Act text.

House Speaker Mike Johnson noted a developing consensus in Congress and called the tighter export limits an important position. Senate Majority Leader John Thune stated there was a high probability of new restrictions before the year's end. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries added Democratic support to the provisions already embedded in the Senate defense bill. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department had not concluded if Alice Huang was a spy. Beijing's foreign ministry rejected the allegations of espionage as groundless.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee stated the scandal proved why export controls are necessary to prevent Chinese technology access. Chip export advocates told The Hill that Huang's exit dismantled the industry's most consequential lobbying infrastructure against legislation. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks jointly urged Congress to pass the AI Overwatch Act to cut off pathways. OpenAI board member Paul Christiano acknowledged that AI developments are not adequately secured against theft. Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo expressed frustration that companies have terrible security while withholding public information.

Epoch AI estimates a median of 660,000 Nvidia H100-equivalent chips were smuggled into China through 2025. The possible upper range of smuggled chips reaches 1.6 million, while the lower bound is 290,000. Alice Huang worked for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm and principal Southeast Asian business partner for Nvidia. Singapore impounded her passport in June 2025 and returned it on February 26, 2026, after a warning. U.S. investigators say Alice Huang used shell companies to access approximately 240,000 banned chips.

Three House committee chairs requested that Huang appear for a closed-door congressional briefing on November 18, 2026. This briefing covers his contacts with Alice Huang and Nvidia's internal protocols against foreign espionage. Colette Kress became interim CEO, and venture investor Harvey C. Jones was named the first board chair. The Trump administration has not publicly committed to signing the stricter semiconductor export controls into law. It remains open whether Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman Roger Wicker will include the provisions in the NDAA.

stories.Headline: Progress Software's Ed Keisling says AI token costs now come out of salaries and bonuses
stories.Summary:
Ed Keisling, chief AI officer at Progress Software, said in a November 15, 2026 CDOTrends article by Winston Thomas that the era of nearly free tokens ended as little as nine to 12 months earlier. He said that money must now come from somewhere, such as employee salaries, bonuses or travel. He described the gap between expectations and reality in AI deployment as far more complicated than executives expect. He compared it to his early career, when his team shipped finished Sun hardware and Oracle software stacks to banks instead of letting each bank install them. He said that work was much more difficult in practice than on paper.

Accenture surveyed 750 executives in 17 countries and found they expect per-token prices to fall 19% over two years while consumption grows 78%. GitHub moved every Copilot plan to token-based billing on June 1, 2026. Accenture found only about one dollar in five of token spend can be tied to a financial return. One in three organizations ran out of its annual token budget before year-end, and fewer than one in 12 use chargeback. By April 2026 Uber had used its full-year budget for AI coding tools and now limits each employee to USD1,500 a month in token spending per agentic coding tool.

Keisling said employees should see their own spend and managers their team's, with budget thresholds that force a conversation about whether work justifies the money. He said nothing should be deployed to a production or even test environment without cost controls in place. He said Progress wired cost telemetry into every agent before release and shut down internal agents after comparing spend with output, saying there was no ROI there. He called dumping everything into a growing context window probably the most expensive route and pointed to retrieval-augmented generation instead. He said getting data ready for a small language model takes months and that governance and observability tooling simply does not exist as a complete package.

The FinOps Foundation notes provider bills show spend by API key or project, not by business unit or cost center, and tooling around a production agent can make up 40% to 60% of feature spend. Gartner predicts companies will use small, task-specific models at least three times as much as general-purpose LLMs next year. IBM found high levels of shadow AI added USD670,000 to the average breach cost, and Ramp data reported by Axios showed 28% of corporate OpenAI chat spending in February flowed through personal consumer plans. Keisling said there is a good chance some data sent to frontier models ends up training them, while OpenAI states it does not train on API or enterprise data by default. Accenture's research suggests only about one-third of workloads must stay sovereign.

Progress describes itself as providing context and control for AI, including control over cost, and bought agentic RAG startup Nuclia in 2025. Progress sells agentic RAG as a service starting at USD700 a month. TypeSafe AI's Jev launched with USD5 in starter credit, which the company says buys about 120 million tokens. Keisling said newer small models are orders of magnitude cheaper than mid-tier ones, and he pins cheap models to routine tasks while saving frontier models for hard ones. He also points to a new class of decision models that classify and choose rather than write.

Keisling scores agents that act on four dials: the access the agent holds, the financial impact of its decisions, how fast a bad change can be reversed and the damage to reputation. He said companies should put a dollar on it and test the agent before it ships. He said what matters is how big a box you were able to put the agent in, in terms of tools, skills and budget. The article says most companies are still drawing theirs. The article ends by saying tokens got cheaper but ready did not.

stories.Headline: Xero launches Xforce to help accounting firms build AI workflows
stories.Summary:
Xero announced Xforce by Xero, a team of forward-deployed engineers and partner consultants who work with accounting firms to design their workflows for the artificial intelligence era, in a media release dated Nov. 11. The team will use XeroForce, Xero's APIs and Xero OS, and it will integrate with other software in a practice's technology stack to automate workflows end-to-end, the company said. Xforce is in beta and is being developed with a handful of design partners in Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, including Liston Newton Advisory in Australia, Nexia Christchurch and Shepherd Hensman in New Zealand, and Azets and Sumer in the U.K. XeroForce, announced in May, is a natural language custom AI agent builder for the financial workflows of small businesses and accountants, helping practices turn manual tasks into durable, scalable workflows.

Xforce brings the expertise of forward-deployed engineers and partner consultants to help accounting firms put XeroForce to work for their practice, their employees and their small business clients, according to Xero. All of Xero's AI innovations, including JAX, its agentic platform, are grounded in what the company calls Accountable Intelligence and sit within the AI-native Xero OS. More information about Xforce by Xero can be found on the company's website, the article said. The article gave no further dates or figures beyond the Nov. 11 release date and the May announcement of XeroForce.

Diya Jolly, president of product and technology at Xero, said that building on positive feedback on XeroForce in beta, Xforce puts experienced experts in the field with firms to help them embed trusted, repeatable and scalable AI workflows. She said those workflows deliver greater consistency and efficiency and give firms time back to reinvest in growing their practice. Jolly said Xero is excited to work with these firms as its first design partners for Xforce, and that together they will explore how AI and automation can make everyday accounting simpler. She said the shared ambition is to champion clients' success by combining great technology with the personal advice and support that help businesses thrive.

Sukhinder Singh Cassidy, chief executive of Xero, said accountants and bookkeepers are being asked to do more with fewer people, and fewer are entering the profession. She said AI can help, but to scale it firms need hands-on support to build it into the way they work. Cassidy said partner consultants provided that support when thousands of firms moved from desktop to cloud, and that Xforce is designed to do the same for AI, with every firm deciding what gets automated on a trusted platform they control. The articles do not say when Xforce will move beyond beta or how firms can join the program.

stories.Headline: US labor authorities launch PERM actions against Microsoft, Adobe and six IT firms
stories.Summary:
United States authorities in October initiated administrative action under the Permanent Labor Certification program against Microsoft, Adobe and six major technology outsourcing firms, including Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Cognizant and Capgemini, according to TechGig. The actions have disrupted the processing and acceptance of these firms' PERM applications, creating uncertainty for foreign professionals awaiting permanent residency. The federal inquiry centers on allegations that certain employers used immigration programs to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign personnel. Officials noted that the ongoing investigations and administrative actions do not constitute a final finding of guilt. The PERM program is a critical step for US employers seeking to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards, and employers must certify that insufficient qualified US workers are available and that hiring a foreign national will not adversely affect American employees.

The Trump administration has introduced a requirement of $100,000 for certain new H-1B petitions while extending related visa restrictions through September 2027. The H-1B program allows US companies to temporarily employ foreign professionals in specialty occupations and has long been central to the Indian IT sector across software development, cloud services, cybersecurity and technical consulting. The administration has not formally announced a complete shutdown or overhaul of the H-1B program, focusing instead on audits, employer accountability and strict compliance. US Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito warned that temporary work visas cannot be treated as a permanent business strategy, stating that visas like the H-1B should only be used when qualified and willing American workers are unavailable for a given role. D'Esposito indicated that the probe is likely to widen and warned that similar actions could soon target additional companies and academic institutions.

His office is coordinating closely with the White House Fraud Task Force, led by Vice President JD Vance, which aims to identify systemic irregularities and abuse within visa programs. The heightened scrutiny directly affects major Indian IT service providers whose US operations rely heavily on deploying specialized talent from abroad. For Indian IT firms, the immediate challenge lies in balancing business continuity in their largest market with rigorous adherence to evolving immigration rules. If federal investigations expand and PERM restrictions persist, Indian service providers could face significant hurdles in talent deployment, foreign hiring and green card sponsorship for employees in the United States. The articles do not say what further steps, if any, the firms or the administration will take next.

stories.Headline: Digital News Publishers Association challenges India's data protection law in Supreme Court
stories.Summary:
The Digital News Publishers Association challenged the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 before the Supreme Court of India. This group represents twenty one news publishers who are concerned about the law and its associated rules. A Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant issued a notice to the Union Government on 27 October 2026. The court declined to grant interim relief without first hearing the government side of the legal dispute. A further hearing on this matter is scheduled to take place on 17 November 2026.

The DPDP Act received presidential assent on 11 August 2023 and regulates digital personal data and digitised non digital data. It defines Data Fiduciaries as entities determining processing means and Data Principals as the individuals whose data is processed. The DPDP Rules, 2025, were notified on 13 November 2025, with principal compliance starting on 13 May 2027. Financial penalties for contraventions can reach Rs. 250 crore, and children under eighteen require verifiable parental consent for processing.

The challenge targets Sections 7, 17, 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37, 44(3), and specific provisions of the 2025 Rules. The publishers argue that the law lacks a specific journalistic exemption, which could hinder the collection of information for investigations. They claim that requiring prior consent from individuals under investigation would undermine the work of journalists investigating public office misuse. The publishers also question Section 44(3), which amends Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act of 2005 regarding personal information. They believe Section 17 raises concerns about the scope of exemptions available to the State for national security purposes.

These groups seek to balance individual dignity with the public right to information and the freedom of the press. Journalists and citizens are affected by this law, as it impacts the ability to scrutinize public institutions and government power. The articles suggest that privacy should not be a shield against legitimate scrutiny, nor should journalism justify publishing every detail. The debate involves the constitutional relationship between Articles 14, 19(1)(a), and 21 of the Indian Constitution regarding expression and privacy. In Jammu and Kashmir, digital rights are significant because platforms are essential for banking, education, employment, and public services.

The region has a specific history with internet restrictions that makes these data protection and privacy issues particularly important. The 2017 case of Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India established that privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right. The 2020 Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India case emphasized proportionality and transparency regarding internet suspensions in Jammu and Kashmir.

Internationally, the European Union uses the GDPR, while the United States uses fragmented laws like the California Consumer Privacy Act. China implemented the Personal Information Protection Law in 2021, which includes specific provisions regarding State organs and national security. These global examples show different ways of balancing individual autonomy, state surveillance, and the right to information or erasure. The Supreme Court will now determine if the law adequately distinguishes public interest journalism from the commercial misuse of data.

It must decide if the legislation protects citizens from information misuse or protects power from the scrutiny of the citizens. The court will examine if State interference with privacy satisfies standards of legality, legitimate purpose, necessity, and proportionality. The articles leave open whether the Data Protection Board will provide an independent and accessible remedy for those affected. It remains unclear how the court will reconcile the right to informational privacy with the public right to know.

stories.Headline: Criminals steal about €100 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa in a cyberattack
stories.Summary:
A highly organized criminal group targeted the French banking and insurance group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa in a major cyberattack during late 2026. The attackers first compromised a third-party service provider on October 27 to infiltrate the bank's infrastructure. Starting on Sunday, November 1, the hackers siphoned approximately €100 million, or about $112 million, from the organization's accounts. They used instant payment systems to move the funds into legitimate European bank accounts before transferring the money to cryptocurrency platforms.

The heist required the creation of fake Fortuneo IBANs to initiate payment orders from the bank's accounts to external destinations. On Tuesday, November 3, the bank discovered the fraud and immediately blocked external access to its information system. To stop the theft, the organization disconnected from the interbank payment system, deleted the fake accounts, and updated its credentials. Blockchain analyst ZachXBT recorded suspicious withdrawals over $106 million on November 2, later raising that estimate to over $133 million. Bitquery tracked $108.8 million in USDC moving through OKX, Crypto.com, and Kraken within 21 hours.

Julien Carmona and the bank's chairman described the incident as a new type of robbery carried out by a well-equipped group. The chairman stated that artificial intelligence was very likely involved in the attack, although he provided no specific technical details. Carmona suggested that advanced AI might have supported the criminals, but the bank has not yet provided concrete evidence of its usage. The bank noted that customer accounts and Fortuneo systems remained unaffected by the breach.

The security breach began outside the bank's network, and the name of the compromised provider remains undisclosed to protect similar companies. Most of the methods used, such as credential theft and money mules, existed long before the mass adoption of artificial intelligence. Experts believe AI could have assisted the group with reconnaissance, coding, or creating documents to open the fraudulent accounts. No criminal group has claimed responsibility for the theft at this time.

stories.Headline: South Korea bans AI-generated fake doctor ads from the 27th
stories.Summary:
South Korea announced on November 15, 2026, that it will ban AI-generated fake doctor advertisements starting on the 27th of that month, according to a report from Chosun Ilbo published the same day. The measure targets promotional material that uses artificial intelligence to create the appearance of medical professionals endorsing products or services. The ban takes effect on the 27th, which falls twelve days after the announcement date given in the article. The report did not specify which agency issued the ban or how the rule will be enforced.

The change means that advertisements featuring AI-generated images of doctors will no longer be permitted in South Korea from the 27th onward. Every number and date the article provides is limited to the announcement on November 15, 2026, and the effective date of the 27th. The article gives no further figures, such as penalties, fines, or the length of any transition period. It also does not describe how authorities will identify AI-generated content or which platforms will be covered.

The article does not name any official, agency, or spokesperson responsible for the ban, and it contains no statements from anyone involved. Because no one is quoted or paraphrased in the source, there are no remarks to report about the reasoning behind the measure. The report likewise does not explain what prompted the decision or whether the rule applies to all advertising or only to certain media. No context about earlier rules or similar bans is given in the article.

The article provides no information about what happens next beyond the effective date of the 27th. It does not say whether there will be inspections, complaints, or penalties after the ban begins. It also does not indicate whether further guidance or details are expected from the government. More to follow.

stories.Headline: John Langford resigns from Microsoft after AI Frontiers restructuring
stories.Summary:
John Langford, a veteran machine learning researcher at Microsoft, has resigned from the company, and his departure follows the dissolution of the AI Frontiers research group, which was established in 2023. The 50-member team focused on exploring new approaches to artificial intelligence, working on projects like Microsoft's AutoGen multi-agent framework and Fara, a computer-use agent. A restructuring in September 2026 moved AI Frontiers from Microsoft Research into Microsoft AI, the company's commercial AI division. Langford stated that this change created differences over how AI development should progress within Microsoft.

The commercial division prioritised scaling existing models using larger datasets and computing resources, while AI Frontiers focused on developing alternative algorithms, optimisation techniques, and model architectures. Langford reported that the team's research was considered "aggressively not research" by the product organisation, which reportedly left several projects without a clear path towards adoption within Microsoft. The research group explored alternative AI technologies including Next Latent, Dion3, and Full Bandwidth Transformers, and these projects aimed to improve AI training and computational efficiency rather than relying on increasing model size. Langford's departure reportedly coincided with other senior researchers leaving the group, which highlights the differences between exploratory AI research and commercial product development.

Langford said the restructuring created differences over how AI development should progress within Microsoft, and he reported that the product organisation viewed the team's research as "aggressively not research." The commercial division's focus on scaling existing models with larger datasets and computing resources stood in contrast to the group's work on alternative algorithms, optimisation techniques, and model architectures. The projects explored by the group, including Next Latent, Dion3, and Full Bandwidth Transformers, aimed to improve AI training and computational efficiency rather than relying on increasing model size. His departure reportedly coincided with other senior researchers leaving the group, and the articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: New Jersey assembly committee advances bills to regulate AI in insurance and tenant screening
stories.Summary:
New Jersey lawmakers advanced legislation to regulate artificial intelligence in insurance, housing and the workplace at a November 16, 2026 meeting of the Assembly Science, Innovation and Technology Committee. The committee took up bills limiting AI use in insurance claim denials, regulating automated tenant screening and imposing new requirements on electronic monitoring of employees. Lawmakers also considered measures requiring greater transparency from data center developers. Assemblyman Chris Tully (D-Bergenfield), the committee chairman, said the legislation reflects the need to protect consumers as AI becomes more widely used. The proposals drew concerns from businesses about higher costs and restrictions on emerging technology.

One bill, A5494, would prohibit certain uses of artificial intelligence in denying homeowners, automobile and flood insurance claims. It advanced with Assemblyman Chris DePhillips (R-Wyckoff) abstaining and every other committee member voting in favor. A second bill, A5495, would regulate automated tenant screening systems used to evaluate prospective renters. It also advanced with DePhillips abstaining and the remaining committee members voting in favor. The committee held a discussion-only hearing on A4981, which would regulate AI-based electronic monitoring systems used in employment and public services. Assembly members Heather Simmons (D-Glassboro) and Cody Miller (D-Monroe) are sponsoring that proposal, along with 16 other Democratic co-sponsors.

Tully said AI systems can improve efficiency and tackle fraud, but that people must be protected from automatic denial by algorithms. He said that when a major decision affects someone's life, there must always be a human in the loop. Tully said mandating human oversight establishes common-sense guardrails to use these powerful tools responsibly. DePhillips said he abstained on both bills because proponents and opponents did not seem that far apart and he saw an opportunity for both sides to collaborate. Assemblyman Balvir Singh (D-Burlington) said he felt like he was learning to ride a bike while riding it.

Assemblywoman Carmen Morales (D-Bloomfield) defended the insurance proposal as a consumer protection measure and said it really is about transparency. Insurance industry representatives raised concerns that the restrictions could limit their ability to use new technology and leave companies at a competitive disadvantage. Nicholas Kikis, vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs for the New Jersey Apartment Association, did not take a position on the tenant screening bill but warned that AI has made it increasingly difficult for landlords to detect fraudulent applications. Kikis pointed to income verification, saying documents landlords previously could verify with relative ease can now be altered using AI. Jeff Kolekowski of the New Jersey Builders Association raised similar concerns without taking a formal position on the bill.

Anthony Russo of the Commerce and Industry Association of New Jersey said the monitoring bill would add a high cost to companies that invent those technologies and that they would have to pay to have it approved. Russo said that if the bill goes through, it just adds to the cost of doing business. Jack Ramirez of the New Jersey Business and Industry Association said the bill's definition of artificial intelligence was too broad and could subject ordinary business tools to additional regulation. Eric Richards, legislative affairs coordinator for the New Jersey AFL-CIO, said AI has the power to change the very nature of work and that without oversight AI companies pose tremendous risk to working people. Richards said the bill puts clear common-sense ground rules for how AI can be used in the workplace and makes sure an employer can't spy on you when you're off the clock.

A5224 would require data center developers to disclose certain information to the public and elected officials before preliminary site plan consideration under the Municipal Land Use Law. S4304, sponsored by State Sens. Linda Greenstein (D-Plainsboro) and Brian Stack (D-Union City), would prohibit agreements intended to conceal certain information about data center developments, and its Assembly counterpart is A2774. Greenstein said that if you don't play by the rules of open government, you don't get to build in New Jersey, and that confidentiality agreements could prevent residents and local officials from learning the full extent of a project's electricity demands and environmental effects. Chris Sotiro of the Climate Revolution Action Network said the developers are not interested in transparency but are interested in hiding. A2774 advanced with bipartisan support, with DePhillips, the only Republican present at the hearing, voting in favor, and Assemblyman Greg McGuckin (R-Toms River) was absent.

Earlier this year, Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation sponsored by Assemblyman Andrew Macurdy (D-Summit) that redirected $250 million in unused data center tax credits to the New Jersey Economic Development Authority. The measure passed the Legislature with nearly unanimous support. The hearings illustrate the competing pressures facing lawmakers as they try to establish protections for consumers, tenants and workers without imposing restrictions that businesses say could discourage innovation or make new technologies more expensive to use. The articles do not say when the full Assembly or Senate might vote on the bills. The articles do not say what happens to A4981 after the discussion-only hearing. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Karen Nyamu denies viral Senate thumb-sucking video and says AI fabricated it
stories.Summary:
Nominated Senator Karen Nyamu denied on November 16, 2026, that a viral video showed her sucking her thumb while scrolling through her phone during a Senate sitting, and she told TNX Africa that the footage had been fabricated using artificial intelligence. The clip, which drew considerable attention on social media, appeared to show the senator seated in the chamber, seemingly distracted by her phone before putting her thumb in her mouth. Nyamu spoke exclusively to TNX Africa and insisted she was being targeted through manipulated digital content. She challenged viewers to examine her manicure, arguing that her nail polish would not have remained intact had she been sucking her thumb as the video portrayed. Nyamu asked whether she could have kept her polish if she had been sucking her thumb, and she said the footage was made using AI.

She added that another one of her posts had recently been doctored as well. She challenged those questioning her conduct to consult the official parliamentary recordings, insisting the footage would expose the alleged fabrication. Nyamu said she had been on the floor debating very serious issues and urged people to check the Senate live feed for any such thing. The denial comes against a backdrop of previous controversies involving the senator and viral footage of her conduct. A month before the November 2026 denial, she trended online after yet another video showed her sucking her thumb on the floor of the house mid-session.

In March 2024, Nyamu was captured on camera scrolling through her phone during a Senate sitting as Nakuru Senator Tabitha Keroche addressed the House, and the footage sparked online criticism from Kenyans who questioned her attentiveness during parliamentary proceedings. In April 2026, an ordinary photograph of Nyamu standing alongside Busia Senator Okiya Omtatah was transformed into a fabricated intimate video that circulated widely online. Nyamu is also the sponsor of the proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, which seeks to establish a framework for regulating the development and use of AI in Kenya. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: US, Israel, UAE and Qatar sign pact to protect AI supply chains and infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The United States, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar signed the San Francisco Declaration on Sunday to protect critical infrastructure and AI supply chains. This agreement strengthens regional cooperation with Washington as the Trump administration attempts to reduce the technological advantages currently held by China. The pact was finalized just before President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping this Thursday. These diplomatic efforts occur while a major scandal involving the chipmaker Nvidia creates further tension in the global race for artificial intelligence.

This accord is a component of Pax Silica, a broader initiative launched in December 2025 to secure advanced manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, and critical minerals. The San Francisco Declaration establishes a common understanding regarding sensitive technologies and proposes the creation of five specific working groups. These groups will focus on resilience, security hubs, supply-chain cooperation, AI adoption, and the development of policy frameworks. While the document does not explicitly name China, it aims to coordinate global partners to challenge Beijing's dominance over the industries that support AI.

The United States State Department is responsible for the agreement and issued a press release explaining the need to safeguard the foundations of AI. Officials indicated that the pact creates a shared understanding of the critical infrastructure and sensitive technologies required for the modern economy. The initiative seeks to build a new grouping of partners specifically tailored for the AI economy to ensure long-term economic security. This strategic move is intended to stabilize the technology race during a period of uncertainty caused by the crisis at Nvidia.

stories.Headline: Nearly 70% of aides and lobbyists expect AI safety rules to pass in the 120th Congress
stories.Summary:
A Canvass survey published by Punchbowl News on November 15, 2026 found that nearly 70% of respondents expect artificial intelligence safety rules to pass in the next Congress, which will be the 120th. The survey combined senior congressional aides with leaders of the wider lobbying world, drawing on top Capitol Hill staff and K Street professionals. Those respondents see the next Congress as the time for action on artificial intelligence safety. The article presenting the survey was dated November 15, 2026, and appeared in Punchbowl News. The survey result points to a shift in expectations for AI guardrails, with nearly 70% of those polled saying they view safety rules as likely to pass in the next Congress.

The 120th Congress is the body the respondents identified as the one that would take up the issue. The article did not give a specific date for when a vote might occur or what the rules would contain. It also did not say how many people took part in the survey beyond describing them as senior congressional aides and leaders of the wider lobbying world. Democrats have rallied behind the idea that artificial intelligence needs legal guardrails, according to the same article, but they are divided on how to tax the tech. That division is the only detail the article offered on the substance of the debate, and it did not say where Republicans stand.

The article also linked to separate coverage on Florida asking a court to stop OpenAI development and on what the Trump-Xi meeting means for tech. No lawmaker or staffer was named as responsible for the push, and the article carried no direct comment from any official. The article did not say what happens next beyond the survey finding, and it did not give a timeline for when AI safety legislation might be introduced or voted on. It presented the 120th Congress as the window respondents expect, without naming a committee, a sponsor or a draft bill. The piece was a preview of premium tech coverage, and the full story was available only to subscribers.

stories.Headline: State regulators find about 62 percent of community banks use or test AI tools
stories.Summary:
More community banks began adopting artificial intelligence technologies around November 16, 2026, to improve their operations. This shift toward generative tools has created new questions regarding how these financial institutions can maintain accuracy. State banking regulators discovered that approximately 62 percent of community banks are currently using or testing these systems. The adoption of such technology requires a careful approach to ensure that the output remains reliable.

The process of using these tools requires bankers to treat AI generated work like the output of a human employee. Experienced professionals must edit the results, perform fact checks, and review the data to ensure it passes a sniff test. If the technology provides inaccurate information, the user should ask the system for a better source or a specific citation. This method allows the banker to maintain ownership of the work while utilizing the speed of the software.

Generative AI consultant Ben Udell is responsible for providing guidance on how to manage these new digital tools. He stated that people often feel they cannot own their work when using artificial intelligence, but this is not the case if used correctly. Udell believes that the process of reviewing AI is not different from managing a human colleague. He suggested that people are simply freaked out because the technology is labeled as artificial intelligence.

More to follow.
