stories.Headline: Albanese government plans mandatory AI safety rules and a new regulator
stories.Summary:
The Albanese Government announced on 10 November 2026 that it will legislate mandatory safety and security protections for frontier AI companies and propose a new regulator to enforce them. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese made the announcement in a joint release with the Deputy Prime Minister and the ministers for Home Affairs and Industry. The ACTU linked the announcement to 850 Qantas jobs it said would be cut and outsourced as the company accelerates its use of AI. Ai Group warned against a regulate-first mindset in its position on a draft workplace AI guide set out on 12 November 2026. The National Tertiary Education Union announced on 12 November 2026 that its Deakin University members will strike next week, with protection from AI among their claims.

The Prime Minister's release said the AI Standards would apply to all frontier AI companies that wish to operate in Australia. It defined frontier AI as the most sophisticated models at the cutting edge of current technological capability. The release said the Government will propose the protections be enforced by a new targeted regulator for AI safety. That regulator would work with the Australian AI Safety Institute and could enforce significant penalties for companies that fail to comply. Companies would have to keep security controls throughout development and deployment, identify and manage serious risks, open their models to independent evaluation, report incidents quickly, and keep and publish safety and security frameworks.

Minister for Employment and Workplace Relations Amanda Rishworth released the draft Best Practice Guide on the Adoption of AI in the Workplace, with consultation open until 27 January 2027 through consultations.dewr.gov.au. The draft followed roundtables and forums involving unions, employer groups, academics and businesses including Microsoft, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores and Ramsay Health Care. The guide is built around 3 themes, Plan, Enable and Embed, and sets out 8 practical principles including cooperative planning and worker engagement, designing work and jobs, establishing AI governance, and managing risks and work health and safety. Its case studies include Brisbane Catholic Education, where 71% of educators reported AI was saving them time on administrative tasks, Commonwealth Bank, where more than 32,000 staff have used personalised career, skills and learning tools, and Blackmores Group, which cut a manual data-entry task from 3 days to 10 minutes. Rishworth said the guide makes it clear that AI works best when the workforce is at the centre of the adoption process.

The ACTU said unions have been calling since 2024 for regulatory protections that are legislated and backed by an empowered regulator. It said Qantas announced the 850 job cuts that day, following what the ACTU called sackings at NAB, ANZ and Canva. ACTU Assistant Secretary Joseph Mitchell said workers need genuine protections against job displacement and against bosses using AI for intrusive monitoring and surveillance. Ai Group Chief Executive Innes Willox called the draft a good start but said elements of what is suggested remain impractical and unrealistic, and named worker consultation as a flashpoint for potential disagreement between unions and industry. Willox said union calls for heavy handed and unrealistic requirements for businesses to engage with them before any decision around implementation will be strongly resisted by employers, and that not every potential use of AI can or should be up for debate with unions.

The NTEU said its Deakin members want a 20 per cent pay rise across the term of the new agreement, protection from the adverse effects of AI, guaranteed job security, and limits on and meaningful consultation about major changes. The union said it has been bargaining with Deakin since July and that management has not responded to staff's key claims. NTEU Deakin Branch President Professor Reece Walters said that after 50 hours of talks, management has dragged the chain and provided nothing in writing to a single staff claim. In a speech to the Australian Labour and Employment Relations Association, Rishworth said the Government has recently legislated to address the rise in AI-generated applications, which she described as often of low quality and with very little prospect of success. She said the legislation gives the Fair Work Commission more discretion to decide matters on the papers without a formal hearing, removes the requirement for hearings to establish whether an applicant in a general protections matter has actually been dismissed, and gives the Commission additional powers to dismiss vexatious or frivolous applicants, including preventing them from making further applications.

Rishworth said the Government will soon introduce a further bill to support the Commission's workload, including the express power to dismiss inactive applications in certain situations. The Prime Minister's release said the protections are consistent with recommendations in the interim report of the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence. The release said further details of the legislation will become available in due course, and it did not set a date for the AI Standards legislation. Minister for Home Affairs Tony Burke said it is not a free-for-all and there need to be clear guardrails to protect Australians. The NTEU said work bans will take place in the days before the strike.

stories.Headline: Kenyan High Court Justice Andayi sets aside ODPC compensation award and questions commissioner's power to decide damages
stories.Summary:
Justice Francis Andayi of the High Court set aside a KSh1.25 million compensation award against a Nairobi healthcare business on a complaint by a patient identified as GW about CCTV cameras in a clinical examination room. The patient argued the cameras compromised her privacy, and the healthcare provider disputed the ODPC's findings and presented forensic evidence on the footage. The High Court did not decide whether the alleged privacy violation occurred, and instead examined whether the Commissioner had legal authority to order compensation. The judgment questioned whether the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner can independently determine damages payable to individuals under the Data Protection Act. The decision came after the ODPC built a record of financial enforcement, with more than KSh30 million paid to individuals during 2025.

The dispute centred on Section 65 of the Data Protection Act and Regulation 14(3)(e) of the subsidiary legislation, and Section 65 gives individuals a right to compensation for damage from a contravention of the Act. Justice Andayi observed that Section 65 does not expressly assign the Commissioner the job of deciding whether damage occurred or calculating compensation payable. He distinguished the regulator's powers to investigate complaints, impose administrative penalties and issue enforcement notices from the separate function of deciding monetary claims between parties. He questioned whether Regulation 14(3)(e) could introduce a substantive power Parliament had not expressly provided in the parent legislation. He relied on the principle that statutory agencies and tribunals can exercise only powers conferred on them by law.

Justice Andayi also questioned the procedure followed when the ODPC issued the award, after the regulator investigated the complaint, considered the provider's response and issued a monetary determination. He was concerned the process had not provided an adequate hearing at which both sides could contest the evidence and address the compensation claim. He questioned whether the same Commissioner could investigate an alleged violation, effectively prosecute the complaint and then determine the financial remedy without safeguards required by natural justice. He said: "Even if a hearing were to be conducted, I again doubt that it would be by the same Data Commissioner to be the one investigating, then prosecuting it and then deciding." He said that would be against all the rules of natural justice.

The patient and the Data Commissioner maintained that Section 65, read with Regulation 14, authorised the watchdog to issue compensation orders, and they relied on previous High Court decisions supporting the regulator's administrative remedies. Justice Andayi found the earlier authorities had not adequately addressed whether the compensation provision in the regulations exceeded the powers granted under the Act. He declined to strike down Regulation 14(3)(e) or declare all previous ODPC compensation awards unlawful, saying such a challenge required proceedings directed at the validity of the subsidiary legislation with the Attorney-General given an opportunity to participate. The judgment does not invalidate previous awards, and the underlying right of individuals to seek compensation under Section 65 remains. The ODPC's compensation decisions have affected financial services, healthcare, lending and digital commerce.

Standard Investment Bank was ordered to pay Andrew Endovo KSh50,000 after sending him an unsolicited promotional email without his consent, and Platinum Credit was ordered to compensate Philip Bolo KSh900,000 after continuing direct marketing despite his objection. Moja Expressway Company, which operates the 27-kilometre Nairobi Expressway, was ordered to pay former employee Cyrus Mwaniki Ndung'u KSh500,000 for using his photograph to promote electronic toll collection services without permission. Tech Limited faced a KSh2.6 million compensation order, which it subsequently challenged at the High Court. In April 2026 the regulator ordered St. Luke Orthopaedic & Trauma Hospital Eldoret to pay Merceline Akoth Odeyo KSh525,000 after she received medical test results belonging to another person on two occasions and her medical information was shared with an external laboratory without her knowledge or consent.

The hospital attributed the incident to human error and argued the information shared was limited to identification details, and the Commissioner found it had not demonstrated explicit and informed consent or adequately protected her personal information. TechTrendsKE reported in April 2025 that the ODPC issued 51 determinations in 2024, with average fines of approximately KSh522,308 per case, and those administrative fines serve a different purpose from compensation awarded to individuals. Immaculate Kassait, the country's first Data Commissioner, is preparing for a leadership transition after a six-year tenure, and a November 13, 2026 assessment listed more than 13,000 complaints handled, 459 determinations issued and 206 enforcement and penalty notice actions. The regulator had also registered approximately 28,000 data controllers and processors, and Kassait has called for amendments to the Data Protection Act on artificial intelligence, sensitive personal information, penalties and data governance.

President William Ruto nominated Lydia Sitienei Chelagat, formerly Director of Legal Services at the Communications Authority of Kenya, to succeed Kassait on November 10, 2026, and her nomination was forwarded to the National Assembly for consideration. In the EU, Ireland's Data Protection Commission found that Tinder's "Download My Data" tool omitted certain categories of personal information or provided only summaries without clearly informing users, and the EU fined Match Group, the owner of Tinder, €11 million. The investigation into Match Group was launched in 2020 and resulted in an order requiring the company to bring its data processing practices into compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation within three months. Match Group rejected the findings and announced plans to appeal, insisting that Tinder maintains strong privacy protections for its users.

The ODPC's ability to investigate complaints and enforce compliance remains intact, and the unresolved issue concerns the legal route through which it can determine compensation. The eventual determination of whether the Commissioner can independently award those damages will depend on a direct judicial examination of the regulation underpinning that authority. The judgment provides businesses grounds to scrutinise the statutory basis and procedures behind compensation orders, while Section 65 continues to recognise the right of individuals to seek compensation when personal information is mishandled. The incoming Commissioner will inherit an institution with a substantial enforcement record and an expanding regulatory mandate.

stories.Headline: Trump launches five billion dollar Genesis Mission to advance science through AI
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump launched a five billion dollar government effort to advance science through artificial intelligence. This initiative, called the Genesis Mission, began in November 2025 via an executive order. It started at the Energy Department and now includes more than 15 federal agencies. The president also issued a second order in June to speed up quantum technology development. These actions occurred during the second term of President Donald Trump.

The Genesis Mission uses Energy Department data, computing power, and facilities to build shared AI tools. In 2025, federal agencies spent about 4.2 billion dollars on AI research and development. The White House Office of Science and Technology Policy released a 123 page report in July. The Energy Department aims to develop error corrected quantum computers by 2028. The Office of Science has a total budget of 8.4 billion dollars for fiscal year 2026.

Darío Gil is the undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy. He called AI, quantum science, and supercomputing the three legs of a transforming stool. Gil stated that 400 million dollars for Genesis is small compared to the total budget. John Sarrao is the director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, California. Sarrao said Genesis created an inflection point for scientists who already used AI.

Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University leads a project combining huge datasets from observatories and instruments. She said the idea is conceptually powerful but noted her cosmology grant was reduced. Brad Marston is a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. Marston said he wants all fields supported because AI and quantum were once backwaters. Researchers in public health and climate research have faced funding cuts and delays.

The National Science Foundation and National Institutes of Health launched Genesis efforts in biology, health, and space. SLAC is involved in 20 Genesis projects and leads two of them. The Energy Department funded nearly 300 projects this year, including nuclear fusion and electric grid simulations. Celia Merzbacher of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium said quantum computing is at the start of a marathon. Some Genesis funding came from a 2025 budget law and some from the department budget.

The government will continue using AI to speed up the development of nuclear reactors. Agencies will keep lining up research spending with the priorities of the current administration. Scientists will continue working on quantum sensors, quantum materials, and quantum error correction. The articles do not say how the government will balance funding for other science fields. It remains open whether the department will talk with scientists about these budget trade-offs.

stories.Headline: Roanoke County students question teachers' heavy AI use as school board adopts AI policy
stories.Summary:
Students in Roanoke County Public Schools are questioning how heavily their teachers rely on artificial intelligence for classroom materials, even as the school board adopted a formal AI policy on Thursday that restricts student use of generative technology. Student Advisory Council representative Addy Weaver told board members that teenagers are noticing an influx of AI-generated content from teachers while students face strict limits on when they can use the same tools for assignments. Weaver said students understand that AI is a very helpful tool for teachers and administrators who might need help with lesson plans or social media graphics, but she said the overwhelming influx of AI-generated content in schools has been a little jarring to students, and many wish for a more balanced approach. She raised these concerns during Thursday's meeting of the Roanoke County School Board.

The school board formally adopted Policy 6.42c on Thursday, codifying rules around artificial intelligence alongside the division's existing three-zone learning framework to prevent what the division calls cognitive offloading by students. District guidelines allow teachers to use AI for routine tasks such as lesson planning and administrative work, while students default to a no-AI zone for most assignments. Some coursework falls into intermediate zones where AI research tools are permitted with proper attribution, and the policy requires students to cite AI assistance when permitted while warning against letting technology replace original thinking. Superintendent Jamie Soltis asked student leaders to bring policy recommendations to their Dec. 9 meeting at the Roanoke County Career and Technology Center.

Weaver also addressed student frustration with Copyleaks, the AI plagiarism detection tool integrated into the Canvas learning management system, saying students reported that the software has been largely ineffective and creates unfair accusations with few ways for students to disprove AI-use claims. She said concerns about Copyleaks were addressed at the meeting, noting that students accused of using AI have few ways to disprove the claim within the tool's current system. Weaver said the discussion helped the council better understand how the use of certain AIs in the county is necessary and benefits both teachers and administrators, and she thanked Soltis for listening to the students' thoughts and discussions. More information is available at the schools website.

stories.Headline: AI Lawsuit Jersey 2026: Settlements, Eligibility and Filing
stories.Summary:
New Jersey faces three major AI class actions in 2026, according to lawfold.com, with the largest, Martinez v. TechHire Solutions, covering over 15,000 job applicants in the Newark metro area who claim an AI tool scored them lower based on zip code. The second, Doe v. SocialAI Corp, involves 8,000 New Jersey residents whose likenesses were used without consent to generate synthetic media. The third targets automated lending platforms and alleges AI loan denials disproportionately affected Black and Latino borrowers, with a class estimated at 12,000 applicants.

The Martinez case was certified by Essex County court in January 2026, the SocialAI Corp motion to dismiss was denied in February 2026, and the lending case began discovery in March 2026. The state attorney general filed two enforcement actions this year, both targeting AI vendors selling untested hiring tools to New Jersey employers. The cases invoke the 2025 AEDT Act, which gives workers a private right of action and requires a bias audit within 12 months of use, annual re-audits every 12 months, public disclosure, and candidate notification before AI use. Penalties run $500 per day for a missed initial audit, $1,000 per day for a missed re-audit, $500 per violation for non-disclosure, and $250 per applicant for missing notification. Deepfake victims can sue for statutory damages of $1,000 per incident under the 2025 privacy expansion, and the updated privacy framework took effect in January 2026, requiring explicit opt-in consent for AI data use.

Damages range from $500 to $2,500 for unauthorized data scraping under the NJ Consumer Fraud Act, $1,000 per violation for hidden AI data use, $1,000 to $5,000 for biometric misuse, and $5,000 per child for children's data harvesting. A 2025 state study found a 34% disparity in AI-driven loan approvals, against a 9% gap for human loan officers. The articles attribute the claims to New Jersey workers who say automated systems denied them jobs unfairly, and to plaintiffs who argue that non-compliance with the AEDT Act itself proves negligence. The articles state that employers must now prove their AI tools are bias-free and that companies that fail face penalties under the 2025 AEDT Act. The articles say the state attorney general filed the two enforcement actions, that penalties could exceed $10 million per case, and that the NJ Division on Civil Rights is actively investigating.

The articles state that the EEOC has referenced New Jersey cases in its own guidance. The articles say staffing agencies are the biggest targets and are named as co-defendants in multiple suits, and that at least four Fortune 500 firms paid undisclosed sums to New Jersey applicants. The articles state that over 20,000 workers have reported suspicious rejections since 2024, that over 40,000 New Jersey workers may be owed compensation, and that most claimants can expect between $200 and $5,000. The articles say the combined class size exceeds 35,000 people, that tech, finance, and staffing face the most exposure, and that the lead court is Essex County Superior Court. The articles state that retail chains face class actions over facial recognition data collected in New Jersey stores and offices.

The articles state that New Jersey passed the AEDT Act in 2025, that it was the first law of its kind in the state, and that the state leads the nation in AI regulation enforcement. The articles say New Jersey expanded its privacy laws in 2025 to cover synthetic media and that the updated privacy framework took effect in January 2026. The articles state that the claims fall under the NJ Law Against Discrimination, the NJ Consumer Fraud Act, the NJ Fair Housing Act, the NJ Biometric Privacy Act, and a NJ COPPA Extension. The articles say the law does not require proof of intentional discrimination and that disparate impact alone is enough under New Jersey law. The articles state that many employers missed the first audit deadline, creating a wave of new claims in early 2026.

The articles state that filing deadlines are approaching fast for several claims and advise workers rejected by AI systems to keep all emails, and deepfake victims to document screenshots, URLs, and timestamps. The articles do not name the defendants in the lending case, the employers or agencies named as co-defendants, the four Fortune 500 firms, or the retail chains facing biometric claims. The articles do not give the filing deadlines, the amounts paid in the undisclosed settlements, or the outcomes of the two enforcement actions. The articles do not state when the three class actions will next be heard or how the 34% disparity study was conducted.

stories.Headline: HFS survey finds only 33% of AI-active enterprises meet their AI business case
stories.Summary:
Only 33% of 502 senior AI decision makers at AI-active enterprises said their biggest AI program met or beat its business case in an HFS Research, Rackspace survey, published November 12, 2026. The survey was conducted in August and September 2026 and reported by MarketScale on November 15, 2026. Success fell to 28% when AI spans several functions and reached 56% where AI is embedded in standard operations. HFS said the pattern points to a fixable gap: unclear ownership of live AI performance, cost and governance as one system. Almost every respondent, 96%, said they have significant governance gaps.

Respondents worked at companies with at least $100 million in annual revenue, across eight industries and four regions. All were running AI pilots or more, and 83% were operating AI in production or beyond. The survey was blind, naming no vendor, and HFS said the results describe AI-active enterprises, not adoption across the whole market. Among single-function users, 37% met or exceeded their business case, falling to 28% across several functions and rising to 56% where AI is embedded in standard operations. HFS cautioned that these are different groups and the data does not show that operating maturity causes better returns.

HFS founder and CEO Phil Fersht said the industry has built a large ecosystem selling models, platforms, infrastructure and consulting, and that when results fall short each party blames another. He said technology and talent are plentiful, but people and partners willing to own how the whole system runs after go-live are scarce. He said the one-third result should make the industry face how hooked it has become on selling AI rather than accepting responsibility for getting it to work. Rackspace CEO Gajen Kandiah said moving from pilots to production requires cost, security, governance and infrastructure readiness handled as one. He said customers need a single accountable operator that integrates, runs and keeps improving the environment across infrastructure, applications, data and AI.

For 78% of respondents, governance failures pose a bigger threat than technology failures to scaling AI, and 44% lack a single, consistent way to run AI in production. The release groups barriers to AI returns into fragmented accountability, unpredictable costs and governance gaps. Of respondents, 58% cite workforce productivity gains, 42% cite measurable cost reductions, 28% report better customer experience and 21% report measurable revenue growth. Across more than 300 banking AI case studies HFS reviewed, productivity made up 44% of use cases, with nearly 20% built around risk and decision-making. HFS president Saurabh Gupta noted the US bank efficiency ratio was 56.9 in 2018 and 55.6 today, attributing swings over 15 years to interest rates and the macroeconomic environment rather than productivity.

Technology spending at global banks has grown close to 9% a year on average, and AI spending is growing nearly 25% a year, yet only 13% of banks and capital markets firms have scaled AI across the business, according to the webinar description. The panel estimated $1.5 trillion in enterprise debt across technology, data, process and talent, which HFS recommends tackling with a two-velocity approach that fixes foundations while capturing value. HFS proposes a fix it calls a Services-as-Software Operator, which could be an internal team, existing providers under one remit or a managed services partner, holding day-to-day responsibility for live AI performance, cost and governance. The enterprise keeps its business context, policy, decision rights and legal accountability. Rackspace describes its Outcomes-as-a-Service model as resting on secure infrastructure, data foundations and forward-deployed engineering for sectors where governance, sovereignty and uptime are non-negotiable, with a Build | Operate | Innovate delivery model, more than 25 years of operating enterprise technology and vendor-neutral, model-agnostic capabilities.

Rackspace reported third-quarter 2026 results after the market close on November 9, with revenue of $609.1 million, down 9.25% from the same period a year earlier, according to Quiver Quantitative. The next day it announced an initial multiyear agreement with Together AI to support enterprise AI inference. HFS states that it has no outside investors and that companies cannot pay to influence its research or ratings, and the report's definition does not require outsourcing since an internal team qualifies. HFS's banking panel recommended that banks own their enterprise AI harness layer instead of renting it. Of respondents, 61% prefer one accountable partner across AI models, platforms and infrastructure, 74% of production-stage firms whose AI has not delivered hold that preference, 73% would pay a premium over raw infrastructure for fully managed AI with governance accountability, and 63% see the operator role as meaningfully different from what they buy today.

The report attaches a condition to the premium: providers have to show clear operational responsibilities and measurable outcomes to earn it. The banking panel offered a tiered pricing model that moves beyond effort-based contracts and a balanced business case built on productivity, prediction, personalization and performance. HFS says enterprises should settle who answers for performance, cost and governance after go-live, and how each is measured, before adding another function to a working AI program. The articles do not say whether any enterprise has adopted the Services-as-Software Operator model. The articles do not give the full report title or the names of the banking practice leaders and senior advisors on the webinar panel.

stories.Headline: St. Paul student says Turnitin flag gave her a zero as district lacks AI policy
stories.Summary:
A St. Paul Public Schools student wrote in a MinnPost opinion piece published on November 16, 2026, that she received a zero on an English essay that Turnitin flagged as 32 percent AI-generated, dropping her grade to a D on the night before her last day of sophomore year. She said she had earned a 98 percent in the class before that and had not used AI for any part of the essay. When she offered the next morning to rewrite sections with pen and paper, her teacher said that was not necessary because she knew the student's writing style and believed the work was original. The teacher had previously raised concerns about Turnitin, an AI detection tool used by the district.

The piece says the district has no official school board AI policy, although Phil Wacker, the district's high school curriculum supervisor, acknowledged Turnitin's limitations in September 2025, particularly for students whose first language is not English, according to St. Paul Publishing. At that time nearly 30 percent of the district's students were English learners. The SPPS Board of Education recently announced a goal of adopting an AI policy by the end of the 2027-28 school year, with details still vague and the board saying the policy will include expectations for how the district prepares students and staff to use, question, evaluate and create with AI. Wacker said conversations about a policy are happening.

The student argues that administrators, not students, should fix the problem, and that she sees a lack of urgency. She writes that the time spent debating a policy means the conversation will take her class's entire high school career, and that some students use AI and have found ways to avoid detection. Turnitin assigns a score based on the percentage of suspected AI sentences, measuring burstiness, or spontaneity of word choice, and sentence length, and the company claims human writing tends to be inconsistent and idiosyncratic. The student notes that her flagged essay was about how high school writing structure strips individuality from students' work.

stories.Headline: Pierre schools begin shaping rules for AI use in classrooms
stories.Summary:
The Pierre School District has spent the past several months working to address the growing use of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with district officials meeting alongside a staff committee to develop procedures for AI use after a community survey was conducted earlier this year. Superintendent Donavan DeBoer said he entered the role knowing that discussions about AI would be necessary as the technology becomes increasingly common, not just in schools, and he noted that AI has been a frequent topic at education conferences and professional retreats because of how quickly the technology evolves. Drawing a comparison to the introduction of cellphones in schools, DeBoer said educators learned that simply allowing students unrestricted access often created challenges that continue today, and he said the district needs to put guardrails on AI sooner rather than later because having some sort of plan is better than having no plan at all.

District conversations began earlier this year with an AI-focused survey sent to staff, students and parents, and about 1,655 responses gave the district a starting point for committee discussions as members work toward establishing AI procedures for the 2027-28 school year. Eighty percent of students surveyed said they had used AI before, and nearly half of those students said they use it monthly or more often, while of the 832 student respondents, 309 said they use AI for homework help and 412 said they use it for research, with others reporting use for writing assistance and studying. Of the 209 staff members who responded, about half said they had used AI for tasks including lesson planning, and most respondents agreed AI can help teachers save time, though many also expressed interest in additional training, recommended tools and established expectations for student use. Across all respondent groups, students, staff and parents expressed awareness that AI tools can sometimes produce inaccurate information, and DeBoer said many students also voiced concerns about academic integrity similar to those expressed by adults in the community.

The district has since formed an AI committee that has met twice, and the group includes principals representing the elementary, middle and high school levels as well as Technology Director Bryan Linn, with DeBoer saying he and Linn are currently working to draft procedures and protocols for AI use. The committee plans to meet again in January to further develop those ideas before sharing them with building leadership teams for additional feedback, and DeBoer said he hopes to bring a proposal to the school board this spring and receive approval before the next school year. Currently, websites such as ChatGPT and Gemini are blocked on student devices because of privacy concerns, though DeBoer said the district may have opportunities to incorporate more secure AI tools into classrooms for activities such as project brainstorming or creating renderings in technical education courses. DeBoer said he does not intend this to be a hard and fast policy because the world is moving at warp speed and the district's AI expectations and protocols will change as things change, and he said the district is looking at a set of processes and procedures to guide staff on consistent expectations for students rather than a policy that would constantly need revision.

DeBoer said he expects AI use to be more common at the high school level than in elementary or middle school classrooms, particularly as students prepare for college, technical school and future careers where the technology is becoming increasingly prevalent, and he noted that AI-detection tools used during grading are not always accurate, prompting some teachers to return to pen-and-paper assignments to avoid concerns about misuse. While the district continues to develop expectations for classroom use, officials also hope to help teachers identify effective AI tools, provide additional training and continue evaluating the technology as it evolves, and results of the district's AI survey are available on the district website. AI policy is expected to remain a topic of discussion at Pierre School Board meetings, and the board meets at 5:30 p.m. on the second Monday of each month at the district administration building, with meetings open to the public.

stories.Headline: Former Commerce officials allege Howard Lutnick failed to act on sensitive computer chip smuggling
stories.Summary:
Former Commerce officials allege Howard Lutnick failed to act on evidence of sensitive computer chip smuggling during his tenure as secretary. These ex-employees describe his leadership as chaotic and marked by micromanaging. The accusations surfaced as scrutiny grew following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. China has denied these spying accusations, calling them a smear attempt.

The department stopped adding firms to the Entity List, which bans advanced chip sales to adversaries. No companies were added between October 9, 2025, and the present, the first such gap since 2008. In May 2025, Lutnick rolled back an interim final rule from January 2025 to avoid stifling innovation. A new rule now requires licenses for exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. This rule was directed by the National Security Council and the Department of Treasury.

Howard Lutnick and his deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, are responsible for the department's export control enforcement. Former staff claim Kessler micromanaged every minor decision and blocked enforcement against suspected smugglers. They allege the career workforce felt stymied and unable to perform their duties. The Commerce Department and the White House did not respond to requests for comment. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressed frustration that Lutnick failed to follow through on chip ban enforcement.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia are affected by the scandal involving suspected agent Alice Huang. Reports suggest $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips reached Chinese firms through her links since 2023. An OpenAI researcher found evidence that banned Nvidia chips trained top Chinese AI models. Epoch estimated between 290,000 and 1.6 million chips were smuggled into China in 2024 and 2025. These smuggled chips provided roughly a quarter of China's acquired computing power.

The Biden administration first issued AI chip export controls in 2022 and 2023. Lutnick began running the department in February 2025, shortly after firing veterans Matthew Borman and Eileen Albanese. This sparked an exodus of up to 50 skilled staff members over 18 months. Departed experts included specialists in AI, Russia, diversion, and chips. The department also pivoted to allow sales of Nvidia H20 and H200 chips to China.

Key roles in the Bureau of Industry and Security remain vacant, including the chief of staff. The principal deputy assistant secretary roles for export administration and export enforcement are also unfilled. It remains unclear if the department will fill these positions or change its enforcement approach. The articles leave open whether the decision to sell H20 chips was made by Trump. They do not state if further investigations into Alice Huang will occur.

He warned that people who failed to understand machine learning, deep learning, or artificial intelligence would become dinosaurs within three years. This prediction appeared accurate as the world approached 2027 because the technology reshaped the finance, tech, and industrial sectors. Business owners who still operate without these tools are now compared to creatures in Jurassic Park.

Investors can seek wealth by using an index fund like the Invesco QQQ Trust to access top companies. The fund carries an expense ratio of 0.18 percent, which costs an investor 18 dollars for every 10,000 dollars invested.

The author of the report believes that investing in artificial intelligence stocks represents the biggest wealth opportunity for this generation. He suggests that owning an exchange traded fund is easier than trying to pick individual winners in a complex market. The Magnificent Seven tech stocks now represent 33 percent of the total market capitalization of the S&P 500. He argues that ignoring the long term potential of this technology could lead to future regret for many investors.

The current infrastructure build out is massive while companies continue to find ways to make these capabilities profitable. stories.Headline: Geoff Woods urges CEOs to use AI themselves before grading employees on it
stories.Summary:
Geoff Woods, founder of AI Leadership and former chief growth officer at Jindal Steel & Power, wrote a Fortune commentary published November 15, 2026, at 7:30 AM ET. In it he described standing on stage at the annual Great Places to Work convention in Las Vegas, where all 500 CHROs in front of him raised their hands when asked if their executive teams had mandated AI use. He said he asks at every speaking engagement whether every executive is using AI to make themselves more valuable. He wrote that leaders are mandating AI and expecting productivity gains from their workforce without holding themselves to the same standard. He argued that delegating AI adoption to IT, a Chief AI Officer or an outside consultant is abdication rather than delegation.

Woods wrote that CEOs and executive teams need to learn to use AI and become AI-driven leaders before they can build AI-driven organizations. He said he is starting to see companies increasingly tying AI goals and skills directly to employee raises and promotions. He wrote that whether compensation should be tied to AI skill depends on the company, and that for organizations that typically tie performance to specific skills that will grow in value it makes sense. He said that for companies that do not, it is a break from precedent but does not mean it is the wrong move. He wrote that his concern is when a CEO who does not use AI is the one making the call, and that by using AI he does not mean writing better emails but truly leveraging it to think strategically.

Woods said he first saw AI in December 2022, when he was Chief Growth Officer at Jindal Steel and ChatGPT had been out for about two weeks. He said he told himself he was really busy and would revisit it later, then thought about delegating it to his huge IT department or hiring a consulting company. He recalled a quote from his college mentor about focusing on mastering skills so valuable they will serve you no matter where you go, and said he knew then that AI would be one of those skills. He committed to using AI once a day, every day, and quickly realized he was using it for things that did not really matter, like writing better emails. He said he never received a promotion for the quality of his emails and began asking what it would look like to major in the majors.

Woods said he started using AI to ask him questions as a thought partner rather than asking it questions like Google, which he called the game changer. A few months into his AI use he spoke with Naveen Jindal, Chairman of Jindal Steel, who asked to see an example, and Woods opened his AI tool using the CRIT framework he had developed, standing for Context, Role, Interview and Task. He attached the annual strategic plan into a secure instance of ChatGPT, set the role as an aggressive, growth-minded board member with deep expertise in the steel industry vertically integrated from distribution to mining, and had it interview him one question at a time up to five questions. He said the AI asked sharp questions only someone who knew the industry would ask, pulled out context that was in their heads and laid out a real analysis of where the plan could break. He said Naveen's mind was blown, that Naveen said "This is incredible," and that he suggested driving it through the whole company with Naveen leading it as Chairman.

Woods said he knew almost nothing about AI but knew the power of asking the right questions, which led to a partnership with Google where he learned a lot about the tech. He said the more he learned about the tech, the less he realized how much the tech mattered, and that you can have the greatest technology in the world but will never unlock the value without winning the hearts and minds of your people. He said it became clear that AI adoption was about leadership, and that over his time at Jindal the market cap grew from $750 million to $12 billion over a four year period. He said this was done with the right strategic thinking, which AI directly supported throughout the company, and that it is not about AI but about the right strategic thinking. He said he resigned from Jindal Steel, wrote a book about what he learned and turned it into a company.

Woods said a question he gets asked often is what first piece of their own work a CEO should test with AI if they wanted to start this week. He advised starting by asking what the biggest problem facing the company is, the one that would unlock huge growth if solved, which he said focuses you on the 20% of work that drives 80% of your results. He advised writing a prompt using CRIT, describing context in detail, naming the kind of expert you wish could advise you, having AI interview you one question at a time and giving it a task such as giving the top three high-impact, non-obvious strategies. He advised not taking the AI response at face value, telling AI what you like, do not like and would change, and iterating until you are confident enough to act. He wrote that most companies measure AI adoption through usage metrics such as 80% of the workforce using AI every week, which he said is a good place to start but does not tell you whether people are using AI for high-value work.

stories.Headline: Mars and Genpact open a 60,000 sq ft Hyderabad centre to run AI-assisted operations for Mars
stories.Summary:
Mars, Incorporated and Genpact inaugurated a Global Capability Centre in Hyderabad, according to announcements published in mid November 2026, with the facility spread across approximately 60,000 square feet and initially housing more than 400 Genpact colleagues. The centre will support Mars' operations across its global markets and will focus on digital innovation and AI-assisted business processes, with plans to scale to 1,000 Mars associates over time, although the announcements do not specify a timeline for reaching that workforce size. The launch builds on a relationship between the two companies that was established in 2018, and the companies plan to use Genpact's Agentic Operations model to redesign processes in order to improve operational speed, consistency and visibility. The Hyderabad centre will develop AI-assisted systems within a governance framework tailored to Mars' requirements, and human expertise and oversight will remain central to these operations, according to the announcement. The centre adds to Mars' presence in India, where the company has invested in seven local factories since 1995 and currently employs more than 2,400 associates across its Snacking, Food and Nutrition, and Pet Nutrition businesses, and its India operations also include a Royal Canin packaging centre.

Mars recently invested $55 million, or roughly ₹516 crore, to expand its Hyderabad Pet Nutrition factory, a move the company said would support domestic demand and exports, and it allocated an additional $12 million, or roughly ₹113 crore, for a Royal Canin distribution and packaging centre, which it said would strengthen localisation and supply resilience. The new GCC forms part of Mars' network of strategic hubs supporting business functions across its global markets. Tarun Chopra, Unit Leader for Consumer Goods at Genpact, said the centre would put the company's approach to work through Agentic-enabled Operations, designing AI-assisted systems that operate within a governance framework tailored to Mars and are meant to deliver measurable business outcomes, and he added that the approach would combine agentic AI capabilities with human expertise. Claus Aagaard, Chief Financial Officer of Mars, said India had remained an important market in the company's growth journey and noted that the Hyderabad centre would strengthen collaboration and advance digital capabilities.

D Sridhar Babu, Telangana's Minister for Information Technology, Electronics and Communications, Industries and Commerce, and Legislative Affairs, attended the inauguration and highlighted Hyderabad's technology ecosystem, skilled workforce and business environment, saying the city had established itself as a destination for global capability centres and that the new facility would connect Mars' established business in India with required technology capabilities and talent. Emilia B Smith, Acting Public Affairs Officer at the US Consulate General in Hyderabad, also attended the launch and highlighted the longstanding commercial relationship between the US and India. For Genpact, the partnership builds on nearly a decade of operational experience with Mars, and the companies intend to combine this process knowledge with agentic AI capabilities to support business functions. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the stated plans to scale the centre's workforce and the absence of a timeline for reaching 1,000 Mars associates.

The legal technology hub known as LexLab at UC Law San Francisco announced a new educational program on November 13, 2026. This initiative is called the Law and AI Certificate Lab, which is designed as a three-day course for building legal tools. The intensive program will take place from December 1 to December 3 for a small group of participants. It provides a condensed version of the AI curriculum that the law school typically offers its students over a full semester.

This training allows professionals to build and evaluate their own software solutions within a short timeframe.

Adjunct professor Damien Charlotin, who created the AI Hallucination Cases database, is directing the program alongside adjunct professor Erin Fraser. Fraser also serves as an associate at the firm McDermott Will & Schulte while helping to lead this lab. These directors intend for the course to support professionals in navigating the complexities of modern legal technology. They aim to bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and the practical application of AI in legal settings.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Massachusetts lawmakers file bills to ban algorithmic rent pricing statewide
stories.Summary:
Massachusetts state Rep. Lindsay Sabadosa, a Democrat from the 1st Hampshire district, and state Sen. Cindy Friedman, a Democrat from the 4th Middlesex district, filed bills in the House and Senate to outlaw algorithmic rent pricing in the state. The Joint Committee on Housing reported the bills out favorably in March, and the proposals now sit before the Committee on Ways and Means. The bills respond to rent-pricing software, often called revenue management software, that many of Massachusetts’ largest landlords use at their properties. The software draws on nonpublic leasing data from nearby properties to recommend how high rents can go. Landlords using such programs have been accused of unfair pricing, intentionally leaving units vacant and colluding with others to reduce competition.

The bills would ban rent-pricing algorithms in Massachusetts, and the session ends Jan. 5. The biggest industry player is Texas-based RealPage, which claims on its website that its customers outperform competitors who do not use the service by up to 7%. RealPage’s algorithm analyzes nonpublic data from landlords using its software, including listed rent, the actual price tenants agree to after discounts and lease length, for new leases and renewals. The software also accesses data on a unit’s future demand and occupancy, including inquiries and applications from prospective tenants. A 2023 report by the Metropolitan Area Planning Council found that 21% of Greater Boston properties sold between 2004 and 2018 were purchased by an investor or speculator, and a 2025 study by the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy found that 8.9% of residential parcels nationwide are owned by a corporation.

Sabadosa compared traditional rent-setting to selling a used car, where the seller checks prices for the same or similar models and sets an asking price accordingly. She said the algorithm is a much more sophisticated way of looking at all the rents than trying to understand the maximum the market will bear in a given community. She said that for someone just trying to make money it is surely a great idea, but for thriving communities where people can afford to live it is a terrible idea, because it is constant upward pressure that pushes everybody out. Friedman said the problem is that it is distorting the market and called it kind of immoral, saying people are taking rental places where people can live and need to live off the market. Friedman said it becomes much more insidious much faster than a landlord going through Zillow or Redfin.

Demetrios Salpoglou, CEO of the real estate platform Boston Pads, said frequent price fluctuations he sometimes sees on the website cause unnecessary issues for renters and landlords. He said he has seen out-of-state landlords rely too heavily on algorithms without understanding neighborhood nuances, and has heard from confused consumers or their agents about a unit’s price changing twice daily. He said it is like over-engineering a Hyundai and calling it a Porsche, and that he has never really had a landlord say the rental software is incredible. Salpoglou said most small- and mid-sized or independent property owners he works with use real-time pricing data on his platform and may lower rent near the lease date but otherwise rarely change prices unexpectedly. He theorized corporate landlords may use the software to satisfy obligations to owners and investors, which he called, in the nicest way he could say it, a CYA.

In 2024 the U.S. Department of Justice and several states, including Massachusetts, sued RealPage and some of the largest landlords in the country, alleging the practice illegally decreases competition. In November of last year RealPage and the DOJ reached a settlement requiring the company to stop using non-public competitor data in price recommendations, not to use active lease data to train its models and to remove or redesign features that limit price decreases. RealPage did not admit wrongdoing and said in court documents that it continues to believe the use of non-public data led to more efficient and procompetitive pricing and reduced vacancies. Massachusetts and other states continued their case, and two landlord defendants, Greystar Management Services and LivCor, have settled, while the case against RealPage, Camden Property Trust, Pinnacle Property Management Services and Willow Bridge Property Company is ongoing. Attorney General Andrea Campbell said in January 2025, when the state joined the case, that her office will seek to hold accountable those who betray renters’ trust and undermine a fair and competitive housing market.

Neither Sabadosa nor Friedman was optimistic the state legislation would pass this session, and Friedman said she thinks the proposal could make it into larger housing-related legislation next session. New York was the first state to ban the technology, with the prohibition taking effect in December 2025, and California and New Jersey have since followed suit. RealPage sued New York seeking to overturn the law, arguing it violated the company’s First Amendment rights to free speech and dissemination of information, and in late September a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction blocking the law while the case plays out. New York Attorney General Letitia James has appealed the decision. Sabadosa said one advantage of Beacon Hill being a little slow-moving is seeing the laws pass in other states and the immediate legal challenges, and that they are looking at what the courts identified as issues and redrafting to be responsive.

stories.Headline: IBM and MeitY Startup Hub sign MoU to support indigenous deeptech startups
stories.Summary:
IBM and the MeitY Startup Hub said on Tuesday that they had signed a Memorandum of Understanding to support the indigenous deeptech startup ecosystem, according to a report published on October 13, 2026. The agreement gives startups access to IBM's technology expertise, skilling programmes and development initiatives. The collaboration combines MeitY Startup Hub's nationwide innovation network with IBM's enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and quantum computing expertise. It is meant to help high-potential startups build, validate and scale technologies for India and global markets. It also complements IBM Ventures' ongoing engagements in India by expanding pathways for enterprise technology startups to connect with customers, investors and industry experts.

As part of the collaboration, startups will get access to IBM's portfolio of enterprise technologies and innovation platforms to solve business use cases. This includes technical guidance and enablement on technologies such as IBM watsonx, an enterprise-ready AI and data platform, IBM Bob, an AI coding agent for enterprises, and IBM Sovereign Core, an AI-ready software stack for digital sovereignty. Startups will also receive technical orientation on IBM's hybrid cloud and quantum computing, along with security and automation solutions. The collaboration will focus on enterprise proof of concepts, sovereign AI innovation, open-source ecosystem development, founder mentorship, technical skilling, and opportunities for startups to showcase their solutions to enterprises and investors. A key priority will be identifying and nurturing promising innovators from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, broadening access to India's growing deep tech ecosystem.

Panneerselvam Madanagopal, the CEO of MSH, said the collaboration with IBM aims to strengthen indigenous deep tech capabilities, foster technology-led entrepreneurship and create greater opportunity for innovators to build solutions that contribute to a Viksit Bharat. Sandip Patel, the Managing Director of IBM India and South Asia, said the collaboration reflects a shared commitment to fostering innovation and strengthening the country's deep-tech startup ecosystem. Patel said these startups are playing a pivotal role in shaping the future of technology-led growth for India and the world. He said that together with MeitY Startup Hub, the aim is to help founders innovate faster, scale responsibly and build solutions that address both national and global challenges. Patel added that the goal is turning promising innovation into real-world impact.

stories.Headline: US Supreme Court agrees to hear Robinhood appeal over IPO shareholder lawsuit
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court agreed on Nov. 13 to hear Robinhood's appeal of a ruling that revived a shareholder class action over its July 2021 initial public offering. The court granted Robinhood's petition, No. 25-944, but limited it to the Section 11(a) omissions question and left out Robinhood's separate Item 303 question. The case, Robinhood Markets v. Sodha, will decide how much interim financial information a company must put in an IPO prospectus before its quarterly results come out. Investors sued in late 2021, saying the registration statement left out material information about a shift in Robinhood's revenue mix and declines in key performance indicators.

The investors also cited falling cryptocurrency trading volume after a first quarter boosted by the GameStop meme-stock surge. Robinhood went public on July 30, 2021, a month after its second quarter closed, and the investors say the registration statement left out second-quarter 2021 data. The court limited its review to whether an issuer can be liable under the misleading-omissions prong of Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 for failing to disclose material interim financial information. The question asks whether such liability applies without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading. The defendants include Robinhood and its IPO underwriters, among them Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan Securities.

A federal judge in San Francisco dismissed the suit, and in an Aug. 29, 2025 decision the Ninth Circuit revived it. A Robinhood spokesperson told CNBC the company was pleased the Supreme Court had agreed to hear its case and looked forward to presenting its argument. The Ninth Circuit panel said the registration statement contained only limited information about second-quarter performance, and the stock fell after Robinhood reported those results. The Ninth Circuit held that an issuer can be liable for omitting material interim data without a separate finding that the omission made a specific statement misleading. Robinhood's petition argued the Ninth Circuit's rule is broader than the statute's text and conflicts with other circuits, including the First Circuit's extreme departure test for interim results.

The court asked the Solicitor General for the government's views in June. The government's brief, filed Oct. 7, recommended granting review limited to a reworded version of Robinhood's first question and said the second question, on Regulation S-K Item 303, did not warrant review. The investors argued that leaving out Item 303 means their Section 11(a) claim will go forward in the district court however the first question is resolved. Business groups including the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association filed briefs backing Robinhood's petition. Law firm Alston & Bird warned the Ninth Circuit's rule could invite forum shopping into the Ninth Circuit.

The investors do not claim any historical figure in the filing was wrong, and their case rests on omissions alone. Section 11 imposes near-strict liability on issuers and underwriters for flaws in a registration statement, so the standard for omissions sets how much intra-quarter data companies feel obliged to disclose before pricing a deal. The ruling will land as the largest IPOs in years come to market, including Anthropic's. The court has not yet scheduled argument.

The case is one of the most closely-watched intellectual property disputes of the generative AI era, and its outcome will shape how UK copyright law applies to AI models trained overseas. The High Court handed down its first instance judgment in November 2025, delivering a mixed outcome that largely favoured Stability AI. Getty succeeded on a small part of its trade mark claim, but its copyright claim ultimately failed, and because Stable Diffusion was trained outside the UK, Getty had dropped its primary copyright claims during the trial. Getty's remaining copyright case was one of secondary infringement, namely that Stable Diffusion was an infringing copy imported into and distributed in the UK.

The High Court accepted that an AI model can be an article even though it is intangible, but held that an infringing copy must be a copy. Because Stable Diffusion's model weights had never stored Getty's images, the model could not be an infringing copy. The key question in the appeal is whether an AI model can be an infringing copy for secondary copyright infringement if the model itself has never contained a copy of those works. The relevant provision of the Copyright, Designs, and Patents Act 1988 is section 27(3), and Getty's position is that making a model includes training it, in turn involving the copying of images.

Getty argues the law does not require the finished model to itself contain a copy of the works it was trained on. The British Recorded Music Industry Limited has been given permission to intervene in support of Getty and warns the High Court's approach could allow AI developers to train models offshore and bring them back into the UK. BPI cites two recent German cases where the Munich Court found that AI models did contain copyright works on which they had been trained, having memorised them. Stability AI argues that whether something is a copy depends on what is actually produced, not on how it was developed.

stories.Headline: Hong Kong lawmakers urge government to tighten AI laws to combat scams and pornography
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers in Hong Kong called for the government to tighten artificial intelligence regulations after a new global index was released on November 14, 2026. The city ranked 50th out of 70 economies for AI governance according to a report from the Switzerland-based International Institute for Management Development. This first-ever World Digital and AI Ranking report placed the region 11th overall and fourth in Asia, trailing behind Singapore and the Chinese mainland. The United States took the top spot on the list for overall competitiveness in the digital and AI sectors.

The current situation requires the government to move beyond general guidelines to create more specific and enforceable laws. Lawmaker Johnny Ng argued that the city must do more to protect young people from scams and pornography. Fellow lawmaker Simon Lee suggested that the city should roll out new AI legislation in several distinct phases. The government is now tasked with balancing technological growth with the need for strict oversight of emerging tools. stories.Headline: Justice Edward Muriithi gives Kenya six months to create a national AI policy and legal framework

This legal action followed a challenge brought by activists John Wangai, Peter Agoro, and Antony Manyara who highlighted the lack of a comprehensive framework. These individuals argued that the absence of governing rules for AI systems across various public offices posed a risk to the citizenry. The court intervened to ensure that the state addresses these regulatory gaps to protect the public.

Justice Edward Muriithi granted the government a period of six months to finish creating a national policy and a legal framework for AI. While the court declined to force Parliament to pass specific legislation within 90 days, it emphasized the necessity of these guidelines. This new requirement aims to prevent violations of fundamental rights, including access to food, clean water, and social security. The framework must also cover essential services such as healthcare, education, sanitation, and adequate housing for all Kenyans.

Justice Edward Muriithi stated that the state carries a constitutional obligation to implement legislative and policy measures for the protection of its people. He explained that these actions are necessary to safeguard the basic rights of citizens from potential harms caused by unregulated technology. The judge emphasized that the government must take proactive steps to ensure that AI deployment does not undermine human dignity. By setting this deadline, the court holds the state accountable for the ethical integration of technology into public administration.

stories.Headline: Scott Loughlin says AI agents on personal devices test whether BYOD programs can survive
stories.Summary:
Employees who use personal devices for work are increasingly running artificial intelligence agents that can read work email, open files and act across applications without a person at the keyboard, and Scott Loughlin, a partner at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader in Washington, DC, wrote in a Bloomberg Law column published on November 16, 2026, that this raises the question of whether bring-your-own-device programs can survive agents in their current form. In a Gartner survey conducted in early 2026, 88% of employees with an enterprise AI tool also used personal AI tools for work, and those tools will likely increasingly include AI agents. Loughlin wrote that the core controls of a BYOD program, a company-managed container for work apps, monitoring of corporate systems and the ability to remotely wipe work data, were designed for apps that people operate and may not work as well for devices running AI agents. Because an agent works inside the employee's logged-in session, company records may show the employee doing what the agent did, and the agent's history and memory sit in the provider's cloud under the employee's account, beyond the reach of a remote wipe. Loughlin wrote that none of this requires hacking, but the exposure is real and no new AI statute is needed to create it, with personal data given to an unapproved agent raising issues under the GDPR and US state privacy laws, protected health information entered into a personal agent possibly being a HIPAA breach, and routine flows of source code or pricing undercutting trade-secret protection.

He wrote that EU law restricts the scope of employee monitoring and may require works-council consultation, and that US laws can limit employers' access to employees' personal accounts. He described three models likely to be applied role by role: access-only BYOD, in which personal devices reach corporate data only through a managed browser, app or virtual workspace; a sanctioned agent, in which an enterprise agent lets the organization control the agent even when it does not control the device; and company-owned devices for people in the most sensitive roles. He noted that the May 2026 guidance on agentic AI from CISA, the NSA and other governments recommends giving agents their own short-lived credentials and requiring human approval for high-impact actions. Loughlin recommended that organizations assign ownership at the leadership level, naming an accountable executive, adding personal and unsanctioned agents to the enterprise risk register and reporting on them to the board committee that oversees cybersecurity risk. He also recommended revisiting the BYOD agreement to address which agents may touch company data, employee disclosure duties, a narrow commitment to preserve and produce work-related agent data, and offboarding certification that connectors are revoked and work-related memories deleted, covering phones and tablets and calibrated to local employment and privacy law.

He advised updating legal-hold and e-discovery playbooks to add agent prompts, outputs, logs and memory to custodian questionnaires and hold notices, mapping roles and controlling the connection points where the law allows, updating incident response with scenarios for a hijacked or misused personal agent, and aligning related policies so they cross-reference each other. Loughlin wrote that organizations that plan ahead will be better positioned to demonstrate reasonable governance to regulators, courts and customers, and that agent risks are developing quickly enough that organizations are changing their BYOD programs in the short term before settling on a longer-term model. He wrote that it is a good idea to make the sanctioned path easier than the personal one and to focus controls on the connection points the organization owns. He wrote that BYOD rests on the premise that a company can manage the risk of devices it does not own, that agents using employees' credentials on those devices test that premise, and that BYOD is unlikely to disappear but programs are likely to change.

stories.Headline: Professor Hoang Van Kiem proposes a three-tiered model to develop talent in gifted schools in the AI era
stories.Summary:
Professor Hoang Van Kiem, former Chairman of the State Council for Professor Titles in Information Technology, wrote in Thanh Nien Newspaper that talent development in specialized and gifted schools needs to change in the age of AI. The article was published on 15/11/2026, in commemoration of the 30th anniversary of the High School for the Gifted, Vietnam National University, Ho Chi Minh City. For decades, specialized schools and gifted schools have contributed to training many scientists, mathematicians, engineers, artists, and others who have made significant contributions to society. The article appeared amid ongoing debates surrounding admissions and training in specialized schools. The piece was presented by Thanh Nien Newspaper and carried by Vietnam.vn.

The article says talent is the result of the interaction of individual potential and biological characteristics, family and social environment, quality of education and teachers, opportunities to access knowledge and technology, training, experience, and creativity, and motivation, passion, and perseverance. It proposes a three-tiered talent development model: Tier 1 foundational competencies including mathematics, language, science, technology, arts, physical education, emotional intelligence, and humanities. Tier 2 is development of specialized talents in mathematics, computer science, natural sciences, languages, arts, social sciences, and emerging fields. Tier 3 is interdisciplinary creativity with scientific research, technological innovation, AI projects, digital art, entrepreneurship, and practical problem-solving. It proposes a model of Gifted High School, Youth Research Center, Creative Space, and Open Academic Community, with five components.

The article says teachers need to discover hidden potential that grades don't reflect, ignite passion and a desire for exploration, and guide students to think independently without relying on AI. It says they should impart research experience and scientific standards and educate students on character, ethics, responsibility, and compassion. It says the philosophy should shift from selecting the elite to unleashing talent, from selecting gifted students, intensive training, student competitions, and achievement to discovering potential, unleashing abilities, research and innovation, talent development, and contribution to society. It says competitions and Olympiads still play an important role in identifying and nurturing exceptionally talented students but should not be the sole objective of gifted education. It says achievement is a milestone, not the ultimate goal of gifted education.

The article says a student who doesn't win an Olympic medal can still become an outstanding scientist, a technological innovator, a talented artist, or an innovative entrepreneur. It says a student who wins numerous awards also needs to continue developing independent thinking, creativity, and adaptability to new problems. It says a student who excels in mathematics shouldn't just study math but needs exposure to computer science, physics, music, art, data science, and practical applications. It says a student who excels in literature shouldn't be judged solely on writing ability but needs philosophical thinking, social observation skills, artistic creativity, and communication skills. It says specialized schools will have to compile statistics on what jobs their graduates are doing after graduation.

The article says the Imperial Academy, established in 1076, is a symbol of Vietnam's tradition of training talent for the nation. It says the modern system of specialized high schools in Vietnam mainly emerged in the 1960s, and specialized mathematics education began in 1965 with a specialized mathematics class at Hanoi University, the predecessor of the specialized school model at the University of Science, Vietnam National University, Hanoi. It says Hanoi ,  Amsterdam High School for the Gifted commenced its first academic year on September 5, 1985, formed by consolidating the specialized classes of several high schools in Hanoi. It says that on July 14, 1993, Deputy Minister of Education and Training Tran Chi Dao signed a decision to establish the specialized high school system for mathematics and computer science at the University of Ho Chi Minh City. It says that on July 4, 1996, Minister of Education and Training Tran Hong Quan signed Decision No. 2693/GD-ĐT establishing the High School for the Gifted, Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City.

The article says future gifted high schools should develop according to the model of Gifted High School, Youth Research Center, Creative Space, and Open Academic Community. It says connecting with universities and research institutes is a key advantage that should be strongly promoted at the High School for the Gifted under Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City, where students can receive guidance from university lecturers, scientists, and business experts and participate in seminars, research projects, and academic activities appropriate to their age. It says student laboratories should provide opportunities for research projects on AI, robotics, biology, materials, environment, energy, music, and digital art. It says the article also covers proposals for admission to specialized schools based on subject groups and subject combinations and proposed changes to the entrance exam for specialized 10th-grade classes. It leaves open what students, parents, and teachers say about those proposed changes.
