stories.Headline: Harvard researchers find 403 US hyperscale data centers used up to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity in a year
stories.Summary:
A study published Monday in Nature Sustainability found that 403 hyperscale data centers across the United States together used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity between May 2024 and April 2025, with the upper estimate equal to the annual electricity use of states such as Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee and the lower estimate close to what Wisconsin or Minnesota consumes in a year. The researchers, led by Harvard data scientist Gianluca Guidi with Francesca Dominici as senior author, built their list of facilities from satellite imagery and estimated each one's annual consumption under a range of operating scenarios, then used U.S. Environmental Protection Agency data to calculate emissions. The facilities produced a combined estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, roughly the annual emissions of Denmark, and more than half of their electricity came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. Half of all the electricity use was concentrated in just four states: Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa, with 142 facilities in Virginia accounting for about 21.4 terawatt-hours and 26 in Iowa accounting for about 7.2 terawatt-hours.

Dominici said that when the team began the research, despite many public and scientific statements about the environmental impact of data centers, there was basically very little or no peer-reviewed data. Guidi said that for the same amount of electricity consumed, the regional electricity mix associated with data centers in Wyoming produces approximately seven times more carbon dioxide than in Oregon, so these environmental impacts are not necessarily inevitable and geography matters. He also said people tend to imagine AI as something almost immaterial, but the infrastructure power is profoundly physical, and behind every algorithm there are enormous buildings, power plants, water resources, and ultimately communities that live with the consequences. The researchers said they hope to continue quantifying the environmental impacts of hyperscale data centers to better understand their effect on air pollution, water, and health, adding that as AI continues to scale, its infrastructure growth must be done sustainably.

The number of data centers worldwide doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100 between 2019 and 2024, with more than half located in the United States, and the research firm Synergy estimates that total U.S. data center capacity will double in the next three years, largely driven by hyperscale growth. In this November's midterm elections, voters in 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country voted to limit or prevent data center development, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. According to a BloombergNEF report, without clean energy alternatives, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than most countries by 2035. The study's figures are likely even higher than shown, because the team did not have enough data to assess every hyperscale data center in the U.S. at the time and more data centers have emerged since the study concluded in April 2025.

stories.Headline: Superintendent Ben Mainka wants AI to enhance student thinking with guardrails in place
stories.Summary:
Ben Mainka, the superintendent of the Novi school district in Michigan, spoke with The Metro about how artificial intelligence should affect learning and thinking, especially for young people, in a conversation broadcast in November 2026. He said he wants AI to enhance student thinking and to assist teachers with administrative tasks, but only so long as guardrails are in place. The same program also featured Daniel Cook, an English professor at Saginaw Valley State University, who in a recent debate argued that college students should have a slower, less digital learning experience. The Metro described the segment as a conversation with Robyn Vincent, and it directed listeners to the full discussion through the media player on the page.

The articles give no further numbers, dates or names beyond those already mentioned, and they do not set out any specific policy, rule or change that follows from the professor's position. What the professor's argument requires is only described in general terms, as a slower and less digital learning experience for college students, without any detail on how that would work in practice. The superintendent's position is likewise general, favoring AI that enhances student thinking and helps teachers with administrative work while guardrails are in place. The articles do not say what those guardrails would be, who would set them, or when any of this might happen.

Responsibility for the discussion rests with the two educators who made the arguments, Mainka for the school district and Cook for the university, and the articles attribute the views to them directly. Mainka is quoted as wanting AI to enhance student thinking and to assist teachers with administrative tasks so long as guardrails are in place, and Cook is described as arguing in a recent debate that college students should have a slower, less digital learning experience. The articles do not record any further remarks from either of them beyond those positions. No other person is named as responsible for any decision or proposal in the coverage.

The context the articles provide is limited to the setting of the discussion, which was a segment on The Metro, a program on WDET 101.9 FM that airs weekdays from 10 a.m. to noon ET and is available on demand. The program framed the conversation around how AI powers smartphones, appears across social media and answers Google searches, and asked how the technology should affect learning and thinking, especially for young people. The articles do not say what happens next, whether any policy will follow, or when the debate or any related decision will continue. The piece was produced by Sam Corey, a producer for 101.9 WDET.

stories.Headline: Young faith voters urge Congress to pause AI data center construction
stories.Summary:
Young people of faith from around the nation, including Texas, met with members of Congress in Washington, D.C., on November 16, 2026, after attending the Ignatian Family Teach-In for Justice 2026 conference. At the conference the students discussed immigration, climate change and artificial intelligence. Robbie McCoy, an undergraduate student at the University of the Incarnate Word, said the meetings with lawmakers centered on a proposed federal moratorium on artificial intelligence. McCoy said the rapid spread of AI data centers across many states should be temporarily paused while future developments and their potential environmental harm are reassessed.

Texas is one of the nation's leading states for data center development, with 123 data center campuses and 36 more under construction. Residents across the state have criticized lawmakers for allowing so many data centers to open in both rural and metropolitan areas. Outgoing Governor Greg Abbott issued a moratorium on rural data centers earlier this year. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said all construction should be halted until the state puts more protections and guidelines in place.

McCoy said that as more facilities have opened, residents are experiencing negative effects, from job losses to quality-of-life issues. He said many of the facilities sit right next to residential communities and schools, and that constituents are rightly asking how the centers will affect their children and their lives. If passed, the legislation would immediately prohibit construction or expansion of qualifying AI data centers until Congress passes additional laws establishing protections for workers, consumers, communities and the environment. It would also restrict the export of computer chips and other technology used to operate AI systems to countries that do not have comparable AI regulations.

stories.Headline: US Commerce Department restricts AI chip sales to stop Chinese companies from using foreign data centers
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Department restricted the sale of top American AI chips on Monday morning, November 16, 2026, to stop export evasion. This move targeted loopholes that allowed companies in China and other nations to access advanced technology through foreign data centers. The Trump administration directed the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council to write this new interim final rule. It aims to prevent Chinese businesses from using high-end hardware remotely to bypass existing American export restrictions. The regulation officially rescinds the AI Diffusion Rule, which was issued during the final days of the Biden administration.

Data center customers in Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand must now obtain a special license to buy chips from Nvidia or AMD. Licenses are also required for overseas customers providing significant computing power to companies based in Russia, Cuba, China, or other banned nations. These rules address billions of dollars in high-end chip purchases by businesses in Southeast Asia that might be smuggled into China. The policy shift follows a year where the Commerce Department had held off on adding any new restrictions to its Entity List. This action closes loopholes that have existed for a year and a half regarding the remote access of computing hubs.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced questions for months about why the department had not updated the Entity List for over a year. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized the Commerce Department last week for its reticence to close these specific export control loopholes. Bessent stated on Friday that only the Commerce Department has the pen to issue these new chip export regulations. The Bureau of Industry and Security issued the rule to stop Chinese companies from accessing chips on foreign territory. The administration framed the announcement as a necessary step to protect national security from growing Chinese access to computing power.

Ryan Fedasiuk of the Foundation for American Innovation called the measure a long overdue step to address remote access in Southeast Asia. Chris McGuire, a former Biden administration adviser, described the update as a major step forward and a good faith effort. Chinese AI companies are affected because they have been banned from buying these advanced chips directly since the year 2022. The rule follows reports that Megaspeed planned to rent computing power to ByteDance and Alibaba using chips from American companies. This pressure increased after a scandal involving Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang and former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang came to light.

The Biden administration and Gina Raimondo first clamped down on AI exports in 2022 to prevent China from acquiring advanced hardware. Experts believe Chinese firms shifted their consumption to data centers in nearby countries to circumvent these original American trade restrictions. Meanwhile, U.S. midterm elections in 2026 showed a bipartisan backlash against AI data centers due to pollution and electricity demand. Voters in states like New York, Ohio, and California backed restrictions on AI expansion or rejected various pro buildout measures. In one Ohio community, nearly 80 percent of voters banned a proposed two billion dollar data center project by Amazon.

The Trump administration will now enforce these new licensing requirements to stop the remote use of American chips by banned nations. Future efforts in Illinois may include renewed data center regulations early next year to prioritize those investing in clean energy. Massachusetts already introduced an executive order in fall 2026 requiring data centers to bring their own clean power sources. The articles leave open how the Responsible Data Center Development Collaborative will coordinate a common framework for responsible industry development. It remains unclear how many overseas data centers will successfully obtain the new licenses required by the Commerce Department.

stories.Headline: OpenSSF CTO Robinson explains Scorecard, SLSA and AI security limits
stories.Summary:
Christopher Robinson, the chief technology officer of the Open Source Security Foundation and chief security architect of the Linux Foundation, spoke on 16 November 2026 about software supply chain security at a time of rising incidents. He explained how tools such as Scorecard, the Security Baseline framework and Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts, known as SLSA, help harden software and secure infrastructure. The discussion also covered global cybersecurity regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act and the role of AI in software engineering. OpenSSF provides guidance, best practices, tooling and training to upstream open-source developers and maintainers.

Scorecard evaluates a project's security posture and signals to consumers whether it follows security best practices, while the Security Baseline, an evolution of Scorecard, lists 41 recommended security controls and practices. The baseline curates actions from regulations such as the EU CRA and frameworks such as the NIST Secure Software Development Framework, and Robinson noted that non-profit open-source maintainers are generally exempt from the CRA while commercial consumers must comply. SLSA addresses provenance, pedigree and integrity by securing development infrastructure, and it defines progressive maturity levels for hardening IDEs, developer workstations, source repositories, CI/CD pipelines and distribution systems. OpenSSF is also deploying an Open Source Software Cyber Reasoning System, a modular harness where developers plug in AI models and apply specific security skills and domain context.

Robinson cautioned that AI makes it easy to bypass foundational security controls when guardrails are not explicitly built in, and he described AI as a helpful assistant that accelerates workflows rather than a replacement for human engineering judgment. He said countries including the UK, India, Japan and Australia are watching the EU CRA's rollout, and he expects other regions to introduce CRA-aligned legislation while hoping for harmonized standards that avoid fragmented compliance burdens. He added that open-source software gives organizations the most reliable foundation for maintaining autonomy and avoiding vendor lock-in. He concluded that open-source projects need clear, explicit contribution guidelines that define their stance on AI tools.

stories.Headline: UK Supreme Court directs UK to adopt Duns principles A to F for assessing patentability
stories.Summary:
The UPC Court of Appeal endorsed the logic of the EPO’s COMVIK and G 1/19 decisions in Abbott v Sinocare, holding that a feature should not be excluded from inventive-step assessment merely because it is non-technical in isolation. The UK Supreme Court held in Emotional Perception AI Ltd v Comptroller-General of Patents [2026] UKSC 3 that the previous Aerotel framework should no longer be followed. The Supreme Court instead directed the UK to adopt principles A to F set out in Duns, drawing on COMVIK and endorsed in G 1/19. The UKIPO subsequently published guidance on how the new approach should be applied during search and examination. The article was first published in Kluwer Patent Blog in November 2026.

Europe has long grappled with exclusions from patentability based on Article 52(2) EPC, including presentations of information, programs for computers, mental acts and methods of doing business. Under the UK’s “any hardware” test, a claim qualifies as an invention if it is directed to, or uses, technical means, and for a computer-implemented invention a reference to a computer, computer-readable storage medium or other hardware will ordinarily be sufficient. This assessment is made without reference to the prior art, and the EPO and UK now have clear guidance on this first hurdle, while the UPC has not yet been required to address it expressly. At the intermediate step, the decision-maker identifies which features contribute to the technical character of the invention as a whole, and features that do not make that contribution cannot support inventive step. The UPC and UK do not generally apply the EPO’s problem, solution approach to inventive step.

Eden Winlow, an associate at Bristows, wrote the article, which was first published in Kluwer Patent Blog in November 2026. The article states that the UPC Court of Appeal expressly endorsed the logic of COMVIK and G 1/19 in Abbott v Sinocare. The article states that the UK Supreme Court held that the Aerotel framework should no longer be followed. The article states that the UKIPO subsequently published guidance on how the new approach should be applied during search and examination. The article states that the UPC has not yet been required to address the first hurdle expressly.

In October 2026, the hearing officer refused the Emotional Perception application on remittal, characterising the technical character of the invention as “Computer hardware running a program (the ANN) that selects and outputs a file” and concluding that outputting a “semantically better” file was not a technical result. In FLIR Belgium BV, the hearing officer disagreed with the examiner in relation to several features, finding that features concerning the operation and display of the virtual gauge contributed to technical character when considered in the context of the invention as a whole. The hearing officer did not, however, accept every display-related feature, and the claimed panning operation was held not to contribute and remained filtered out. Because inventive step had not been assessed by reference to the correct set of contributing features and a full Pozzoli analysis had not been carried out, the FLIR Belgium BV application was remitted for further examination. In Abbott v Sinocare, the disputed features concerned the display of event icons alongside sensor-derived glucose data, and the Court concluded that they contributed to improved human-machine interaction, helping the user to manage diabetes and achieve glycaemic control.

The article states that the UPC Court of Appeal’s decision in Abbott v Sinocare arose in preliminary injunction proceedings and concerned a relatively discrete challenge to a particular group of user-interface features. The article states that the decision does not provide a complete methodology for assessing technical character and contribution of features in more complex AI or computer-implemented claims. The article states that the EPO continues to apply the technical-character filter within its problem, solution approach. The article states that the UK must now integrate the intermediate step with its own obviousness principles. The article states that the UPC has taken an initial step by endorsing the COMVIK/G 1/19 interaction analysis but continues to develop its own approach to inventive step and must similarly integrate these principles.

The article states that the interesting recent development is not a change to the categories of exclusions but a growing convergence in how their effect on patentability is assessed, through a structured inquiry into which features of a claim contribute to its technical character. The article states that the low “any hardware” threshold and the intermediate step are two parts of a single structured assessment, the breadth of the former making the latter necessary. The article states that the intermediate step does not simply involve classifying each feature as inherently technical or non-technical, and that the analysis must be performed feature by feature but by reference to the technical character of the invention as a whole. The article states that a feature that appears non-technical in isolation may nevertheless contribute through its interaction with other features, so the inquiry must consider the interrelationship and combined functioning of the claim features. The article states that this is essentially the discipline established by COMVIK and elaborated in G 1/19, and that what is new is its express adoption in the UK and its emerging application outside the EPO’s problem, solution framework.

The article states that the UPC’s endorsement of G 1/19 suggests it may take a similar approach to the first hurdle, although that remains to be tested. The article states that the two early UKIPO decisions show why the intermediate step cannot be reduced to categorisation. The article states that the critical question in Emotional Perception was whether the claimed computational features contribute to a technical purpose or effect, rather than merely producing an output with greater semantic or cognitive value to the user. The article states that Abbott v Sinocare should not be made to bear too much weight and is best treated as a useful but limited indication of the same direction of travel. The article states that it would be an overstatement to say that European approaches to excluded subject matter and inventive step have been harmonised.

stories.Headline: Thirty-one states enact AI election laws while nineteen states have none as of October 2026
stories.Summary:
Thirty-one states enacted laws regulating artificial intelligence in election campaigns by October 2026, according to reporting from SciLine. These state laws primarily target the use of deepfakes and require labels on content generated by AI. Nineteen states had no such laws on the books as of that same date in October 2026. The United States still has no federal rule written specifically for political advertising using artificial intelligence. This creates a patchwork of rules where campaigns face different duties depending on the state.

The Federal Communications Commission banned AI-generated voices in robocalls in 2024 under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. The Federal Election Commission declined to create a dedicated AI rule in 2024, calling its fraud provisions technology neutral. These federal actions leave a gap because neither agency has a mandate to police AI video on social platforms. State laws focus on synthetic media and candidate deepfakes rather than general-purpose AI or chatbots. These statutes often focus on windows before an election and provide fast civil remedies for targeted candidates.

The Federal Election Commission stated that a lie in a campaign ad is a lie regardless of the producer. This agency confirmed that its existing fraudulent misrepresentation provisions apply to all AI-generated communications. The commission chose case-by-case enforcement over a bright-line statute, leaving definitions and penalties open until complaints arise. The Federal Communications Commission acted on a delivery channel it already regulates to ban voice cloning. These two agencies hold the federal levers that touch artificial intelligence in campaigns today.

Campaigns must now map labeling rules across different states, which increases costs for legal review and creative workflows. Broadcasters must decide if they are responsible for missing labels, while platforms manage moderation at scale. AI vendors face reputational risks and often adopt refusal policies for named political figures during election windows. Model providers tend to adopt the strictest common denominator, such as watermarking, to avoid tracking thirty-one rulebooks. The 19 states without laws may rely on older fraud or defamation statutes.

The AI industry has watched these cycles closely, and Sam Altman of OpenAI spoke about the 2024 race. In January 2024, Altman told Bloomberg House in Davos that America and AI would be fine regardless of the election. The current legal front is widening, including questions about whether unfair competition suits can freeze frontier AI. Washington has tied technology rules to alliances, such as the Pax Silica pact signed by the US and eight allies. Federal power often flows toward national security framing before addressing consumer or election framing.

The next phase of policy may be defined by the fight over federal preemption of state laws. A single federal standard could set uniform definitions and disclosure rules while displacing stricter state requirements. If no federal framework arrives, the split between the thirty-one and nineteen states will probably persist. The record does not yet show a specific policy change tied to the most recent election. It remains unconfirmed if the election produced any federal AI law, regulation, or executive action.

stories.Headline: David Kyler urges public support for laws and a treaty to rein in AI
stories.Summary:
David Kyler, director and co-founder of the Center for a Sustainable Coast, based in St. Simons Island, Georgia, wrote a guest column for The Atlanta Journal-Constitution published on November 16, 2026, about efforts to rein in artificial intelligence. He said his group has been concerned about AI systems and the data centers that serve them because both pose grave threats to the environment, public health and quality of life. He said the group's commentary on these technologies has been published in the AJC and other Georgia media outlets over the past 18 months. He said the group devotes a special section of its website to AI and data centers, where links to informative articles and reports are frequently posted, because public understanding is required to support vital legislative reforms. The column describes five proposals in Congress.

The FRONTIER Act, sponsored by Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., and Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., would require frontier labs to publish transparency reports, implement whistleblower protections, report critical safety incidents to the Commerce Department and give the government power to halt deployment of higher-risk models while preempting certain state laws. The AI Kill Switch Act, introduced by Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., and Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, would require developers to build shutdown capabilities into the most advanced systems and authorize the Department of Homeland Security, in consultation with the Commerce Department and the director of national intelligence, to order temporary slowdowns or termination of models threatening catastrophic harm. The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, introduced by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, would permanently ban artificial superintelligence, pause advanced AI development until a new federal body called the Department of Artificial Intelligence establishes safeguards, and severely penalize violations. The Stop Rogue AI Act, sponsored by Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to set standards for tracking, verifying and controlling autonomous AI agents that operate without human supervision. The AI Incident Reporting Act, advanced by Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, would require developers to report security breaches and incidents to the Commerce Department.

The column says Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., and Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, are negotiating a broader national safety framework holding companies legally responsible for mitigating model harms. Kyler writes that international legislation might partially reduce these risks, but that global harm from AI could be impossible to predict unless safeguards are publicly protected. He says individuals in the United States can call for advancement of a treaty, and he urges readers to support petition signing to take effect until national and international leadership controls development. He also writes that data centers consume large amounts of power and water, and that their pollution, climate damage and health risks sometimes fall on communities that receive few of the benefits. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Utah board creates AI student taskforce to advise on classroom use
stories.Summary:
The Utah State Board of Education formally established an Artificial Intelligence Student Taskforce a few weeks before mid November 2026, placing it under the board's existing Student Advisory Council, and the group is set to meet roughly four times during the school year, alternating between in-person and virtual meetings. The task force was approved during the board's October meeting, and although students have not yet been assigned to it, several students helped set the effort in motion. One student from one of Utah's largest districts contacted the technology director about a year earlier to ask how to start a task force, a high school senior recently interned at an AI law office, a charter school student wants to bring his experience with learning disabilities to the conversation, and another student is running projects with the STEM Action Center. The council currently has 15 students serving on it.

The task force is meant to advise the state board on how AI is used in teaching and learning, and it gives students a chance to share their views on decisions adults make for them. Matt Winters, the board's former AI Specialist, said the board regularly hears from parents, superintendents and advocacy groups but does not hear from students and teachers as consistently. LeAnn Wood, vice chair of the board, said she hopes the group provides a boots-on-the-ground perspective on how AI is affecting students' education, for better or for worse, because students are the ones who see it in action. The article ties the effort to wider debate since generative AI went mainstream in late 2022, noting that a 2025 Project Tomorrow survey found 63% of students in grades six through 12 worry about being wrongly accused of cheating with AI, while more than 400 CEOs, including leaders from Adobe, IBM and Microsoft, have signed an open letter advocating mandatory computer science and AI education in schools.

Winters credited the students for driving the work, saying the story is entirely about the kids and that the work flows through him rather than because of him. He said he would expect companies such as NVIDIA, OpenAI and Anthropic to pay attention, describing the students as savvy and able to help influence the state's long-term vision. Wood said one challenge may be engaging students beyond the 15 on the council, since some may want careers in governance, law or public policy while others have different goals, and Winters has already prompted students on bringing in more peers, with ideas such as a hackathon taking shape. Wood said that if students make recommendations or raise concerns and the board disregards them, the experiment will have failed, and she hopes the experience leads students to engage civically as adults.

stories.Headline: Canada and the UK renew their AI security partnership with shared standards and joint evaluations
stories.Summary:
On 13 October 2026, Canada and the UK renewed their AI security partnership, which was first signed in 2024 as the AI Safety Partnership. The renewal aims to foster the safe and responsible development and deployment of AI. The agreement commits both countries to three priorities: interoperable standards, enhanced information-sharing and closer technical cooperation. The Canadian AI Safety Institute and the UK AI Security Institute will hold regular exchanges and coordinated evaluation activities. The Canadian Institute of Advanced Research contributed CAD $1 million to the UK AI Security Institute's Alignment Project.

The renewed partnership covers mutually recognised or shared AI security standards, improved information exchange including on frontier risk, and expanded technical arrangements. Neither country has passed a single comprehensive law governing AI across every sector. Canada's proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act was abandoned when Parliament was dissolved in 2025. The UK has deliberately chosen not to legislate. No legislation in either country sets out exactly how organisations must assess AI risks.

The article recommends that organisations implement a consistent and repeatable process to answer the same questions both regimes ask. These questions are whether the impact of the AI system has been assessed before deployment, whether decisions have been documented, whether there is meaningful human oversight and whether there will be ongoing monitoring. Such a process would let organisations respond to the partnership priorities, evidence compliance in both jurisdictions and prepare for any future legislation. The article was co-authored by Carole Piovesan, Managing Partner at INQ Law in Toronto. It was published by Stephenson Harwood on 16 November 2026.

Canada's legal environment is fragmented across jurisdictions and sectors, including privacy, human rights, consumer protection and competition law. The federal Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems sets out commitments on accountability, safety, fairness, transparency, human oversight and robustness. The Directive on Automated Decision-Making is binding on federal institutions and is supported by the Algorithmic Impact Assessment, which scores a system's risk and scales safeguards accordingly. In June 2026 the federal government tabled Bill C-36, which would enact the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act as Canada's new private-sector privacy law. A companion bill, the Safe Social Media Act (Bill C-34), would impose digital safety duties on social media platforms and chatbot services, with both regimes overseen by a new Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada.

Health Canada has issued pre-market guidance for machine learning-enabled medical devices. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions' Guideline E-23 on Model Risk Management, in force from 1 May 2027, expressly captures AI and machine learning models at federally regulated financial institutions. The Standards Council of Canada has convened work on AI standards and trust frameworks. In 2017 Canada became the first country to launch a national AI strategy, and its successor, AI for All, launched in June 2026, aims to lift business AI adoption from just over 12% to 60% by 2034. Canada now has a dedicated Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation, whose priorities flow from the Prime Minister's May 2025 mandate letter to Cabinet.

Budget 2026, tabled on 5 November 2026, includes access to 500 MW of sovereign AI compute, approximately CAD $1 billion over five years for a Government Transformation Fund, a new Digital Transformation Canada, CAD $176.3 million over five years for the Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission and a plan to explore a Technology Stability Board. The UK has adopted a principles-based approach covering safety, security and robustness, transparency and explainability, fairness, accountability and governance, and contestability and redress, enforced by sector regulators. The Financial Conduct Authority's AI Update outlines how existing financial services rules apply to AI, and the Information Commission has issued guidance on AI and data protection and has been tasked with preparing a formal Code of Practice on AI and automated decision-making. The Competition Markets Authority's AI Strategic Update sets out six principles aimed at fostering competition and consumer protection. If an AI system uses personal data, a data protection impact assessment is one of the most useful tools available to assess risk.

Reforms under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 removed the general prohibition on solely automated decision-making that produces legal or similarly significant effects, replacing it with a requirement for a lawful basis such as legitimate interests, provided no special category data is involved. Organisations must still ensure transparency, provide individuals with the opportunity to make representations, allow access to human intervention and enable individuals to challenge decisions. The EU AI Act came into force on 1 August 2024, and its broad extraterritorial reach applies to organisations based in the UK and Canada that place AI systems or general-purpose AI models on the EU market. The EU's digital omnibus on AI has deferred the rules for high-risk AI systems from 2 August 2026 until 2 December 2027 for Annex III and 2 August 2028 for Annex I. Providers of high-risk AI systems must operate a robust risk management system, keep detailed technical documentation and records, design systems to allow effective human oversight, demonstrate compliance via a conformity assessment before the system is placed on the market and conduct post-market monitoring.

stories.Headline: Al Kingsley writes a plain English guide to explain how AI works and where it may go
stories.Summary:
Al Kingsley wrote in School Management Plus on 16 November 2026 that school leaders and staff often pretend to understand artificial intelligence during meetings rather than admit they do not know the basics, because teaching is a profession built on knowledge and an information gap can feel like a failing. He said the problem is not the technology itself, since AI is not a scary human overlord yet, but that without knowing how it works and what its quirks are, leaders and staff cannot make informed decisions for colleagues and students. He argued that anyone who does ask what others may regard as simple questions will find their colleagues grateful, and he guaranteed it. He described his book, Unpicking AI ,  one token at a time, as deliberately and definitively not a book about AI in schools, with no education jargon at all.

The book is a simple, accessible guide to AI in general, written for anyone who wants to understand what it is before deciding how to use it, and it emphasises plain English. It first explains where AI came from, showing that the ideas started many, many years ago, which makes media headlines seem less futuristic and less overwhelming. It then explains how AI actually works, and once you realise it learns from vast amounts of data, you can see why it is so impressive and why it sometimes gets things oh-so confidently wrong. The book also looks at where AI might end up in the future, in easy language, because at this point nobody actually knows, even the tech bros.

Kingsley said that when we get our questions answered we all gain confidence, whatever the subject, and that with a new understanding of AI your questions will improve. Asking whether to ban it will become a question of what it can do, where to look out for problems and how to help students use it constructively in school. He returned to the meeting scenario, where someone who knows how AI works fearlessly asks to check that everyone knows what they are talking about before deciding. Kingsley is due to speak at the Schools and Academies Show in Birmingham this week at a talk entitled Choosing the Right Technology for Your Secondary School: The Questions Leaders Should Be Asking.

stories.Headline: Malaysia plans full AI exposure in schools next year as PAGE urges a balanced approach
stories.Summary:
The Parent Action Group for Education Malaysia successfully conducted its 16th annual general meeting in September 2026 to continue its campaign for English language instruction. This educational lobby group previously advocated for the use of smartphones as teaching aids, though many teachers initially insisted that these devices remain at home. While some developed nations are now restricting technology, the Madani government has decided to implement full scale exposure to artificial intelligence within the Malaysian education system. This new curriculum is scheduled to begin next year for students entering Year One and Form One.

Several countries are currently spending significant funds to return to traditional learning methods to combat digital fatigue and protect cognitive focus. Sweden spent more than 2.1 billion krona, or 875 million ringgit, over two years to bring printed textbooks and teaching guides back into classrooms. Denmark committed 540 million Danish krone, which is 330 million ringgit, over ten years for physical books while making schools and after school clubs handphone free. Other nations including Finland, Italy, France, and Norway have restricted or banned phones, while Madrid, Spain, is capping primary student screen time to two hours per week.

Datin Noor Azimah Abdul Rahim, the chairman of the Parent Action Group for Education Malaysia, expressed concerns regarding the eagerness to put screens in front of developing children. She argued that implementation must be guided by child safety, equity, and educational outcomes so that students do not surrender their ability to think independently. She noted that professors at Harvard University are increasingly banning laptops, as an analysis by The Harvard Crimson in September 2026 found such bans had more than doubled. She believes pupils still need physical books and handwriting practice to avoid being distracted by digital notifications.

The group suggests that Malaysia should learn from developed countries that have come full circle by finding a healthier balance between digital and traditional education. The author warns that excessive self promotion without adequate preparation could lead to failure, citing the recall of 8,878 Chery Omoda 5 cars and 600 other vehicles. The goal is for students to use technology to solve problems and make informed decisions rather than depending on it to think for them. The group will continue to serve as a channel between concerned parents, the Ministry of Education, and other stakeholders.

stories.Headline: Bureau of Industry and Security requires licenses to export advanced AI chips to certain data centers
stories.Summary:
The Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule on November 16, 2026. This rule requires licenses to export, reexport, or transfer advanced artificial intelligence chips to data centers. It targets facilities supplying significant computing power to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5. The rule also applies to companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those locations. These restrictions apply to chips shipped to data centers anywhere in the world.

The rule covers chips under ECCNs 3A090 and 4A090 providing over 12 million aggregate total processing performance. It requires licenses for shipments to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. The rule formally rescinds the January 2025 AI Diffusion Rule and its associated authorizations. It applies to chips already in place, treating new restricted service as an in-country transfer. Data centers already supplying this power must obtain a license within 90 days of the effective date.

The Bureau of Industry and Security is responsible for enforcing these new semiconductor export controls. Officials stated the rule relies on existing power over chip shipments rather than direct remote access regulation. They explained that the diligence requirements prevent companies from evading controls through corporate spinoffs or restructurings. BIS will review license applications on a case by case basis for restricted destinations. They will consider the effectiveness of each country's export control regime and its cooperation.

Cloud providers, chip suppliers, and data center operators are affected by these new compliance requirements. They must now identify who runs workloads on chips and who owns those companies. Some reports indicate ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent used chips in Japan, Malaysia, and Thailand. Exporters must obtain know your customer information to prove they lacked knowledge of restricted end uses. A data center's refusal to provide this information is now considered a red flag.

The rule follows Executive Order 14434 and uses the term Super Intelligence instead of artificial intelligence. Previous BIS opinions from 2009 and 2014 stated that providing cloud computing capacity was not controlled. The Remote Access Security Act passed the House on January 12, 2026, to amend the Export Control Reform Act. A companion Senate bill, S. 3519, was introduced on December 17, 2025, to target foreign persons of concern. These legislative efforts aim to give BIS explicit statutory authority over network access to controlled items.

The rule takes effect on its publication date in the Federal Register with a 60 day comment period. The Secretary of Commerce may add more high risk destinations to the license requirement list. BIS may impose import restrictions or Entity List designations on parties that tolerate evasion. The Remote Access Security Act still awaits action in the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs. The articles leave open whether the Senate will pass the broader House definition of remote access.

stories.Headline: EU science and ethics advisors urge public AI evaluation capacity
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors and the European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies issued a joint statement warning that traditional public policy guardrails cannot govern rapidly advancing artificial intelligence. The two senior advisory bodies called on the European Union to establish sovereign capacity to evaluate complex AI models rather than delegating safety assessments to commercial technology firms. The statement, titled ‘The next phase of artificial intelligence ,  Governing for safety, security and human agency,’ sets out four core principles for European policymakers. The advisors delivered the four primary recommendations to the College of Commissioners. The joint statement was published on 16 Nov 2026.

The first recommendation is to keep existing rules strong, with safety, cybersecurity and human agency remaining mandatory prerequisites for AI development. The advisors warn against regulatory backsliding and say political hesitation risks weakening statutory obligations under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and that lobbying to dilute compliance deadlines must be resisted. The second is to calibrate development and deployment to degrees of danger, so the pace at which foundation models and autonomous systems are released correlates with potential hazards. Where models pose severe cybersecurity, biosecurity or critical-infrastructure risks, deployment must be contingent on verified mitigation rather than post-incident response. The third is to build independent public evaluation capacity, with the advisors urging the EU to develop public testing facilities and warning the bloc cannot remain dependent on self-attestations or proprietary safety benchmarks supplied by commercial developers. The fourth is to establish an ecosystem for continuous learning, in which regulatory frameworks and scientific risk assessments evolve dynamically alongside advancing model capabilities, since static compliance checklists are obsolete and authorities must create adaptive monitoring loops that ingest empirical evidence from operational deployments.

The Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, established under the Scientific Advice Mechanism, comprises seven eminent researchers appointed in their personal capacity to deliver evidence-based policy counsel. The European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies operates as an independent advisory body examining where scientific discovery intersects with fundamental European rights. Officials within the Directorate-General for Research and Innovation confirmed that the move reflects mounting concern that commercial market pressures threaten to bypass fundamental safety reviews. The GCSA and EGE argued that relying exclusively on commercial developers to determine whether their proprietary models trigger GPAI systemic risk thresholds introduces an inherent conflict of interest that undermines European safety objectives. The advisors asserted that safety and market competitiveness are complementary, and that reliable, audited and trustworthy systems form the only durable foundation for widespread societal adoption in medicine, public administration and critical engineering.

In independent coverage by Wisevoter, titled Scientists Urge Europe to Enforce AI Rules, observers underscored that the European advisory apparatus is pivoting attention away from theoretical rule-drafting toward concrete technical verification capabilities. European academic organizations welcomed the advisors’ insistence on public evaluation infrastructure. Policy commentators at European Interest had previously pointed out that public scientific research risks marginalization if access to frontier models and evaluation tools remains gated behind commercial licensing agreements. University consortia emphasized that independent evaluation capacity within member states would provide academic researchers with transparent benchmarks and reproducible verification protocols. For universities, research hospitals and academic research offices, the recommendations highlight procurement due diligence and audit trails, expansion of research ethics committee remits, academic participation in public evaluation testbeds, and safeguarding scientific reproducibility.

Both bodies have previously advised the Commission on computational technologies, delivering opinions on artificial intelligence in crisis management and publishing detailed guidance on the successful and timely uptake of artificial intelligence in science in the EU. The joint statement arrives as the operational burden of the AI Act, finalized in 2024, has shifted toward secondary rulemaking and practical enforcement. Critical milestones currently under negotiation include the general-purpose AI Code of Practice and implementation frameworks that clarify downstream compliance obligations. The European Commission has introduced legislative proposals including the Cloud and AI Development Act (COM(2026) 502 final). The advisors warn that without substantial budgetary investment in public technical staff, automated evaluation tooling and independent laboratory verification, regulatory bodies risk becoming rubber-stamping entities for proprietary commercial claims.

Following publication of the joint statement on November 16, 2026, the Directorate-General for Research and Innovation and DG CONNECT are scheduled to review the advisors’ recommendations. Attention will center on whether the European Commission incorporates explicit funding for independent evaluation infrastructure into upcoming Horizon Europe work programmes and the implementation roadmaps for the Cloud and AI Development Act. In parallel, the European AI Office is preparing the final administrative drafts of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, where stakeholder negotiations over independent auditor access remain under way. Under existing voluntary frameworks, major model providers conduct internal red-teaming exercises and issue selective model cards. The articles leave open whether the Commission will adopt the recommendations and how the negotiations over independent auditor access will conclude.

Articles.Title: EU Scientific and Ethics Advisors Call for Independent AI Model Evaluation - CASRAI

stories.Headline: Los Angeles schools survey parents, students and staff to shape generative AI policy
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District is distributing a survey to parents, students and staff to help inform its policy on generative artificial intelligence in schools, LAist reported on November 16, 2026. The district wants to hear from community members about how the technology should be used in classrooms across the system. The survey is meant to gather input that will shape the district's formal policy on generative AI. The report was published by Elly Yu, who covers early childhood issues for LAist.

The survey follows a surprise moratorium that LAUSD implemented in September on student use of generative AI on school-issued devices for this school year. Before that moratorium, district policy allowed students 13 and older to use the technology under supervision. The school board has an ad-hoc committee on generative AI that examines the new technology and what its role should be in the classroom. The committee was formed as part of a resolution that was passed to limit screentime in the district.

The ad hoc committee is scheduled to meet four more times this school year, on Dec. 9, 2026, Jan. 20, 2027, March 3, 2027 and April 7, 2027. The committee plans to make policy recommendations that the full board could vote on. The survey of parents, students and staff is intended to help inform the district policy that emerges from that process. The committee's work and the survey together will feed into the recommendations the board may eventually consider.

The context is a district still working out how generative AI fits into its classrooms after the September moratorium paused student use on school-issued devices. The ad-hoc committee's four remaining meetings this school year give the board a schedule for turning community input into recommendations it could vote on. The survey gives parents, students and staff a way to weigh in before those recommendations take shape.

Articles.Title: LAUSD wants to hear from parents about how the district should use AI - LAist

stories.Headline: City leaders at Global AI Cities 2026 set out five priorities for making AI and digital infrastructure resilient
stories.Summary:
At Global AI Cities 2026, more than 300 local government leaders from over 50 cities gathered in Manchester to discuss artificial intelligence and digital resilience. The event was organised by Global Government Forum and co-hosted by Greater Manchester Combined Authority. Sarah Wray reported on the conference for Global Government Forum on 16 November 2026. The discussions were captured in the report Making AI work for people and places: Five priorities for cities. The report draws on insights from the event and includes examples from Romania, Westminster and Alberta.

The report sets out five priorities for cities, including fixing the fundamentals and prioritising according to criticality. It also calls for governing AI throughout its lifecycle and making digital infrastructure itself resilient. The report says resilience depends on people and partnerships as well as technology. Global AI Cities 2027 is to be held in Manchester on 24-25 May. The report is available to download.

Alexandru Georgescu, senior researcher at Romania's National Institute for Research and Development in Informatics, said local authorities are not actually ready for AI in itself. He said generative AI and large language models are not comparable to traditional software and need new processes and new cybersecurity practices, including adversarial testing and red-teaming. He said many large organisations are not ready to do this, let alone local administrations that probably have not budgeted for it. He said cities are agglomerations of critical infrastructures that serve wider regions and become targets for criminals, rogue states or state-sponsored organisations. He concluded that many local authorities are not adequately prepared and do not have the level of support they need from central authorities.

Gurpreet Muctor, chief data and technology officer for Westminster City Council, said a late 2025 cyber-attack took five months to recover from and forced the shutdown of all systems. He said the attack was perpetrated by somebody who impersonated a council employee and was still a manual process, not an AI attack. He said AI increasingly adds a new layer to that threat in the form of deepfakes that can impersonate council workers, politicians or senior officials. Richard Henderson, corporate chief information officer for the Government of Alberta, said many local governments make it too easy for hackers because they are not getting the fundamentals right. He said Alberta built AI-assisted tooling to scan 400 million lines of government code for vulnerabilities, work he estimated would have taken a human 125 years of development time.

Henderson advised cities not to wait for the most advanced tools and said they can probably build their own reasonable facsimile relatively quickly for not a significant amount. He said the only way to survive the deepfake threat is through good governance and protocols, such as an agreed challenge phrase to ascertain that someone is genuine. Georgescu said there is too much focus on the cutting edge when good enough is often adequate for both attackers and defenders. He said his institute prioritises based on criticality, identifying which systems would cause the greatest harm if compromised and hardening those first. He highlighted the most basic AI-related risk as someone pasting citizen data into a public LLM to save time, and said the human factor and security culture matter.

Georgescu said there is not enough talk about the lifecycle of AI products and systems and how decommissioning will be handled. He warned of AI agents stuck in systems and attached to data that an adversary could exploit long after the department that built them has moved on. Henderson said staff are not interested in waiting for discussions about AI and will use it whether organisations like it or not. One senior leader at the summit described facing a pandemic, a major snowstorm and an energy blackout, which highlighted the difference between having technology and having resilience. The city is now strengthening resilience through a city brain supported by AI, improved cybersecurity, closer partnerships with telecom providers, resilient government buildings, district-level citizen refuges with power and connectivity, and new platforms providing real-time information on infrastructure.

The articles do not state what specific measures, funding or deadlines follow from the report's five priorities. They do not name the city whose leader described the succession of crises. They do not give the outcome of the Westminster attack beyond the five-month recovery and system shutdown. They do not say what action, if any, Romania's central authorities have taken in response to Georgescu's comments. They do not give details of the Global AI Cities 2027 agenda beyond its dates and location.

Articles.Title: AI’s double-edged sword: why cities must prioritise digital resilience - Global Government Forum

stories.headline_source: AI’s double-edged sword: why cities must prioritise digital resilience

stories.Headline: AI-Generated Election Posters Spark Controversy in Japan
stories.Summary:
A city council by-election in Amagasaki, Hyogo Prefecture, on November 15, 2026, drew 12 candidates for one vacant seat, and at least four of them displayed posters with AI-generated faces rather than their own photographs. Former prefectural assembly member Hikoharu Konishi acknowledged that four candidates had used artificial images, and the Amagasaki City Election Administration Commission confirmed at least four posters were suspected of using generative AI. In one case, officials said the man depicted on the poster of candidate Hiroyoshi Hara was not Hara himself, and an election official who had met Hara said the person shown looked completely different. The controversy emerged during a closely contested race in which voters also chose a mayor on November 15, with incumbent Kazumi Matsumoto winning a second term and Hiromi Ikeshita securing the council seat. Some posters depicted men with tattoos on their arms, while others showed attractive, distinguished-looking older men alongside simple campaign messages.

Japan's Public Offices Election Act has regulated posters through requirements on dimensions and identification of responsible parties but has not required candidates to use photographs of themselves. After the July 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election, when campaign poster boards displayed sexually explicit images of women and other material unrelated to candidates, lawmakers revised the law to require candidates' names to be clearly visible and to prohibit material damaging another person's reputation or violating public morals. The amended law contains no provision requiring a candidate's actual face to appear on a poster, and election authorities said they had no legal grounds to order the posters removed. Under the publicly funded election campaign system, public funding for poster production in the Amagasaki by-election was available up to approximately 610,000 yen per candidate, depending on reimbursement conditions. Each of the four candidates received enough votes to qualify for the return of the 300,000 yen deposit required to stand in the municipal election, though all four were defeated.

An Amagasaki election official said the commission could not intervene simply because a photograph or image was misleading, citing freedom of political activity and freedom of expression. Konishi, who with his secretary had submitted the candidacy registrations on behalf of the four individuals, reportedly responded that he found officials' requests for identity verification unpleasant. Speaking on behalf of candidate Koichi Sato, number 12, on November 14, the final day of campaigning, Konishi told voters the posters were the ones everyone in Amagasaki had been talking about and asked whether people genuinely felt suspicious about the images. He confirmed to Kansai Television that the images were produced using AI, saying of Sato's poster, "This was made with AI," and calling it "an image." Konishi said production costs were matters to be settled between candidates and contractors, that he had followed the Public Offices Election Act properly with the election commission's approval, and that outsiders should not make a fuss.

One Amagasaki resident said the artificial appearance immediately discouraged closer examination of the candidates' messages, and another said it made them wonder how committed the candidates really were and that it was difficult to sense any sincerity. Another resident said candidates should not engage in such unusual practices, while another questioned whether the individuals were seriously attempting to win office. Reporters searched Amagasaki for campaign vehicles and tried to contact the individuals by telephone but could not locate them or obtain interviews. Ono Planning Office, a local poster production company that has worked on more than 1,000 campaigns, restricts AI use to image correction and set its own guidelines in November. Company representative Satsuki Ono said AI can create a completely different face from the original material, that this is no longer simply correcting a photograph, and that charging nearly 600,000 yen for posters made with AI for practically nothing and paying only for printing could yield a substantial profit.

Election consultant Takuma Ohamazaki said that normally someone who runs for election incurs expenses and finishes with a financial loss, and that in this case he suspected some people may have ended up making money. Ohamazaki also warned that increasingly sophisticated AI could make future cases far harder to detect, saying the cat-and-mouse game between technological advances and the Public Offices Election Act will continue. Legal experts said Japan's election legislation has historically been designed to regulate specific, identifiable practices, making it difficult to anticipate abuses from new technologies, and that restrictions on political expression must be balanced against democratic freedoms including the right to participate in elections and communicate political messages. There has been no confirmation that the four candidates or their associates improperly received public funds or profited, and the allegations remain suspicions rather than established wrongdoing. Similar concerns circulated on social media, where users questioned whether obtaining publicly funded poster payments might have been one motivation for entering the election.

Further changes to the Public Offices Election Act are scheduled for March 2027, including a requirement to disclose when AI has been used in election-related materials. The planned disclosure requirement has drawn criticism because it carries no penalties for violations and does not necessarily require detailed explanations of which elements of an image were generated or altered. Experts questioned whether a simple declaration that AI was used would provide meaningful protection against misleading campaign imagery. Without clearer definitions of prohibited conduct or enforceable penalties, they warned, candidates may continue exploiting gaps between rapidly developing technology and election regulations. The Amagasaki controversy has highlighted a broader challenge facing Japan's democratic system.

Articles.Title: AI-Generated Election Posters Spark Controversy in Japan - News On Japan

stories.Headline: Amazon withdraws Ashburn data center plan and will convey 25 acres to Loudoun County
stories.Summary:
On October 20, Amazon agreed with Loudoun County, Virginia, to withdraw its plan for four data center buildings totaling more than 800,000 square feet on its 122-acre Ashburn campus, the former George Washington University campus. Amazon had purchased the campus for around $427.3 million in March 2026. In July, Amazon filed a site plan called Bridgefield Tech Center, with four two-story data center buildings and three parking garages. Amazon sought a by-right approval, an administrative process with no Planning Commission, public hearing or Board vote. On November 17, Loudoun County supervisors are set to take a final vote on pausing new legislative data center applications for up to 12 months.

Under the October 20 deal, Amazon will convey about 25 acres to the county and seek to rezone the rest, mainly for housing. Amazon cannot construct data centers or host their supporting infrastructure on the Ashburn campus, and it will not sue to do so. The pause would cover rezonings and special exceptions, the longest gap Virginia law permits, but not administrative applications, including at least 17 grandfathered applications totaling over 11 million square feet. The Board can still consider grid reliability substations during the period. On September 15, supervisors voted 7-1-1 to pause Board consideration of certain legislative applications for data centers and electrical substations, and the written resolution was deferred from October 20 to November 17.

Board Chair Phyllis Randall announced the agreement, called Project Potomac Promise, and said the campus was just the wrong location for a data center, owing to the infrastructure it would need and residents' opposition. Amazon's Josh Weissman said the company had heard the community's pointed concerns and took them seriously. He said Amazon and the county have differing views on the site's legal potential, and it chose a shared vision over costly litigation. Neither Amazon nor Randall cited power supply as the reason for calling off the planned construction. Supervisor Juli Briskman had vowed on July 30 to fight the plan every step of the way.

Business Insider reported that some AWS sites had space for Nvidia GB300 racks but not enough power to run them, so finished racks were held in warehouses. Amazon called staging equipment best business practice and disputed that it lacked a path to bring the racks into its data centers. AWS CEO Matt Garman cautioned that over 100 data center moratoriums are being considered across the U.S. Governor Abigail Spanberger said the decision on approving or blocking data center projects should rest with the community and not the state. State Senator Russet Perry has drafted a three-year statewide moratorium on data center approvals.

Loudoun County hosts about 233 data center buildings and 56.5 million square feet built or under construction as of March 1, 2026, plus 35.7 million square feet approved but not yet built. In 2025, the county issued permits for over 10 million square feet of data center space, the highest in a year. A 2000 zoning ruling assigned data centers as office buildings, letting companies build them by right in office-zoned areas, and since March 2025 new data centers have required a special exception approved by a Board vote. The county generated $1.2 billion in tax revenue in fiscal 2026, 39% of its budget, with about 40%, or $1.3 billion, projected for fiscal 2027. In early October, county staff told supervisors that Amazon would need additional county approval before building, citing a zoning determination that data centers were not a permitted primary use on the property.

AWS reported a $578 billion backlog and $46 billion in Q3 sales, up 39%, and Amazon's leases signed but not yet started rose to $164.9 billion in Q3 from $137.2 billion in Q2 and $96.4 billion at the end of 2025. Amazon plans to spend meaningfully more in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion planned for 2026, and it purchased $77.3 billion of property and equipment, with $159.6 billion of property and equipment commitments. CEO Andy Jassy said AWS added 3.9 GW of power capacity in 2025 and expected to double it by the end of 2027, but still had capacity constraints that yield unserved demand. On October 2, Garman pledged more than $1 billion over five years to support communities near its data centers and confirmed Amazon would stop using NDAs with government agencies. On September 24, Oracle issued a force majeure notice to Blue Owl Capital over its 2.45 GW Stargate campus in Doña Ana County, New Mexico.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Amazon AI Data Center Expansion Faces Permitting Delays - I/O Fund

stories.Headline: Ethics professor Domènec Melé argues AI shapes habits and desires but cannot replace human wisdom or communion
stories.Summary:
Dr. Domènec Melé, an emeritus professor of business ethics at IESE Business School and an emeritus member of the Royal European Academy of Doctors, published an article titled “Christian Spirituality and Artificial Intelligence: Discernment in a Global Technological Economy” in the journal Religions on 27 October, the academy reported on 16 November 2026. In it he reflects on how artificial intelligence and new technological environments affect the spiritual development of human beings. He writes that artificial intelligence has shown it not only expands human capabilities but also shapes habits, desires, attention and forms of relationship. He argues that processing information or generating plausible responses is not the same as wisdom, which requires integrating knowledge with experience, moral judgement and an orientation towards worthy ends.

Melé holds that fluid and personalised interaction may simulate attention or empathy but does not amount to communion, because communion requires reciprocal presence, vulnerability and the capacity for self-giving between persons. He notes that in an economy rewarding engagement or productivity, optimising means does not automatically settle which ends are worth pursuing. He says artificial intelligence can reduce repetitive burdens and broaden access to knowledge or assistance, but replacing activities whose value includes human participation, such as teaching, care, professional judgement or personal accompaniment, carries risks. He also warns of an unequal distribution of human presence, since those with greater resources may keep access to teachers, doctors or advisers in person while others increasingly receive automated substitutes.

The article further underlines the material footprint of the technology, noting that although it may appear immaterial to users, artificial intelligence depends on data centres, chips and electricity grids whose consumption of energy and water is considerable. Melé does not advocate rejecting technology or absolutising it, and he suggests technical creativity can be understood as a form of participation in the care and development of creation, while the power it confers is a responsibility entrusted to human beings rather than absolute dominion. In a context of concentrated infrastructure, data and capital, he argues that the social doctrine of the Church offers criteria of dignity, the common good, subsidiarity and solidarity to keep individuals and communities from becoming passive recipients of decisions taken elsewhere. He concludes that progress is genuinely human when directed towards the integral development of persons and, within the Christian horizon, towards communion with God and with others.

Over the past 30 years Melé has researched and written extensively on business and economic ethics, corporate social responsibility, Christian social ethics, spirituality in management, management philosophy and humanistic management. He has published more than 70 book chapters and scientific articles in journals including the Journal of Business Ethics, Business Ethics Quarterly, Business Ethics: A European Review, Business and Society Review, Philosophy of Management and Humanistic Management Journal. He is also the author of several books that have become reference works in humanistic economics, among them “Ethics in Business Management”, “Anthropological Foundations of Business Management”, “Business Ethics in Action. Seeking Human Excellence in Organizations”, “Christians in Society” and “Ethics in the Family Business”, the last co-authored with fellow READ emeritus member Miguel Ángel Gallo.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence and spirituality - Real Academia Europea de Doctores

stories.Headline: Microsoft outage creates Zoho opportunity for India Inc, says Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw
stories.Summary:
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, the founder of Biocon, said on the social media platform X that the recent disruption of Microsoft services could create an opening for the Indian software company Zoho to serve as a backup management information system for Indian businesses, according to TechGig. She made the suggestion as companies were re-evaluating their reliance on global technology providers following the outage. The Microsoft 365 outage affected users in more than 70 countries, including India, according to Downdetector data cited by the report. Microsoft announced on Saturday that its services had been fully restored and that all products were operational, confirming the Microsoft 365 disruption was resolved.

The report said Microsoft's Microsoft 365 suite has more than 450 million commercial users, a figure Bloomberg reported, and the scale of the disruption renewed concerns about the risks of businesses relying heavily on a single technology provider. Zoho already has a significant presence in India's government email infrastructure, with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology stating in December that nearly 12.68 lakh official email accounts across various ministries and departments had migrated to a Zoho-based platform. Approximately 7.45 lakh of those accounts belonged to central government employees, according to the ministry. Union ministers publicly backed domestic products, including Zoho's software and its messaging platform Arattai, as alternatives to foreign technology services in October last year.

Mazumdar-Shaw is the person behind the suggestion, and she posted on X that Zoho could emerge as a backup management information system provider for India Inc given such unforeseen events, the article said. The report did not say whether Zoho or Microsoft responded to her remarks. The articles give no further statements from Microsoft, Zoho or government officials beyond the ministry's December figure and the ministers' earlier public backing of domestic products. The articles also do not say what steps, if any, Indian businesses plan to take in response to the outage or to her suggestion.

Articles.Title: Microsoft outage creates Zoho opportunity for India Inc, says Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw

stories.Headline: Ivy Tech hosts a free Zoom AI essentials course on Wednesday
stories.Summary:
Ivy Tech is hosting an artificial intelligence essentials course on Zoom this Wednesday, according to Star City News. Instructors will go over how AI can be used in professional environments and how it can actually help improve work flow. They will also emphasize the crucial role of human oversight of AI. Those who attend will also get hands-on experience with Google AI tools.

It's happening Wednesday, Nov. 18, from 9-10 a.m. The course is free, and more information is available online. The session is listed among the Things to Do items on the starcitytv.com site. The article was published on Monday, November 16, 2026, and was written by multi-media journalist Lincoln Schlemmer.

The article does not name a specific instructor or spokesperson for Ivy Tech, so no one is quoted directly in the story. The details about the course come from the Star City News listing rather than from a named Ivy Tech official. The article describes the course as covering professional uses of AI, improved work flow and human oversight. It also notes that attendees will work with Google AI tools during the session.

The listing appears in the Things to Do section of the Star City News website, which covers Lafayette, Indiana. The article gives no further context about enrollment, capacity or whether the course will be repeated. It also does not say what happens after the Wednesday session or how participants sign up beyond checking online. More to follow.
