stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Accelerates Microbial Biosynthesis of Functional Bio-Based Nanomaterials
stories.Summary:
Microbial biosynthesis has emerged as an environmentally friendly alternative to traditional physicochemical nanoparticle production techniques, offering a versatile platform for generating functional nanoscale materials under mild reaction conditions. Conventional production routes, including chemical reduction, sol-gel processing, and laser ablation, routinely rely on hazardous reducing agents, toxic organic solvents, and high energy inputs that create environmental hazards and leave harmful surface residues. Microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, algae, cyanobacteria, and actinomycetes circumvent these issues by deploying enzymatic pathways, metabolic by-products, and active biomolecules to reduce metal precursors and stabilize nanoscale structures. Recent synthetic evaluations demonstrate that these biogenic nanomaterials possess superior biocompatibility and surface functionality compared with their chemically manufactured counterparts. However, translating microbial synthesis into industrial production has long been impeded by complex biological dynamics, unstandardized parameters, and erratic batch-to-batch variation, prompting researchers to integrate artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-driven materials informatics across every stage of the fabrication workflow.

Microbial nanomaterial generation operates through distinct biological mechanisms, primarily categorized into intracellular and extracellular pathways, alongside specialized biomineralization processes. In intracellular routes, metal cations traverse microbial cell envelopes through dedicated ion channels or electrostatic interactions with surface carboxyl and hydroxyl groups, undergoing reduction via intracellular enzymes, reduced cofactors such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, and thiol-bearing molecules like glutathione. Although intracellular synthesis yields smaller, highly monodisperse nanoparticles, product harvesting requires cell lysis that complicates downstream recovery. Extracellular synthesis circumvents this limitation by secreting reductive enzymes, extracellular polymeric substances, and redox-active metabolites into the surrounding culture medium, facilitating direct particle nucleation and capping without cellular disruption. Concurrently, biomineralization allows organisms such as magnetotactic bacteria to synthesize single-domain magnetic crystals of magnetite or greigite within membrane-bound magnetosomes, producing structures with tight size distributions and permanent magnetic dipole moments under strict genetic regulation.

The biochemical diversity across microbial classes dictates the morphology, yield, and catalytic activity of the resulting nanoparticles. Bacteria such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Escherichia, and Shewanella offer rapid growth and accessible genetic manipulation, using redox enzymes like nitrate reductase to yield metallic and metal oxide architectures. Fungi provide exceptional biomass yields and robust extracellular secretion rates, releasing high volumes of enzymes and secondary metabolites that simplify downstream purification while generating silver, gold, and zinc oxide nanoparticles. Photosynthetic microalgae and macroalgae utilize light and carbon dioxide to produce polysaccharides, polyols, and pigments that drive phyco-nanotechnology, yielding crystalline structures under sustainable cultivation regimes. Cyanobacteria contribute distinct phototrophic pathways that continuously supply reducing equivalents, whereas actinomycetes, particularly Streptomyces species, leverage diverse secondary metabolite profiles to assemble antimicrobial silver and gold particles with unique surface functionalization.

Despite the inherent flexibility of biological systems, native microbial synthesis remains exquisitely sensitive to extrinsic and intrinsic cultivation parameters. Small fluctuations in metal precursor concentrations, ambient pH, reaction temperatures, dissolved oxygen levels, nutrient feeds, and agitation rates trigger profound shifts in particle size, crystal structure, dispersity, and overall stability. For instance, alkaline reaction environments alter the ionization state of functional groups and boost biomolecular reducing capacity, favoring smaller, more uniform nanoparticles. Elevated temperatures accelerate reduction kinetics up to the threshold of thermal protein denaturation, while microbial physiological status during the logarithmic growth phase provides peak metabolic activity for efficient nucleation. Because these environmental parameters exhibit complex, multidimensional interactions, traditional one-variable-at-a-time experimentation and standard response surface methodologies fail to resolve nonlinear interdependencies, leaving bioprocess optimization labor-intensive and frequently unrepeatable.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning models are fundamentally transforming this landscape by replacing trial-and-error laboratory cycles with predictive modeling. Supervised learning algorithms, including artificial neural networks, support vector machines, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting regressors, can map multi-parameter inputs directly to nanoparticle size, yield, and morphology. Hybrid algorithmic frameworks, such as neural networks coupled with particle swarm optimization, have successfully isolated precursor concentrations, feed rates, and agitation speeds as primary drivers of particle dimensions. Furthermore, convolutional neural networks, graph neural networks, and transformer-based architectures automate feature extraction from electron microscopy and spectroscopy imagery, quantifying structural properties without subjective operator intervention. Integrating these predictive algorithms with high-throughput multi-omics profiles, spanning transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, allows researchers to anticipate cellular states and systematically dial in desired nanomaterial specifications with minimal experimental iteration.

Beyond primary synthesis, post-synthetic surface functionalization is critical for adapting microbial nanomaterials to demanding technological environments, as native biomolecular capping layers alone rarely satisfy rigorous industrial or clinical benchmarks. Polyethylene glycol coatings provide steric hindrance that limits non-specific protein adsorption, extending circulation half-lives and preserving structural integrity even under extreme thermal stress. Natural biopolymers like chitosan introduce reactive amine groups that promote mucoadhesion and support covalent drug conjugation, while targeted protein functionalization utilizing antibodies, transferrin, and cell-penetrating peptides enhances receptor-mediated uptake in pathological tissues. Researchers are also constructing hybrid nanocomposites by embedding biogenic nanoparticles within bacterial cellulose scaffolds or coupling them with graphene oxide and reduced graphene oxide sheets, achieving synergistic mechanical strength, superior electrical conductivity, and amplified catalytic performance. Stimuli-responsive functionalization represents an advanced frontier in biogenic material engineering, enabling dynamic structural and functional adaptations in response to environmental triggers.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Accelerates Microbial Biosynthesis of Functional Bio-Based Nanomaterials

stories.Headline: Cloud provider leak exposes personal data of 46,000 TSMC employees
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company confirmed on November 16, 2026, that personal data of current and former employees was leaked online. A threat actor using the alias SmithBianl posted a sample text file on a hacker forum on November 8. This individual claimed the sample came from a larger 6.9GB dataset containing 46,000 employee records. The leaked information was offered for auction with a starting price of 3 BTC, which is roughly $65,000.

The breach requires the company to notify affected staff and provide them with necessary support. The compromised data includes sensitive details such as national ID numbers, banking information, addresses, and contact details. TSMC determined that the leak originated from the system services of a cloud service provider rather than its own internal infrastructure. Consequently, the company has engaged a third-party cybersecurity firm to help manage the ongoing situation.

TSMC stated that its operations and customers remain unaffected by this external security incident. In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company noted there is no evidence that its own systems were compromised. The chipmaker, which produces hardware for Nvidia and Apple, is focusing on supporting the employees whose data was exposed. The company continues to investigate the breach through its partnership with external cybersecurity experts.

Articles.Title: TSMC employee data leaked from cloud provider

stories.Headline: Oracle's Natalia Rachelson urges businesses to measure AI success by delivered improvements, not agent counts
stories.Summary:
Natalia Rachelson, a Senior Vice President of Applications Development at Oracle, said in an interview with PTI that businesses adopting artificial intelligence should judge success by the improvement the technology delivers rather than by the number of AI agents they deploy. She said the number of agents deployed matters less than the improvement they deliver, a view that shifts how organisations should evaluate their AI investments. Her comments were published by TechGig on November 16, 2026, in a report that also said AI is moving from merely helping employees to actively performing work for them. The report said this evolution requires a re-evaluation of traditional AI adoption metrics.

Rachelson advised business leaders to select a measurable goal for AI implementation from the outset, so that AI initiatives stay aligned with tangible business outcomes and improvements. The report said this approach is crucial as AI transitions from assisting employees to performing tasks autonomously. It said businesses should measure success by delivered improvements, not by the number of AI agents deployed. The report framed the shift as a change in how organisations should think about the value of their AI spending.

Rachelson is responsible for applications development at Oracle, and she gave her assessment directly to PTI, according to the TechGig report. She said the number of agents deployed matters less than the improvement they deliver, and she tied that view to the need for a measurable goal chosen at the start. The report presented her position as guidance for leaders weighing how to evaluate their AI investments. It did not give any figures for agents deployed or improvements measured.

The report described the technology as transitioning from merely helping employees to actively performing work for them, which it said necessitates a re-evaluation of traditional AI adoption metrics. It said business leaders should therefore pick a measurable goal from the outset to keep AI initiatives aligned with tangible outcomes. The article gave no further details on specific companies, timelines or results beyond Rachelson's comments. It did not say what happens next beyond the advice to measure delivered improvements.

stories.Headline: Researcher maps four decades of AI growth in echocardiography research
stories.Summary:
An investigator conducted a bibliometric analysis of artificial intelligence research in echocardiography and published the results in the Journal of Cardiovascular Imaging. This comprehensive study mapped worldwide growth in the field by evaluating literature spanning more than four decades of cardiovascular imaging. The researcher analyzed 2,682 peer-reviewed and conference documents published between 1984 and November 10, 2025. These documents collectively accumulated 35,083 citations across global scientific databases. The analysis revealed a dramatic surge in publication volume and citation visibility following 2018.

The study required a dual-source search strategy querying both Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection through November 10, 2025. Scopus provided 2,472 documents, while the Web of Science supplied 1,928 records, resulting in 2,682 unique publications after deduplication. The research tracked 1,509 original research articles, 534 conference papers, and 300 review articles. In 2024, there were 572 records, and 2025 saw 573 records before the data collection ended. The analysis focused on diseases like heart failure, valvular heart disease, coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathy, and congenital heart disease.

The investigator stated that citation metrics measure scholarly visibility rather than translational effectiveness, diagnostic rigor, or patient safety. They noted that unadjusted observational comparisons reflect scholarly attention rather than underlying methodological quality or independent causal effects. The researcher explained that reliance on two databases may have underrepresented non-English literature and unindexed regional validation studies. They also mentioned that bibliometric databases remain susceptible to positive publication bias regarding successful algorithmic benchmarks. The author concluded that future research must transition toward rigorous multicenter prospective trials.

The study found that the United States led productivity with 1,404 publications, followed by China with 784 and the United Kingdom with 512. The Mayo Clinic ranked first in institutional output with 142 publications, while the University of California had the highest average citations. Top investigators included Francisco Lopez-Jimenez with 55 publications, Zachi I. Attia with 54, and Paul Andrew Friedman with 52. Open access publishing and dedicated funding were associated with higher citation counts for the researchers involved. The United States and United Kingdom formed the most productive partnership with 237 co-authored papers.

Echocardiography has been the most widely used clinical cardiac imaging modality since Inge Edler and Carl Hertz introduced ultrasound in 1954. Over subsequent decades, ultrasound instrumentation incorporated technological advancements that expanded daily procedural workloads and created highly complex diagnostic studies. Traditional manual acquisition and interpretation encountered structural limits under growing demands for precision cardiovascular medicine. Artificial intelligence emerged as a transformative methodology to provide computational solutions for automated view classification and myocardial quantification. These tools also offer diagnostic classification and structured electronic reporting across various clinical settings.

Future efforts must prioritize algorithmic explainability and dataset diversity across different ultrasound equipment platforms. Researchers need to integrate these technologies directly into clinical guidelines and real-world cardiovascular care. The study suggests a shift from retrospective single-center model development to more rigorous prospective trials. The articles leave open how these tools will specifically impact patient safety and diagnostic rigor in practice. They also leave open the exact timeline for the full integration of AI into standard clinical guidelines.

stories.Headline: MoEngage builds Merlin AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for secure tenant-scoped data access
stories.Summary:
MoEngage built Merlin AI, a set of artificial intelligence agents that work with live platform data, and described the work in a post published on aws.amazon.com on 2026-11-16T06:00:00Z. The post was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das and Karthik Baile from MoEngage. MoEngage is the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use across channels including push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and Rich Communication Services (RCS). MoEngage treated the work as an architecture problem, asking how to give agents secure, tenant-scoped access to live data without rebuilding hundreds of existing APIs. MoEngage solved it with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model.

The MoEngage Model Context Protocol (MCP) Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand's segments, campaign history, and content library. Merlin AI runs four kinds of agents, and all four share foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for reasoning and generation, AgentCore runtime for hosting, and MCP for standardized access to data. Across all four modes, Merlin AI uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, tool-call planning, and content generation. Merlin AI Studio places purpose-built agents in the workflow: Copywriter, Designer, Segment Assist, Jinja Assist, In-app Template Builder, and Flow Assist. The architecture has four layers, namely clients, an MCP server on AgentCore runtime, MoEngage platform APIs, and foundation models in Amazon Bedrock.

MoEngage made three design choices to keep tenants isolated and identity out of the model's reach. First, the MCP server reuses the existing JWT-based authentication that MoEngage APIs already use, and AgentCore runtime validates each token before a request reaches the server. Second, workspace and user context travel in request headers that AgentCore runtime forwards to the server rather than as tool arguments, so the model does not see these values and cannot change them. Third, AgentCore runtime runs each user session in its own isolated environment, so one user's conversation cannot read another's session state. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content safety and personally identifiable information (PII) filters to agent responses, and a backend-for-frontend layer validates the structure of generated content before the MoEngage interface renders it. Users set guardrails on what each agent can do, review every action in its activity log, and choose between autonomous and human-reviewed execution.

One customer, Glance, saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates as a result. The Campaign Insights Agent, embedded on the analytics page, delegates to specialized sub-agents, one running analysis across several metrics at once, a second diagnosing why a metric is underperforming, and a third comparing performance across time periods or segments. Custom agents let lifecycle and customer relationship management (CRM) teams design agents that run continuously on MoEngage data and tools, inside rules the product and marketing team defines. Offer Decisioning selects the best offer on web and app surfaces, and Campaign Decisioning delivers 1:1 decisions across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp. MoEngage's platform APIs for campaigns, analytics, segments, content, and flows were already OpenAPI 3.0-compatible, so MoEngage used the FastMCP framework to generate MCP tools from those specifications.

The tools fall into five groups: campaign tools that create, edit, schedule, and send campaigns across channels, analytics tools that query delivery funnels, click-through rates, conversions, and cohort performance, segmentation tools that list, inspect, and create segments from behavioral and attribute filters, content tools that manage content blocks, templates, and dynamic content rules, and flow tools that inspect, pause, or modify automation journeys. The tools come from the specifications, so they stay in sync with the APIs, and when a team updates a specification, the tool definitions update with it. AgentCore runtime scales sessions as demand changes, so MoEngage does not plan capacity for traffic bursts across its customer workspaces. The built-in JWT authorizer validates tokens against MoEngage's existing identity provider, so the MCP server uses the same authentication model as the APIs. Built-in metrics, logs, and traces through Amazon CloudWatch give MoEngage engineers visibility into every session.

Hosting on AgentCore runtime is framework-agnostic, so MoEngage can change models or agent frameworks without touching the MCP server. MoEngage moves between the Claude Sonnet versions through the same Amazon Bedrock API and pays per token instead of operating GPU infrastructure. Amazon Bedrock does not use customer prompts or responses to train foundation models, which matters for a system that processes customer engagement data at scale. In a typical request, a user signs in to MoEngage and asks a question, the client sends the request with the user's existing JSON Web Token (JWT), and AgentCore runtime validates the token and starts an isolated session for that user. The agent asks a model in Amazon Bedrock which tools to call, the MCP server calls the MoEngage APIs with the user's tenant context and returns the results, and the agent then composes the answer.

In the campaign example, the user types a request to draft a weekend flash sale push for the high-value segment using the same tone as the best-performing December campaign. The agent calls the analytics tools to find the top December campaign, the segmentation tools to confirm the high-value segment, and the content tools to pull the brand voice. The post says it covers the four agent modes in Merlin AI, how MoEngage exposed its existing APIs as MCP tools, and how the architecture keeps each tenant's data isolated. The post closes with the results MoEngage customers have seen and the pattern other software providers can reuse. The article text ends mid-sentence in the campaign example, so the rest of that walkthrough is not given.

stories.Headline: Researchers say AI cuts drug discovery timelines to 12 to 18 months and costs by up to 40%
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping drug discovery by compressing timelines from a historical average of five years to as little as 12 to 18 months, according to a narrative review published on November 16, 2026. The review examines how machine learning, deep learning and advanced computational frameworks address high attrition rates and massive capital requirements in conventional pharmaceutical research. Researchers are shifting from reactive, descriptive analyses to proactive, predictive modeling that guides experimental design and uncovers non-obvious relationships between molecular structures and disease mechanisms. Modern drug discovery draws on unprecedented volumes of biological data from next-generation sequencing, proteomics and metabolomics platforms. Machine learning and deep learning have become essential for extracting meaningful insights from this biological big data.

The review says AI reduces development costs by up to 40% while compressing timelines to 12 to 18 months. Machine learning supports quantitative structure-activity relationship modeling and prediction of absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity properties. Convolutional neural networks analyze cellular phenotypes and 3D molecular structures, graph neural networks treat atoms as nodes and bonds as edges, and transformers enable context-aware modeling of protein sequences and SMILES strings. DeepMind's AlphaFold predicts 3D structures from amino acid sequences with accuracy approaching X-ray crystallography and has generated over 200 million predicted structures. AlphaFold 3 models complex assemblies containing proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules and ions, and diffusion-based tools like RFdiffusion enable de novo protein design.

The review attributes these advances to researchers integrating machine learning, deep learning and computational frameworks across the pipeline. It says AI-driven biomarker analysis groups patients to develop personalized medicine approaches considering individual genetic and molecular profiles. Machine learning algorithms identify optimal patient populations, predict treatment responses and design adaptive trial protocols that adjust based on interim results. The review states that explainable AI and uncertainty quantification methods such as Bayesian deep learning attempt to address the black-box nature of deep learning models. It says balancing complexity with interpretability remains an ongoing trade-off.

Public databases support computational modeling, including PubChem with data on more than 322 million chemical compounds, the Cambridge Structural Database for crystallography, DrugBank for pharmaceutical information and metabolomics databases like HMDB. Relay Therapeutics and Nimbus Therapeutics used AI models to design selective inhibitors for FGFR2 and TYK2 and moved them into clinical trials with greater speed. Insilico Medicine's AI-driven, end-to-end pipeline for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis moved from target identification within fibrotic pathways to generative molecular design and faster clinical testing. Researchers designed the antibody AU-007 to target the interleukin-2 pathway, activating anti-tumor T cells while preventing cytokine release syndrome. Other platforms identified PVRIG for the antibody COM-701 and mapped receptor networks for HMBD-001.

Computational models predict patient-specific neoantigen epitopes to guide personalized immunotherapies such as EVX-01 for melanoma and GRANITE-001 for solid tumors. An AI-designed HIV vaccine candidate was discontinued, which the review cites as an experimental setback in translation. Drug repurposing advanced dexmedetomidine into Phase 3 trials for agitation in Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia, evaluated talabostat for prostate cancer and identified bevantolol to reduce chorea in Huntington's disease. The NLM-Chem corpus contains 150 full-text articles annotated with approximately 5,000 chemical entities, supporting automated text-mining pipelines. Domain-adapted transformer models such as BioBERT and SciBERT achieve high relation-extraction accuracy, and architectures combining Relation BioBERT with bidirectional long short-term memory networks detect and categorize drug-drug interactions.

Biological datasets often suffer from missing values, experimental variability and systematic biases that can impact model performance and generalizability. Algorithmic bias, particularly when models are trained on datasets that fail to represent diverse populations, risks creating disparities in medical outcomes. Large-scale training and high-performance computing resources often remain inaccessible to smaller institutions and organizations in developing countries. The field lacks standardized, large-scale benchmarks and rigid evaluation protocols, and inflated performance claims often result from data leakage or inconsistent data splitting. Federated learning offers collaborative research that preserves patient privacy by training models across decentralized data sources without sharing raw sensitive information, and digital twins could enable in silico clinical trials simulating how populations might respond to new drug regimens.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Significantly Accelerates Drug Discovery and Molecular Development Timelines

stories.Headline: Autonomous agents turn static knowledge graphs into dynamic Context Graphs under six GraphRAG patterns
stories.Summary:
A practitioner's guide published on Towards Data Science outlines six agentic GraphRAG patterns that show how autonomous agents can turn static knowledge graphs into dynamic Context Graphs. The guide, reported by TechGig on November 16, 2026, describes patterns that let these graphs retain operational history and user intent. According to the content, autonomous agents carry out this transformation so that knowledge graphs can evolve beyond static data repositories. Context Graphs built this way gain the ability to remember past decisions and user interactions, which the guide says enhances their utility in complex AI workflows.

The guide sets out six distinct agentic GraphRAG patterns, and each one describes a way for autonomous agents to reshape how a knowledge graph holds and uses information. The central change it describes is the shift from static knowledge graphs, which serve as fixed stores of data, to Context Graphs that keep a record of what has happened and what users intended. Retaining operational history and user intent is presented as the main gain, because it lets the graph carry forward past decisions and interactions rather than starting fresh each time. The guide explains that autonomous agents facilitate this transformation, and it frames the resulting Context Graphs as more useful in complex AI workflows.

The guide comes from Towards Data Science, and TechGig reported on it on November 16, 2026, describing it as a practitioner's guide to the six patterns. TechGig presents the guide as detailing how autonomous agents transform static knowledge graphs into dynamic Context Graphs, and it credits the content with the explanation of how agents facilitate that change. The report says Context Graphs gain the ability to remember past decisions and user interactions, a capability it ties to their utility in complex AI workflows. TechGig frames the patterns as enhancing AI workflows with operational history, which is the benefit it draws from the guide.

The context the articles give is that knowledge graphs have worked as static data repositories, and the guide positions agentic patterns as the way past that limit. By keeping operational history and user intent, Context Graphs are said to remember past decisions and user interactions, which the guide links to better performance in complex AI workflows. The articles do not say what happens next, beyond describing the six patterns and the transformation they enable. No further steps, timelines or adopters are named in the coverage.

stories.Headline: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh forms a task force to study AI's impact on jobs and the economy
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh convened a conference in San Francisco on Monday, November 16, 2026, to examine how artificial intelligence affects the economy. He gathered technology executives and economists to discuss whether this revolution could cause massive job displacement for white-collar workers and lower the prices of services. The event served as a public forum for Warsh to explore these questions through his newly assembled task force on productivity and jobs. While he offered no immediate conclusions regarding interest rates, the findings from this group could eventually inform future monetary policy.

The Federal Reserve is currently contemplating raising interest rates in December to slow price increases caused by vast spending from AI firms. This occurs as the AI lab Anthropic prepares to price shares for an initial public offering on Wednesday, potentially raising 64 billion dollars at a 1.4 trillion dollar valuation. Meanwhile, voters in the November 3 midterms passed several state-level measures to slow the construction of essential data centers. Warsh is utilizing a task force including venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, and Stanford economist Chad Jones to provide outside expertise.

Chairman Warsh suggested that AI might create a service-sector version of the China shock, which followed China joining the World Trade Organization in 2001. He noted that while that event lowered prices for goods, it caused the loss of one million manufacturing jobs and 2.4 million jobs overall. Marc Andreessen expressed optimism about the technology but argued that heavy government regulation in healthcare and education might prevent rapid job displacement. Former commerce secretary Gina Raimondo called the anti-data center trend a very troubling sign that would be bad for the country.

The three task force members must now assemble their perspectives into a formal report for the chairman within the next few months. After this report is submitted, the Federal Reserve will debate the results to decide if they should shape official monetary policy. The central bank must determine if AI will lead to medium-term disinflation, which might eventually require the Fed to lower interest rates over the long term. Because the technology is racing ahead, the institution may need to reach a conviction on these answers sooner than originally planned.

stories.Headline: Researchers at Guangxi Medical University outline a machine learning roadmap for mapping cardiac regeneration barriers
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University conducted an analysis published in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. The analysis establishes that the adult mammalian heart has virtually no capacity to regenerate lost cardiomyocytes after injury. Machine learning algorithms applied to high-dimensional biological data offer a systematic strategy to map regulatory networks governing repair. The authors caution that direct experimental validation of artificial intelligence in cardiac regeneration remains scarce. They position their work as a methodological roadmap rather than a synthesis of settled clinical conclusions.

Heart failure is the terminal stage of numerous cardiovascular conditions and a principal cause of mortality globally. Its escalating disease burden is driven by population ageing. After myocardial infarction, most adult cardiomyocytes withdraw permanently from the cell cycle. This leads to permanent scar formation, progressive ventricular remodelling, and irreversible loss of contractile function. Adult zebrafish retain lifelong regenerative capacity, and neonatal mice have a brief window of complete myocardial regeneration that closes during the first postnatal week.

The authors state that the adult mammalian heart keeps its regenerative machinery strictly restrained. Previous cell-based therapies, including bone marrow-derived cell and cardiosphere infusions, yielded only modest clinical efficacy in trials and meta-analyses. This was due to poor graft survival, inefficient engraftment, imprecise control over lineage fate, and active suppression by the hostile host microenvironment. The biological barriers span transcriptional circuits, post-translational protein interactions, and spatial cell-to-cell communication networks. Single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and high-throughput proteomics each illuminate distinct facets but cannot alone resolve integrated biology in sparse, heterogeneous datasets.

Deep learning architectures, variational autoencoders, and graph neural networks are being deployed to model multi-omics layers jointly. Frameworks such as Weighted Nearest Neighbour, Graph-Linked Unified Embedding, and scGPT project modalities into unified latent spaces. Unsupervised dimensionality reduction including Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection and SC3 clustering identifies atrial, ventricular, and conduction-system cardiomyocyte populations. BayesSpace, GraphST, and Tangram combine spatial adjacency matrices with transcriptomic profiles to map border-zone niches. The authors emphasize that spatial co-localisation and computational neighbourhood enrichments establish descriptive statistical associations rather than proven causal mechanisms.

Delivery of transcription factors GATA4, MEF2C, and TBX5 converts fibroblasts into cardiomyocyte-like cells in vitro and enhances ventricular function in animal models of myocardial injury. The Hippo-YAP pathway, Neuregulin1 and ErbB4 signalling, Meis1 expression, and metabolic shifts away from fatty acid oxidation control cardiomyocyte cell-cycle exit and re-entry. The review identifies a persistent gap: proteomic and phosphoproteomic validations lag substantially behind transcriptional and genetic manipulations. Interpretable machine learning applied to spatial transcriptomics revealed macrophage-niche programmes driving pathological fibrosis, and targeted in vivo gene silencing using lipidoid nanoparticles attenuated myocardial fibrosis in mice after infarction. An artificial intelligence model trained on thousands of cardiac fibrosis publications mapped ten nodal pathways, confirming that fibroblast-specific deletion of Jak1 and Jak2 prevents pressure-overload fibrosis.

Monocle, diffusion pseudotime, and CellRank leverage RNA velocity and Markov chains to predict cell state transitions. Applying standard trajectory inference to adult cardiac regeneration is limited because regenerative cells exhibit extremely low basal proliferation, leaving few intermediate states. Cardiac repair involves non-linear jumps such as dedifferentiation, proliferation bursts, and redifferentiation that violate assumptions of continuous progression. Longitudinal spatiotemporal profiling of the injured adult heart remains exceptionally scarce. An artificial intelligence agent analyzing single-cell maps encompassing 1.8 million cardiac nuclei nominated a small-molecule activator of mitochondrial biogenesis that conferred cardioprotection in experimental models, and quantitative proteomics showed glutathione peroxidase 4 downregulation drives cardiomyocyte ferroptosis.

stories.Headline: Ralf Seifert proposes a five stage model to move procurement teams from AI pilots to autonomy
stories.Summary:
Ralf Seifert proposed a five stage maturity model for procurement teams on November 16, 2026. He wrote this guide to help organizations move from AI pilots to full autonomy. The model aims to map the journey toward scaling artificial intelligence in sourcing. Seifert argues that many teams currently test AI without a clear plan. He suggests a structured approach to build organizational readiness for these tools.

The model requires moving through five stages called aligned, organized, data-ready, augmented, and autonomous. It demands a spend data platform, ERP integration, operational platforms, and strict model governance. Organizations must develop their mindset, skillset, and toolset together to reach the final stage. This process requires defined decision guardrails, quality data, and a dedicated owner for AI. Success depends on matching agent autonomy to risk through spending limits and access rights.

Ralf Seifert is responsible for the model and emphasizes that pilots alone do not scale. He states that organizations must validate business value before expanding the responsibilities of AI agents. Luca Nanni, former supply chain lead at Philip Morris International, says spreadsheets hinder AI scaling. Nanni explained that his company redesigned its operating model and accelerated its process transformation. He believes a holistic change in systems and capabilities is necessary for success.

Dirk Holbach, former chief supply chain officer of Henkel Consumer Brands, says the industry is in a hype cycle. He notes that while value exists, it is not yet available at scale. A ProcureAbility survey from October 2026 found that 68 percent of leaders test AI without plans. Only 8 percent of senior procurement leaders have a defined plan for AI implementation. These figures show that a lack of organizational adoption affects many procurement teams.

SAP showcased the autonomous enterprise at its Connect conference in October 2026 with procurement featured. Novartis presented a sourcing assistant pilot co-developed with SAP to handle heavy manual tactical work. This pilot promised 35 percent higher productivity and 25 percent faster cycle times for sourcing. The articles state that the first three maturity stages provide little more than visibility. Savings leakage and supply risk are only addressed once a team reaches Stage 4.

Next, procurement leaders should ask ten specific questions about ambition, leadership, value, ownership, and skills. They must also evaluate governance, data security, scaling, autonomy, and competitiveness to determine their standing. Advanced teams must rank a portfolio by value and validate savings with finance departments. The articles leave open how many organizations will successfully move past the pilot phase. They do not state the specific timeline for reaching the autonomous stage.

stories.Headline: Max Roser finds every high-quality US survey shows more negative than positive views on AI
stories.Summary:
Max Roser of Our World in Data published an article on November 16, 2026, comparing recent high-quality surveys of American views on artificial intelligence. He wrote that he searched for a range of recent high-quality surveys and put them together in one chart. He said he was cautious about surveys because answers can shift when a question is worded slightly differently or when respondents can choose from different options. Every survey he included found that more Americans have a negative view of AI than a positive one. He wrote that he was surprised by how consistent the overall result is.

In Pew's survey, 52% say they are more concerned than excited and 9% are more excited than concerned, a ratio of more than five to one. When Pew first asked this in 2021, the ratio was about two to one. When a middle answer is offered, 37% took it in Pew's recent survey, and in both Pew's and Gallup's surveys only 9% chose a positive view. In the Ipsos survey, 17% said AI is an extremely bad thing for society and just 2% said extremely good. In a Quinnipiac poll in September 2026, 35% said they are somewhat concerned and 38% very concerned that future AI systems could threaten human survival, and 73% believe such a risk exists.

Pew's survey found that 56% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans are more concerned than excited about AI, and in both parties only around one in ten are more excited than concerned. Roser wrote that many find the prospects of AI exciting, but for more Americans the concerns are larger. He wrote that if the industry wants to earn the public's trust, it will have to take these widespread concerns much more seriously than it has so far. Pew's survey covered 3,488 US adults on the American Trends Panel, conducted June 22 to 28, 2026, with November 2021 data from the same panel conducted November 1 to 7, 2021. The Gallup and Bentley University survey covered 3,270 US adults on the Gallup Panel, conducted May 4 to 11, 2026.

The Quinnipiac poll was released March 30, 2026, based on a telephone survey of 1,397 US adults conducted March 19 to 23, 2026. The Annenberg Public Policy Center survey covered 1,320 US adults, conducted June 16 to July 19, 2026. The Ipsos survey for ABC News and The Washington Post covered 2,545 US adults on the Ipsos KnowledgePanel, conducted October 9 to 13, 2026. In the same Ipsos survey, 50% said AI is a good thing for them personally and 49% a bad thing, while 15% said it is extremely bad for them personally against 3% who said extremely good. In Quinnipiac's March 2026 poll, 55% expected AI to do more harm than good in their day-to-day life against 34% who expected more good.

Roser included only surveys based on probability samples, and Quinnipiac called randomly generated landline and cell phone numbers. The other four surveyed members of online panels recruited at random, mostly by mail to randomly selected addresses: Pew's American Trends Panel, the Gallup Panel, the panel used by the Annenberg Public Policy Center, and Ipsos's KnowledgePanel. All five surveys weight their results to match the US adult population and publish the full wording of their questions and their results. Roser did not include polls based on opt-in online panels, citing an opt-in poll that found 20% of Americans under 30 agreed that the Holocaust is a myth, when Pew's probability-based panel found 3%. In 2021, Pew introduced the question with a short definition and referred to artificial intelligence computer programs rather than artificial intelligence (AI), and Pew reports the results as one trend.

The Quinnipiac poll on concern about human survival was a telephone survey of 1,202 US adults conducted September 24 to 27, 2026 using random digit dialing, with live interviewers calling landlines and cell phones. In that poll, 14% were not so concerned, 11% not concerned at all, and 1% did not know or gave no answer. A Quinnipiac release on September 30, 2026 reported that 86% support independent safety standards for AI companies. Pew's September 16, 2026 report by Monica Anderson and William Bishop was titled Democrats are now more worried than Republicans about AI and its impact on jobs. The article leaves open how the industry should address these concerns, beyond Roser's statement that it will have to take them much more seriously than it has so far.

Articles.Title: No matter how you ask, more Americans are negative than positive about AI

stories.headline_source: No matter how you ask, more Americans are negative than positive about AI

stories.Headline: Amazon identifies AI agent campaign stealing API keys from exposed AI applications
stories.Summary:
Amazon's threat intelligence team uncovered a campaign using AI agents to steal API keys from exposed AI applications. These agents hunted for weak spots in internet-exposed apps to extract provider keys stored inside. The team captured records of this activity using decoy servers from October 3 until late last week. The agents used stolen keys to run AI models that powered the search for more keys. The team believes separate China-linked groups operated the agents based on time zones and prompts.

The campaign targeted LiteLLM, One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. It exploited default credentials like LiteLLM's master key and flaws in Langflow and RAGFlow. One API family systems were targeted via an authentication bypass through the isCliRequest header. Attackers used server-side request forgery to reach cloud metadata services and searched GitHub, npm, and PyPI. The agents also tried bypassing identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes.

Amazon's team said they cannot verify the reported outcomes but the records show what actors pursued. They stated that AI agents change the speed and persistence of attackers rather than using new techniques. The team noted that agents succeeded where basic security was missing, such as hard-coded credentials. They recommended treating AI apps like production systems and watching for unusual usage or spending. The team expressed moderate confidence that the agents ran on the open-source tool ARTEX.

Cloudflare responders saw ARTEX use a compromised CI/CD API token to make 400 database dump requests. The company noted that static tokens without expiry dates granted broad access across customer cloud setups. Microsoft reported that attackers used agentic AI tools for GitHub secret hunting to find AI inference keys. The FBI stated that attackers have used ARTEX since August against organizations in many global sectors. South Korean financial institutions were affected, with personal information of 67,000 people stolen in one campaign.

The agents used internet scanning services and certificate transparency logs to find leaked keys. They searched container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels. ARTEX uses a planner agent to split goals into tasks for worker agents running security tools. The developer made the ARTEX GitHub repository unavailable on October 8, but commercial versions remain. CISA added a related flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on May 5, 2025.

AWS customers who may have been affected have been notified by the Amazon threat intelligence team. Cloudflare suggests looking for Worker scripts named artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-*, or artex-do-*. Users should rotate exposed credentials and limit client IP addresses for their API tokens. Researchers at Cisco Talos linked more than 2,500 IP addresses to the ARTEX tool. The articles leave open whether the deepfake ID photos passed checks or if database requests returned data.

Articles.Title: Amazon Uncovers AI Agent Campaign Targeting LiteLLM, Dify, and Other Apps for API Keys

stories.Headline: APA publishes guidance urging employers to put people at the centre of workplace AI adoption
stories.Summary:
The American Psychological Association published new guidance on 16 November 2026 to help organisations introduce artificial intelligence into the workplace responsibly, warning that unclear policies and conflicting expectations risk undermining employee trust and wellbeing. The guide, titled Deploying AI Into Workplaces: What Leaders Need to Know, sets out seven recommended practices informed by established psychological research and emerging evidence about AI use. It is intended to help employers balance the potential benefits of AI with the need to protect workers, maintain meaningful human oversight and consider how technology changes the design of jobs. The guidance comes amid growing pressure on employees to incorporate AI into their daily activities, often without clear organisational policies governing its use. According to the APA's 2026 Work in America Survey, fewer than 40% of workers for whom the question was applicable knew whether their employer had an official policy on acceptable AI use, pointing to a potential disconnect between the pace of AI adoption and the development of workplace policies to support it.

Among the guide's recommendations are ensuring that safeguards reflect the potential consequences of AI errors, involving employees and others affected by AI systems in decisions about their introduction, and protecting opportunities for workers to develop expertise and learn through experience. The APA also encourages organisations to consider how AI might affect professional judgement, knowledge sharing and the development of skills over time, rather than focusing exclusively on efficiency or productivity gains. Developed with input from specialists in human-technology interaction and several branches of psychology, the guide includes practical examples of effective implementation and warning signs that organisations should recognise. APA CEO Arthur C. Evans Jr. said the rapidly growing use of AI at work is creating new behaviours and social judgments while raising questions about trust, all of which are fundamentally questions of psychology, and he asked whether using AI to write emails should change how someone is judged. He said psychological science can help organisations understand not just what AI tools can do, but how their use affects trust, decision-making and employee well-being, and that the guide gives leaders a practical framework for introducing AI thoughtfully, with people at the centre of the process.

Dennis P. Stolle, executive lead psychologist for applied psychology at APA, said purchasing an AI tool and telling people to use it without further direction is not a sound strategy. He said organisations need to invest in the people who will work with the technology, not just the technology itself, which means giving workers the information they need to judge where AI tools are reliable and where they are not, making sure human oversight is meaningful and rethinking how jobs are designed. Although aimed at employers across sectors, the guidance raises questions relevant to universities, research organisations and scholarly publishers, where AI is increasingly being incorporated into research, editorial, administrative and knowledge-management workflows. For these organisations, the APA's recommendations underline the importance of establishing clear expectations around acceptable AI use while preserving professional expertise, accountability and trust in human decision-making.

Articles.Title: APA urges employers to put people at centre of workplace AI adoption

stories.Headline: China showcases AI and robotics to world leaders at a summit in Shenzhen
stories.Summary:
China is hosting world leaders in the city of Shenzhen this week. US President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin are attending a global economic summit. The city is presented as a high-tech wonderland powered by artificial intelligence. This event showcases China's home-grown innovation and robotics to the visiting dignitaries. The city is touted as the origin story for a high-tech future.

The summit highlights a city where drones deliver dinner and driverless taxis play music. Humanoid robots at DexForce Technologies serve coffee and play chess for visitors. The city is located in south-eastern China and is close to Hong Kong. It has evolved from a fishing village to a hub for electric vehicles. Some coffee costs 30 yuan, while breakfast noodles cost under 3 yuan.

Engineer Huang Shihua says that Shenzhen is a miracle for young people. He believes that robots will serve humanity by taking on dangerous tasks. Huang claims that AI can foster equality and help emerging economies catch up. He compares the opportunity in Shenzhen to the dreams found in America. He hopes that AI will help the entire world become one family.

A construction worker says that life is hard and factories have relocated. A delivery driver in his 40s says the city is no longer a place to thrive. Ms Lu earns 200 yuan per day delivering food inside the SEG plaza. A taxi driver says his house is worth a third of its original price. Canadian and Vietnamese tourists call the drone delivery technology amazing and great.

Shenzhen grew from a fishing village into one of China's wealthiest cities. It manufactured cabbage patch dolls, then televisions, iPhones, and now advanced humanoid robots. The city is central to the bold vision for China held by Xi Jinping. However, the second-largest economy faces a property crisis and sluggish consumer spending. Many manufacturers have downsized or moved to find cheaper labour for production.

Gig work now supports 200 million workers, or 40 percent of the urban labour force. Job agent Li Xiaohe offers temporary factory jobs paying around 22 yuan an hour. Some drones now fly at night to warn people not to cause trouble. The articles leave open how many workers will fit into the AI future. They do not say if the property market will recover its original value.

Articles.Title: China is hosting the world's leaders in Schenzhen's AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see

stories.Headline: CDW's Hang Tan says CIOs must redesign core workflows so AI improves business performance
stories.Summary:
Hang Tan, chief strategy and transformation officer and executive vice president at CDW, wrote in a Nov 16, 2026 opinion article on cio.com that AI is getting smarter at remarkable speed. He said employees can now draft, analyze, search and automate routine work faster than they could a year ago. He said recent research on the state of AI shows organizations continuing to expand adoption across functions and use cases. He said that in many organizations the business still works the same way, with the same work moving through the same systems. He said AI speeds up a task and the benefit disappears into a process designed for another era.

Tan said CDW works across thousands of customer environments and has made AI assistants available to more than 14,000 coworkers. He said CDW has built more than 12,000 agents and started redesigning core workflows. He said the CIO's challenge is no longer simply enabling access to AI. He said the challenge is helping the business move quickly without creating fragmented technology, uncontrolled cost and risks that IT will ultimately have to manage. He said usage climbed quickly inside CDW but usage alone couldn't tell whether the business was performing better.

Tan said the task is not the real unit of business performance and the workflow is. He said the next phase of AI value creation will come from improving how work moves across the enterprise. He said leaders who see the workflow as the constraint are tempted to apply AI to every step, an instinct that is often a mistake. He said the better approach is to start with the business challenge, not the technology, and define the outcome that matters and work backward. He said not every problem needs an agent and sometimes a simple rule works better and costs less.

Tan said employees experiment and surface opportunities but can only change the tasks they control, not the handoffs before and after them. He said business leaders choose which workflows matter and own the outcomes and have the authority to bring functions together. He said a workflow designed from the top will struggle if the people running it have never used AI or don't trust it. He said CDW needs both broad access so coworkers build fluency and leadership focus on a few core workflows where redesign can change performance. He said neither scales if every team has to solve for tools, data, security and cost on its own.

Tan said the CIO's mandate is to build the enterprise AI foundation quickly enough and make it useful enough that business teams build on it rather than around it. He said that foundation combines approved AI tools, trusted data and business context, connections into enterprise applications and workflows, security and governance, and visibility into performance, cost and value. He said business teams won't wait for IT and will find their own tools and build their own connections if the foundation isn't there. He said the CIO then inherits fragmented data, duplicated spending, inconsistent governance, cyber risk and little visibility into what AI is doing across the company. He said a foundation that is too restrictive or hard to use drives people around it, while one that works becomes the default.

Tan said AI will keep getting more capable and the competitive difference will come from what companies are willing to change around it. He said the measure of that change isn't how much AI a company has deployed but whether the business performs better. He said that is the standard CDW is applying inside the company and the standard he would encourage every CIO to use. He said CIOs should not stop at licenses, usage or hours saved but should ask whether AI has changed an outcome the business cares about. He said companies should build the highway for AI transformation or spend the next several years managing the risks created on the side roads.

Articles.Title: Your AI is smarter. Is your business still working the same way?

stories.Headline: Northwest Arkansas Community College plans MIT partnership to create employer-specific AI training
stories.Summary:
Northwest Arkansas Community College announced last week that it plans to enter a one-year letter of intent with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Pathways for AI Training and Hiring program, according to a news release from the college. NWACC, which is described as Arkansas' largest community college, is planning to work with MIT to establish artificial intelligence training for employers in the region. The PATH program is a workforce development initiative that helps individuals find jobs as artificial intelligence becomes more prominent. The program specifically focuses on helping two-year colleges like NWACC create artificial intelligence training programs.

NWACC is seeking businesses based in the region that hope to better prepare employees as the use of artificial intelligence grows, the release states. If the new curriculum is successfully established and implemented, unique coursework will be designed for each participating employer, according to the release. The letter of intent states that success will be measured by whether the institutions can identify a significant workforce need and determine a credible, responsible and sustainable way to address it together. Officials from NWACC and MIT met in July for a workshop that also included regional business leaders, and the workshop aimed to identify sought-after skills related to artificial intelligence across different industries.

Dennis Rittle, president of NWACC, said in the release that as the region's leader in artificial intelligence education and workforce development, it is the college's responsibility to keep looking for ways to best prepare the Northwest Arkansas workforce for the AI economy at home and around the world. He said the PATH team from MIT is outstanding at helping learners, regardless of background, secure jobs in the growing AI economy. He said the two organizations will look to develop hyper-local, industry specific AI training to solve actual workforce needs. He also said he is deeply grateful for the trust PATH has placed in NWACC and excited for the opportunities it brings to the businesses and workforce of Northwest Arkansas.

stories.Headline: Executives trust AI over their own judgment twice as often as other workers, survey finds
stories.Summary:
New research from Charter's AI Pulse survey of 5,002 full-time U.S. desk workers who use AI on the job found that executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file employees to trust AI over their own judgment, Fortune reported on November 16, 2026. About a third of managers and executives say they trust AI more than their own judgment on work decisions, compared with 16.3% of non-managers, and executives are also more than twice as likely as workers to trust AI over a knowledgeable colleague. The same article notes that Gen Z approaches AI with some skepticism, since 69% of employed Gen Zers in the Voices of Gen Z study from Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation and GSV Ventures say they trust work completed without AI more than AI-assisted work. That study surveyed 1,572 Americans ages 14 to 29, and only 3% of them put the most faith in work produced entirely by AI, even though 51% of Gen Zers use generative AI at least weekly. The survey also found that 81% of executives say they always or usually fact-check AI output before using it, versus 71% of workers, and that executives are 3.3 times as likely as workers to use outputs they doubt.

In Charter's survey, 85% of executives are at least somewhat optimistic about AI's impact on their organization, compared with 56% of employees. The article recalls that in 2025, SAP research shared with Fortune found that 74% of executives trusted AI more for business advice than colleagues or friends. It adds that misplaced trust in AI carries a bigger price at the top, because when an executive leans on a flawed AI answer to decide who gets promoted, where the money goes, or how a team is restructured after a merger, employees absorb the consequences without getting a vote. Brian Elliott, Charter's executive-in-residence, who co-led the AI Pulse research, says where someone sits at the table matters more than the year they were born, and that the survey of over 5,000 AI users at work found sharper divides by career stage than by age. He says AI is great at summaries and high-level answers, which is much of what a leader needs, while workers deal with specifics where AI's gaps show.

He says executives fact-check AI more but are also far more likely to use outputs they doubt, almost certainly because they have less fear that a mistake might cost them their job. In his view the biggest driver may be pressure, since many leaders are expected to move fast and have all the answers, and he says that combination explains how a CFO might drop the CMO's campaign into ChatGPT and quiz her on it, trusting the tool over a peer who knows the context and spent weeks on the work. The article says younger workers' wariness stems from institutions they feel have failed them, from schools to employers, and that Gen Z treats AI as an assistant rather than giving it main character energy. It notes that executives are finalizing next year's budgets and AI strategies now, and that the open question is how many of those calls will rest on a leader's judgment and how many on a chatbot's general answer. It concludes that leaders who treat AI the same way Gen Z does could make 2027 a better year for the employees who live with their decisions.

Articles.Title: Everyone worries Gen Z trusts AI too much. Executives trust it over their own judgment twice as often

stories.Headline: Attackers use AI to bypass security patches and find vulnerability variants
stories.Summary:
This summer, maintainers of the vm2 JavaScript library shipped fixes for 34 sandbox-escape vulnerabilities. Anthropic's Claude co-wrote 19 of these patches, but a security researcher later used AI to bypass one. Shayaun Nejad of Rubrik performed this variant analysis for a talk in San Francisco. He presented his findings at the recent [un]prompted AI security conference.

The vm2 library sees 1 million downloads per week and uses open-source code. In June, FIRST projected 66,000 CVEs for the year, but the number is approaching 100,000. Microsoft's October Patch Tuesday addressed 1,415 vulnerabilities, compared to 180 in October 2025. Bank of America added 1,000 contractors in the second quarter to help 3,000 staff. Meta used AI for 40% of critical fixes by July, though code grew 100% year over year.

Shayaun Nejad warned that AI-assisted patches can serve as blueprints for attackers to find variants. He noted that the same bugs were often rediscovered in new testing runs. Anthropic stated that software security is now limited by how quickly humans verify and patch AI findings. David Molnar of Meta said humans are drowning in reviews and need more automation. Taesoo Kim of Microsoft warned that AI drastically reduces time for binary-diff analysis and exploit creation.

The Microsoft Edge Security team warned that attackers are using AI for patch-gap abuse. This affects downstream browsers like Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge that use the Chromium base. Epoch AI researchers used GLM 5.3 to compromise every Firefox release from September 17 to October 26. These researchers spent 1,000 dollars in credits and 12 hours per target. The process did not trigger any provider safeguards or refusals.

Rubrik and 1Password's Off-by-1 Labs observed that AI offense currently outperforms AI defense. Off-by-1 Labs found that half of 6,080 AI patches for six vulnerabilities left attack paths open. P2Patch tests showed an AI agent successfully bypassed 41 of 101 patches. Trail of Bits found one in eight human-written patches for 2,265 vulnerabilities also failed. Anthropic's Glasswing program found 37,966 vulnerabilities, but only 217 of 7,349 public flaws were fixed.

Mozilla will stop releasing regression tests associated with security fixes to prevent patch gap abuse. Fudan University researchers used an LLM framework to find 56 incomplete patches across 62 closed-source applications. This work resulted in 19 CVE assignments and 28,100 dollars in bug bounties. Some users now employ open-weight models like Qwen, Kimi, and GLM to avoid API guardrails. The articles leave open how the industry will fully automate the review pipeline.

Articles.Title: AI-written patches are becoming attack maps for hackers

stories.headline_source: AI-written patches are becoming attack maps for hackers

stories.Headline: German students use AI for homework as PISA finds lowest scores in 25 years
stories.Summary:
Young Germans have used artificial intelligence tools for two and a half years to complete school assignments. Students use these applications for subjects like math, German, English, chemistry, and physics. Many students use these tools to solve problems or explain complex academic topics. Some students admit to using AI for homework when they feel stuck. This practice is described by scientists as cognitive outsourcing of the thinking process.

The 2024 JIM study found ninety-one percent of Germans aged 12 to 19 use AI. Seventy-four percent of these students use AI for learning and homework. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani banned AI in public schools up to eighth grade for 2026 and 2027. The KMK has issued vague statements on AI use since 2024 in German federal states. These guidelines suggest students should engage with AI in a critical and responsible manner.

Teacher Franziska Müller says some students can no longer think for themselves or comprehend texts. She notes that students often read AI prepared answers aloud during her gymnasium classes. Julian Hinn believes AI can respond better to student needs than some teachers can. He suggests introducing AI in the 10th grade for students aged 15 or 16. Hinn encourages his senior students to critically question the quality of AI solutions.

Andreas Schleicher of the OECD reported that AI chatbot users get lower average science scores. The Brookings Institution argues that AI risks outweigh benefits by eroding critical thinking and memory. Students with knowledge gaps may adopt AI errors and fall further behind their peers. Affluent children may benefit more, which the PISA study says widens the existing gap. This phenomenon is called the Matthew effect, where early success leads to more progress.

The PISA study from September evaluated 15-year-olds from more than 90 countries worldwide. German 15-year-olds posted their lowest scores in the 25-year history of this specific study. The Brookings Institution conducted research with young participants from around the world on cognitive skills. The Matthew effect is based on a biblical verse from Matthew 25:29 regarding wealth. These reports highlight a decline in independent judgment and perseverance among students.

Teachers are now more motivated to challenge students to think independently and maintain personal autonomy. Students must solve problems without AI during exams or they risk failing their courses. One student told Müller he felt unable to think for himself after a poor result. The articles leave open how to balance AI support with the development of basic skills. It remains unclear if bans or strategic integration will better prevent the dumbing down.

Articles.Title: AI in German classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

stories.Headline: AI models scan filings and court records to map cross-border holding chains
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is changing how institutional investors and international founders handle cross-border due diligence and asset protection, according to an article published by Rebellion Research on November 16, 2026. The article says specialized AI models now scan corporate filings, shareholder registers and court records at the same time to map complex holding chains across three or four countries and languages. Automated Know Your Customer workflows trace ultimate beneficial owners through multiple tiers of holding companies, giving compliance teams an instant visual map of control and voting rights instead of manual cross-referencing of PDFs. Continuous screening algorithms monitor global watchlists and adverse media in real time and alert users when a counterparty's risk profile shifts, which the article says cuts onboarding delays and lowers data-entry errors.

The article says moving intellectual property, equity stakes or liquid securities into an international holding vehicle requires strict adherence to local statutory rules, because courts and tax authorities look past paper registrations to where real management decisions happen. It advises confirming that a chosen jurisdiction offers predictable commercial courts and clear creditor-protection laws, and keeping independent bank accounts, local accounting records and formal board minutes separate from operating businesses. For banks, it lists four checks: proof of economic substance such as physical operations or qualified directors, documented source of wealth through audited statements or tax filings, clarified intercompany flows of royalties, dividends or management fees, and updated beneficial ownership records ready for annual reviews. The article also warns that algorithms struggle with legal nuance and might flag a legitimate restructuring involving three jurisdictions or a newly formed trust as suspicious.

The article attributes guidance to the U.S. Mission to ASEAN, which it says highlights AI-driven threat analysis and fraud prevention as ways to strengthen cross-border defenses, and to IMTF, which it says shows financial institutions pairing automated tools with human-in-the-loop oversight for transparency and accountable decision-making. It cites Astra Trust offshore services as an example of specialists who align corporate formation, board governance and cross-border compliance across financial centers. The article's stated position is that licensed fiduciary professionals should verify statutory compliance and oversee governance while automated platforms handle repetitive KYC checks and watchlist monitoring around the clock. It concludes that software alone cannot replace the legal standing that properly licensed corporate service providers bring to multi-jurisdiction structures.

stories.Headline: Gen Z buyers use AI to shortlist homes and estimate mortgage costs
stories.Summary:
Gen Z consumers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to research homebuying, according to a 2026 Homebuyer Insights Report from Bank of America. These young buyers use the technology to shortlist properties, estimate mortgage payments, and calculate closing costs before contacting agents or lenders. The report found that 32 percent of Gen Z, 28 percent of millennials, and 20 percent of all prospective buyers or homeowners used AI tools in the past year. Most users focused on financial affordability, with 57 percent estimating costs and 55 percent learning about the general homebuying process.

The shift requires real estate firms to scale their technology, though JLL research shows 90 percent of companies are testing AI while only 5 percent have met their goals. More than 60 percent of these firms are unprepared to scale beyond pilots, and only 33 percent of workers feel adequately trained. In early 2026, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac introduced governance frameworks for accountability and human oversight, while MISMO released a voluntary toolkit in June. Additionally, a revised law in Colorado regarding automated decisions is scheduled to take effect on January 1.

Matt Vernon, the head of consumer lending at Bank of America, stated that AI is now a meaningful first step in the journey for buyers. Despite this trend, the report indicates that 55 percent of buyers still prefer humans for touring homes and 54 percent want human legal advice. The Urban Institute noted that AI already assists with underwriting, valuation, and fraud detection to lower costs and speed up servicing. They suggested that lenders should measure success by how many more people become and remain homeowners.

The real estate industry is currently undergoing its largest transformation in a generation, which the World Economic Forum compares to the early days of the internet. Companies with C-suite sponsors for their technology programs are three times more likely to succeed than those without such leadership. The Urban Institute has launched a new initiative on AI in mortgage finance to track these developments. Future success for firms will depend on training their staff and proving measurable results to keep pace with AI-savvy buyers.

Articles.Title: Gen Z Turns to AI to Navigate Homebuying

stories.Headline: Moonshot AI uses Kimi models to pursue scientific discoveries in biology and chemistry
stories.Summary:
The Beijing-based artificial intelligence start-up known as Moonshot AI recently announced its intention to utilize Kimi models for scientific discovery. This strategic move was highlighted by the company during a keynote address delivered at the Web Summit technology conference in Lisbon late last week. The organization is now competing with rivals from the United States to transform artificial intelligence into a powerful engine for research. By focusing on these goals, the company aims to push the boundaries of what current machine learning models can achieve. This new direction requires the development of more advanced reasoning capabilities to handle complex data in specialized fields.

The company is specifically pushing into the realms of biology, chemistry, and pharmaceutical research to find new breakthroughs. These scientific applications demand a much higher level of intelligence than those used for standard coding tasks. The transition involves moving beyond general purpose AI to create tools that can solve intricate problems in the natural sciences. Giacomo Ficari, who serves as the director of international for Moonshot AI, spoke about the potential of this shift.

He stated that the real excitement for the company lies in the field of science. Ficari explained that while finance and legal applications are at the same intelligence level as coding, science pushes that level even higher. He believes that the ability to reason through scientific problems represents the next major frontier for their technology. More to follow.
