stories.Headline: NTT Data's supply chain head urges firms to connect isolated AI uses through multiagent systems
stories.Summary:
Pedro Béjar Castán published an article on 13 November 2026 on nttdata.com urging organizations to stop doing isolated AI and to implement multiagent systems. He wrote that the CEO talks about AI in broad terms while the innovation team runs proofs of concept and some business functions have started pilots. He said demonstrations, vendor conversations and internal experiments are all happening at the same time. He wrote that proof is emerging that AI adds value, yet he keeps hearing the same thing: "We don't know what to do next." His answer is that organizations probably don't need another use case and need to connect the ones they already have.

He described multiagent systems, where multiple AI agents work together across a business process to interpret what is happening, coordinate the response and take action. For a manufacturer that wanted to define and implement agentic intelligence throughout its value chain, NTT DATA ran 14 workshops for customer service, production, logistics and warehousing departments. The team spoke with more than 60 people and cataloged 129 improvement opportunities by the end of the process. Following a multiagent approach let NTT DATA group the 129 individual improvement opportunities into just 36 prioritized AI use cases. In one project, some shifts needed 10 frontline operators and others 4, and truck arrival patterns drove much of the staffing volatility.

Béjar Castán, managing director and global head of supply chain at NTT DATA, said he is responsible for leading NTT DATA's work with the World Economic Forum's Advanced Manufacturing and Supply Chain initiative. He wrote that NTT DATA combines deep industry and process knowledge with AI strategy, consulting, engineering and implementation expertise. He said NTT DATA can look across a value chain to identify where AI can make the biggest difference, connect opportunities that might otherwise be treated in isolation and then design, build and integrate the multiagent systems. He said plenty of firms will help you think, some partners specialize in strategy and others are strongest at implementation. He said what is harder to find is a partner that can do both.

He wrote that in supply chain management AI is already improving forecast accuracy, flagging changes in demand patterns, surfacing supplier risk earlier and optimizing transportation routes. He said each use case enhances only a single activity and a human is still required to pass the separate pieces of intelligence on. He described a multiagent environment where the system reads an order, checks the quantity against expected demand, identifies anomalies, evaluates stock-out risk over a two-week horizon, recommends a revised quantity, updates the planning system and notifies the people who need to know. He said multiagent systems are mostly used in software at the moment but will increasingly extend into the physical world through autonomous handling equipment, vision systems and connected assets on plant floors. He said a logistics specialist thinks about transportation and a warehouse manager thinks about staffing, and AI creates more value when you look at the process connecting the two.

He wrote that organizations have introduced AI capabilities function by function, launched pilot programs and encouraged employees to experiment with AI tools. He said this has led to many small use cases that save individual teams time and effort, but those use cases must be organized and connected for the organization as a whole to benefit. In one project, warehouse managers worried about staffing while the logistics team reported that trucks turned up early, late or in clusters at the docks. He said the two problems were in reality one use case, and looking at them together has allowed NTT DATA to synchronize operator availability with inbound and outbound truck movements. He said that if you can predict an important truck will be two hours late, you can place fewer employees in loading and more in preparing customer orders before the gap opens up.

He listed six steps: set the ambition, identify improvement opportunities, define the use cases, prioritize the use cases, choose your technical architecture and build a roadmap. He said most discussions and arguments are about prioritizing use cases, weighing the value each could create and whether the organization is ready to deliver it. He asked whether an organization has the data availability, process maturity and systems integration to make an effective AI use case. He wrote that the processes connected today could eventually be executed by physical AI, so it makes sense to prepare for that transition. stories.Headline: Damac chairman Hussain Sajwani says his Anthropic stake earned more in under two years than 30 years of investing

Hussain Sajwani, the 72-year-old chairman of Dubai-based luxury real estate developer Damac Properties, said at the Bloomberg Invest Dubai forum that what he made in 30 years he made in Anthropic in less than two years, according to Livemint. He said that between only three companies, OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic, the group is making a few billion dollars of profit.

Sajwani founded Damac Properties in 2002, and according to Forbes he started out in the food services business, catering to the US military and construction giant Bechtel, before shifting to real estate in 2001 after Dubai allowed foreigners to own property. Forbes puts his net worth at $15.3 billion, making him the 185th richest man in the world. stories.Headline: CoreWeave partners with Wayve to accelerate AI training for autonomous vehicles
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, a provider of cloud computing for artificial intelligence, announced a multi-year agreement with Wayve on November 15, 2026. Wayve develops embodied intelligence and is currently building an AI Driver intended for use in robotaxis and personally-owned cars. This partnership aims to accelerate the training of AI for autonomous vehicles by utilizing specialized cloud infrastructure. The collaboration focuses on improving the driving intelligence layer through advanced computing resources.

Wayve will now train its foundation models on CoreWeave Cloud using Nvidia Blackwell GPUs to expand its simulation, evaluation, and training capabilities. This transition follows a period where Wayve utilized Weights & Biases before scaling its operations to the CoreWeave platform. The AI Driver learns from real-world data collected across more than 70 different countries to ensure safety and physics are integrated. Such complex workloads require purpose-built cloud solutions that offer high reliability during long training runs and detailed observability.

Silvius Rus, the senior vice president of engineering at Wayve, stated that accessing this specialized cloud helps accelerate the commercial deployment of their AI Driver. He explained that their system improves by gathering real-world experience, training on that data, and deploying only the versions that outperform existing software. Gavin Jackson, the vice president of international at CoreWeave, noted that the agreement brings one of the most demanding physical AI programs in the world to their platform. He added that companies moving AI into the physical world need infrastructure designed for training and simulation to work together.

CoreWeave has demonstrated its performance through record-breaking MLPerf benchmark results and a top Platinum ranking from SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX three times in a row. The company also earned a number-one ranking for price-performance and inference speed for Moonshot AI’s Kimi K2.6 and Kimi K2.7 Code during independent benchmarking by Artificial Analysis. These technical achievements support the reliability needed for Wayve to validate safety at scale. The partnership represents a shift toward integrating AI more deeply into physical world applications.

stories.Headline: Rackspace and Together AI sign binding inference infrastructure agreement for 2027 deployment
stories.Summary:
Rackspace and Together AI announced an initial multiyear inference infrastructure agreement on November 10, 2026, and the CASRAI Editorial Board published its account on 15 Nov 2026. The agreement is binding, and deployment is planned for 2027 subject to financing and other conditions. Rackspace and Together AI signed the inference infrastructure agreement, with deployment planned for 2027. The announcement says the deal does not establish general availability of a new research service. The companies also entered a nonbinding letter of intent to explore joint enterprise offerings.

Rackspace says it expects to operate dedicated NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems, including power, liquid cooling, networking and storage. Together AI expects to provide the managed platform. GPU financing had not been finalized, and facilities, power and equipment availability are also conditions. The nonbinding letter of intent covers joint enterprise offerings, which need further agreement. Data residency, security and compliance features would depend on the specific offering and customer arrangement.

For research offices assessing a future offering, CASRAI's reading is that the service arrangement needs to specify data flows and operational responsibilities. Dedicated hardware alone does not answer where prompts, outputs and logs will go or who can use them. That assessment belongs alongside the institution's research data governance review. NIST's AI RMF Govern playbook recommends connecting AI risk management to data governance, model testing, monitoring and incident response. Applying that approach means identifying who approves the workload, who reviews model outputs and who handles operational incidents.

Together AI's existing privacy documentation says prompt storage is on by default, while sharing data for model training is a separate opt-in that is off by default. Its organization settings govern requests made with that organization's API keys. The zero data retention documentation distinguishes request content from other records, and enabling the option affects subsequent requests. Usage metadata remains, and explicitly uploaded fine-tuning or batch files remain stored until deleted. A university should establish which settings, retained records and deletion arrangements apply to its proposed workload.

The CASRAI article cites Rackspace's strategic agreement with Together AI of November 10, 2026, checked 2026-11-15. It cites Together AI's privacy and security documentation and its zero data retention documentation, both checked 2026-11-15. It cites the NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern section, checked 2026-11-15. stories.Headline: Knightcorp warns that silent AI policies leave technology firms facing disputed claims
stories.Summary:
Knightcorp has published its Forerunner Report - Technology, which examines insurance issues tied to AI, cyber risk, cloud exposure, directors' liability and connected devices, according to a report dated 15 November 2026. The research argues that insurance reviews are struggling to keep pace with how technology businesses now operate, especially where companies rely on AI tools, cloud infrastructure and third-party software platforms. It presents insurance less as an annual procurement exercise and more as part of broader risk governance for finance leaders, boards and technology teams. One central finding is that policy wording may not clearly address AI-related claims, since some professional indemnity and cyber policies are silent on AI. The report says that silence could leave room for disputes over whether cover applies when businesses build AI into their own products or use AI embedded in third-party platforms.

Citing Lander & Rogers, it says AI exclusions are appearing in some policy wordings, which adds pressure on companies to check whether their existing insurance arrangements match their use of the technology. On cloud and vendor platforms, it says undeclared systems, or systems that do not fit a policy's wording, can become a point of dispute during claims, and it suggests businesses map third-party systems that handle client data and then test how each one is treated in policy applications and wording. The report applies the same logic to connected hardware, saying companies that make or supply smart devices should check whether new mandatory security standards apply to them, including rules banning universal default passwords on in-scope consumer devices manufactured after a specified threshold, and it adds that undeclared connected devices may affect how insurers assess a claim. On governance, the report highlights recent action by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission over misleading sustainability claims, noting that penalties in greenwashing cases involving Mercer Superannuation and Vanguard Investments fell on the companies involved. It says that focus raises wider questions for boards about how they substantiate public governance statements, and it advises organisations to examine how directors' and officers' cover would respond if directors were drawn into proceedings, whether that insurance sits in a standalone policy or within management liability cover.

The report also notes that organisations covered by the Privacy Act which use automated decision-making in certain ways will need to disclose that use in their privacy policies, and it refers to a Federal Court development in the Medibank matter, where Deloitte reports prepared after the cyber incident were found not to be protected by legal professional privilege. Trent Brown, chief executive officer of Knightcorp, said the issue for companies is whether insurance arrangements still reflect the pace of change inside technology businesses, and he asked whether risk and insurance arrangements still reflect the business a company has become, since in technology a business can change faster than the systems around it. Justin Geldart, an account director at Knightcorp, said that where a policy is silent on AI the outcome is uncertain and coverage can be disputed, and he encouraged technology leaders to ask how their cover treats AI they build versus AI they buy, because the answer can differ. Jessica Tanner, key account manager for technology at Knightcorp, said claims tend to be tested on what was declared and how the policy defines it, and that for a technology business the practical question is whether the wording and the application reflect the platforms the business actually relies on. The report includes tools to help organisations assess that question, among them a matrix of exposures, a broker checklist for AI risk, examples of where claims uncertainty can begin and an 11-question insurance readiness checklist.

stories.Headline: ESET survey finds 66% of Australian businesses faced AI-related cyber threats in the past year
stories.Summary:
ESET reported on 15 November 2026 that 66% of Australian businesses faced at least one AI-related cyber threat over the past year, based on a survey of 400 cybersecurity decision-makers and influencers across Australia. The research also found that AI use is already widespread, with 92% of organisations either using or piloting it in at least one business function, including fraud detection, customer service, content generation, document processing, threat detection and software development. As AI use has spread, businesses have reported a mix of internal and external risks, with employee misuse of generative AI cited by 34% of respondents and 33% saying they had experienced data leakage through AI platforms. Another 30% reported AI-generated phishing or impersonation attacks, while 29% said they had faced AI-enabled deepfake or voice-cloning attacks.

Most respondents said their organisations had introduced at least some measures to manage those risks, with 89% having at least one safeguard or policy in place or planned and 11% having none. The most common steps were monitoring access to AI tools and their outputs, cited by 49% of respondents, internal responsible-use guidelines followed at 48%, and restrictions on uploading sensitive data to AI platforms at 47%. Beyond AI-linked threats, 72% said they had experienced at least one major cybersecurity incident during the past year, and of those, 35% said they had dealt with three or more incidents. Cloud environment breaches and business email compromise were the most commonly reported incident types, followed by credential theft or abuse and insider threats, while 80% of affected organisations said they could detect and respond to their last significant incident within 24 hours.

Parvinder Walia, President of the APAC region at ESET, said AI was becoming more closely tied to day-to-day operations and decision-making, and that as it gains access to more data and influence over decisions, organisations must ensure the right oversight and safeguards are in place. He said trusting AI also means knowing how and where it is being used, and that in cybersecurity speed changes the outcome, since a threat left undetected for hours can quickly become a business-wide incident. He said organisations need continuous visibility, rapid response and access to deep expertise to contain threats early and protect business continuity, and that phishing and social engineering show why the human layer of cybersecurity cannot be overlooked. He said that as AI makes malicious communications more convincing and personalised, organisations need to continuously build employee awareness through relevant training and realistic simulations, and that technology can stop many threats but a well-prepared employee can help stop the one that gets through.

The survey found no single dominant cause behind cyber incidents, with weak, stolen or compromised passwords the most commonly cited cause at 37% among affected organisations, followed by phishing or social engineering and user actions or human error at 34% each. Training is already common, with 92% of organisations saying they provide cybersecurity training at least annually, yet employee awareness and training remained the top cybersecurity challenge, cited by 50% of respondents. The report said security priorities are shifting as businesses expand their use of AI, cloud services and connected technologies, finding that 69% of organisations are using or planning to adopt managed detection and response, while 48% are currently covered by cyber insurance and 33% are planning to obtain cover. However, 95% reported challenges in obtaining or maintaining cyber insurance, with rising premiums the most common barrier at 47%, and among organisations affected by incidents, 14% reported significant financial loss.

stories.Headline: MiTAC Computing unveils full-stack infrastructure to scale agentic AI for enterprises
stories.Summary:
MiTAC Computing Technology Corporation unveiled a comprehensive AI infrastructure ecosystem at the SC26 event in Chicago on November 16, 2026. The company showcased its full-stack innovation at Booth 4615 to address compute, thermal, and data bottlenecks associated with enterprise AI deployment. This initiative involves strategic collaborations with partners including AMD, Canonical, DDN, Intel, NVIDIA, and Rafay to build scalable AI factories. The system utilizes high-density liquid cooling, disaggregated inference, and end-to-end orchestration to handle the surge in inference workloads.

The infrastructure requires a disaggregated AI inference engine developed with Skymizer, using the MiTAC G8825Z5 server with AMD EPYC 9575F or 9755 processors and AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs for prefill processing. For the decode stage, the air-cooled MiTAC G4520G6 server uses Intel Xeon 6 processors and eight Skymizer HTX301-4S accelerator cards to provide 2 TB of aggregate memory. This configuration allows the on-premises execution of massive models like the 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 large language model. Additionally, the upcoming ORv3 44OU Helion Agentic AI Rack will scale up to 32,768 AMD Zen 6 CPU cores.

Rick Hwang, the President of MiTAC Computing Technology, stated that cohesive infrastructure is necessary for scaling agentic AI rather than using fragmented systems. He explained that MiTAC provides the foundational full-stack solution required to make sustainable AI factories a reality for enterprises. The company also integrated Canonical Ubuntu for security, DDN Infinia for low I/O latency, and Rafay for GPU-as-a-Service orchestration. These components are managed by the proprietary MiCoreView software, which provides unified visibility and deep telemetry across the entire data center.

The company is also showcasing rack-scale innovations, including a 52U liquid-cooled rack with 96 AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and a ZutaCore waterless two-phase cooling system. This cooling technology supports thermal design powers exceeding 4,000W and achieves an annualized pPUE of 1.03. MiTAC further offers various server platforms, such as the G4827Z6 and G2610Z6, which leverage NVIDIA MGX architecture and Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. These diverse hardware and software integrated solutions are designed to empower businesses to meet future challenges in high-performance computing.

stories.Headline: Imec and ASRA publish ACIR requirements for automotive chiplets
stories.Summary:
Imec and ASRA unveiled the document “Automotive Chiplet Interoperability Requirement,” or ACIR, on November 12, 2026. The two partners presented ACIR as an open architectural requirements catalog for interoperable chiplets in the automotive sector. According to imec, the document is intended to facilitate the introduction of a cross-vendor chiplet ecosystem. Imec is a European semiconductor research organization, and ASRA is a Japanese organization. The announcement was reported by igorslab.de on November 15, 2026.

ACIR complements existing standards and focuses on what chiplets in automotive applications must deliver at the system level. The document covers fault and system management, boot procedures, power management, functional safety and automotive-specific interoperability. It addresses coordination of key die-to-die connectivity requirements so that independently developed chiplets can communicate reliably after integration into a larger system. Another focus is a shared fault-reporting infrastructure, so that faults are reported and handled in a way that allows safe and predictable responses. ACIR was published less than a year after imec and ASRA announced their strategic collaboration on automotive chiplet architectures.

Imec states that ACIR is intended as an open reference for OEMs, Tier 1 suppliers, semiconductor manufacturers, IP and software providers, system integrators, tool vendors and research institutions. According to this approach, the document describes what interoperable automotive chiplets must support without prescribing how individual companies implement these capabilities internally. Imec and ASRA describe ACIR as a tool for reducing risk and accelerating the adoption of automotive chiplets. The partners say the first version, made publicly available, will also incorporate feedback from the industry. According to imec, the document was jointly developed by ASRA and imec’s now-expanded Autonomous Edge Chiplet Program.

The article states that ACIR brings together the European semiconductor research community and Japanese automotive and SoC development. The article says a shared requirements catalog from Europe and Japan increases the likelihood that chiplet architectures in cars will not split into several isolated camps. The article states that the involvement of two established industry and research networks gives the document considerably more weight than an internal specification from a single manufacturer would have. The article says the automotive industry is organized globally, while standardization is often fragmented along regional or company-specific lines. The article states that vehicles are built through a long chain of OEMs, Tier 1 suppliers, semiconductor companies, software providers and integrators.

The article states that computing requirements in vehicles have been increasing for years, driven by driver assistance systems, semi-autonomous and autonomous functions, high-resolution sensor processing, AI-assisted decisions, and increasingly complex infotainment and cockpit systems. The article says this demand has so far been met primarily by monolithic SoCs that integrate CPU cores, accelerators, memory controllers and other functional blocks on a single die. The article states that larger dies drive up development costs, increase the risk of costly design errors and make economical use of advanced manufacturing processes more challenging. The article says high-performance CPU cores, AI accelerators, I/O logic, safety units, and analog or specialized controllers do not necessarily benefit from the same process node or have to be developed by the same manufacturer. The article states that chiplet architectures combine multiple specialized dies in a shared system, which can make development and cost structures more flexible.

The article states that ACIR is not the end of a standardization process but rather its visible beginning. The article says the practical relevance of ACIR will likely depend on how widely the requirements are accepted and adopted in real designs. The article states that whether ACIR is sufficient in practice depends on how the requirements are translated into concrete products and validation procedures. The article says a document alone does not create interoperability, but merely creates the conditions for different companies to align their components toward a common goal. The article states that ACIR is initially a requirements catalog, not a finished standard with guaranteed market success.

stories.Headline: Arist CEO Michael Ioffe predicts AI agents will recommend most major corporate decisions including layoffs
stories.Summary:
Michael Ioffe, the cofounder and CEO of the startup Arist, said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on November 16, 2026, that AI agents will increasingly recommend major corporate decisions, including layoffs, while executives keep the final say. He predicted that within the next few years the majority of significant enterprise shifts, such as products being launched or layoffs being made, will be recommended by agents. Arist uses AI agents to interview employees, comb through company data and recommend solutions to business problems, and it already works with more than 15% of the Fortune 500. Ioffe said the technology can gather insights from thousands of employees in just 72 hours, a process that traditionally requires teams of consultants.

Ioffe said an executive will always make the final call, and he sees AI's biggest opportunity in helping companies identify problems and act on them faster rather than replacing executives or consultants. Before an agent can recommend something as consequential as a layoff, it must understand what is happening inside a company, so Arist's agents can decide whom to interview, ask questions and weigh responses against information such as an employee's tenure, performance and past engagement scores. Ioffe said that helps the system distinguish the loudest complaints from problems affecting the wider organization, and that the agents will push back if an executive frames a question to get the answer they want. He argued that employees may be more candid with AI agents than with another person, and he said that if a company can get to the truth much faster, a 50,000-person enterprise can move at the speed of a 50-person startup.

Ioffe said he did not set out to compete with consulting firms, and he described how at 19 he became interested in delivering education to students in war-torn Yemen and built a text-message-based learning platform before shifting Arist toward training employees at Fortune 500 companies and becoming one of OpenAI's early partners. He noticed that companies would pay consultants millions to diagnose a problem and then pay Arist a few hundred thousand dollars to train employees to fix it, and in his experience the consultants got the diagnosis wrong about 90% of the time, which prompted Arist to move from training employees to diagnosing problems. He pointed to a major software company whose data was merely pointing out what was happening instead of why.

The prediction comes as more companies cite AI when cutting jobs, sometimes drawing accusations of "AI washing," or blaming technology for cuts made for other reasons, and the article says that even when companies genuinely expect AI to replace workers, moving too quickly can backfire. HR leaders have warned that companies risk losing valuable talent when they cut workers without a clear plan for how AI will replace their work, according to previous reporting cited in the article. The article also notes that gathering information through AI agents could raise concerns about how candid employees are willing to be with an agent working on behalf of their employer, especially when its findings could influence decisions about their jobs.

stories.Headline: South Korea orders audit of IT assets to counter AI-driven cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
The Presidential Office of South Korea ordered a comprehensive audit of information technology assets on November 15, 2026, to combat cyberattacks powered by artificial intelligence. This initiative targets the private sector, the government, and the military to ensure that security vulnerabilities are addressed before they become public. The National Security Office held a joint response meeting on November 13, which was chaired by third deputy director Song Ki-ho. During this session, participants reviewed a full survey of network and system configurations that has been ongoing since August.

The new strategy requires the establishment of a management system to accurately identify hardware and software assets across all sectors. This effort involves close cooperation between the National Intelligence Service, the Ministry of National Defense, and the Ministry of Science and ICT. Officials plan to accelerate the adoption of a software bill of materials to quickly identify systems affected by specific vulnerabilities. Additionally, the government will seek early warnings about security flaws from software vendors, overseas government agencies, and related professional communities.

The National Security Office explained that AI-enabled attacks are increasing while existing network diagrams often differ from the assets actually being operated. This discrepancy makes it difficult for individual institutions to respond quickly when new security vulnerabilities emerge in their systems. By securing information before it is publicly disclosed, the office intends to implement preventive measures more effectively. The goal is to create a more agile defense mechanism that can keep pace with the evolving nature of AI-driven threats.

stories.Headline: Nvidia board investigates CEO Jensen Huang over conduct and potential foreign intelligence ties
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares dropped as much as 8.79 percent to 170.24 dollars on November 9 after reports emerged regarding Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang. The company founder admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a recent internal memo, while the board of directors launched an independent investigation into his conduct. This probe examines whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation involving Alice Huang, a former senior executive at a semiconductor firm. U.S. intelligence authorities suspect that Alice Huang may have been recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security to approach the executive.

The current scrutiny follows a 40 page report published on May 13 by Culper Research which alleged that Nvidia evaded U.S. export restrictions. Culper Research estimated that over 20 percent of computing revenue for fiscal 2026 was linked to China through a Singaporean firm called Megaspeed. The report claimed Megaspeed received funding from Alibaba and saw its debt and equity grow from 33 million dollars in 2023 to 3 billion dollars by late 2024. It also noted that 2.9 billion dollars in refundable deposits of unclear origin were transferred to subsidiaries like the Malaysian company Speedmatrix.

The board of directors hired outside legal experts to lead the investigation but stated they have no reason to believe company secrets were compromised. They expressed continued confidence in Jensen Huang, although the executive previously described his interactions with Alice Huang as routine business contacts. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives warned that Huang might have to step down depending on the investigation results, which could create a leadership vacuum. Such a vacancy might disrupt product launches and investment decisions for the broader artificial intelligence ecosystem, including partners like OpenAI.

The controversy may lead to tighter regulatory scrutiny of Nvidia's business in China despite previous requests from Huang for the U.S. government to ease export restrictions. Since the Culper Research report was released, Nvidia shares have fallen about 20 percent while the S&P 500 has gained approximately 2 percent. The Chinese government has denied all allegations of espionage, and no specific spying activity has been confirmed by officials. Analysts believe that prolonged uncertainty regarding the future of the chief executive could threaten the overall stability of the company's management.

stories.Headline: Nvidia board removes CEO Jensen Huang following reports of extramarital affairs
stories.Summary:
The board of Nvidia prepared to remove CEO Jensen Huang around November 11, 2026, following several serious personal allegations. Huang eventually resigned as president, CEO, and board member after reports of affairs with two different women emerged. One woman is suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence, while the other is a senior executive at Nvidia. These events created the most serious leadership crisis in the history of the world's largest AI semiconductor company. The board considered meeting as early as November 11 to determine the future of the company's founder.

The board's decision followed allegations involving Alice Huang of Megaspeed in Singapore and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Powell joined the company in 2008 and reported directly to Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 with two engineers. Huang owns about 3.6 percent of the company, which lacks a dual-class share structure for enhanced founder voting rights. The board will now adopt a full chairmanship structure, and Colette Kress will serve as the interim CEO. Kress will also keep her current roles as the company's chief financial officer and executive vice president.

Independent directors hired attorney Joon Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to lead an independent investigation. Huang wrote a letter to employees on November 8 admitting he was unfaithful to his wife and apologizing. He initially expressed his intention to remain in his position before the allegations regarding Kimberly Powell became public knowledge. When the New York Times contacted him about the reports, Huang told the reporter not to reach out directly. Neither Kimberly Powell nor the company issued an official response to the reports regarding the alleged extramarital relationship.

Investors fear a leadership vacuum because Huang personally managed over 60 direct reports and led all major company decisions. The FBI and U.S. intelligence officials are investigating whether Huang shared national security secrets with Alice Huang of Megaspeed. China's Foreign Ministry denied the spy allegations and told the United States to stop fabricating narratives for technology blockades. Market reactions were sharp, with shares dropping 8.1 percent to 159.59 dollars, erasing 340 billion dollars in market value. Analysts like Stacy Rasgon noted that the transition would be difficult because Huang and Nvidia were essentially one.

Huang transformed Nvidia from a gaming chip maker into an AI leader, introducing the GeForce 256 GPU in 1999. In 2006, he developed CUDA, and he later secured early support from Sega and cooperation with TSMC founder Morris Chang. He built strong ties with Samsung Chairman Lee Jae-yong, SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, and firms like Microsoft and Google. Huang also persuaded President Donald Trump to ease export restrictions and committed 90 billion dollars to various partnership deals. Despite these successes, the New York Times reported that Huang had rejected internal succession planning for several years.

The board is now searching for a permanent successor to replace the founder who led the company for 33 years. Potential candidates mentioned by media include Apple's Johny Srouji, Arm CEO Rene Haas, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, and Lori Huang. Other unlikely candidates include AMD CEO Lisa Su and Intel's Lip-Bu Tan, while the U.S. Congress tightens export controls. The investigation will now examine internal controls and compliance with the company's code of conduct regarding the reported affairs. It remains open whether the leadership change will ripple across the broader AI ecosystem and affect global capital flows.

stories.Headline: Nvidia probes CEO Jensen Huang over relationship with suspected Chinese intelligence asset
stories.Summary:
Nvidia launched an independent internal probe into CEO Jensen Huang on November 8, 2026, after he admitted to marital infidelity. The investigation follows allegations that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset for China's Ministry of State Security. Intelligence officials believe Alice Huang may have attempted to use the relationship to obtain sensitive information about advanced semiconductors and U.S. administration developments. While Huang apologized to shareholders and colleagues in a memo, it remains unproven if any classified secrets were leaked or if espionage occurred.

The board of directors formed a special committee of independent directors and external legal counsel to review potential risks to national security. This process occurs as House Committee Chairmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford requested a closed-door briefing with Huang on November 18. Additionally, Senator Chris Coons announced a congressional investigation on November 8 to examine the company's security protocols. The situation caused Madison Huang, a senior director at Nvidia, to cancel her November 8 visit to Seoul for Nvidia AI Day 2026.

The board stated they have no reason to believe company secrets were compromised and expressed continued confidence in the leadership of Jensen Huang. In his internal memo, Huang admitted he was not faithful to his wife and stated there is no excuse for his actions. Regarding broader security, Nvidia claims that meetings with Asian cloud customers involve only ordinary business information rather than trade secrets. The company is now requiring some Southeast Asian customers to use the Fleet Intelligence system to track the location of AI accelerators.

This controversy coincides with reports that Chinese firms Neumatrix and MagInfra may have bypassed export restrictions to obtain H200 chips. Allegations suggest Neumatrix is linked to the sanctioned private equity firm Wise Road, while MagInfra shares ties with the sanctioned server company Inspur. These findings have intensified government scrutiny of Nvidia's customer screening and the U.S. approval process for chip exports. The company continues to operate while facing increased political pressure and potential constraints on its global business strategy.

stories.Headline: S&P Global rates AI-linked debt as analysts warn concentrated exposure may magnify credit risk
stories.Summary:
S&P Global has taken a central role in rating a growing wave of AI linked debt instruments that are attracting institutional demand, according to a report published on November 16, 2026. S&P Global Ratings has assigned relatively high grades to structures backed by AI related projects that are drawing capital from insurance companies. Analysts have raised concerns that complex repayment terms and concentrated exposures within these AI themed securities could magnify credit risk. The report says the growing use of S&P Global ratings on AI related debt should not be the only factor investors consider today.

The report says S&P Global operates in the capital markets industry as a provider of benchmarks, data and analytics, and its credit ratings on AI related debt directly influence how insurers and other large investors assess and compare risk across this emerging segment. It says the S&P Global narrative rests on the group using AI, data and capital markets activity to turn complex financing trends into high margin, repeatable services. The report says the main condition for this thesis is that S&P Global converts its investments in AI driven productivity, private markets transparency and energy data into high margin growth across divisions. It says the news leans into the catalyst that S&P Global can monetise an 8 trillion dollar maturity wall through more structured and themed issuance.

The report says the catch is that concentrated exposure to a handful of tech borrowers means those ratings are now more exposed to a single theme than traditional diversified securitisations. It says that pressure point sits squarely in the risk section that already flags dependence on healthy issuance volumes and investor confidence in Ratings. The report says that if analysts start questioning whether AI related tranches are understood as well as they are scored, it gives critics of traditional ratings models fresh material, including at rivals like Moody's and Fitch. It says the more scrutiny builds, the more investors may look at S&P Global's own debt disclosures and risk frameworks for clues.

The report says raw headlines about AI debt only become useful once you link them back to the S&P Global Narrative, because that is what turns a single theme into a full investment decision. It says readers might want to see where analysts expect the business to be a few years from now and how far that is from today. The article is general in nature and was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St, and it states that it is not intended to be financial advice.

stories.Headline: Hari Suciono says AI construction drives inflation before productivity gains arrive
stories.Summary:
Hari Suciono wrote an opinion piece on November 15, 2026, about artificial intelligence. He explains that AI is currently driving inflation during its construction phase. This happens before the technology can provide long term productivity gains. The physical economy behind the software is creating these higher costs. This process involves building data centres, power plants, and transmission networks.

Data centres consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, which was 1.5 percent of global consumption. Demand may reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, exceeding the current electricity use of Japan. Global investment in these centres reached approximately US$500 billion in 2024. In Ireland, data centres used 22 percent of electricity in 2023. Virginia regulators approved a 2027 tariff for customers using more than 25 megawatts.

Hari Suciono, an economic practitioner at Bank Indonesia, says AI requires enormous capital and skilled labour. He argues that the cloud is not weightless and relies on physical infrastructure. Suciono suggests that governments should require large data centres to bear their own infrastructure costs. He believes projects must demonstrate additionality by financing new generation and grid capacity. He urges the use of macroprudential oversight instead of relying on interest rates.

Ordinary ratepayers and households are affected when data centres compete for limited electricity capacity. In Ireland, one study estimated that this demand added 360 euros to average household costs from 2015 to 2023. Manufacturers and retailers may eventually pass higher electricity costs on to their consumers. Emerging economies might import inflationary costs before they receive any productivity benefits. Some studies found data centres caused only 4 percent of US utility rate increases.

The articles state that AI is expected to automate routine work and optimise supply chains. It promises to improve forecasting and reduce the cost of producing various goods. However, the infrastructure is expanding faster than regulatory frameworks and energy systems can adjust. This creates a paradox where a cost reducing technology first raises local prices. The boom also creates financial stability risks for banks and nonbank lenders.

Central banks must now decide how to respond to inflation caused by capacity investments. They risk making power plants and housing more expensive if they tighten policy too aggressively. Financial authorities need to monitor corporate leverage and credit concentration linked to AI. The articles leave open whether expected AI revenues will actually materialise for lenders. It remains unclear if the productivity dividend will arrive before the economy is destabilised.

stories.Headline: Federal Reserve economists find AI data center commitments top $1 trillion while productivity gains stay muted
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board published working paper FEDS 2026-074, titled Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence, with DOI 10.17016/FEDS.2026.074. Federal Reserve Board economists Nick Carollo, Leland D. Crane, Daniel Garcia Molina, and Joseph Nichols authored the paper. The paper documents that U.S. capital commitments for artificial intelligence data centers have surged past $1 trillion. It also finds that aggregate macroeconomic productivity gains and labor market disruptions remain muted. The paper evaluates how generative AI infrastructure is rippling through national accounts.

Planned domestic data-center construction climbed from roughly $300 billion in 2024 to more than $1 trillion in announced pipelines by 2025. Using the project forecasting methodology from Brandsaas et al. (2025), the authors estimate baseline annual data-center investment will step up from $100 billion in 2024 to over $880 billion by the end of 2027. That exceeds 2.0% of U.S. GDP, with approximately one-third of the outlay funding physical structures. Two-thirds is absorbed by high-tech equipment including GPUs, TPUs, high-density memory, and server cooling systems. The authors calculate an import share of roughly 50% for high-tech compute hardware, with components primarily sourced from East Asian fabrication and packaging corridors.

Carollo and colleagues report that high-bandwidth memory and specialized printed circuit boards saw annualized price increases of nearly 8% through early 2026. This reversed a multi-decade trend of technological price deflation. Surging electricity requirements prompted a sharp rise in power-generation interconnection requests in late 2025. The paper finds generative AI has yielded negligible measurable impact on aggregate U.S. labor productivity and Total Factor Productivity. Econometric decomposition indicates recent post-2023 productivity pickups primarily reflect cyclical supply-chain normalization rather than AI diffusion.

On November 13, 2026, at the UC San Diego Economics Roundtable, Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson delivered a keynote titled New Technology, Old Questions: Productivity Puzzles and the Macroeconomy. Jefferson invoked Robert Solow's famous 1987 paradox that you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics. Jefferson noted that early personal computer investment in the late 1980s required more than a decade of organizational adaptation before aggregate productivity accelerated. Daron Acemoglu (2025) estimates cumulative TFP gains of only 0.7% over the next decade, while Filippucci et al. (2025) reach 0.3 to 0.9 percentage points annually. Jones and Tonetti (2026) and Demirer, Musolff, and Yang (2026) confirm coding agents accelerate syntax generation, but software deployment remains tightly bounded by human review and integration testing.

On November 12 at Yale University, Governor Michael S. Barr presented remarks on American Inequality and the Future of AI, analyzing findings from the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances. Barr warned that because AI infrastructure requires massive capital reserves, financial gains are heavily concentrated among top software firms and high-wealth equity holders. Governor Christopher J. Waller, in his November 10 speech at the Bank of England Watchers Conference on The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism, emphasized labor resilience. Waller noted that aggregate claims, vacancies, and payrolls show no sign of widespread displacement. New York Fed research (Abel et al., 2025) and independent market analysis from TradingView report that only ~10% of workers use AI daily, with firms primarily augmenting existing roles rather than reducing headcounts.

The Federal Reserve's November 13, 2026 Financial Stability Report says equity valuations are partly driven by enthusiasm for super intelligence and details rapid growth in data center debt. The working paper keeps its analysis distinct from the central bank's semi-annual Federal Reserve Financial Stability Report, which focused on debt liquidity and bank credit exposures. Foundation model providers capture ~19% of U.S. software gross output, and broad experimentation contrasts with limited intensive daily integration. NBER research by Alvarez et al. (2026) shows that data centers generate brief construction bursts but minimal long-term local employment. The findings carry operational lessons for university research offices, campus HPC directors, and sponsored programs teams navigating hardware scarcity and escalating compute costs.

stories.Headline: DataMeds AI interim co-CEO Gerald Commissiong outlines a 2026 turnaround and healthcare AI roadmap
stories.Summary:
DataMeds AI, Inc. released a fourth quarter 2026 corporate outlook on November 16, 2026, from Interim Co-CEO Gerald Commissiong. The release was issued through ACCESS Newswire from Tampa, Florida, and was updated to remove a word from the first line of the original subhead. The company trades on NASDAQ under the symbol MEDS and was formerly known as Wellgistics Health, Inc. The outlook covers strategy across recent investments in what the release calls the company's emerging healthcare ecosystem. The release states the company is in an ongoing turnaround focused on financial discipline, strategic investments and proof-of-concept revenue generation before driving for scale in 2027.

The release describes a roadmap to consolidate future U.S. healthcare intellectual property, which it calls a once-in-a-generation opportunity for consumers to fight back. It cites a recent Menlo Ventures report finding healthcare is AI's biggest vertical market, with spend growing 2.5x to $3.7 billion, more than double the next largest vertical, legal. The company says it has 5,724,857 common shares outstanding, including 2,745,900 common shares deposited in the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation available for trading. Stockholders holding approximately 1,333,930 common shares entered lock-up agreements precluding sale of their shares into the market for at least ninety days from the release date. The release states there are no debt, preferred equity or warrant securities eligible to convert into free trading common shares as of the release date, and that 80,826 cash warrants are outstanding, each with a fixed exercise price of $35.00 per share, currently eligible to be exercised into free trading common shares.

Commissiong said healthcare in America is broken and that the focus must go back toward helping the patient, insured or uninsured, who ends up subsidizing the costs. He said the business model is rooted in cutting out the middleman so the payor pays a fair price and receives beneficial health outcomes. He said DataMEDS' objective is to narrow the arbitrage between what you are paying for and what you are getting. He said the company must leverage patients' data to rein in what he called the army of middlemen gouging the industry, initially in GLP-1 patient management, one of the most expensive pockets of the healthcare ecosystem. He said the company aims to improve regimen compliance, manage titrating up as therapy is initiated and titrating down as the need for therapeutic intervention lessens, help patient behavior, provide support products at the right time to manage side effects and help physicians monitor patients more efficiently.

Commissiong said a Florida-based Health Maintenance Organization decided to work with DataMEDS around its Health Lives Here initiative to implement a formulaic process around helping members manage their health journey. He said success in providing useful insights and delivering better outcomes, lower costs or both would prove a scalable business model allowing the company to capture more institutional payors. He said the company's physical healthcare infrastructure leverages its own pharmacy, lab and telemedicine platforms together with its proprietary independent pharmacy network. He said the recent acquisition of Helomics underscores the vision to improve outcomes while reducing costs, calling cancer one of the most devastating diagnoses and simultaneously one of the most profitable healthcare industries. He said most patients are willing to allow their data to be used in a de-identified way to help improve treatment paradigms, and the company expects to create new intellectual property that will add to its proprietary positioning.

The Menlo Ventures report, titled "2026: The State of AI in Healthcare," states that domain-specific spend is 50% of healthcare organizations' AI spend, more than 2x the average enterprise. It states AI for drug discovery spend jumped from $30 million to $700 million, a 23x increase, as pharma deploys AI at scale. It states Microsoft and Epic took 68% of new scribing dollars, while early scribes are extending into new categories. It states clinical copilots grew 5.5x to $550 million and patient engagement 4.5x to $450 million, versus 1.3x for coding and billing. It states payer AI spend lags 19x less versus providers, while 43% say provider AI coding has increased their costs.

DataMEDS incorporates its EinsteinRx artificial intelligence platform and PharmacyChain blockchain-enabled smart contracts platform into the Health Lives Here mobile application from Tollo Health, LLC. Its pharmacy-related Corexa Health subsidiary provides pharmacy dispensing and pharmacy-related services, including distribution of products developed by Tollo Health. DataMEDS owns Helomics Corporation, a Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania-based commercial clinical molecular diagnostics laboratory focused on the ChemoFx Assay chemotherapy selection diagnostics test that aims to help oncologists make chemotherapy treatment decisions. The release states the company is headquartered in Tampa, Florida, and directs readers to https://datamedsai.com. The release includes forward-looking statements under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 and states the company undertakes no obligation to update or revise them except as required by law.

The release lists media contact James Lambert, Vice President at Rubenstein Public Relations, at 212.805.3024 and jlambert@rubensteinpr.com, and investor contact IR@datamedsai.com. It states investors should refer to the company's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission for additional information regarding capitalization and outstanding securities. It states the forward-looking statements are based on management's current expectations and are not predictions of actual performance. It states actual results may differ materially due to risks and uncertainties described under "Risk Factors" in the company's most recent Annual Report on Form 10-K and subsequent filings. It states readers are cautioned not to place undue reliance on the forward-looking statements, which speak only as of the date of the release.

stories.Headline: Stanford review finds AI boosts task completion but not durable learning across 52 causal studies
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, Stanford University's SCALE Initiative released an expanded evidence review examining 52 causal studies on artificial intelligence in education. The review found that AI tools frequently enhance real-time task completion and student confidence. It found that durable learning gains remain highly inconsistent. The review cautions university researchers, institutional review boards, and evaluation teams that passive cognitive offloading often undermines conceptual retention compared to structured pedagogical scaffolding. The report is titled The Evidence Base on AI in K-12: A November 2026 Review.

The report was published by the AI Hub for Education within the Stanford Center for Opportunity Policy in Education, the SCALE Initiative. It was authored by Seth Walker, Lily Fesler, JP Martinez Claeys, Chris Agnew, and Susanna Loeb. The synthesis expands a March 2026 baseline of 20 papers by adding 32 newly published causal studies released between October 2025 and June 2026, bringing the total evidence base to 52 rigorous investigations. The Stanford repository enforces strict methodological criteria, including only randomized controlled trials and well-identified quasi-experimental designs. The March 2026 review included zero student-facing causal studies in operational U.S. elementary and secondary schools, while the November update captured the first five domestic K-12 trials, though most research remains concentrated in adult and higher education contexts.

The authors highlighted a notable shift in setting toward the first five domestic K-12 trials. The core finding across the 52 evaluated studies is that educational outcomes diverge sharply based on whether AI provides cognitive scaffolding or enables cognitive offloading. When tools deliver Socratic guidance, clarify misunderstandings, and structure problem-solving steps, students achieve modest gains in conceptual mastery comparable to human tutoring. When students use models to offload intellectual tasks such as generating complete essays, code, or mathematics solutions, durable learning declines. In-session task completion accelerates, but unassisted post-tests reveal marked performance deficits compared with peers using traditional learning materials.

In multiple randomized experiments, students using AI reported elevated confidence, decreased anxiety, and perceived mastery, yet their objective exam scores failed to demonstrate measurable academic advantage. Generative fluency often conceals genuine comprehension deficits. Generative platforms reduced teacher preparation time for lesson plans, reading level adaptations, and grading rubrics without compromising curricular quality as assessed by subject-matter experts. Automated diagnostic systems providing feedback to novice tutors improved pedagogical technique and pupil outcomes. In classrooms where teachers relied heavily on automated instructional prompts, spontaneous teacher-student interaction declined, occasionally dampening student motivation.

Across evaluated platforms, students rarely logged the dosage required for measurable academic impact unless usage was mandatorily integrated into structured class periods. Following the rollout of foundational models in 2023, vendors widely promoted AI as an automated one-on-one tutor capable of rapid learning acceleration. Commercial claims overwhelmingly rested on correlational customer surveys lacking control groups. The Stanford SCALE Initiative established the AI Hub for Education Research Repository in early 2025. Independent coverage by Education Week underscored the tension between school district technology procurement and the finding that homework offloading undermines student retention.

Analysts emphasized that districts have deployed significant funding without established pedagogical guardrails governing home use. Reporting in Chalkbeat highlighted equity concerns, noting that under-resourced schools often lack the staffing needed to guide student AI interactions effectively. Researchers quoted across both outlets echoed Susanna Loeb's conclusion that AI is not a uniform intervention, but a medium whose efficacy is defined by how educators structure student engagement. Educational AI studies must incorporate delayed, unassisted post-tests to distinguish real skill retention from transient tool assistance. Investigators should formalize outcome measures and analytical models in advance by completing a study protocol preregistration, preventing selective reporting in a field facing commercial pressure.

Institutional review boards must adjust evaluation standards, and protocol assessments in classroom environments must evaluate cognitive risks and control-group fairness alongside privacy protections when students are exposed to task-offloading software. Experimental reproducibility requires detailed sharing of prompt templates, model versions, and interaction logs. Researchers should support their findings with an open data availability statement and maintain compliance via institutional responsible conduct of research training programs. The Stanford AI Hub for Education will continue updating its repository monthly.

stories.Headline: A systematic review finds AI achieves high accuracy in cancer imaging but needs prospective multicenter validation
stories.Summary:
A systematic review of 180 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 found that artificial intelligence systems, particularly those using deep learning, show consistently high performance in cancer detection and prognostic modeling across imaging modalities and tumor types. The review was published in Discover Artificial Intelligence, volume 6, issue 1, Article 1531, by N. A. R. Mohamed in 2026. Scienmag reported on it on November 15, 2026, in an article by Nathaniel Bowman. The study selection followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines to identify original research applying AI to major oncological imaging tasks. Early research focused on convolutional neural networks for basic pattern recognition, and the field has since evolved toward architectures integrating imaging with clinical and genomic information.

The review covered computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography, mammography, histopathology, dermoscopy and endoscopy, and assessed each study with the QUADAS-AI framework. Several high-quality cohorts reached area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values above 0.90 for cancer detection, and certain curated whole-slide histopathology datasets reached an AUC of 0.99. Mammography-based deep learning models for breast cancer screening reported AUC values between 0.89 and 0.96, while lung cancer screening studies using 3D convolutional neural networks trained on over 42,000 CT scans achieved an AUC of 0.94. Approximately 20 percent of studies lacked clear documentation of recruitment methods or exclusion criteria. Only 21 percent of included studies performed external validation using independent datasets, and only 14 percent incorporated multicenter datasets.

The authors emphasize that prospective, multicenter trials are the necessary next step to verify robustness in routine clinical workflows and reliable performance across populations and technical environments. The reviewers identified persistent limitations in reporting standards concerning patient selection, data flow and timing. They note that deployment must occur without increasing the reporting burden on clinicians or introducing workflow complexities. The review states that ongoing monitoring of system performance is essential, as models may require periodic updates against evolving scanner technologies and changing clinical protocols. The authors identify future priorities including robust outcome-based clinical endpoints, federated multicenter validation strategies and continued development of explainability frameworks.

The review notes that saliency mapping and feature attribution techniques have been used to improve clinician trust by visualizing the diagnostic basis of predictions. Regulatory science frameworks increasingly emphasize structured reporting standards such as CLAIM to ensure clinical deployments are safe, effective and consistent. Federated learning approaches were noted for mitigating privacy and data-sharing constraints, allowing collaborative training across institutions without centralized patient data. The review states the highest clinical evidence currently supports AI as an adjunctive tool in breast and lung cancer screening, metastatic detection in digital pathology, and classification of dermatologic and endoscopic lesions. The review says AI could reduce workload pressure on radiology and pathology services while maintaining standards for patient care and early disease intervention.

Benchmark datasets such as BRATS facilitated advancement of U-Net and V-Net architectures, with more recent transformer-based models like UNETR further improving accuracy of 3D tumor segmentation and characterization. Handcrafted feature extraction allowed researchers to predict tumor phenotypes, survival outcomes and potential responses to immunotherapy in patients with lung cancer and glioblastoma. Vision transformers and self-supervised pretraining methods have emerged as particularly influential in enhancing representation learning for volumetric and cross-domain data. These methods reduce dependence on large, manually labeled datasets, which have traditionally been a bottleneck in training and generalizability across institutions and scanners. Multiparametric MRI applications for prostate cancer provided automated lesion localization and Gleason grade prediction.

The review notes that integrating tools into picture archiving and communication systems and existing electronic health record workflows requires overcoming medico-legal, technical and process-oriented hurdles. The ability to predict responses to therapies such as neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy in rectal cancer without excessive manual intervention highlights the practical utility of advanced architectures. The research landscape is shifting toward large-scale foundation models and more tightly coupled molecular-oncology frameworks. The review leaves open how prospective, multicenter validation will be conducted and how reporting gaps in patient selection, data flow and timing will be closed. It also leaves open how regulatory, workflow and monitoring requirements will be met as scanner technologies and clinical protocols change.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Collin Hansen warns pastors that AI cannot replace scripture and prayer
stories.Summary:
Collin Hansen, editor-in-chief of The Gospel Coalition website, raised the question of whether pastors can trust artificial intelligence in an essay titled "Why AI Will Write Your Next Sermon," and he discussed the issue further in a telephone interview with columnist Terry Mattingly, whose piece was published on November 15, 2026. Hansen said AI had become a nearly daily part of his life over the past couple of years, as it has for many others, and that he has found help with home repairs, diet and exercise plans, meal preparation, trip planning, personal health assessments, and even baseball swing and pitching advice for his son. The deeper question, he said, is how AI will handle the problems pastors face as the faithful wrestle with parenting and careers, marriage and morality, sin and forgiveness, questions that affect work in the pulpit as well as private hospital conversations and prayers. Hansen said the software professionals who build these platforms struggle to separate factual questions from those focusing on ethics and morality, and he warned that pastors who seek AI help with sermons need to understand that. He asked whether AI means people do not have to study and remember the Bible as much, and said that doing so turns what used to be Bible study into some kind of science that can be chopped into pieces and processed, perhaps with another AI program.

He said the computer system does not recognize what happens in counseling, evangelism, apologetics and deathbed ministry, where there is a difference between asking AI to supply the answers you need and your own personal, intimate familiarity with the scriptures, and he said those distinctions will be lost on people who think these tools will make things more efficient. Religious leaders and pastors need to pause and ask what they are being efficient for, what they are trying to accomplish, what they will say to these people and how they will pray for them if they are not formed in the scriptures and in prayer themselves, he said. The article cited the third annual "State of AI in the Church" survey, conducted by AIforChurchLeaders.com, ChurchTechToday.com and others, which found that AI has moved from novelty to normal, with 93.5% of church leaders actively engaging with or exploring AI in their ministries. Two years ago 13% totally opposed the use of artificial intelligence in church work, and now only 2.4% say that, while 43% of church leaders reported using AI every day, double the 2024 rate, and 78% used AI weekly or more, up from 43% in 2024. The survey also found that 64% of participants used AI when doing sermon research or writing, and that a mere 9% of churches have a formal policy on using AI agents.

A Lifeway Research survey of Protestant pastors yielded more modest numbers, with less than 50% saying they are using AI, only 10% describing themselves as regular users and 32% experimenting with it, while 18% were intentionally avoiding AI and 20% claimed they were simply ignoring AI trends; 62% of pastors in that survey worry that users are not being honest about how they were using AI in ministry, and 55% affirmed that God has always shared His Word through people and AI isn't a person. Hansen said everyone knows AI programs can help users who are not gifted writers or speakers appear more literate, but it is also clear that these platforms struggle to separate questions about facts and those about doctrine. He said AI knows better how to answer Bible questions than a seminarian or an average pastor, but that a person will not get good, ethical, trusted advice from AI unless they ask for it. If pastors ask about the Ten Commandments, he said, they will hear the mean ethical take of an AI engineer in Silicon Valley in the year 2026, a human pretending to be an objective computer, and they will not hear the God who thundered on Mount Sinai.

Articles.Title: MATTINGLY: Can pastors trust AI?

stories.Headline: Career experts advise job seekers to build networking relationships before asking for help
stories.Summary:
Online job applications have become easier to send but harder to get noticed through, because employers increasingly use automated screening tools to evaluate large numbers of applicants, according to the Associated Press. Employment experts say that having inside connections from professional networking can help job seekers stand out when the robots threaten to reject a resume outright. LinkedIn career expert Catherine Fisher said networking is important whether or not someone is searching for a job, and that it is not just a nice-to-have because it sets a person apart and gives an edge. The advice was reported by Newser on November 15, 2026, in an article that also carried an unrelated item about Kalshi dropping Donald Trump Jr.

The experts offered several tips, starting with developing relationships before asking for help. Indeed career strategist Matt Berndt said networking is about relationship-building and that a common mistake is approaching it transactionally, meaning people reach out only when they need something. Instead of asking about job leads straight off, he suggests approaching contacts for specific career information or advice, such as asking about the job market and compensation where a contact works if you are thinking about relocating. Another way to start a conversation is to follow people on social media and comment on their posts.

Nisha Chittal, chief of staff at Vox, said first messages to a hoped-for professional contact should be brief and to the point. If you are inquiring about openings, she advises against asking vaguely about upcoming opportunities that would match your qualifications, and suggests instead asking whether the contact has or knows of openings for a specific position. Chittal also said a quick no to an online application does not necessarily close the door, because a personal recommendation is worth a shot since many recruiters are bombarded with applications and appreciate hearing about promising candidates. She said that generally if you have that kind of referral, someone will give the application a serious look, and that it is a tough environment to be job searching right now, so anything that makes a personal connection helps when there are many hundreds of applicants for a job.

stories.Headline: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander corrects reporter who cites false AI stat and warns against trusting AI
stories.Summary:
On Friday, the Oklahoma City Thunder lost 113-112 to the Los Angeles Clippers at Intuit Dome in an NBA Cup game, their third straight defeat, despite Shai Gilgeous-Alexander scoring 40 points. During the postgame press conference, a Los Angeles reporter asked Gilgeous-Alexander a question built on a statistic about his first-half assists that the reporter had taken from an AI-based search engine. Gilgeous-Alexander, the reigning back-to-back NBA MVP, corrected the reporter by saying the figure was a false stat. After Gilgeous-Alexander gave a routine answer about his efficient 40 points, the reporter admitted in a joking way that the incorrect stat had come from AI. The reporter then quipped, "Gotcha, don't trust AI," and Gilgeous-Alexander replied as he walked off the podium that people should definitely not do it.

The exchange changed nothing about the result, which saw the Clippers score the final seven points to escape with the one-point win, and Gilgeous-Alexander missed a shot at the buzzer. The loss was Oklahoma City's third in a row and dropped the Thunder in the NBA Cup, while Gilgeous-Alexander's 40 points came in a losing effort. The articles give no further numbers, dates or names beyond the 113-112 score, the 40 points, the two MVP awards and the Intuit Dome setting. Coverage of the moment spread through HoopsHype, ClutchPoints, Awful Announcing, Thunder Wire and other outlets, with headlines calling Gilgeous-Alexander the NBA's preeminent Anti-AI King. The articles do not say whether the reporter or his outlet faced any discipline, correction or policy change after the exchange.

The reporter is responsible for the incorrect statistic, having relied on AI search results without cross-checking the information, as Awful Announcing noted most people hardly do. Gilgeous-Alexander said the stat was false and, when the reporter joked about not trusting AI, told him not to do it and definitely not to do it. The articles do not name the reporter or identify his outlet beyond describing him as an LA reporter. The Thunder star's response drew praise online, with fans saying they love when players put media in their place and calling him the man. The articles do not quote the reporter beyond the few words of the quip.

The context is a difficult stretch for Oklahoma City, which the articles describe as a growing injury crisis and a depleted roster, with fans noting half the team is out. Gilgeous-Alexander has admitted the Thunder are maybe having their toughest stretch ever, and coverage says coach Mark Daigneault cannot ask him to become everyone as supporting players must step up. The articles do not say what happens next for the reporter or his outlet, and they give no follow-up beyond the exchange itself. Oklahoma City's next game and any response from the team or the reporter are not covered in the articles provided.
