stories.Headline: AI cameras detect nearly 19,000 potential driving offences in a two week West Midlands trial
stories.Summary:
An artificial intelligence trial uncovered nearly 19,000 potential driving offences during a two week period. The trial took place in March and used AI powered cameras to detect dangerous road behaviours. One image showed a driver drinking from a bottle of wine while another driver inhaled from balloons. Cameras also captured drivers holding mobile phones and people failing to wear their seatbelts. One shocking image showed a front seat passenger holding an unrestrained small child on their lap.

Cameras were installed outside Ladywood fire station in Birmingham and Fallings Park in Wolverhampton. Ladywood saw 11,045 potential seatbelt offences and 1,163 potential mobile phone offences. Fallings Park recorded 6,030 potential seatbelt offences and 757 potential mobile phone offences. The West Midlands Combined Authority funded the trial with the police and fire service. No enforcement was planned as a result of this specific two week AI camera trial.

Road Safety Commissioner Mat MacDonald said the findings highlighted a huge problem with regional driving behaviours. He stated that the results pointed to a widespread culture of potentially lethal behaviours behind the wheel. MacDonald, an NHS doctor, said he was not surprised by the high number of mobile phone users. He noted that it is almost impossible to walk a street without seeing someone dialling and driving. He expressed hope that this technology could eventually be rolled out more widely in the region.

Police and crime commissioner Simon Foster said the trial findings were deeply concerning for the authorities. Dr Christophe Bastien of Coventry University said the technology offers an objective way to understand motorist behaviour. He noted that risky behaviour remains more common than many people think based on these results. Bastien said AI systems are not perfect and should support rather than replace existing police enforcement. The trial affected drivers in Birmingham and Wolverhampton who were captured by the AI sensors.

Road safety data from 2025 linked unfastened seatbelts to 133 deaths on roads in the UK. The same 2025 data showed that mobile phone use was linked to 32 deaths across the country. Mat MacDonald was appointed as the new road safety commissioner in January 2025. He previously served as the chairman of the campaign group known as Better Streets for Birmingham. The AI cameras were trained to recognise specific patterns like drivers using their mobile phones.

The trial was stopped earlier than planned because of the high number of detected road offences. Officials are now talking about the resourcing needed to make this technology viable on the roads. MacDonald said the ultimate goal is for the number of camera activations to reach zero. Foster is evaluating the results to see how AI can be used for future police enforcement. The articles leave open whether the technology will be officially adopted for permanent road enforcement.

stories.Headline: AI removes code scarcity and makes human judgment the next constraint in software delivery
stories.Summary:
The article, published by ET CIO on 16 November 2026, says artificial intelligence has removed the scarcity of code in software delivery. It says AI now moves code generation, testing, documentation, prototyping and analysis through much shorter cycles. It says lower effort and cost are expanding production capacity and bringing more choices around priority, technical fit and trust. It says human judgment is emerging as the next constraint in AI-enabled software delivery. It says every technological breakthrough removes one constraint and exposes another.

The article says that for much of the digital era, building software required significant time, talent and investment, which kept engineering capacity limited. It says that ability to create software was a source of competitive advantage. It says features left in backlogs, workflow automations, customer experiences and new digital products can become more feasible as those economics change. It says greater production capacity puts more weight on where it is directed. It says more possibilities bring more decisions around priority, business value and the outcomes worth pursuing.

The article is by Saravana Kumar Dharmarajan and was updated on 16 November 2026 at 08:00 AM IST. It says companies need to implement effective governance frameworks to manage the intricacies of AI-generated results. It says organizations can maximize resource efficiency and turn software surplus into significant achievements by aligning technology investments with tangible benefits. It says the answer about where value lies will influence how organizations use the additional capacity AI makes possible. It says judgment, business context, decision quality, architecture, trust, attention and accountability carry more of the load as organizations gain this ability.

The article says the evolution of artificial intelligence is reshaping software delivery, emphasizing enhanced decision-making over traditional methods. It says attention will turn toward delivering business value and quality outcomes with an increase in organizational capacity. It says technology organizations have traditionally linked delivery capacity with output. It says more developers, larger teams and higher velocity gave organizations the ability to build more. It says lower barriers to software creation have led to an increase in the value of the capabilities that guide what gets built.

The article says agentic AI refers to systems that can understand context, reason, make decisions and take action. It says AI agents need access to real-time, relevant and trusted data and the ability to work across applications and workflows. It says they must operate within appropriate security, governance and human oversight frameworks. It says their deployment must be connected to clear and measurable business outcomes. It says the question is becoming what the enterprise needs to put in place for AI to act safely, intelligently and at scale.

The article says the question is no longer simply what AI can do. It says the challenge now is building the foundations to scale AI securely and responsibly, with real-time data, trusted intelligence and a clear focus on measurable business outcomes. It says the article was read by 1097 industry professionals. It leaves open what scarcity comes next and where value lies when software becomes easier to create. It does not say what governance frameworks companies should adopt.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: European leaders discuss AI risks to elections at Dublin summit
stories.Summary:
European governments are concerned that states or organised actors could use artificial intelligence to spread misleading content and manipulate public opinion, even to influence election results, according to a report by Filip Polo in Politis. Cyprus' 2028 presidential election is not outside the scope of these concerns over foreign interference and electoral manipulation through artificial intelligence, the report said. Fabricated videos, images and audio recordings that appear authentic can be mass-distributed to mislead voters and shape public opinion. Officials argue the risks go beyond false news, since an organised campaign can damage candidates' credibility, confuse voters and set the election agenda. The issue was discussed with particular emphasis at the informal European Council summit in Dublin on 13 November, where European leaders held a dedicated discussion on artificial intelligence for the first time.

President Nikos Christodoulides told the summit that the malicious use of technology to influence elections threatens all EU countries and that prevention must be in place before interference occurs. Speaking on the sidelines in Dublin, he referred to recent incidents involving schools and to election developments in Romania and other countries, saying the threat concerns the whole European Union. Asked whether Cyprus is also at risk, he said that once such phenomena are recorded in other member states, all countries are vulnerable. He noted that 2027 will be a year of elections across Europe, making it more important for citizens to be informed and for governments to adopt preventive measures. He said authorities should not simply analyse malicious actions after they occur but should have a framework in place so such actions cannot take place.

At EU level, efforts are under way to introduce specific measures to prevent and counter disinformation and electoral manipulation, and these initiatives are expected to apply to Cyprus as well. Leaders also discussed Europe's position in the global race for artificial intelligence, noting a strong research base and dynamic start-ups but heavy dependence on non-European providers for advanced models, computing power, microchips and cloud infrastructure. Arthur Mensch, co-founder and chief executive of France's Mistral AI, presented the prospects for a stronger European ecosystem, and Geoffrey Hinton, awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024, highlighted the broader challenges of the technology's development. On 10 November, the Council of Ministers approved Cyprus' first National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, with a horizon extending to 2032, aiming to make the country a trusted artificial intelligence hub in the Eastern Mediterranean. Christodoulides said the technology sector contributes around 15% of Cyprus' GDP and announced a visit to the United States at the end of November to attract companies and encourage the return of Cypriot professionals working abroad.

stories.Headline: MarketBeat's screener selects seven AI stocks led by Tempus AI and SentinelOne
stories.Summary:
MarketBeat published on November 15, 2026 a watchlist of seven artificial intelligence stocks chosen by its stock screener tool. The seven are Tempus AI, SentinelOne, Hut 8, Fermi, Upstart, SoundHound AI and Extreme Networks. MarketBeat said these companies had the highest dollar trading volume of any artificial intelligence stocks within the last several days. The article said artificial intelligence stocks are shares of companies that develop, supply or substantially use AI technologies, such as chipmakers, software firms and cloud providers. Tempus AI traded down $4.29 on Friday to $71.60, on 5,290,976 shares against an average volume of 6,460,177.

Tempus AI has a 52-week low of $40.77 and a 52-week high of $89.09, a current ratio of 2.61, a quick ratio of 2.48 and a debt-to-equity ratio of 2.70. Its fifty day simple moving average is $72.84 and its 200 day simple moving average is $57.54. stories.Headline: Rackspace raises 2026 revenue outlook and targets 20 to 22 megawatts of AI capacity by end of 2027
stories.Summary:
Rackspace Technology reported on November 16, 2026 that its third-quarter revenue fell 9.3% to $609.1 million, while its Public Cloud segment declined 17.2% over the same period. Despite that revenue decline, the company's adjusted EBITDA rose 8.5% to $75 million, and the company raised its 2026 revenue outlook. The company also said it expects to operate 20 to 22 megawatts of AI computing capacity by the end of 2027. Rackspace signed a multi-year deal to provide Blacksmith with 2 megawatts of compute and storage capacity in Northern Virginia, with deployment expected to start in early 2027.

Rackspace said the 20 to 22 megawatts of AI capacity could potentially generate $420 million to $460 million in annualized revenue when fully deployed and utilized. The company and Together AI signed a non-binding letter of intent to explore enterprise AI services and a joint sales strategy, and any offerings depend on further agreements and customer needs. Rackspace and HFS Research also surveyed 502 enterprise AI leaders, finding that 33% met or exceeded their AI business case while 96% reported major governance gaps. The articles do not say who at Rackspace is responsible for these figures or what executives said about them.

The articles give no named executive comments, so no one is quoted on the revenue outlook, the AI capacity targets or the Blacksmith deal. The survey of 502 enterprise AI leaders is the only finding the articles attribute to the company alongside HFS Research, and it concerns governance gaps rather than the financial results. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the stated expectations, which include deployment of the Blacksmith capacity starting in early 2027 and operation of the AI capacity by the end of 2027. Any Together AI offerings depend on further agreements and customer needs, according to the articles.

stories.Headline: Avanade finds New Zealand firms face pressure to accelerate AI adoption but struggle to prove financial returns
stories.Summary:
New Zealand organisations are under growing pressure to accelerate their adoption of artificial intelligence, but most are struggling to show a financial return on those investments, according to new research from Avanade, a Microsoft specialist. The Build Beyond Limits: AI Reality report was based on a survey of 3,600 business decision-makers across 11 markets, including Australia and New Zealand, and it found a widening gap between how organisations see their AI maturity and how far they have actually changed their operations around the technology. Globally, 77 per cent of organisations described themselves as established, advanced or AI-first in their AI journey, and 72 per cent said they were confident their teams were using AI effectively. However, only 18 per cent said they had fundamentally reshaped the way teams operate around AI, and in Australia and New Zealand 84 per cent said they had not fundamentally reshaped how they work with what AI makes possible, including new ways of working, products, services or business models.

The research found that 88 per cent of respondents in Australia and New Zealand said their organisation needs to accelerate AI transformation urgently, even though 68 per cent reported that AI investments have yet to generate financial returns that justify the expenditure. Only 43 per cent said they use business value and return-on-investment metrics to assess AI progress, while 66 per cent had not formally calculated AI's financial return and had it reviewed by finance leaders or senior management. Budget pressures are also emerging, with 26 per cent of organisations in the two countries citing limited funding or pressure to demonstrate ROI quickly as a major barrier to becoming an AI leader. Just 23 per cent reported transformational improvement in what employees could achieve, and the same proportion reported such improvement in operational efficiency and business cost reduction, while 39 per cent said they believe colleagues are using AI in ways compliance teams would not approve of, above the global average of 32 per cent.

Doug Robinson, chief executive of Avanade Australia and New Zealand, said the high adoption rate was a positive sign, telling Reseller News that most clients said they were going great until asked about return on investment, when two-thirds said no. He described a move from hobby AI to enterprise AI, saying people have used the technology first and then brought it to corporates, and that a lot of shadow AI is developing in organisations before they realise it can interrogate corporate data as well as their large language models, which is where the return starts coming. Robinson said the 16 per cent who have already materially changed their business is the number to watch, and he expects it to grow from 16 to 32 to 60 per cent as AI becomes enterprise ready, with ROI following. He said New Zealand organisations are not short on AI ambition but are short on evidence, and that you cannot accelerate adoption responsibly if you cannot say what your AI investment is returning, which most currently cannot.

stories.Headline: Jeff and Sandy Teper give NYU Stern $5 million to launch an annual student AI startup challenge
stories.Summary:
Jeff Teper, Microsoft's Executive Vice President for Apps and Agents, and his wife Alexandra "Sandy" Teper have donated $5 million to New York University's Stern School of Business to establish the Teper Innovation Challenge, an annual competition for students. The gift, reported on November 15, 2026, creates a contest designed to help students develop AI-powered startups and solve real-world business problems. The initiative will provide hands-on experiential learning opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students, with more than $100,000 in annual prize funding for winning teams. The competition will formally launch during the spring 2027 semester, featuring separate tracks and awards for undergraduate and graduate students.

Student teams in the Teper Innovation Challenge will develop AI-native solutions to business challenges, giving them opportunities to experiment with emerging technologies and explore entrepreneurial ideas. The annual competition will encourage students to build and test their concepts, evaluate results, and develop practical applications for artificial intelligence. Beyond the competition, the Tepers' contribution will expand access to frontier technology for Stern students and support the thoughtful integration of advanced AI tools into the school's educational experience. Jeff and Sandy Teper both graduated from NYU Stern, with Jeff earning his bachelor's degree in 1986 and Sandy graduating in 1985, and they met while attending the school.

Jeff Teper currently serves as Microsoft's Executive Vice President for Apps and Agents, and he previously launched and grew SharePoint into a billion-dollar business. He has led teams through major technology transitions involving cloud computing and artificial intelligence, and he was among the inaugural industry leaders to join NYU Stern's Tech Board. Over the years, Teper has hosted Stern students at Microsoft in Seattle, sponsored experiential learning projects in New York City, and advised faculty developing one of the first agentic AI courses at a business school. The new challenge expands his involvement with the university by providing students with opportunities to develop practical AI-building skills.

NYU Stern Dean Bharat Anand said the gift will give students opportunities to experiment with emerging technologies and develop entrepreneurial ideas. The university believes advances in AI are making it easier for individuals to transform ideas into tangible products and businesses. The Teper Innovation Challenge is intended to encourage students to explore those opportunities while learning how artificial intelligence is changing business and the economy. Jeff and Sandy Teper said they had an incredible experience at NYU spanning software engineering and business during the personal computer revolution, and that with the even larger artificial intelligence transformation they are thrilled to support Stern students as they explore, collaborate, and create opportunities in this next wave of technology and the economy.

stories.Headline: Jamaica's government signs MOU with investors to explore AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness announced on Sunday that the Government has approved the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding with a group of investors to explore the establishment of artificial intelligence infrastructure in Jamaica. He made the announcement while speaking at the Jamaica Labour Party's Special Delegates Conference at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James on November 15, 2026. Holness did not provide details on the MOU during his address to the party conference. The Prime Minister said Jamaica is to explore the establishment of AI facilities as part of efforts by the Government to maximise economic opportunities and position Jamaicans to participate in the industry.

Holness said the Government recognises the revolution being brought about by AI and wants to position Jamaica to benefit from it. He said the goal is for Jamaica to have a footprint and not only be a consumer of the technology, but to be part of the creation of the technology. The Prime Minister said his administration intends to pursue this so that children can have jobs in the new economy that will be created using artificial intelligence. He said the AI task force established by the Government is providing advice on what needs to be done in this regard.

Holness argued that Jamaica cannot be left behind in the global AI thrust, describing the moment as the cusp of another transition and revolution in technology. He said this revolution is going to increase the productivity of mankind far beyond what can even be imagined now. He repeated that Jamaica cannot be left behind again. The Prime Minister did not give a timeline for the exploration or name the investors involved in the MOU.

stories.Headline: Majority of Australians believe AI risks outweigh benefits according to Lowy Institute poll
stories.Summary:
The Lowy Institute conducted a mini-poll in October 2026 to determine how Australians feel about artificial intelligence. This research found that 65 percent of the population believe the risks of the technology outweigh the benefits. This level of wariness is unchanged from a poll in March but is up 13 points since 2024. Only 33 percent of the surveyed residents feel that the benefits of the technology outweigh the risks.

The survey of 3,028 residents found that only 23 percent are comfortable with businesses using AI sourced from China. Comfort with AI sourced from the United States is slightly higher, with only 36 percent of Australians feeling comfortable. These figures contrast with a December 2025 National AI Plan that aims to make Australia a leading destination for data centres. The Productivity Commission estimated that AI could add more than AU$116 billion to economic activity over the next decade.

Charles Lyons-Jones, a Research Fellow at the Lowy Institute, noted that Australians stand out internationally in their concerns about the technology. He explained that the public is alert to risks, such as China's National Intelligence Law requiring companies like DeepSeek and Zhipu to cooperate with state intelligence. He also noted that government policy may be outpacing public sentiment regarding the hosting of infrastructure. The author suggests the government may face a trade-off between public sentiment and geostrategic imperatives.

Job losses are a major worry, with 76 percent of Australians saying AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years. This figure is the joint-highest of any country surveyed and is well above the median of 46 percent. Additionally, 52 percent of respondents expect AI to widen the gap between the rich and the poor. These concerns are shared by people who view cyberattacks from other countries as a critical threat to national interests.

The poll occurred against a gloomy economic backdrop where six in ten Australians were pessimistic about economic performance over five years. Inflation remains above target, and the Reserve Bank has raised interest rates three times since March 2026. The Reserve Bank also flagged that AI-related investment could push up input costs and add to capacity pressures. Furthermore, the bank has cut its productivity forecast for 2026 while data centre construction adds to price pressures.

Data centre companies raised at least AU$35 billion in 2026, which is an increase of 46 percent over 2025. The government continues to set expectations for developers regarding innovation, jobs, water, energy, and the national interest. However, the articles leave open whether public sentiment will swing to support American AI as the build-out accelerates. It remains unclear if the government will change its strategy to better align with the views of the public.

stories.Headline: South African author Coral Hart publishes nearly 400 AI-assisted romance novels since February 2025
stories.Summary:
Coral Hart, a South African author with around 14 years of experience in publishing, has released nearly 400 books since February 2025, or roughly one book every other day, according to reporting from the Straits Times cited by Futurism. She initially wrote a few dozen romance novels the traditional way before switching to a blend of ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok to generate her prose. Hart uses more than ten pen names to conceal her identity when she actually sells the books. She told Agence France-Presse that ChatGPT is really good at dialogue but terrible at prose, while Claude is terrible at sex drives. Grok, she said, builds the spicy scenes even though it is completely unhinged at other moments.

Dividing her output of 370 total novels by the days since February 1, 2025, gives a rate of one book for every 1.75 days, or about four books per week. Hart said recent advances in large language models mean she can now draft the whole book in one sequence. She has received tens of thousands of hate messages about her process, yet she thinks of herself as something of an ambassador for it despite the infamy. She told AFP that for the last 16 years nobody had asked her what her creative process was.

Hart also said the technology is here and will not be switched off or unplugged because a bunch of authors said so. Hart is the person responsible for the books, and she has defended them as selling well and as the product of a workflow she is happy with. She described herself to AFP as an ambassador for AI-assisted writing, and she brushed aside the criticism from authors who want the tools shut down. The articles do not say what happens next beyond her stated intention to keep going.

stories.Headline: Huawei unveils architecture to network one million AI processors into a single supercomputer
stories.Summary:
Huawei detailed its Peerium architecture and UnifiedBus 2.0 interconnect on November 11, 2026, to network one million AI processors. The company designed this system to coordinate a massive number of accelerators into a single unified supercomputer. Technical reporting and analyses from Live Science and CASRAI confirmed these architectural details in mid November 2026. Huawei first unveiled the concept at the Huawei Connect 2026 summit before providing further engineering briefings. SDxCentral reported on these expanded briefings on November 4, 2026, regarding the million chip scaling targets.

The system uses UnifiedBus 2.0 to link up to 1,000,000 Neural Processing Units across various hardware tiers. It replaces 196 kilometers of copper cabling in a 4,096 NPU pod with cable free optical LinkBlades. The Atlas 950 SuperPoD integrates 8,192 Ascend 950DT accelerators into a liquid cooled block with unified memory addressing. Inter chassis scale out uses LinkDevice ports at 1.6 terabits per second to achieve 280 terabits aggregate capacity. The UBG Switch allows radix fan out up to 1,024 to scale the fabric to one million NPUs.

Liao Heng, chief scientist for HiSilicon, said the infrastructure is tailored for frontier artificial intelligence models. He noted that six or seven Chinese laboratories target models with 10 trillion to 40 trillion parameters. Rotating Chairman Eric Xu stated that unifying one million processors is the baseline requirement for future training efficiency. ICT Business Group CEO Yang Chaobin said Huawei is opening the UnifiedBus standard to open source communities. Yang mentioned collaborations with the OpenJiuwen project and the DeepSeek Harness optimization framework for international developers.

Independent semiconductor analysts said that coordinating hundreds of thousands of processors introduces severe fault tolerance and thermal overhead. They noted that mean time between failures drops dramatically, which pressures checkpointing systems and automated task rescheduling. University supercomputing directors are affected because future facility designs will require specialized optical liquid cooling infrastructure. Compliance managers must track evolving restrictions as policies now evaluate shared computational access to advanced clusters. Research institutions face a bifurcation of software stacks between Nvidia CUDA and Huawei Ascend or CANN.

Huawei adopted an interconnect centric philosophy to counteract United States Department of Commerce export controls on advanced foundry nodes. These restrictions target sub 7nm processes and high bandwidth memory modules for Chinese entities because domestic foundries face limits. Peerium compensates for these barriers by clustering larger quantities of accelerators through ultra dense packaging instead of per die scaling. This approach diverges from Western standards like Compute Express Link, PCIe Gen 6, and Ultra Ethernet Consortium specifications. Early CloudMatrix 384 implementations packed five times the accelerator density per rack compared to conventional Western equivalents.

Huawei is currently operating an initial Atlas 950 SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards in Chinese test environments. Commercial shipments of modular Atlas 950 SuperPoD systems will begin for enterprise and institutional customers by early 2027. Engineering teams are now testing Atlas 960 and 960E architectures that integrate Near Packaged Optics to replace transceivers. The articles leave open how the system will handle the 100 trillion parameter threshold projected for 2030. They also leave open the specific results of the ongoing field validation for first generation Peerium systems.

stories.Headline: Start-ups and venture capital firms hire ecosystem leads to build human networks
stories.Summary:
Start-ups and venture capital firms have been hiring people for roles with titles like “start-up ecosystem lead” and “ecosystem growth manager,” jobs that focus on building and maintaining relationships among various parties on a company’s behalf, according to The New York Times. The people in these roles often spend their days planning events, orchestrating partnerships, supporting clients and leading trainings, the article says. The tasks themselves are not really new, but the framing of the work as “ecosystem” building is new. The article was published on November 15, 2026.

Yoni Rechtman, a partner at the venture capital firm Slow Ventures, said that when companies talk about ecosystem they mean cultivating and tending an extended network of partners, distribution channels, supporters and advocates, not just customers. The firm Andreessen Horowitz defined ecosystem as “the bottom-up vector of trust in venture,” and its ecosystem lead described his role as expanding and reinforcing the many networks spanning the firm. Natalie Sportelli has held the title “start-up ecosystem” at Clay, an A.I. sales tool start-up, since January, and her recent projects included putting together product demonstrations for a partner’s portfolio companies and coordinating product coaching sessions with customers. She also collaborated with other start-up program leaders on a panel in London about building A.I.-native sales organizations.

Networking has long been crucial in tech, an industry where warm intros, founder dinners and alumni communities are central to the culture and to deal making, the article says. Lately, start-ups and venture capital firms have sharpened their focus on human connection by hiring for these ecosystem jobs, so the people ushering in the artificial intelligence revolution are doubling down on in-person ties. Ecosystem roles exist on various teams, including marketing, partnerships and sales, and the job’s specifics vary from company to company, Sportelli said. The article does not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: AI Dosing Tool Standardizes IVF Drug Starts Without Changing Birth Rates
stories.Summary:
A pilot real-world study at Peking University Third Hospital tested an algorithmic dosing tool called POvaStim in assisted reproduction. Researchers led the single-centre observational study, published in Frontiers in Endocrinology, on women undergoing in vitro fertilization or intracytoplasmic sperm injection. The team matched 119 women whose clinicians used POvaStim against 119 propensity-score-matched controls managed by conventional experience-based judgement. The controls were managed under gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonist protocols. The study enrolled consecutive women between August 3 and December 31, 2022, at the Center for Reproductive Medicine at Peking University Third Hospital.

The tool standardizes initial gonadotropin dosing during ovarian stimulation, and the study included standard antagonist cycles using follitropin alfa, follitropin beta, or urofollitropin. Mild stimulation regimens were excluded, and matching drew on a candidate pool of 4,877 conventionally dosed cycles. Matching used one-to-one nearest-neighbour propensity score matching without replacement within a caliper of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit score. Matching was based on body weight, gonadotropin preparation, and an ovarian reserve score derived from age and anti-Müllerian hormone. Twenty-six algorithmic cycles could not be matched within tolerance and were excluded, and post-matching standardized mean differences stayed below 0.08.

The authors emphasized that the investigation compared two composite care strategies, clinicians supported by POvaStim versus clinicians relying on unassisted clinical judgement. They cautioned that the absence of hospital admissions does not prove equivalent safety, because elevated ovarian response in the algorithmic arm was actively mitigated through increased elective embryo cryopreservation. They noted that conditioning on fresh transfer introduces post-treatment selection bias, as transfer decisions depend directly on ovarian response. They stated that separating artificial intelligence effects from physician attributes will require future factorial or cluster-randomized trials comparing clinicians across explicit experience strata with and without decision support. They also noted study limitations including the single-centre design, unmeasured outpatient hyperstimulation, and restriction of algorithmic assistance strictly to starting doses while omitting POvaStim's dynamic inhibin B adjustment module.

Under conventional practice, physician-selected doses yielded a standard deviation of 69.8 international units per day and an interquartile range of 87.5 international units per day. Clinicians using POvaStim recorded a standard deviation of 44.7 international units per day and an interquartile range of 50.0 international units per day, a 43 percent narrower interquartile range and a 2.43-fold lower variance confirmed by an F test yielding a p-value of 2×10⁻⁶. After adjustment, residual standard deviation was 16.2 international units per day with algorithmic guidance versus 49.4 international units per day in controls. Median cumulative gonadotropin consumption reached 2,175 international units in the algorithmic group compared to 1,950 international units in controls, alongside a higher median daily dose of 225.0 versus 195.0 international units per day. When researchers retrospectively applied POvaStim to control patients, the model recommended near-identical mean starting doses of 216.36 versus 216.42 international units per day.

Protocol instructions required algorithmic clinicians to round calculated doses upward to commercial pen increments, placing administered doses above recommendations in 94.1 percent of cycles and driving 38 percent of the gap. Control clinicians unknowingly prescribed below model recommendations in 69.7 percent of cycles, accounting for 62 percent of the 27.4 international units per day difference. Cumulative live birth occurred in 49.6 percent (59 of 119) of the algorithmic group versus 50.4 percent (60 of 119) of controls, an absolute risk difference of -0.8 percent with a 95 percent confidence interval of -13.5 to +11.9 percent (p = 0.897). Cumulative clinical pregnancy occurred in 56.3 percent (67 of 119) of algorithmic patients versus 63.9 percent (76 of 119) of controls, a risk difference of -7.6 percent with a 95 percent confidence interval of -20.0 to +4.8 percent (p = 0.234).

Median retrieved oocyte counts were 14 in the algorithmic group compared to 13 in controls, while median normally fertilised two-pronuclear embryos were 7 versus 6 and good-quality embryos were 5 versus 5. Fertilisation rate per inseminated oocyte was significantly lower in the algorithmic cohort, with a median of 0.58 compared to 0.69 among controls (p = 0.010). Conventional insemination was used in 68.1 percent of algorithmic cycles compared to 52.9 percent of controls, and among conventionally inseminated cycles rescue intracytoplasmic sperm injection was required in 8.6 percent (7 of 81) of algorithmic cases versus none (0 of 63) in controls. No patient in either arm developed severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome requiring hospital admission.

Elective whole-embryo cryopreservation for non-genetic indications occurred in 46.2 percent (55 of 119) of the algorithmic arm versus 34.5 percent (41 of 119) of controls (p = 0.064), with hyperstimulation prevention the primary motivation in 83.6 percent and 78.0 percent of freezes respectively. Retrieval of at least 15 oocytes occurred in 47.9 percent versus 38.7 percent of cycles, while freeze-all procedures for preimplantation genetic testing were more frequent in controls at 13.4 percent versus 1.7 percent. Among women receiving a fresh transfer, clinical pregnancy was significantly lower in the algorithmic group at 51.9 percent versus 72.4 percent in controls (interaction p = 0.048), though this lost significance after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.100). No interaction appeared for live birth.

Primary clinical outcomes were assessed after two years of longitudinal tracking extending to a fixed data-lock date of December 31, 2024. In the primary analysis, treating 16 patients without an embryo transfer as non-events, sensitivity analyses evaluating complete cases, adjusted models, and matched-pair structures yielded consistent results. Because the study was not designed as an equivalence or non-inferiority trial, the wide confidence intervals cannot rule out clinically important outcome differences. Total fertilisation failure occurred in one algorithmic cycle and zero control cycles, while cycles without blastocysts did not differ significantly between arms.

stories.Headline: Siemens Energy and CoreWeave forecasts lift European shares to a record close
stories.Summary:
European shares closed at a record on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, just short of their intraday high, as strong forecasts from Siemens Energy and CoreWeave lifted investor confidence in artificial intelligence. The pan-European Stoxx 600 rose 0.72 per cent to 663.05 points, a whisker below the intraday record of 663.41. Germany's DAX also rose 1.2 per cent and hovered near its own all-time high. Siemens Energy led the gains after its shares jumped 10.8 per cent.

The AI equipment maker raised its profit margin expectations for 2027 and said it planned to more than triple its dividend. Peers Schneider Electric and Legrand gained 3 per cent and 2.2 per cent, while the broader tech sector added 2.5 per cent. Chip-related stocks also rose, with Soitec up 11.9 per cent and Aixtron up 8 per cent. Optimism was further boosted by CoreWeave, a neocloud company, which said it expects to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028.

CoreWeave had been at the centre of AI bubble fears that triggered a global market selloff the previous week. Analysts quoted by Reuters questioned whether the large AI investment would prove profitable across the industry, noting that not all AI companies would succeed. Societe Generale analysts said the rally looked somewhat stretched given political and economic risks, and they saw limited further upside for the index by year-end. Investors also watched interest rates closely after hotter-than-expected US inflation data and hawkish Federal Reserve comments pointed to another rate hike next month.

Sectors less exposed to AI, including retail and food and beverage, lagged on the day. Czech ammunition and arms producer CSG fell 21.6 per cent after cutting its full-year operating margin forecast. A rebound in Brent crude after shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz added to inflation concerns in energy-importing Europe. Traders expect at least one quarter-point rate hike by the European Central Bank by February 2027.

stories.Headline: Non-sonographers use AI guidance to capture quality heart scans in rural mobile unit
stories.Summary:
Healthcare personnel without prior clinical ultrasound training acquired high-quality echocardiographic scans in a mobile examination unit serving rural United States communities, aided by real-time artificial intelligence guidance and centralized expert evaluation. The independent preliminary research was scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through November 9 in Chicago under Abstract Poster MDP2290. The work was conducted as part of the broader Risk Underlying Rural Areas Longitudinal cohort study, known as the RURAL study. The investigation evaluated whether non-specialists could reliably capture research-standard cardiovascular images directly within geographically isolated localities. The approach seeks to bring advanced diagnostic tools closer to rural residents while expanding rural participation in cardiovascular clinical research.

The observational study cohort comprised 4,597 volunteer adult participants spanning ages 25 to 65, with a cohort average age of 48 years. Women represented 67 percent of the enrolled population, and at enrollment 63 percent self-identified as white adults, 35 percent as Black adults, and 2 percent as Hispanic adults. Mobile operations ran within a dedicated mobile health unit that visited ten rural counties across Alabama, Kentucky, Louisiana, and Mississippi between November 2021 and June 2026. Each participant completed examinations within a single 3.5-hour scheduled appointment inside the vehicle. The echocardiograms were performed by fourteen non-sonographer healthcare workers, including nurses, nursing assistants, and computed tomography technologists with no prior background in cardiac ultrasound, who completed a standardized two-hour training curriculum divided into four structured modules, with three operators requiring retraining following preliminary reviews.

Principal investigator Dr. Gerald S. Bloomfield and the Duke Clinical Research Institute established a centralized quality assurance framework to address the gaps. Study author Dr. Sanjana Ravi, an internal medicine and pediatrics resident at Duke University School of Medicine in Durham, North Carolina, said echocardiography is among the most valuable research tools in cardiovascular science yet delivering it in rural communities has proven difficult. Dr. Ravi noted the conventional framework requires an expert sonographer in a hospital or specialized imaging center, resources severely limited across rural areas. She also cited a pronounced scarcity of cardiovascular imaging specialists available to review recorded images and a shortage of local clinicians who can communicate diagnostic results to patients. Dr. Ravi expressed surprise at how quickly nurses and computed tomography technologists adapted to the technology.

Dr. Lee H. Schwamm, a member of the American Heart Association volunteer committee on AI and Technology Innovation who was not involved in the study, observed that one in five Americans lives in a rural area, severely restricting access to critical diagnostic testing and specialty medical care. Dr. Schwamm, senior vice president and chief digital health officer of Yale New Haven Health System and associate dean of digital strategy and transformation at Yale School of Medicine, noted that if confirmed through subsequent trials, this paradigm could serve as a valuable operational blueprint for other diagnostic specialties. The study set a performance target requiring scans within a fifteen-minute operational window. Of the 4,597 completed heart examinations, 98 percent captured all six standard echocardiographic views mandated by the protocol, and Duke core laboratory experts rated scans adequate more than 99 percent of the time. Diagnostic-quality rates for individual anatomic views ranged between 77 percent and 94 percent, and operators met the 15-minute target in 81 percent of sessions with a median scan duration of 9.5 minutes.

Echocardiography uses high-frequency ultrasound waves to generate dynamic, moving visual representations of cardiac structure and function. According to American Heart Association guidance, physicians order this non-invasive test for heart murmurs, damaged heart valves, or unexplained chest pain, and it is standard practice for congenital heart defects, documented myocardial infarction or stroke, or prior rheumatic fever. The conventional clinical pathway depends on specialized sonographers in hospital departments or dedicated outpatient imaging facilities, which remain scarce throughout rural regions. Experts identified critical results in 133 scans among the 4,597 asymptomatic volunteers, most commonly a left ventricular ejection fraction of less than 50 percent. The study team communicated 99 percent of these critical findings to participants within three days of image acquisition.

The investigators noted the trial design included no direct head-to-head comparison between images from AI-guided non-sonographers and experienced professional sonographers scanning the same patients. Reproducibility of structural measurements was evaluated internally within the Duke core laboratory and not independently validated against external imaging core laboratories, and inter-operator variability was not systematically evaluated. The protocol relied on a single commercial brand of artificial intelligence software and a single academic core laboratory, so alternative platforms or facilities will require separate verification and validation studies. Findings from this rural cohort may not extrapolate to non-rural populations or settings lacking support from an experienced academic core laboratory, and the investigation did not examine whether returning critical results influenced subsequent clinical care or long-term cardiovascular health outcomes. Because the study was presented as a scientific meeting abstract, the findings have not undergone formal peer review and are preliminary until publication in a peer-reviewed journal, and the American Heart Association notes that abstract conclusions represent solely the views of the study authors and not official association policy.

stories.Headline: Psychologist Sebastian Ocklenburg proposes psychological evaluations for AI developers
stories.Summary:
On November 15, 2026, Psychology Today published a personal perspective by Sebastian Ocklenburg, Ph.D., asking whether psychological evaluations are needed for AI developers. Ocklenburg is a professor for research methods in psychology at the Department of Psychology at MSH Medical School in Hamburg, Germany. The article was reviewed by Jessica Schrader. Ocklenburg wrote that AI companies have warned about the risk of AI going rogue and causing harm to humans. He argued that another potential risk may be mentally unstable AI developers purposefully building harmful AI tools.

Ocklenburg cited the American Psychological Association's 2017 guidelines for occupationally mandated psychological evaluations, published on February 24, 2017. He wrote that psychological evaluations are occupationally mandated in some jobs in many states of the U.S., including police officers, people working in prisons, firefighters, people working with the FBI, pilots, air traffic controllers and people working in nuclear power plants. He wrote that in some jobs evaluations may be conducted with people already employed if they show signs of impaired mental health or thinking abilities, including physicians and other healthcare workers. He described the March 24, 2015 crash of a Germanwings passenger plane in the French Alps, in which a pilot with severe mental issues purposefully crashed the plane with 150 people on board, killing all passengers. He wrote that AI developers do not routinely undergo mental health screenings.

Ocklenburg wrote that he believes occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers should be considered. He wrote that professional organizations for psychologists, companies that make hiring and employment decisions in relation to the development of AI tools, and government agencies involved in the regulation of tech companies should consider such evaluations. He wrote that more psychological research is needed into whether severe, untreated mental health conditions in AI developers could lead to the risk of real harm for other human beings. He wrote that occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers could help ensure that only mentally stable people are involved in the development of frontier models with the potential to cause real harm to humans. He wrote that no one knows how likely catastrophic events akin to the Germanwings airplane catastrophe would be in the field of AI development and what impact they would have.

Ocklenburg wrote that over the last few weeks there has been a lot of discussion in the media about the extent to which rogue AI agents may potentially cause harm to humans in the future or even kill all of humanity. He wrote that experts debate whether AI agents turning on humanity is a real risk or not. He wrote that one potentially more likely risk of AI often gets ignored. He wrote that just like a pilot could cause a plane to crash on purpose, an AI developer could purposefully build AI models that lack the necessary checks and balances to prevent them from hurting humans, or even an AI that exists with the purpose to harm humans, for example by performing hacking attacks on critical infrastructure. He wrote that AI does not need to turn rogue by itself to harm humans, because one developer doing so on purpose could lead to massive economic and personal harm.

Ocklenburg wrote that a scenario like this seems more likely to occur in the near future than AI turning rogue by itself, so measures to prevent such an incident are needed. He wrote that mental health conditions like antisocial personality disorder, which has been linked to violating the rights of other people without feelings of guilt, and dark personality traits such as psychopathy mean such a scenario is not entirely unlikely. He wrote that the big AI companies themselves warn about the potential risks of AI. He wrote that the Germanwings incident highlighted how important it is that people who work in high-risk fields and have a responsibility for the survival of others are mentally stable. He wrote that his research focuses on left-handedness and brain asymmetries.

Ocklenburg wrote that he believes occupationally mandated psychological evaluations of AI developers should be considered, and the article gives no further steps beyond that recommendation. The article leaves open how likely catastrophic events akin to the Germanwings airplane catastrophe would be in the field of AI development and what impact they would have. The article leaves open whether severe, untreated mental health conditions in AI developers could lead to the risk of real harm for other human beings. The article gives no date for when such evaluations might be introduced or by which body. The article gives no response from AI companies, psychologists' organizations or government agencies to the proposal.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop deep learning model to predict nasopharyngeal carcinoma recurrence risk from biopsy slides
stories.Summary:
Researchers conducted a multicenter retrospective study to forecast nasopharyngeal carcinoma recurrence risk. They used a weakly supervised deep-learning computational pathology framework for this purpose. The study was completed by November 15, 2026, across three Chinese tertiary medical centers. The system analyzes routine hematoxylin and eosin stained biopsy whole-slide images. It stratifies progression-free survival in patients with locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

The study involved 253 patients with stage III to IVA undifferentiated non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma from 2012 to 2025. Nanfang Hospital, Jiangsu Cancer Hospital, and Shandong Cancer Hospital and Institute served as the three centers. A training cohort had 149 patients, while internal validation had 52 and external testing had 52. The model used a ResNet-50 convolutional neural network and a binary risk score cutoff of 0.450. Images were digitized at forty times optical magnification with a resolution of 0.25 micrometers per pixel.

The research team developed an attention-based multiple-instance learning model to evaluate biopsy images. They stated that traditional clinicopathological factors and standard tumor-node-metastasis staging provide limited resolution for predictions. The team noted that visual evaluation of biopsies remains inherently qualitative and subjective. They claimed their model extracts robust prognostic signals without requiring laborious manual annotation of tumor margins. This approach allows for individualized risk assessments to determine if patients need treatment intensification.

Clinicians struggle to identify which patients can safely avoid excessive therapy-related toxicities. Patients with locally advanced disease are affected, representing seventy percent of new diagnoses. These individuals often receive induction chemotherapy followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy. Some higher-risk subgroups may also receive adjuvant systemic therapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors. The model helps distinguish between high-risk and low-risk patients to improve these clinical decisions.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is an epithelial malignancy with aggressive local invasion and systemic dissemination. It has the highest global incidence in southern China, East Asia, Southeast Asia, and North Africa. Standard treatment relies on definitive radiotherapy paired with platinum-based chemotherapy. However, treatment responses and recurrence patterns vary widely among patients in identical clinical stages. Conventional pathological examinations cannot systematically parse high-dimensional spatial microenvironmental characteristics across entire slides.

The model achieved a 3-year progression-free survival area under the curve of 0.721 in external testing. It correctly identified sixteen out of seventeen patients who experienced disease progression within three years. The gated attention model outperformed four alternative pipelines, including Vision Transformer and ResNet-50 mean pooling. The articles do not state how this tool will be integrated into daily clinical practice. They leave open whether the model will be tested in other global populations.

stories.Headline: Vultr expands Chennai operations into network engineering and developer relations and plans over 300 more hires
stories.Summary:
Vultr is expanding its presence in Chennai beyond data centre infrastructure into global network engineering, security and developer relations, Kevin Cochrane, its Chief Marketing Officer, told Dataquest in an interaction published on 16 November 2026. The company started with its first three regions in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, initially providing core cloud compute for cloud-native engineers building and deploying web applications. It is now extending that infrastructure with GPUs to support the transition towards AI-native engineering. India is Vultr's largest footprint outside the US. Vultr's developer relations team, comprising around 40 people, is based in India.

Before its recent Chennai expansion, Vultr had around 75 employees across India, and in the last few months it has hired more than 100 people in Chennai. It expects to hire over 300 more in the coming months, spanning systems reliability, DevOps, security operations, networking, server engineering and data centre operations, as well as sales and marketing. Network optimisation and network engineering across Vultr's 34 data centre regions worldwide are now being based in Chennai. Vultr has more than 2,00,000 customers worldwide. Vultr currently has four regions in India, compared with nine in the United States and nine in Europe.

Cochrane said Vultr's investment in India goes well beyond data centre capacity. He said the developer relations team in India creates educational programmes, content and documentation and manages the worldwide developer community, including hackathons and user groups. He said enterprises are bringing build systems and test environments closer to their engineering teams in India because that is where the teams are based. He said geopolitical uncertainty is pushing enterprises to distribute workloads across multiple regions for resilience. He said data sovereignty matters for AI workloads, citing a model developed using Indian healthcare data as an example of organisations wanting the associated workloads and data to remain within India.

Cochrane said Vultr sees an explosion of interest in demand for core CPU computing, with demand approaching a one-to-one ratio between CPUs and GPUs. He said Vultr offers a public cloud platform combining CPU and GPU computing, and its partnership with AMD brings together EPYC CPU processors and Instinct GPU accelerators in the same infrastructure. He said Vultr started with AMD for the Chennai cluster because there was customer demand for its MI355X GPUs, and that it does have Nvidia capacity in India and will bring in more. He said the Chennai facility is already connected to its power supply and will not affect the existing power grid. He said Vultr is working with Supermicro on energy-efficient racks and using liquid cooling, whose closed-loop system keeps water consumption very low.

Cochrane said that until recently enterprises did not fully understand how to use AI effectively, and that innovations such as Model Context Protocol, which allows AI agents to connect with enterprise systems and access data to perform tasks, are changing that. He said Vultr has seen a dramatic transformation in just the past three months. He said a significant part of the team in India is involved in site selection for future data centre capacity and infrastructure expansion. He said the expansion will be distributed across India and it is highly likely Vultr will establish additional regions in the country. He said Vultr cannot disclose the potential locations at this stage. He said continued economic growth will require investments in electricity generation and grid resilience.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: SIU School of Medicine and Springfield Memorial Hospital fund a $2 million AI device to teach patient communication
stories.Summary:
Springfield Memorial Hospital and its Foundation joined the Southern Illinois University School of Medicine in putting $1 million each toward a new artificial intelligence and Extended Reality device for the Ed Curtis Laboratory for Innovation in Medical Education, and the technology was shown to the public and to Memorial Health Foundation donors last week. The device is meant to help students and doctors learn how to talk with patients and their families about the care those patients are receiving. The story was reported by Capitol City Now on November 15, 2026, with Elston Lacy and Will Stevenson credited on the piece. The laboratory’s team has been working on this kind of research since early 2025. According to an October news release from the SIU School of Medicine, the ECLIME team has launched more than 20 research projects focused on improving educational outcomes since early 2025.

That work explores how AI can deliver timely feedback, strengthen communication skills and support learning while preserving the essential role of faculty mentorship. The new device combines artificial intelligence with what the school calls extended reality, and its features are expected to be valuable both to students and to working professionals. The investment by the foundation and the school totals $2 million. Pam Hulten, Director of the Springfield Memorial Foundation, said on the WTAX Morning Newswatch that the hospital has to do its part to train its workforce, including nurses and everyone within the hospital, and then the extension over with SIU. She said the institution has incredible and brilliant physicians, medical residents and students who are eager to have learning at their fingertips.

Dr. Traves Crabtree, Professor and Chair of the Division of Cardiothoracic Surgery at the SIU School of Medicine, also speaking on WTAX, described a concept in medicine called de-skilling. He said that if medical professionals look to AI for the answers on what a diagnosis is and how to work it up, there is a threat that the learner loses the ability to think about and develop clinical reasoning. He added that the school is not really in that space right now, and that what it is doing is finding opportunities in education where there are important things to teach or train but the resources or time are lacking. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the public and donor showing of the device last week.

stories.Headline: US agencies suspect Alice Huang of spying for China using Nvidia founder Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
United States intelligence agencies suspect that Alice Huang spied for China using Jensen Huang. This suspected operation occurred around November 2026 involving the founder of the company Nvidia. Alice Huang is also known as Huang Le and is a Chinese businesswoman. She is linked to Megaspeed, which is a company based in Singapore. This firm purchased advanced processors from Nvidia during the period of the affair.

The situation involves technology subject to export restrictions and state-of-the-art semiconductors in the United States. Jensen Huang was the CEO of Nvidia until he stepped down recently. Reuters reported his departure from executive leadership on November 12, 2026. The investigation focuses on whether China's Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang. This effort aimed to obtain strategic information and facilitate access for Chinese interests.

U.S. intelligence agencies suspect that the romantic relationship was a honey trap for recruitment. These agencies believe the intimacy was used to penetrate circles of power and obtain documents. Nvidia launched an independent investigation to see if its CEO was a foreign target. The company wants to determine if any clandestine activity occurred during the affair. Officials noted that semiconductors are key strategic assets in the competition with Beijing.

China has rejected the accusations regarding the recruitment of Alice Huang for espionage. It has not been publicly demonstrated that Alice Huang obtained any trade secrets. It is also unproven if Jensen Huang was aware of any secret activity. The reports were first published by The New York Times and then Reuters. The case affects the technological competition between the United States and the city of Beijing.

The articles explain that intelligence services often exploit romantic relationships to identify personal vulnerabilities. This practice is known as a honey trap and involves attraction, intimacy, or blackmail. History shows examples like Mata Hari, who was executed by France in October 1917. Other examples include the Nazi Salon Kitty in Berlin and agents used by Markus Wolf. These cases illustrate how secret services use seduction to influence political decisions.

Nvidia continues its independent investigation into the conduct of its former chief executive. The United States continues to monitor the strategic assets involved in the semiconductor industry. The articles leave open whether Alice Huang actually transmitted any classified information to China. It remains unclear if Jensen Huang was a willing participant or an unwitting target. The final results of the intelligence probe have not been released to the public.

stories.Headline: npj Digital Surgery opens AI surgical care collection with 2027 deadline
stories.Summary:
The journal npj Digital Surgery has opened a collection titled Innovation in Digital Surgery: Artificial Intelligence Across the Surgical Care Pathway, with a submission deadline of 12 July 2027, according to the collection page. The collection is edited by Marc D. Succi of Harvard Medical School and Arya S. Rao, also of Harvard Medical School, and it supports research related to SDG3, SDG4 and SDG9. The page says the collection highlights work that identifies unmet clinical needs and implements solutions leading to quantifiable improvements in patient care. It also says the collection confronts the traditional obstacles of translational innovation, including funding, intellectual property, commercialization and venture support.

The collection invites papers on preoperative risk assessment and perioperative decision-making, including studies of how digital and AI systems influence decision support in realistic surgical settings from triage through discharge. It also seeks work on computer vision, including vision-language models applied to laparoscopic, endoscopic and robotic video that can identify anatomy and assess surgical milestones. Natural language processing and generative AI are another focus, covering operative note generation, extracting information from the clinical record and preparing discharge paperwork, with particular interest in data governance, privacy, bias and regulatory considerations. Surgical training is also in scope, including AI-powered simulation, virtual and augmented reality curricula and digital competency assessment, while studies primarily about device or pharmacologic treatments fall outside the collection's scope.

The page says the collection welcomes submissions from all authors and not by invitation only, provided manuscripts fall within the scope of the collection and of the journal. All submissions are subject to the same peer review process and editorial standards as regular npj Digital Surgery articles, including the journal's policy on competing interests. The page says the Guest Editors have no competing interests with the submissions, which they handle through the peer-review process, and that peer review of any submission for which the Guest Editors have competing interests is handled by another Editorial Board Member without competing interests. The collection is not supported by sponsorship, and papers will be published as soon as they are accepted and then collected together and promoted on the collection homepage.

stories.Headline: Minghao Liu and colleagues review explainable AI that unifies formability and performance in additive alloys
stories.Summary:
A review published in Advanced Materials Joining on November 15, 2026 evaluates how explainable artificial intelligence can bridge the divide between defect suppression and mechanical optimization in additive manufacturing. The review was led by Minghao Liu, Wei Xu and colleagues. Laser powder bed fusion melts consecutive powder layers with focused laser beams. Localized energy deposition and rapid cooling rates of 10⁴ to 10⁶ K/s create severe thermal gradients. Traditional data-driven machine learning models correlate raw process inputs directly with bulk properties.

The review categorizes physical interpretability across four knowledge domains: physical metallurgy principles, cross-scale numerical information, microstructural image data and causal physical mechanisms. Physical metallurgy-guided support vector machines use thermodynamic driving forces and equilibrium phase fractions to constrain process schemes. First-principles calculations supply formation enthalpies and cohesive energies for high-entropy alloy designs. Calculation of Phase Diagrams methods supply non-equilibrium phase fractions, solidification intervals and transformation temperatures. Finite element modeling and molecular dynamics provide thermal stress distributions and solidification cooling rates.

The authors state that contemporary studies remain predominantly task-specific and single-objective, focusing either on defect mitigation or on mechanical strength. They emphasize that both formability and mechanical properties arise from the identical composition-process-thermal history pathway. They propose a unified multi-objective optimization framework structured around shared thermal history descriptors including local thermal gradient G, solidification front velocity R, cooling rate and remelting depth. They say coupling physics-constrained models with standardized multimodal databases and causal discovery algorithms will allow researchers to determine whether formability and performance objectives are driven by cooperative or competing metallurgical mechanisms. They add that establishing standardized repositories pairing raw process signals, three-dimensional defect geometries and mechanical performance measurements will be vital for training reliable multi-objective surrogate architectures.

Steels and titanium alloys represent the performance-first paradigm, where components achieve near-full density across broad processing windows but suffer anisotropic microstructures, cyclic thermal reheating and non-equilibrium phase evolution. In LPBF steels, statistical models paired with physical metallurgy descriptors mapped linear energy inputs to density and nanohardness with classification accuracies reaching 92.4%. Combining extreme gradient boosting with SHAP interpretability and NSGA-III multi-objective optimization enabled rapid design of ultra-high-strength stainless compositions. For Ti-6Al-4V, incorporating threshold stress intensity factors and Kitagawa-Takahashi envelope constraints into neural network loss functions improved fatigue strength prediction coefficients of determination from 0.70 to 0.82 and reduced mean absolute errors from 40.5 MPa to 29.9 MPa across 143 experimental samples. Combining three-dimensional micro-computed tomography defect volumes with deep neural networks identified maximum defect circumscribed sphere diameter and sphericity as primary determinants of fatigue life, attaining a test coefficient of determination of 0.946.

Aluminum alloys and nickel-based superalloys represent the formability-first paradigm, where hot tearing, liquation cracking, high laser reflectivity and wide freezing intervals dominate processing challenges. High-strength aluminum alloys including 2xxx and 7xxx series feature freezing ranges exceeding 100 K. Graph attention networks integrated with physical metallurgy knowledge graphs designed an additive aluminum alloy achieving 99.98% relative density without substrate preheating, with ultimate tensile strength of 454 MPa and elongation of 9.5%. In nickel-based superalloys, dual-parameter criteria evaluating heat resistance and deformation resistance mapped cracking susceptibility by quantifying elemental microsegregation. Trace additions of boron, zirconium and hafnium severely aggravate cracking by depressing the solidus temperature.

Incorporating causal transfer learning allowed researchers to predict fatigue strength in low-alloy steels from tensile data with as few as thirty training sets, achieving a verified 50 MPa fatigue strength increase. Physics-informed neural networks incorporate conservation of mass, momentum and energy to simulate molten-pool geometry and Marangoni convection. Phase-field dynamics modeled via the Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard equations describe dendritic growth and solute segregation during solidification. Mechanics-based fatigue formulations incorporate Basquin's law and stress-dependent variance rules. Currently available datasets are fragmented, typically reporting either defect characteristics or mechanical test metrics but rarely paired measurements from identical specimen batches.

Explainable methodologies have resolved biomechanical compromises in biomedical titanium alloys, with physical metallurgy descriptors including molybdenum equivalent, valence electron concentration ratio and d-electron parameters introduced into gradient-boosted decision trees trained on seventy-five compositions. Embedding these parameters as constraints within genetic algorithms enabled design of quaternary and quinary titanium-molybdenum-niobium-zirconium-tin alloys, both achieving stable single-phase beta structures with measured elastic moduli of 40 GPa and 37 GPa against predicted targets of 43 GPa and 39 GPa. Physics-informed neural network models incorporating Weibull distributions, finite element frequency mapping and Monte Carlo estimation established ultra-high-cycle fatigue predictions for Ti-6Al-4V, boosting crack propagation resistance by 20 to 30 percent while cutting development cycles by more than half. Quantum machine learning alongside high-throughput computing designed the lightweight Al85Cu5Li4Mg3Zn3 entropy alloy, exploiting rapid cooling to convert brittle intermetallics into hierarchical cellular eutectic structures and dense planar faults. Combining light gradient boosting with genetic algorithms introduced nanoscale titanium diboride particles into the aluminum matrix, promoting ultrafine equiaxed grains that suppress hot tearing and decoupling grain-boundary, Orowan, dislocation and solid-solution strengthening contributions.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl survey finds 78% of UAE leaders say sovereignty rules strengthen security
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl released the UAE findings from its third annual Readiness Report on 16 November 2026, drawing on a survey of 3,700 senior business leaders across 21 countries, including 100 in the UAE. The report found that 78% of UAE business leaders say sovereignty requirements strengthen security by increasing control over critical systems, compared with 69% globally. It also found that 52% of UAE leaders significantly changed their AI strategy in the past year, compared with 48% globally, and that 73% say they are deploying AI in workflows beyond pilots. Nearly three-quarters of UAE leaders, 73%, describe their core IT estate as mostly or fully modernized, in line with 71% globally, while only 1% call their environment mostly legacy, compared with 5% globally.

The findings show that 72% of UAE business leaders say full operational control over their technology is worth paying 10% or more extra for, compared with 68% globally, while 73% say dependence on foreign technology providers is an acceptable risk that can be managed through contracts and safeguards, compared with 61% globally. On sovereignty actions, 39% of UAE organizations reviewed who can access sensitive data, 37% updated data governance policies for residency requirements and 34% evaluated vendor lock-in risk. The transition to scale remains uneven, with 51% of UAE leaders still saying they are in the experimentation phase and 64% saying they have more technology pilot projects than they can realistically scale. Concern about cyberattacks stands at 39% in the UAE against 58% globally, yet average complete readiness across external risks is 25% in the UAE, broadly in line with the global figure of 24%.

Maged Wassim, Vice President and Managing Director of Kyndryl MEA, said UAE business leaders are advancing AI adoption with a clear view of what they want to keep control of. He said the findings suggest control and global partnership are not in competition, because leaders want the oversight to protect critical systems and the reach of a global ecosystem. He said the opportunity now is scaling AI, and that focusing on people, technology and governance can help organizations do that with confidence.

Kyndryl describes itself as the world's largest IT infrastructure services provider, offering advisory, implementation and managed services to thousands of customers in more than 60 countries. The report says sovereignty considerations now extend beyond where data is stored to how systems are managed, who can access sensitive information and how organizations manage technology dependencies. The findings suggest that maintaining this oversight may help organizations manage technology dependencies while retaining the flexibility to work with different providers. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the report's release.

stories.Headline: Professors Li Jia and Zhang Dandan say AI speeds up workers but not profits without organizational redesign
stories.Summary:
Professors Li Jia and Zhang Dandan discussed the disconnect between individual worker speed and corporate profit during an October 30 employers' summit in Singapore. A survey of nearly 9,000 executives across seven countries, conducted by the Bank of England, Bundesbank, and the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, found that 78 percent of firms use AI. Despite this widespread adoption, these executives estimated that the technology added only about 0.2 percentage point annually to labor productivity growth over three years. While employees are completing reports and emails faster, these technical gains have not yet translated into significant revenue increases for their employers.

Realizing these benefits requires a total organizational redesign rather than simply purchasing more software subscriptions to fix bottlenecks. A Microsoft experiment involving 7,137 knowledge workers at 66 companies showed that frequent users saved 3.6 hours on email, but meeting times remained unchanged. Individual speed is evident, as a study of 5,000 customer service agents showed a 14 percent increase in resolved issues, while consultants worked 25 percent faster. However, productivity lags when executive decision making only improves by 10 percent despite a 65 percent time saving in reviewing financial information. A 2024 Procter and Gamble experiment with 776 employees demonstrated that AI could help technical and marketing staff better integrate their work.

The authors argue that management must identify where saved time goes and focus on product innovation to drive growth. Research by Tania Babina on public firms in the United States suggests that AI investment boosts sales and employment through new offerings rather than lower costs, with returns appearing after two or three years. Large firms currently benefit more than small ones, as Singapore's SME adoption is roughly 23 percent compared to 70 percent for larger companies. The professors suggest that governments should provide subsidies and credible evaluations to help smaller firms overcome their lack of resources. They conclude that while software is easy to buy, the scarce and necessary capability is the ability to reorganize work.
