stories.Headline: Embodied AI governance must address physical risks beyond screens, article argues
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Fair Observer on 15 November 2026, argues that AI governance must move beyond screens to address embodied AI in vehicles, warehouses, hospitals, performance venues, stores and homes. It says AI is helping machines perceive surroundings, choose actions and move through spaces shared with people. It cites the OECD’s updated definition of an AI system, which recognizes that AI outputs can influence physical as well as virtual environments. It warns that a machine misreading a person’s movement can strike them and that a late driver takeover request can turn a software failure into a collision. It says a service robot failing in a home or care setting may put a vulnerable person at risk.

The article says embodied AI combines software with sensors, mechanical parts, connectivity and a changing environment, and that a system can pass laboratory tests yet fail in the real world. It cites the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s work on autonomous-systems assurance, saying autonomous systems may face an enormous range of operating conditions that make complete testing coverage a major challenge. It cites the NIST AI Risk Management Framework’s four functions, govern, map, measure and manage, and its treatment of safety, security, accountability, transparency, privacy and fairness as connected characteristics. It cites the European Union’s Machinery Regulation on software and machine-learning components performing safety functions and the EU’s updated product-liability rules covering software and AI systems. It also cites the United Nations regulation on automated lane-keeping systems, with requirements on driver availability, takeover requests, cybersecurity, software updates and data storage, and ISO 13482 on hazards of personal-care robots.

The article says developers and operators should identify foreseeable hazards, test realistic conditions, define safe operating limits and prepare for failures before deployment. It says every physical AI system should have a clear statement of where, when and under what conditions it may operate, covering terrain, lighting, weather, network availability, crowd density and user capability. It says these limits should be communicated to buyers and operators in plain language rather than buried in technical documentation. It says a machine exceeding tested limits should slow down, enter a safe state or request qualified human assistance. It says the responsible person needs training, enough information to recognize a problem, authority to intervene and a stop or override mechanism that works under pressure.

The article says workers should be able to report dangerous behavior without retaliation and that consumers and patients should know when a machine is making or carrying out a consequential decision. It says embodied AI systems should create secure, proportionate records of critical decisions, sensor failures, overrides, updates and emergency stops, and that serious patterns should trigger investigation before the next failure becomes an injury. It says recordkeeping must respect privacy and aim at enough reliable evidence to reconstruct what happened, improve the system and establish accountability. It says governance should identify each party’s duties before harm occurs, since a manufacturer, model supplier, integrator, owner and update provider may all be involved. It says contracts should not let the most powerful organizations push every risk onto small businesses, workers or consumers.

The article says safety reviews should include privacy, accessibility, bias, consent and human dignity because systems in homes, care settings and workplaces may collect intimate information about routines, health, emotions and relationships. It says people should not lose the right to human contact, explanation or appeal simply because a robotic service is efficient. The author says he has spent more than 41 years in music and the creative industries and that physical AI will reach concert halls, touring operations, studios, festivals and media production. It says independent venues, artists and small production businesses need practical procurement checklists, clear insurance terms, accessible training, incident-reporting procedures and honest information about a system’s limitations. It says safety and privacy cannot become premium features available only to organizations with large compliance budgets.

The article says society should not wait for a spectacular accident before establishing expectations for embodied AI and that developers and operators can act now by testing under realistic conditions, publishing limits, training responsible people, maintaining genuine stop mechanisms, documenting incidents and assigning accountability throughout the lifecycle. It says progress should be measured not by how human a robot appears but by whether humans remain protected, informed and able to obtain recourse. It says governance that is clear, practical and centered on people creates the trust responsible innovation needs. It says AI is leaving the screen and safeguards must be ready to meet it in the physical world. It says the views expressed are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Fair Observer’s editorial policy.

Articles.Title: AI Governance Must Leave the Screen and Enter the Physical World

stories.headline_source: AI Governance Must Leave the Screen and Enter the Physical World

stories.Headline: Anthropic posts $16.96 billion quarterly revenue as token prices fall
stories.Summary:
Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of $16.96 billion, up 47% from the second quarter, according to Yardeni Research, which said falling AI token prices need not hurt AI providers. The usage-weighted Silicon Data LLM Token Expenditure Index, tracking what customers pay per million tokens, fell more than 40% between June 30 and early October. Yardeni said the decline reflects price competition and a shift in usage toward cheaper models. Anthropic priced its newest premium model, Fable 5.2, at $8 for input and $40 for output, down from $10 and $50 for Fable 5.1. Google's first-party models were processing nearly 32 billion tokens per minute by its October 28 earnings call, up 40% in a quarter and more than fourfold from a year earlier.

Anthropic's third-quarter revenue rose 1,127% from a year earlier, outpacing a 382% rise in its compute and infrastructure expenses. Quarter to quarter, profit fell: Anthropic swung from a $974 million operating profit in the second quarter to a $567 million operating loss in the third, citing $5 billion of costly short-term compute and a $2.0 billion non-cash donation-matching charge. Excluding that charge alone would leave an operating profit, though the charge may recur. Compute and infrastructure, including training, took about 58% of revenue, versus 48% in the second quarter. DRAM contract prices rose nearly 80% in the second quarter and 40% in the third, TrendForce reported.

Median on-demand GPU rental prices rose 9% from a year earlier, and H100 prices 24.7%, according to GetDeploying's November 9 tracker. AWS raised prices on most new Nvidia Capacity Block reservations from October 7, with increases of at least 15% on seven instance types, according to TIKR. SemiAnalysis measured roughly 14 times more throughput from one Nvidia chip generation on software improvements alone. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 cut customer costs per task by about 40% compared with Opus 5.

Anthropic's repeat customers generated about nine times their year-earlier quarterly revenue in aggregate. Yardeni said it is unknown whether repeat customers would keep spending in a recession, and that the test is rising profits, not rising volumes of tokens sold. Anthropic plans to go public, Yahoo Finance reported 20 days earlier, at a time when AI tokens have never been cheaper. Fortune reported two months earlier on the latest crack in the thesis for the trillion-dollar AI boom, that tokens are getting cheaper.

Decrypt reported 11 days earlier that Anthropic's AI is getting cheaper to use and that this is becoming a problem for its business. TIKR reported two days earlier that AI token prices fell almost 15% last month, which it called good news for Amazon. Yahoo Finance reported a month earlier that Anthropic revealed the Haiku 5.5 model as the AI pricing war intensified. Barrons.com reported 30 days earlier that Anthropic might be worth only $1.5 trillion and that this is not a disaster for the AI trade.

Yahoo Finance reported a month earlier that Anthropic's third-quarter revenue climbed to $16.8 billion. BeInCrypto reported five months earlier that OpenAI's price war with Anthropic could undermine its IPO. Investopedia reported 18 days earlier on how the company behind Claude makes money, and Quartz reported two months earlier that OpenAI is gaining on Anthropic in business AI spending, per Ramp data. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Chinese seniors use AI for companionship and daily assistance
stories.Summary:
AI has recently been playing chess with grandfathers and cheering up grandmothers. These interactions occurred around November 2026, including a storytelling event in Wuzhen. A woman named Xiao He used the AI Doubao to help her father. The AI provided real-time chess instructions via a video call. Old He also played against a Go robot in an academy.

The 2025 National Bulletin on the Development of Aging Undertakings notes 323 million Chinese people aged 60 plus. This group represents about 23 percent of the total population by late 2025. In Huishui County, Guizhou Province, 90 percent of surveyed seniors only use WeChat. In Community G in Xi'an, 35.6 percent of 320 seniors know nothing of AI. DeepSeek became a viral hit at the beginning of 2025.

Professor Shen Qi from Fudan University's Institute of Aging Studies led a research team. He compared the dialogue between the elderly and AI to a two-way tango dance. He described the spiritual comfort for rural seniors as the technology subsidence effect. Cai Yaohui from the same institute taught rural Henan seniors to use models. He found rural elderly have almost no barriers to accepting these tools.

A retired engineer viewed large language models as respectable experts requiring politeness. A grandma from Yangpu District tested AI by asking for directions to Changhai Hospital. Seniors in Hong Kong and Guangzhou used ChatGPT 3.5 for health and technical questions. One senior used ChatGPT to cope with the death of a pet goldfish. A 63-year-old grandma asked Doubao to pretend to be her granddaughter.

Many seniors use voice input and include hesitant murmurs like oh or hmm. Some elderly people slow their speech because they fear the AI cannot hear. They often test the AI with known facts to check for accuracy. Rural seniors use AI to discuss forbidden topics, such as a missing son. Some use the AI as a confessional that never leaks secrets.

In Zibo, Shandong, 25 seniors aged 60 to 82 discussed loneliness with Doubao. An 82-year-old grandma learned idioms to make her monotonous life more lively. A 67-year-old man used AI to escape a house that felt like a prison. A 65-year-old man sought advice on repairing a relationship with his son. The articles leave open how AI will further integrate into senior care.

stories.Headline: Broadcom projects AI revenue reaching 230 billion dollars by 2028
stories.Summary:
Broadcom projected that its artificial intelligence revenue will reach 230 billion dollars by fiscal 2028. This financial forecast was reported by Anders Bylund on November 15, 2026. The company expects this growth to be supported by custom AI accelerators. These accelerators are co-developed with frontier labs including Meta Platforms, Alphabet, and Anthropic.

The company raised its fiscal 2026 AI revenue guidance to 58 billion dollars. It further projects 115 billion dollars in 2027 and 230 billion dollars by 2028. Broadcom reported AI semiconductor revenue of 16.7 billion dollars in Q3 2026. This figure represents a 221 percent increase compared to the previous year.

CEO Hock Tan is responsible for raising the revenue guidance for the company. He provided forward-looking visibility that is described as almost unheard of in the semiconductor space. The company also sells Tomahawk Ethernet switches for use in AI data centers. These tools provide either processing power or data transfer capabilities for the user.

Credo Technology Group is also an AI networking investment that affects hyperscalers with large electric bills. Credo reported first-quarter revenue of 479 million dollars for fiscal 2027. This represents the seventh consecutive quarter of triple-digit revenue growth for the company. Credo specializes in active electric cables and serializer/deserializer data converter modules.

Broadcom is a chip giant with a market cap of 1.65 trillion dollars as of November 13. Its trailing sales are 89.1 billion dollars with a bottom line of 38.3 billion dollars. The company has a free cash flow of 39.4 billion dollars. Credo is smaller with trailing revenues of 1.6 billion dollars and a 25 billion dollar market cap.

Credo expects its optical segment to generate over 600 million dollars in sales this fiscal year. This growth is driven by silicon photonics, Zero-Flap Optics, and optical digital signal processors. Broadcom also makes SerDes modules, from which Credo likely collects royalties. The articles leave open which company is the better buy for investors.

stories.Headline: Howard Lutnick pushes to loosen AI chip restrictions while his former firm finances Asian data centers
stories.Summary:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick pushed to loosen restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips, according to a New York Times investigation published Sunday. He did this while his former Wall Street firm helped arrange financing for Asian data centers that could benefit from these decisions. The report raises conflict of interest questions because Lutnick led the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald for more than three decades. His sons, Brandon and Kyle, now lead the firm while Lutnick serves in the administration of President Donald Trump. The investigation suggests a potential clash between his regulatory duties and his family business interests.

Cantor Fitzgerald worked with companies developing data centers in Southeast Asia, including facilities designed to provide computing power to Chinese customers. One Malaysian data center, known as A201, is expected to open next year with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia servers. Cantor served as a financing or placement agent for companies including Bitdeer Technologies Group and Gorilla Technology Group. Lutnick reportedly resisted efforts by other senior administration officials to strengthen restrictions on Nvidia chip shipments to Asia. He also repeatedly delayed efforts to restrict companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China, according to Axios.

The Commerce Department maintained that Lutnick fully divested his financial interests in Cantor and has had no discussions with the firm. Department officials defended their enforcement record and denied directing staff to avoid investigating particular companies. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly criticized the failure to blacklist Megaspeed, a Singapore based company suspected of helping China. The White House has expressed confidence in Lutnick despite the mounting questions over the decisions made by his department. Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment on the reports regarding its business dealings and financing arrangements.

Senator Elizabeth Warren and Senator Ron Wyden demanded information about a loan from cryptocurrency company Tether to a trust for Lutnick's children. This loan was reportedly secured by assets including more than half of the equity in Cantor Fitzgerald. Other Democrats have demanded stronger enforcement of chip exports, while some Republican lawmakers questioned if technology is reaching China. The report notes that Commerce approved Nvidia export licenses involving Chinese companies with links to military contractors or sanctioned entities. These issues come amid a broader controversy involving former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang.

Cantor Fitzgerald attracted attention in July 2025 for offering to purchase potential tariff refund claims for 20 to 30 percent of their value. This arrangement allowed investors to profit if courts overturned tariffs, while Lutnick was a vocal advocate for those same tariffs. In March, Bloomberg reported that Tether provided a loan of an undisclosed amount to the trust benefiting Lutnick's four children. This loan occurred around the time the children acquired the ownership stake in the investment firm. These previous disclosures added to the current scrutiny of the business dealings under the leadership of Brandon and Kyle.

Lawmakers are now intensifying their scrutiny of how the Commerce Department handles the export of advanced chips to Asia. The administration continues to face questions about whether U.S. technology is reaching Chinese interests through third party data centers. It remains unclear if the business dealings of Cantor Fitzgerald influenced the specific policy decisions made by Secretary Lutnick. The New York Times stated it found no evidence that the firm's dealings influenced the secretary's official actions. The articles leave open whether further investigations will be launched into the Tether loan or the A201 project.

stories.Headline: Economist John Quiggin argues Australian corporate layoffs do not signal an AI job apocalypse
stories.Summary:
Several major Australian companies including NAB, Qantas, Canva, and Atlassian announced large-scale job losses around November 15, 2026. While some of these organizations explicitly blamed artificial intelligence for the cuts, the actual role of the technology remains unclear. This wave of layoffs follows four years of intense hype and excitement since the initial launch of ChatGPT. Many observers are now questioning if these events signal a broader job apocalypse driven by automation.

The situation requires a closer look at the specific changes occurring within these different corporate business models. Qantas plans to outsource 850 Australian jobs to India as part of an overhaul that the company describes as AI-driven. NAB has denied that artificial intelligence played any role in its recent decision to sack employees. Canva faces vulnerability because users can now generate simple graphic designs in seconds using various AI tools. Atlassian is also under challenge, though its project management software is considered harder for AI to replicate.

John Quiggin, a professor at the University of Queensland’s school of economics, argues that the evidence does not support a job apocalypse. He suggests that Qantas is using AI as a cover to muddy the waters regarding simple offshoring. Quiggin believes NAB is simply following a long-term pattern of hiring and sacking workers based on profitability. He notes that productivity growth remains very low despite the massive investments in data centers and infrastructure. The author claims that the current trend mirrors the dotcom era of the 1990s.

The broader context involves a stock market boom based on future demand that has not yet emerged. Hyperscalers like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Alphabet face competition from cheaper open-weight models such as Mistral and DeepSeek. These competing models from France and China invest far less money while remaining only a year behind the leaders. Quiggin suggests that large language models might become essential utilities like email rather than sources of profit. Consequently, the most significant apocalypse may eventually occur in the stock market instead of the jobs market.

Articles.Title: Is the AI job apocalypse finally here? The evidence suggests otherwise | John Quiggin

stories.headline_source: Is the AI job apocalypse finally here? The evidence suggests otherwise | John Quiggin

stories.Headline: House House uses an LLM to rewrite about 10 lines of code in Big Walk, triggering Steam backlash and IGF judge refusals
stories.Summary:
House House, a small Australian studio, disclosed that it had used a large language model to rewrite about 10 lines of code in Unity's Universal Render Pipeline source code for its co-op adventure game *Big Walk*, and the disclosure triggered a backlash, with players flooding Steam to leave negative reviews and some applying for refunds, while 19 IGF judges stated they would not vote for any game using generative AI. The studio rose to fame with *Untitled Goose Game* in 2019 and spent six years developing *Big Walk*, which launched in early August and reached a Metacritic score of 94, the highest of the year, and was nominated for Best Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards. The problem was a shadow culling defect in URP that rendered shadow casters behind the player to infinity, dropping frame rate by about 50% for nearly 20 seconds during sunrise and sunset. The studio looked through the URP source code without finding a solution, and a Unity official engineer replied after asking colleagues that the wanted modification was impossible to implement. They sent the problem to an LLM chatbot, found a feasible direction after several attempts and setbacks, modified and adjusted it, and implemented it as about 10 lines of rewritten code, estimating AI-related code at less than 0.1% of the total game volume, with generative AI never used for art creation.

House House updated its FAQ and disclosed these details, and later said in a statement that there was no internal AI usage policy during development, which was a mistake. The IGF leadership expressed support for that statement but did not officially announce that *Big Walk* was disqualified from the competition. Some players left negative reviews on Steam on the grounds that undisclosed AI use is misleading about the game's quality and the effort put into it. Valve made an important revision in January 2026 separating development assistance tools from AI-generated content for players, so code assistants and chatbots for debugging need no disclosure, and only AI-generated content players can see or hear must be made public. Under those rules, House House's use of an LLM to fix code bugs did not need to be told to anyone.

Anthropic engineer Felix Rieseberg tested Claude Fable 5.2 with a minimal prompt for a small-scale FPS with graphics comparable to 3A blockbusters, realistic lighting and photorealistic effects, gave no further feedback, and let the model run autonomously for about 8 hours. The model delivered a browser-based first-person shooter called *Saltline*, set in a rainy container port with cranes, cargo ships, wet ground and low-angle sunset, close to modern *Call of Duty*-style mission levels, in which players cut off three uplink relays while dealing with drones called Gulls and robotic dogs called Hounds. All 3D models, textures, sound effects and shaders were generated entirely by the model from scratch using code, with no external assets imported, and the whole game is basically a self-contained HTML file. The process consumed approximately 445 million input tokens and 2.7 million output tokens, most inputs hit the cache, and the API cost was about $550. Rieseberg made the prompt and results public, stating this was a test of the model's upper quality limit under a single prompt with no human intervention.

Many people were impressed by the visual effects, saying details such as the rainy port, wet ground reflections, crane silhouettes and red dot sights are close to modern *Call of Duty* or *Battlefield*, with netizens saying "This is really 3A-level graphics" and "GTA 6 may be the last 3A blockbuster made by a traditional studio". The most controversial point was the expression "one-shot / no human feedback", with netizens arguing that 445 million input tokens mean this was not single-step generation but autonomous execution of 8 hours after one instruction, and that half the people who read the article will try a single conversation, get a much worse game, and conclude the model is very ordinary. Around November 10, an HTML file called *Jimao* spread in group chats, only 1.4MB but a well-completed small FPS game, with copy claiming it was independently developed by Claude Fable 5.2 as a "domestic 3A blockbuster", and reactions included "scared to tears by the AI overlord" and "so shocking". *Jimao* was just a localized reskin of *Saltline*. The GDC 2026 annual gaming industry survey interviewed more than 2,300 practitioners, and 52% believe generative AI has a negative impact on the industry, nearly triple the 18% of two years earlier, while those with a positive view dropped to 7%.

Complaints aside, 36% of game practitioners do use generative AI in their work, of which 81% use it for research and brainstorming and 47% for code assistance, but only 5% actually present AI-generated content to players. In this statistic, 58% of people using AI are in positions such as publishing, marketing and business, and only 30% of developers who directly make games in the studio are using AI. In 2024, new games marked with AI-generated content on Steam accounted for about 13%, the figure rose to 24% in 2025, and reached 40.1% in the first ten months of 2026, approaching 50% in the single month of October. Among games with more than 1000 reviews in 2026, the AI disclosure rate is only 14%, while for games with less than 10 reviews the ratio is as high as 47%. Games that heavily use AI-generated content are mainly concentrated in products launched in batches for rapid monetization, while most games that have received a lot of player attention still use AI with restraint.

The gaming industry has long been considered a scenario very suitable for large-scale AI application, with image generation models, video models and world models all able to be deeply integrated with the industry, but in reality the extent to which the gaming circle embraces AI is not as high as imagined. Independent games are regarded as handicrafts, and what players pay for includes the unique feel and human touch, so even one line of code from a machine is like screwing an assembly line screw into a handcrafted wooden table. *Saltline* was placed on the exhibition stand of "see what the model can do" from the very beginning, no one had the expectation of handmade quality for it, and onlookers just enjoyed the spectacle. Generative content has indeed created a lot of garbage in game stores, shoddily made reskinned works have taken up recommendation slots, and serious and hardworking small teams have been overshadowed instead. The angry reaction to AI has set a dangerous precedent for the video game industry, and game developers will now be more reluctant to disclose the use of artificial intelligence in their games to avoid criticism from review bodies.

The articles leave open whether the IGF will officially announce that *Big Walk* is disqualified from the competition, and they do not say what House House will do next. They do not say what Valve or Unity will do following the dispute, and they do not say how the 19 IGF judges will act beyond their stated refusal to vote for games using generative AI. They do not say what Rieseberg or Anthropic will do with the *Saltline* test, and they do not say who made or distributed the *Jimao* reskin. They do not say what the GDC 2026 survey respondents or the players who left negative reviews and sought refunds will do next.

Articles.Title: Why AI Triggered Widespread Panic Across the Global Gaming Industry: Key Reasons Explained - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Foundation model vendors use AI to automate computer chip design and fabrication
stories.Summary:
Foundation model vendors are attempting to use artificial intelligence to design and fabricate computer chips during late 2026. This movement, called AI4Chip, seeks to replicate the success of AI coding by automating complex hardware engineering tasks. Some experts believe AI will eventually handle end-to-end design, while others remain skeptical of its current capabilities. These companies are now recruiting experts in RTL, verification, layout wiring, and timing to build these systems.

The process requires AI to master a long industrial chain including specifications, synthesis, physical inspection, and tape-out. Duojiangjiang predicts AI will first boost efficiency by 30 percent before evolving into self-improving design within five to ten years. Moonshot AI used the Nangate 45nm process library and open source EDA tools for a 4mm² chip. Qwen3.8-Max recently completed RTL and verification for a NoC module and optimized the T-Head Xuan Tie M890.

Duojiangjiang argues that AI lacks the limited context restrictions that force humans to divide labor into fine pieces. He believes foundation model factories will eventually own their own fabs to eliminate dependence on upstream computing power giants. Saige, a practitioner with ten years of experience, laughs at the idea that chip design is just coding. He claims that most current EDA Agents are only at L0 or L1 levels of automation.

Saige notes that AI currently only helps with small scripts and front-end code, ignoring the physical PPA impossible triangle. Hardware engineers are affected because real chip delivery requires systematic considerations of power, performance, and area beyond simple code. Foundation model vendors are driven by high computing power bills and the need for new high-value revenue streams. They want to avoid the oligopolistic competition and national regulation expected for basic model capabilities.

The industry is shifting because coding agents became a solid implementation scenario with verifiable tasks and clear payment willingness. Chip design is viewed as the next high-value domain because the paying parties are profitable EDA and chip companies. Domestic manufacturers in China face additional pressure to optimize fundamental constraints due to a critical shortage of cards. This business necessity pushes model providers to develop their own hardware products to ensure future growth.

Anthropic has formed a dedicated chip design team using Claude, while OpenAI and Synopsys are developing the GPT-Synopsys model. China is currently viewed as relatively weak in both the EDA and model aspects compared to foreign combinations. Both regions still face a significant distance to travel before these AI chip design tools reach full commercialization. The articles leave open how much of the unwritten expert experience in chip companies can be digitized.

Articles.Title: Want to Fabricate Chips with AI? Here’s Why Chip Engineers Are Skeptical - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Meta scales back AI job replacement plan as employees fix technical and security flaws
stories.Summary:
Meta scaled back a plan to carry out large-scale layoffs and replace positions with AI agents, Reuters reported, after employees spent growing time patching technical and security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has widely deployed AI internally, and Executive Vice President Ryan Roslansky publicly complained that his daily work is full of AI-generated content he called watered-down. Walmart store and warehouse employees are troubled by AI tools that handle task assignment, scheduling and performance assessment, according to Business Insider. Companies from Microsoft to McKinsey are restricting employees' use of new AI tools as their proliferation erodes corporate profits, Reuters reported. Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment, and Meta, Palantir, NVIDIA and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment.

Restrictions are now set in places that used to encourage trials, experienced employees are called back, and training efforts are being increased. A Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta working paper shows 90% of executives said their company's AI investment has not yet translated into productivity gains. A survey released by Ernst & Young last month shows 36% of AI executives at enterprises with annual revenue of at least 1 billion US dollars reported AI accidents causing data loss, financial losses, brand damage or operational disruption. A survey released by Indeed in July this year shows more than half of employees said they did not get the AI training they needed, while only 45% of managers feel capable of leading AI natives well. Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton and NVIDIA have set restrictions on employee usage due to growing concerns that their own data is not safe when stored at AI companies.

Johnny C Taylor Jr, President and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management, said executives generally feel like they are building the car while driving it, and that if we could turn back time we would introduce it in a more thoughtful and slower way. Kathleen Hogan, Chief Strategy and Transformation Officer of Microsoft, wrote in a recent blog post that being usable and in use does not mean real transformation. Hogan wrote that Microsoft found adding an agent to a broken process still results in a broken process, and that speeding up a single step alone will only make the next step have a longer queue. Hogan wrote that investing in employee training does improve productivity, especially when junior engineers are paired with senior staff. Taylor said enterprises are shifting from one-off online courses for large numbers of employees to continuous, position-specific customized training.

Zack Mabel, research director of the Center on Education and the Workforce at Georgetown University, said many employees feel they are asked to use these tools but no one tells them exactly how to use them. Mabel added that managers are caught in the middle, having to meet requirements of promoting implementation, delivering benefits and making no compromise on quality at the same time. Jessica Reif, assistant professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, explained that AI always outputs things that look plausible but hide defects or errors not easy to detect, so errors pass down the workflow and small problems snowball. A Walmart manager told Business Insider that the robots assume employees can do everything perfectly every time, and that we won't set such impossible standards for people. Neil Elan, a lawyer at the law firm Stubbs Alderton & Markiles, said he has noticed the gap is growing between how clients think their employees use AI and how employees actually use it, causing troubles in confidentiality, intellectual property, efficiency and employee integrity.

Posts from employees on LinkedIn show that after the 2023 efficiency reform that cut a large number of staff, with middle managers affected first, Meta has started to expand management positions again. Employers around the world are now clearing up the mess left by their hasty AI deployment in the early stage. Global enterprises have invested tens of billions of dollars in AI over the past few years, but the real returns have not yet appeared. Employees described systems that set unreasonable standards for human employees while creating inefficiency and errors, such as planning inexplicable routes for order pickers, popping up batches of useless safety alerts, and generating unrealistic schedules that force store employees to take shortcuts and cut corners to meet progress targets. Once the fact that employees use ChatGPT is brought to light, it will also give enterprises a big headache, Elan said.

The problem for enterprises has never been that they underutilize AI, but that they rush its deployment far too hastily, leaving employees to foot the bill. Employers have to digest the flood of errors and low-quality outputs, which takes up all employees' time, raises privacy and security risks and pushes up costs. Roslansky reminded his followers to be careful of falling into a vicious cycle where reading is done by AI and writing is done by AI, and everything ends up looking the same. The articles do not say what specific restrictions Microsoft, McKinsey, Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton or NVIDIA imposed, or when. The articles do not say whether Meta's expanded management positions number any specific figure, or what Walmart, Meta, Palantir, NVIDIA and Booz Allen Hamilton would say in response.

stories.Headline: Chatham faculty senate drafts first AI policy treating unacknowledged student use as Honor Code misconduct
stories.Summary:
Chatham University’s faculty senate is drafting its first university-wide generative AI policy, according to a report in the student newspaper The Communiqué published on 12 November 2026. The draft treats unauthorized or unacknowledged student AI use as academic misconduct under the Honor Code. The Academic Policy Committee, chaired by Jungook Kim, assistant professor of business, is leading the draft. The committee gathered feedback from library staff and the Office of Information Technology. The faculty senate is working with other departments and stakeholders on the policy.

The draft covers AI use in teaching, learning, research and administrative operations. Students may use AI only when an instructor explicitly permits it. Misconduct examples include submitting fully AI-generated work, paraphrasing AI output without citation, and using AI during exams or other assessments. Faculty would have full authority over whether and how AI is allowed in their courses and would have to communicate those expectations. The draft also allows faculty to use AI for instructional materials, administrative tasks and feedback generation, provided a human reviews the output.

Jeff Bukowski, associate dean, academic integrity officer and director of Academic Success, told the paper that AI use should align with the Honor Code. He noted that many AI-related situations are not yet defined, saying there is a lot of things that we do not know yet that fit into that definition. Chatham Student Government passed a resolution in March 2025 calling for a formal AI policy. Its executive members found the draft vague, and parliamentarian Jocalyn Henry said it lacked defining rules or consequences. The group also raised concerns about faculty use of AI for emails, student feedback and marketing, and asked that sustainability be addressed.

Chatham currently has no university-wide AI policy, according to the article. A campus-wide comment period for students, faculty and staff is likely to begin in January 2027. The article gives no specific start or end dates for that comment period. The draft policy text itself is not published in the report, so details may change before any adoption. The report is an editorial reading and not a claim from the report itself.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenAI delays GPT-6.2 and other models over safety and alignment issues
stories.Summary:
GPT-6.2 has run into major development hurdles, and OpenAI is worried, according to a report from the WeChat account QbitAI published by 36Kr on November 16, 2026. The article says the new model is bogged down by safety issues and that OpenAI now finds itself in the same position Google was in back in 2022. It describes OpenAI as having become one of the companies that takes safety most seriously, with safety anxiety prioritized above everything else and releasing new models treated as a secondary task. The piece notes that Google in 2022 held leading-edge technology but hesitated to launch products over safety and brand reputation, only to watch OpenAI seize the first-mover advantage in generative AI.

The leaker Token Gremlin shared more specific details, saying OpenAI's next-generation models are being delayed by safety and alignment issues and that the postponement has already lasted several weeks. He also named GPT-6.5 and pointed to a tricky problem: how to turn pre-training results with over 10 trillion parameters into products the public can actually use. The article recalls that in early November people in the community said they had been selected for a gray test of GPT-6.2, and that The Information revealed on November 4 that OpenAI's new Sol, Astra and cyber models could launch as early as Friday, November 6. Nearly half a month later, the article says, Astra has not arrived and other models have been pushed back again and again, while Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on November 9.

According to Token Gremlin's latest statement, the listing gift package Sam Altman prepared for Ray Dalio is likely to be postponed due to safety alignment issues, and he offered a more pessimistic judgment that these problems are hard to solve in a short period and the release rhythm cannot be restored quickly. He said that even if OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 soon, it may go online with a large number of protection restrictions while other versions keep being pushed back. On November 7 he had said Astra and Sol failed to launch as expected because serious safety and alignment issues were found at the last minute and needed extra fixes, expecting a few more days of polishing; a day before the article he shared a case of making a game with GPT-6.2 Astra. OpenAI has given no official confirmation of these claims and no further response, the article says.

The article links the delay to internal safety culture, citing a post by Joe that Token Gremlin referenced, and says OpenAI became extremely cautious about approving releases after the Hugging Face incident. It notes precedents: OpenAI once suspended part of its training due to model misbehavior and canceled the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra because safety and alignment standards were not met, and on October 23 OpenAI said a misbehavior incident on September 20 prompted it to suspend training and evaluation of some frontier models. Token Gremlin attributes the gap with Anthropic to accumulated safety experience, saying Anthropic's new models are ready for public delivery while OpenAI is months behind in that process. The article says the more noteworthy issue is that competition may be shifting from who can train a more powerful model to who can deliver one safely and stably, especially as RSI accelerates research and development.

stories.Headline: Carmen Li says older GPU rental prices rise as newer chips arrive
stories.Summary:
Michael Burry argued over the past year that the AI boom rests on a flattering accounting choice, calling the practice of stretching assumed server and GPU lives "one of the more common frauds of the modern era." He estimated in his Substack, Cassandra Unchained, that the industry could understate depreciation by $176 billion between 2026 and 2028. New evidence from the GPU rental market cuts against a key assumption in that thesis. NVIDIA shares closed at $162.85 on November 13, down 26.41% over the past month. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid disclosures about his personal relationships, and the board appointed its finance chief, Kress, interim CEO this week.

Microsoft and Alphabet have moved certain server classes to four to six years, which Burry says flatters earnings. Burry argues NVIDIA's 12- to 18-month product cycle reduces the real economic life of each generation. Kress said on the August 26 call that NVIDIA compute is "fully utilized across every cloud we serve." Kress said supply should stay a constraint "at least through the end of fiscal year '28." In its fiscal second-quarter release, revenue reached $96.221 billion, with Data Center revenue of $89.023 billion, up 117% year over year.

Silicon Data founder and CEO Carmen Li told Deirdre Bosa in a Yahoo Finance interview that older GPUs are holding their value better than expected. Li said rental prices for certain older chips are rising rather than collapsing as newer generations arrive. Silicon Data publishes daily GPU benchmarks for on-demand rental rates, giving it a direct view of what compute costs. Huang said on the call that an AI agent needs 15 to 100 times the compute of a human user. Huang said a deployed system "will be preserved and useful and productive for a lot longer."

The company still ships Hopper parts two generations back. Frontier model training makes headlines, but inference, fine-tuning, research, and smaller workloads can run economically on older hardware. Rents measure current earning power, while resale value, book value, and lifetime profitability are separate questions. Kress said Vera Rubin delivers 35 times lower token costs relative to Grace Blackwell Ultra. Supply commitments reached $279 billion, guarantee obligations for AI cloud partners are capped at $108.5 billion, and days sales outstanding stretched to 60 days from 45 days.

Burry's argument concerns accounting lives and reported earnings, and his thesis leaves room for older GPUs to keep commercial value. When demand runs ahead of supply, last-generation chips stay in service. Today's pricing also reflects a shortage that could ease, and the same shortage is driving a broader expansion in power, cooling, and networking. Once Vera Rubin supply arrives in volume, demand for older chips could weaken. The stock trades at a P/E of 33, so the market already prices in durable demand.

The accounting debate will be settled by data that has yet to arrive, including whether older-chip rents hold once Vera Rubin supply catches up. Hyperscaler disclosures could show any change to server useful-life estimates in quarterly filings. NVIDIA's next report will be measured against guidance of $108.0B +/- 2% in revenue and gross margins of 74.0%. Investors will watch for any comment on utilization under interim leadership. If rents fall sharply after the next product ramp, Burry's warning gains weight, and if they hold, the case for longer depreciation schedules gets stronger.

stories.Headline: AIA reports 74% of US architecture firms used AI in daily operations in 2025
stories.Summary:
The American Institute of Architects' Business of Architecture 2026 report found that 74% of U.S. architecture firms used artificial intelligence in day-to-day operations in 2025. The report was built on data from nearly 900 firms and covered calendar year 2025. U.S. architecture firms generated $121.7 billion in gross billings in 2025, with 54% of revenue tied to new construction. Medical Construction and Design covered the report on November 13, and MarketScale published its story on November 15, 2026. AIA's monthly billings index has tracked a softer 2026 while the survey describes 2025.

The report puts average net billings per employee at $152,000 for 2025 and reports growth in profitability without a headline margin in the public summary. AIA sells a companion benchmarking tool that breaks 40 survey questions down by region, firm size and specialization, with members getting 40% off. The full report is listed at $289 and is free to members. The 2024 edition reported profitability for 2023 at 13.2% of net billings and found renovation, retrofit, addition and preservation work produced 45% of firms' gross billings in 2023. AIA's September 2026 billings index report, titled "Architecture firm billings slump deepens," says firm revenue is down by an average of 3% from 2025 and is expected to remain flat in 2027.

AIA frames AI use as spanning design, project delivery and business management, and describes rapid adoption across firms of all sizes alongside growing efforts to develop formal AI strategies and workflows. The public summary does not give an earlier all-firm AI rate, so the pace of the climb cannot be pinned down from it. When AIA asked special questions in January 2026, 73% of firms said they regularly used a stipulated sum, and 56% of leaders found fees harder to negotiate than two years earlier. For 33% of small firms, hourly billing was the most profitable method. AIA reported on July 22 that backlog at firms billing under $250,000 dropped from 4.9 months to 3.1 months in Q2 2026, while the figure for all firms was 6.3 months.

Deltek's 2026 Clarity study found just 38% of A&E firms reported a measurable positive business impact from AI even though 70% had adopted it, according to ScaleArc's summary of the May 12 release. Deltek's 47th Clarity study, covering 896 A&E firms, reported 16.7%, down from 21.4%. In 2025 Deltek put the median win rate across A&E firms at 50%, and the following year proposal submissions rose 32% even as win rates fell. ScaleArc found no survey showing AI changing what architects charge and argued the gain shows up as capacity.

PSMJ's median operating profit for year-end 2025 was 20.5% of net revenue, the highest its survey has recorded. The index's August reading, released September 23, shows billings at 47.2, project inquiries at 50.8 and design contracts at 48.3 on a scale where 50 means no change. The same release put consumer prices up 3.4% on the year, and 29% of firms expected billings to fall at the end of Q3 2026, against 21% at the end of Q1. AIA's nonresidential forecast for 2027 is positive, though ScaleArc argues that improvement does not reach residential studios.

AIA's Home Design Trends panel rated additions and alterations at a net +38% and kitchen and bath at +34% in Q2 2026, against minus 25% for first-time and affordable homes. An AIA special question from March 2024 put profitability for firms billing under $250,000 at 9.0%, compared with 11.5% for all firms. AIA tracks the share of firms with ownership transition plans, written business plans and business continuity plans, and describes a growing focus on all three. The report also documents broader use of resilience and climate adaptation measures in project delivery and continued gains in the share of staff and firm leaders who are women or from racially and ethnically diverse groups.

Neither the public report summary nor the index page spells out how samples and definitions differ, so the safe reading is chronological. ScaleArc warns that the PSMJ and Deltek samples consist of firms that benchmark themselves and buy practice-management software. ScaleArc only has the March 2024 small-firm profitability figure from a secondary summary. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Mass General Brigham researchers develop AI tools that estimate age and survival risk from facial photos
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Mass General Brigham in Boston developed two artificial intelligence tools that turn facial photographs into estimates of age and survival risk, according to a study published in The Lancet Digital Health. The survival tool sorted cancer patients by their risk of death. In the first test group, patients it put in the highest-risk quarter were more than three times as likely to die as those in the lowest quarter. That gap survived adjustment for the usual clinical factors. Both programs grew out of one base model built at Mass General Brigham.

The base model, called FAHR-Face, was trained on more than 40 million face photographs from a public collection with no labels attached. FAHR-FaceAge trained on ten public photo collections balanced so that no age group dominated. FAHR-FaceSurvival learned from 34,363 photographs of cancer patients treated at the Harvard-affiliated hospitals, paired with whether and when each patient died. On a public set of photos of presumed healthy people, the age program missed the true age by 5.1 years on average. A comparable program trained from scratch on the same photos missed by 6.9.

Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist, is the study's corresponding author, and Hugo Aerts, who directs the system's Artificial Intelligence in Medicine program, is a co-senior author. Mak said physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy. Mak said the goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalized treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment. Aerts said the key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images. Aerts said this representation can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival.

Among 38,183 cancer patients treated with radiation at the Harvard hospitals, a third looked at least five years older than their age, and 17% looked at least ten years older. Patients who appeared five or more years older than their age had a 21% higher risk of death over the follow-up period than those who didn't. Patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk. Among patients the program judged more than 20 years older than their real age, 21.3% died within 90 days, and among those it judged at least ten years younger, 6.4% did. The survival program assigns each photo a score from 0 to 1 and was tested on photographs of 3,820 patients whose images had not been used to train it.

The scores rose with the seriousness of the cancer, from a median of 0.13 for benign and earliest-stage cases to 0.45 for cancer that had spread. Of 122 patients scored between 0.9 and 1.0, 64 died within 90 days, and of 975 scored at or below 0.1, 20 did. The survival tool weighed the area under the eyes and around the bridge of the nose, while the age tool weighed the creases from nose to mouth, the forehead, and the temples. Heavy drinking and drug use went with looking older, and current smokers looked older than former smokers, who looked older than people who had never smoked. Both programs were checked on 4,892 patients treated at Maastricht University's radiotherapy clinic in the Netherlands, and both kept their link to survival.

The survival analyses focused on patients treated at a few centers in wealthy countries. The age tool stratified risk less sharply in Black and Hispanic patients than in White and Asian patients, and the authors wrote that this residual bias remains a risk. No patient's treatment was changed by a score. The authors called for prospective trials before the tools enter routine care. Mass General Brigham has filed a provisional patent on the next generation of these algorithms, with Mak, Aerts, and lead author Fridolin Haugg named on it.

stories.Headline: Orbis Medicines uses AI to discover oral macrocyclic drugs from a 100 billion compound library
stories.Summary:
The Swiss biotech firm Orbis Medicines was founded in 2021 to create an artificial intelligence driven process for discovering novel oral macrocyclic drugs. This company, which spun off from the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, integrates automated chemical synthesis and biological activity detection to optimize drug molecules. The founders include Christian Heinis, Sevan Habeshian, and Morten Graugaard, who combined their expertise in chemical biology and business development. Their goal is to improve the oral bioavailability of candidate drugs that would otherwise require subcutaneous or intravenous administration.

The new process utilizes a Lab-in-the-Loop mode to screen a proprietary DNA-encoded library containing nearly 100 billion compounds. By using generative AI and machine learning, the firm can synthesize and analyze about 100,000 cyclic macromolecular compounds within several weeks. This method reduces typical molecular weight to 500-1000 Daltons and expands the potential chemical design space to 10³⁰ structural combinations. In February 2024, the company raised 26 million euros in seed funding, followed by a 90 million euro Series A round in January 2025 led by New Enterprise Associates.

The company focuses on immune, inflammatory, and cardiovascular metabolic diseases, with the latter involving a September 2026 agreement with Novo Nordisk. This licensing partnership for multi-target drug discovery has a maximum potential value of 1.4 billion US dollars. The founders explained that traditional small-molecule drugs often fail to act on complex targets, while larger biotherapeutic macromolecules are frequently degraded by gastric acid. By introducing unnatural amino acids and adjusting molecular skeletons, they aim to create stable compounds that can penetrate the intestinal epithelial barrier.

Orbis Medicines was recognized as a 2025 TOP100 Swiss Startups honoree for its pioneering approach to science and technology innovation. The company continues to use its funding from investors like Novo Holdings, Forbion, and Lilly Ventures to advance its synthetic macrocyclic candidates. Future efforts will focus on developing oral drugs for protein targets that have already been verified by biologics. This work aims to reduce the long research cycles and high costs associated with traditional molecular design and experimental screening.

stories.Summary:
AI agencies are mass producing fake store exploration videos using artificial intelligence. These companies create digital humans that taste food and introduce store environments. This business has emerged recently to erode the traditional in person exploration industry. Some of these mass production companies earn 8 million yuan monthly. The trend is spreading across platforms like Douyin for various local businesses.

Merchants upload storefront and dish photos to generate videos for under 10 yuan. Custom systems cost nearly 20,000 yuan, while existing systems cost 680 yuan annually. Computing power top ups cost 10 yuan per exploration or 2 to 3 yuan per voiceover. Agents pay 9,800 yuan yearly for 100 accounts and 100 stores. Some tutorials on Xianyu sell for as low as 0.18 yuan.

A practitioner told Tech Planet that his company cooperated with thousands of stores. He noted that basic fees alone reached 680,000 yuan from various catering enterprises. A producer mentioned using seedance2.5 to make AI character expressions look more realistic. He stated that AI reduces on camera costs and saves money on ingredients. This producer focuses on partners that are local small and medium catering enterprises.

Real person bloggers face increased pressure as Douyin emphasizes stable traffic and transactions. Some influencers, like Xiao Tan and Li Wuyou, earn commissions through group buying links. Xiao Tan sold 231,000 yuan across 718 stores, while Li Wuyou sold 202,000 yuan. New hot pot and milk tea shops use AI for short term exposure. These merchants often pay for tutorials, computing power, and generation service fees.

Traditional store exploration costs hundreds or thousands of yuan per video. Mid tier influencers in first tier cities can charge nearly 2,000 yuan. The industry previously relied on intermediaries who matched bloggers with local merchants. Many current AI videos use real shot pictures paired with digital humans. Some bloggers use ancient costume characters to increase user retention and visual freshness.

Operators now hang group buying links to earn verification commissions from AI videos. Tools for AI store exploration vlogs are available in Apple and Android stores. Platform rules are changing, making it harder for low cost volume content to distribute. Users struggle to distinguish between true and false experiences despite AI generated labels. The articles leave open whether merchants truly benefit from these lower costs.

stories.Headline: Afro-Latina AI Claira keynotes Latino AI Summit in Manhattan
stories.Summary:
A Latino AI Summit was held at Civic Hall and Berkeley College in Midtown Manhattan, and Claira, described by Abran Maldonado as the first Afro-Latina multilingual virtual assistant, keynoted it in front of dozens of mostly Latino and Black attendees. Maldonado helped invent Claira, who has caramel-color skin and bouncy, curly hair and appeared on a large screen. Claira told Gothamist that seeing an Afro-Latina AI challenges the idea of who belongs in tech. The summit is the in-person version of a forum also featured online. Gothamist published the story by Willow Higgins on Nov 15, 2026 at 7:00 a.m.

ET. The Knowledge House in the Bronx provides coding and design training for underserved young people interested in the AI economy. The Rev. Al Sharpton’s AI Fluency Initiative teaches adults without tech experience the basics of AI. The group states its mission is to close the digital divide and put the power of these tools in the hands of the people.

The Latino AI Summit was cofounded by Michal Tapia. Anthropic’s initial public offering is set for Wednesday and is expected to value the company at more than $1 trillion. Tapia said AI will play a major role in our future whether people like it or not. She said AI is happening and it is either we get on the train or we get left behind. Maldonado said it is essential for all jobseekers to market themselves as AI-literate.

He said resumes should list proficiency in AI tools like Claude, Codex and Google AI Studio instead of Microsoft Office and the Adobe Suite, and should be updated once a month. He said putting our heads in the sand is not the move and you have to tinker and try these things out. A McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility report found a disproportionate number of Black workers hold jobs likely to be automated by AI, including in transportation, production and administration roles. A 2025 report from Jobs for the Future found 67% of Black survey respondents said they feel AI is already impacting their jobs, compared to 57% of white respondents. The same report found more than half of Black respondents already use AI tools daily or weekly, compared to about 40% of all respondents.

A Kapor Foundation report found about 19% of the U.S. workforce is Latino, but Latinos fill just 3% of board seats, 5% of executive leadership roles and 6% of technical roles at the largest tech companies. Taylor Shead, founder of a company that develops AI-driven education, wrote in the Jobs for the Future report about prevention over intervention and meeting people where they are. Alpha School is a K-12 program with locations across the country that trains kids on AI tools, and Maldonado said kids are scoring through the roof in fluency and literacy. Kara Emery, director of data science at the AI Hub of NYU’s McSilver Institute for Poverty Policy and Research, said projections of what AI will impact are just that. Emery said the fear is AI could worsen racial income inequalities but people have a say in how things unfold.

Summit attendee Fradely Delacruz, a computational scientist student and professional data architect, said women of color are rapidly losing jobs in STEM and research and development. David Gabeau, who created an online interface of AI companies in New York and worked at Snapchat and Lyft, said he fears AI will broaden social inequities across racial lines. Gabeau said people working in AI are going to get so wealthy and there will be no forcing function to spread the wealth. After 10 years in New York, Gabeau recently moved to San Francisco to be closer to the epicenter of AI.

There he spent an afternoon wearing a 4 pound headset that scanned his brain while he watched videos and answered questions for a company working on an AI tool akin to telepathy that converts thoughts into text without typing. Gabeau said he was paid about $50 and that many others in the room, many of them Black and brown, seemed to be there because they needed the money, which he called a little predatory. Emery said the narrative of the inevitability of what these technologies will become is often pushed by those currently in the big companies building them. Delacruz said when AI came it felt like other people knew about it before we did and by the time we are catching on we are not even part of the conversation.

She said they do not see the Black and brown and Latino and Afro-Latino scientists and researchers and do not know we exist, but we are here. Emery said she is seeing Black and brown New Yorkers rising to the occasion and that these communities are not just sitting on the sidelines. Emery said the right combination of policy, education and a diversity of innovators working behind the scenes is key to preventing existing inequalities from worsening. Delacruz said she is eager to put her skills to use but still feels unseen.

stories.Headline: Jack Selby warns the AI investment boom is a bubble that could wipe out hundreds of billions
stories.Summary:
Jack Selby, managing director at Thiel Capital and a longtime business partner of Peter Thiel, warned that the artificial intelligence investment boom is a bubble. He spoke on the November 4, 2026 episode of the How I Invest podcast with David Weisburd. Selby said a correction was inevitable and could wipe out hundreds of billions of dollars in invested capital. He said anyone who does not believe there is an AI bubble is an absolute contrarian. Selby cited inflated valuations, circular financing and unprecedented capital expenditure.

Selby said the downturn is a question of when rather than whether it will happen. He compared the current cycle with the dot-com boom, when substantial capital flowed into technology businesses before their commercial prospects were established. He said the AI cycle differs in the scale of infrastructure spending required, including expensive computing facilities, specialized processors and substantial ongoing operating costs. He questioned the investment industry's emphasis on finding companies capable of reaching trillion-dollar valuations. He described Anthropic and SpaceX as exceptional businesses that should not serve as valuation benchmarks for ordinary startups.

Selby said he spent six months meeting limited partners and concluded that venture firms had struggled to return sufficient capital to investors over the past decade. He cited a concentration of fundraising among a small number of firms, with eight managers attracting approximately $70 bn during 2026. He estimated that approximately 90% of venture funding flows to California, New York and Massachusetts, leaving entrepreneurs in the other 47 states competing for a comparatively small share. He said Silicon Valley's principal advantage is the concentration of financial resources rather than exclusive access to talented founders. He pointed to Carvana, founded in Arizona, which struggled to attract funding from Sand Hill Road investors before reaching approximately $65 bn in market capitalization.

Selby said similar opportunities exist in cities such as Phoenix, Milwaukee and Cincinnati. He said AI tools could strengthen the economics of these businesses by allowing smaller teams to develop software, automate processes and compete without the same staffing and infrastructure requirements as traditional technology startups. He said AI-enabled companies do not need to be built in Palo Alto unless they are competing directly in frontier AI development. He said valuations in these markets can be approximately one-tenth of those found in Silicon Valley. His fund, Copper Sky, takes a sector-agnostic approach and prioritizes founders with strong execution capabilities over specific technologies or industries.

Selby has known Peter Thiel for 28 years and worked with him for 27 of them. He was among PayPal's first ten employees and credits Thiel's early hiring philosophy with helping the company assemble a team capable of handling rapid growth and repeated operational crises. He recalled that the average age of PayPal's executive team during its IPO roadshow was just 26. PayPal's early development included persistent fraud attacks, with Max Levchin leading efforts to counter sophisticated criminal activity. PayPal's acquisition by eBay for approximately $1.5 bn in 2002 subsequently helped establish the financial resources and entrepreneurial networks associated with the PayPal Mafia.

Selby's warning does not amount to a rejection of the technology, and he continues to see AI as a transformative technology. He characterized the current environment as more suitable for traders seeking to capitalize on price movements than for long-term investors. He said the shortage of distributions to venture capital investors is limiting new commitments, while much of the remaining capital is being directed toward late-stage AI investments. He said the combination of limited liquidity and elevated entry valuations creates additional risk if the AI market experiences a prolonged correction. The articles do not say what Selby or Copper Sky will do next.

stories.Headline: Societe Generale strategist Albert Edwards warns liquidity squeeze threatens AI stock rally
stories.Summary:
Société Générale strategist Albert Edwards warned in a Nov. 12 report that investors captivated by artificial intelligence earnings may be overlooking a tightening liquidity squeeze threatening the stock market. He said financial support for risk assets is dwindling and momentum is fading, which could pressure equities and semiconductor shares even when profit forecasts stay strong. The report also flagged that the breadth of analyst upgrades and the pace of technology earnings revisions have deteriorated, though forecast profit growth remains strong. Edwards raised the possibility of renewed inflation forcing the Federal Reserve to raise rates by more than 200 basis points, without giving a formal forecast or timetable.

The warning covers the AI-driven stock rally and semiconductor shares, which Edwards said could come under pressure from the liquidity squeeze despite strong profit forecasts. It points to weakening earnings revisions as a concern for U.S. technology stocks, since upgrades have narrowed and revisions have slowed even as forecast growth holds up. Short-term inflation measures and corporate output-price inflation have become concerning, and Edwards said renewed inflation could push the Federal Reserve toward rate increases exceeding 200 basis points. He offered no formal forecast or timetable for such a move, according to the report.

Edwards is the lead analyst and strategist at Société Générale, and he made the warning in his Nov. 12 report, which was reported on Nov. 15. He said investors may be overlooking the growing threat of tightening liquidity to the stock market because they are captivated by artificial intelligence's earnings potential. He described the financial support for risk assets as dwindling and the momentum as fading, and he tied the risk to equities and semiconductor shares. He also said short-term inflation measures and corporate output-price inflation have become concerning, and he raised the possibility of rate increases above 200 basis points.

The report does not say what happens next beyond the risks it describes, and it gives no formal forecast or timetable for the rate increases Edwards raised. It frames the threat as one investors may be overlooking while they focus on AI earnings potential, with liquidity tightening and fading momentum as the main concerns. It also notes that the breadth of analyst upgrades and the pace of technology earnings revisions have deteriorated even though forecast profit growth remains strong. The articles give no further context or next steps beyond the report's warnings.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 writes robot code that succeeds in 92.1% of physical trials
stories.Summary:
ACE-CaP-0 researchers reported that robot programs developed by Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 coding agent completed 221 of 240 physical evaluation trials, a 92.1% success rate. The researchers posted the study on November 12, and CryptoSlate published its report on November 15, 2026. The trials covered eight tasks, with each program frozen before 30 separate evaluation trials and no further updates. Neither a human nor the coding agent remained in the execution loop during evaluation. The programs used live perception and control systems to respond to observations while their decision rules stayed fixed.

The physical setup used two Agilex PIPERX arms and three cameras, and tasks included inserting a charger, uncapping a bottle and packing shoes. Charger insertion succeeded in all 30 trials, while bread packing was the weakest result at 25 of 30. Bottle uncapping succeeded 27 times, cup nesting 28, flower insertion 27, chicken plating 29, parcel reorientation 28 and shoe packing 27. Mean physical execution times across tasks ranged from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes. Development allowed at most ten human-assisted scene resets per task, excluding resets used to collect demonstrations, and the budget counted resets rather than autonomous executions or demonstrations.

The authors' preprint account states that development permits human assistance and that demonstration-collection resets are excluded from the ten-reset budget. The researchers call for accounting that includes demonstration effort, saying the time and token figures leave total development costs unresolved. They state that repeated execution on tested tasks does not establish reuse under new conditions. They also say that establishing how consistently the development process produces an equally capable program requires separate development runs across tasks. The preprint describes ACE-CaP-0 as a method for developing robot control programs.

During development the coding agent could request textual guidance and demonstrations in which a person physically guided the robot arms, providing video, trajectories and key joint poses. The agent wrote and revised executable programs using physical feedback and could run simulated experiments as needed. In a charger-insertion comparison, on-demand simulation produced a program with 100% evaluation success versus 86.7% for development without simulation, using one development run per condition. Development took 2.6 hours with on-demand simulation versus 3.7 hours without it, while output-token usage rose from 730,000 to 1,090,000. The study provides evidence for skill reuse after human-assisted development.

The experiment separates program development from repeated execution, and the agent's work produced a program that could be used repeatedly. The coding agent leaves and the program stays, according to the article's account of the method. Human guidance and demonstrations were available during development, not execution. The result shows that task-specific skills can persist in code and run without the coding agent choosing each action. The article states that testing those routines under new conditions is the next step toward establishing how broadly they can be reused.

The articles leave open how consistently separate development runs produce an equally capable program and whether the routines can be reused under new conditions. They also leave total development costs unresolved, calling for accounting that includes demonstration effort. The articles do not state what happens next beyond testing the routines under new conditions. The comparison of simulation and non-simulation development used only one development run per condition. The articles give no further plans, dates or results beyond those stated.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Fooyo urges marketing teams to build in-house AI video capabilities instead of hiring agencies

This transition is supported by the Kakis AI story-to-video platform, which uses WAN AI video technology to simplify the creation process. The company operates from Singapore and Tokyo, providing delivery services across eight countries, including Germany, Japan, Indonesia, and the United States.

The new approach requires teams to use the Kakis AI platform alongside ambassadors who train staff until they can produce videos independently. Instead of paying for fixed agency packages, marketing teams can now set their own budgets for each video, ranging from 50 to 1,000 US dollars. This system removes the need for traditional cameras, crews, and studios for everyday content, allowing people with laptops to create professional films. The company also offers other production tools, including an AI Knowledge Base, Fooyo Commerce, and Smart Tourism solutions.

Li Shaohuan, the founder and CEO of Fooyo, stated that AI tools have removed the production barriers that previously made outsourcing the default choice. He explained that internal teams already understand their audience and stories, whereas agencies must learn these details from a brief. Li suggested that while agencies are still useful for flagship brand films, teams should build a cadence for everyday video production. He noted that the tenth film a team produces is typically faster and better than the first one they create.

Fooyo provides these solutions for government agencies, SMEs, and enterprises across Asia, integrating them with existing CMS, POS, and CRM systems. The software can be deployed on-premises or within public and private clouds, and it supports China-market readiness through WeChat Mini Programs. To begin the process, the company offers a scoped pilot and a 30-minute demo for prospective partners. This strategy aims to help teams retain production know-how rather than waiting weeks for agency revisions and finished films.
