stories.Headline: Luke ellis outlines seven realistic ways to make money with AI in 2027
stories.Summary:
Luke ellis published the article "7 Realistic Ways to Make Money With AI in 2027 (Without Falling for the Hype)" on vocal.media on 2026-11-15T06:00:00Z, about two hours before it was read. The article says the initial gold rush and speculative fever surrounding artificial intelligence have finally cooled as we transition into 2027. It says the days of low-effort AI-generated content dominating search results or social media feeds are a thing of the past. It says major platforms and search engines have deployed sophisticated detection and filtering systems that prioritize depth, unique perspective, and the human touch. It says profitability is no longer about who can generate the most text, but who can best integrate AI into existing workflows to solve real problems.

The article gives seven methods, starting with a hybrid Human-in-the-Loop content service in which you act as the expert strategist and spend most of your time humanizing output. It says you should build a portfolio of Before AI and After Human Edit comparisons and focus on technical niches like cybersecurity, renewable energy policy, or telemedicine. It says pricing has shifted from per word to per project value. The second method is AI implementation consulting for small to medium-sized businesses, using the 2027 no-code ecosystem and tools like Zapier, Make, and autonomous agents, with robust Service Level Agreements on data handling. The third is hyper-specialized, AI-integrated digital products such as Notion dashboards with custom AI prompts or legal document frameworks that auto-fill by jurisdiction.

The article says the fourth method is a high-quality, AI-curated newsletter using specialized LLMs to monitor hundreds of sources, including technical journals, patent filings, and niche forums, with a micro-niche example of AI applications in vertical farming and two hours spent refining the narrative. The fifth is Optimization-as-a-Service for sellers on Shopify, Etsy, and Amazon, using generative AI for product photography and SEO-optimized listings for visual-first discovery engines. The sixth is short-form video of 15-60 seconds, with AI scriptwriting, synthetic voiceovers, and AI-driven editing, aimed at brands needing 20+ videos per month. The seventh is RAG-based assistants for local businesses, built on Private LLM instances so proprietary data is never used to train public models.

The article says many jurisdictions now require explicit labeling of AI-assisted content and that the US Copyright Office and international bodies have specific rulings on AI-generated works. It says the AI-generated portions often cannot be copyrighted, only the human-authored arrangements and edits. It gives a 30-day plan: Days 1-7 the Specialist Phase, choosing only one method and mastering 2-3 specific AI tools; Days 8-14 the Proof Phase, producing three high-quality pieces for free or for your own brand; Days 15-21 the Outreach Phase, identifying 20 potential clients and sending personalized, value-first messages; Days 22-30 the Refinement Phase, securing your first paying client and using their feedback to refine workflow and pricing. It says success is not about being a prompt engineer but about being a professional who uses the best tools to deliver exceptional results to other humans. It says the hype has faded and the real work begins now.

The article says it will release a series of accompanying short videos following the article to show exactly how these AI-assisted edits are performed, and that these videos are currently in production and will be released separately. It says the article is a 6 min read, with a photo by Igor Omilaev on Unsplash. It says the piece was published under Futurism and lists navigation links for Home, Top Stories, Latest Stories, and AI-Generated. It says readers can subscribe for free to receive all of luke ellis's stories in their feed. It says there are no comments for the story and invites readers to be the first to respond and start the conversation.

The article says the market for pure AI-generated writing has effectively collapsed by 2027 due to over-saturation and declining engagement, while demand for high-quality, specialized content is higher than ever. It says mainstream AI tools are powerful but most small to medium-sized businesses lack the internal bandwidth or technical expertise to implement them effectively. It says business owners are often skeptical of automation due to privacy concerns. It says generic templates are worthless in 2027 and intellectual property theft is rampant. It says we are in an era of extreme information density and most professionals are overwhelmed.

The article says monetization of a newsletter usually requires a significant subscriber base or a high-ticket sponsorship model, and consistency is the primary barrier to success. It says major platforms are rapidly integrating their own basic AI tools, so you must offer superior quality, custom branding, and a higher level of creative direction than the free built-in options. It says platforms are constantly changing their algorithms and what works this week may not work next month. It says RAG assistants require ongoing maintenance, and as a business changes its prices or policies you must ensure the knowledge base is updated immediately. It says you should never upload sensitive client information such as customer lists or private financial data into public AI models, and should use secure, enterprise-grade instances that guarantee data isolation.

stories.Headline: AI creators post Seinfeld and Office parodies that mock socialists and Democrats
stories.Summary:
An AI-generated Seinfeld parody posted by NYC Common Sense on Nov. 14 sends Jerry, George and Elaine to a Democratic Socialists of America convention, and the account TBC shared it with a caption calling it "AI Seinfeld goes to the DSA convention." The roughly two-minute, 43-second sketch follows Jerry to the convention at the invitation of a woman he is dating, while George asks about the free buffet and Elaine wants to hear men who have never lifted anything explain labor. When Jerry wonders why the attendees are not at work, his date tells him that socialists do not need jobs, and the jokes keep coming with a demand for a nondisclosure agreement before a discussion of transparency and an unemployed attendee living rent-free in his parents' second apartment. Security personnel remove Jerry after someone objects to his support for police, and a closing card labels the video AI-generated satire that depicts neither real events nor real statements and disclaims affiliation with the DSA.

A separate Office spoof posted by TBC on Nov. 6, which Clay Travis shared the next day, runs roughly 95 seconds and turns workplace political correctness into a staff meeting at Dunder Mifflin. Michael Scott wears a rainbow sweater and a Black Lives Matter pin and calls for a moment of silence, while Dwight Schrute goes to the whiteboard to diagram who a political wave will hit first and Jim supplies the familiar deadpan reactions. Travis wrote alongside his post that AI is getting scary good and that the episode could have existed, and the parody is framed around Democrats winning on Tuesday. Asked in the thread beneath the Office video whether humans write the dialogue, TBC replied yes.

The satire also reaches the right, because creator @sikoraimagine posted a separate AI parody on Oct. 16 that sends a synthetic version of President Donald Trump into Dunder Mifflin. That video pairs him with Michael Scott, Dwight, Jim and Pam in a fictional workplace visit, and it gives the president the same sitcom treatment the other clips give Jerry and Michael. The clips give familiar sitcoms an unofficial second life, with creators using AI versions of their characters and settings to stage new political comedy that blends television nostalgia with jokes about socialists, Democrats and Trump. AI-generated political imagery has also appeared in Texas campaign messaging, as The Dallas Express has reported, which brings that technology into the rhythms and settings of sitcom comedy.

stories.Headline: Sebastian Raschka explains how large language models represent token positions
stories.Summary:
Sebastian Raschka published an article on November 15, 2026, explaining how large language models represent token positions. He wrote this technical guide to cover both classic and contemporary positional encoding methods. The author created this standalone piece to serve as a foundation for future architecture trends. He specifically wanted to provide a tutorial on relative positional embeddings after many readers asked. This work follows his previous materials on building a large language model from scratch.

The guide compares GPT-2, which uses absolute embeddings, to MiniMax-M3, a model released in 2026. GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the first transformer block. MiniMax-M3 uses Rotary Positional Embeddings, or RoPE, inside the attention of each transformer block. GPT-2 XL uses specific dimensions for these vectors, while the original GPT-2 has 1,024 learned vectors. MiniMax-M3 features 60 feedforward layers, where the first three are dense rather than mixtures of experts.

Sebastian Raschka is responsible for this technical explanation and the accompanying PyTorch implementation. He stated that he had not previously covered positional information methods in any of his articles. The author noted that the content is very technical and might be too detailed for some. He mentioned that his next article will return to a more comfortable writing style. Raschka also explained that he is now experimenting with a new perks system on Substack.

The author explains that these methods affect how models distinguish word order in sentences. Without positional encoding, swapping words like red and gray would result in the same attention scores. Causal masks provide some implicit order, but they cannot distinguish a separation of one position from ten. Therefore, explicit positional signals are essential for the attention mechanism to function accurately. This process ensures that identical tokens, such as fox, receive different representations based on their location.

The articles explain that tokenizers first encode input text into token IDs. An embedding layer then maps these IDs to vectors of numbers called features. Transformer blocks modify these vectors using feedforward layers and attention mechanisms. Finally, the output layer produces logit scores that are converted into probabilities for the next token. In absolute methods, the model learns a table of position vectors during the training process.

The author will next use this foundation to analyze the latest large language model architecture trends. He provides a gallery of 2026 open-weight models grouped by their specific positional encoding choices. The text leaves open how the context window of absolute models can be extended. It notes that increasing the context length to 100k would make the embedding table very large. The author suggests reading the article in a web browser to use the navigation bar.

stories.Headline: Upwork survey finds 77% of AI users say their workload increased
stories.Summary:
The article, published by eu.36kr.com on 17 November 2026 and written by Wei Xi, argues that AI is making people busier rather than more productive. It says AI can produce a decent draft in three minutes, but writing a heartfelt, engaging article people want to read has not become easier. It reports that many former colleagues at large tech companies use AI daily while bosses raise requirements, and many product managers must bring a working demo to the review meeting. It says AI does not save time but makes people busier and busier. It presents three paradoxes: the Cowan Paradox, the Solow Paradox and the Jevons Paradox.

The article cites Ruth Schwartz Cowan's 1983 book More Work for Mother, which observed that washing machines, vacuum cleaners and electric stoves were widespread by the 1970s yet she was busier than her mother's generation. It says full-time housewives in the US spent about 52 hours a week on housework in 1924 and around 55 hours a week by 1966. It says economic historian Joel Mokyr named this the Cowan Paradox. It says Cowan found the work of one housewife in 1950 would have needed three or four people in 1850. It says new tasks such as driving to the supermarket and picking up and dropping off children did not exist in the horse-drawn carriage era.

The article reports that the staffing agency Upwork surveyed 2,500 people, finding 77% of employees who use AI say their workload increased and 81% of executives admit they raised work requirements in the past year. It says Aruna Ranganathan and Xingqi Maggie Ye of UC Berkeley published an article in Harvard Business Review in February 2026 titled AI Has Not Reduced Work, It Has Made Work More Intensive. It says they spent eight months observing a tech company with about 200 employees and found product managers started writing code and researchers took on engineering tasks. It says renowned developer Simon Willison shared the article and said it matches his own experience. It says Stanford Social Media Lab coined the term "workslop" in September 2025 for AI outputs that look decent but cannot push work forward.

The article says the lab surveyed 1,150 full-time American employees, 40% of whom received such outputs in the past month, each spending an average of 116 minutes processing them, an implicit loss of $186 per person per month. It says engineer Siddhant Khare wrote AI Fatigue Is Real, No One Is Talking About It in February 2026, which topped the Hacker News leaderboard, arguing every task gets done faster so you take on more tasks but your brain cannot expand its capacity. It says John Maynard Keynes wrote Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren in 1930, calculating that with 2% annual capital growth and usual technological advance, by 2030 people need work only three hours a day, 15 hours a week. It says Swiss and Spanish economists calculated in 2024 that annual working hours per capita in the US fell from 2,316 hours in 1929 to 1,765 hours in 2019, a 23.8% reduction in 90 years, while Keynes' target is about 780 hours a year. It says Sam Altman said publicly this summer that every technological revolution promised more leisure but society never lived with less work, and he does not think AI will change this because humans are naturally competitive.

The article says economist Robert Solow wrote in a July 1987 New York Times book review that "You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics," and won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in October of that year. It says US non-farm labor productivity grew at an average annual rate of 3.19% from 1948 to 1973, fell to 1.53% from 1974 to 1995, returned to 3.15% after the internet boom in 1996, and dropped to 1.39% after 2004. It says Anders Humlum of the University of Chicago linked survey data of 25,000 Danish employees with official tax and employment archives and found AI users save an average of only 2.8% of their time, with no significant impact on income or working hours. It says MIT's Generative AI Divide report last July found enterprises invested 300 to 400 billion US dollars in generative AI but 95% of institutions saw no measurable returns. It says Callum Williams of The Economist posted a US productivity curve in February 2026 captioned that the AI productivity boost is still not visible in US statistics, and Indeed Hiring Lab pointed out US total factor productivity slowed from 1.5% to 0.8% in 2025.

The article says Stanford economist Paul David explained that electricity faced the same paradox: power stations were built as early as 1881, but by 1900 there was barely evidence of efficiency gains in factories, and US manufacturing productivity exceeded 5% per year only in the 1920s, 40 years after commercialization. It describes this as the productivity J-curve, in which productivity first declines then rises as enterprises adjust processes and train employees, and says today's AI is stuck at the bottom of the J-curve. It says Workday research found that in 89% of institutions less than half of jobs have been redesigned to match AI capabilities. It says American economist Erik Brynjolfsson is the flagbearer of the optimists, and in March 2026 the US Bureau of Labor Statistics announced productivity grew 2.8% in 2025, against an average of only 1.2% in the decade before the pandemic. It says he tweeted that it is still hard to determine how much of this growth AI contributed, but the Solow Paradox might be ready to retire.

stories.Headline: Australia weighs binding standards for AI data centres as researchers propose a legislated social-licence floor
stories.Summary:
Australia is considering tougher rules for AI data centres, and the harder question is what happens to the promises after the servers switch on. The Commonwealth released five national expectations in March covering energy, water, jobs, research and the national interest, and a September consultation explored binding minimum standards for large facilities. That consultation raised the prospect of published compliance plans, ongoing reporting and different obligations for owners, operators and AI developers, and it closed on 9 October. These are proposals, not a single national law already in force.

The authors, Zhixi Liu and Chong Zhou, researchers affiliated with Basalt-X Australia Pty Ltd, propose in a recently published Telecommunications Policy study what they call a legislated social-licence floor, meaning minimum enforceable duties covering what a company owes the places and people affected by its infrastructure. They say Parliament can require evidence, consultation and remedies but cannot order a community to trust a developer. They propose a record that follows a large project from planning to operation, showing for each material commitment what was promised, the baseline used, who can deliver it, what evidence counts, when it is due and what happens if it falls short. They say a statutory duty, a planning condition, a contract and a voluntary public statement are not interchangeable, and a voluntary commitment should be labelled as such rather than presented to residents as enforceable protection.

On electricity, they note that signing a power-purchase agreement does not bring a new generator online, and a data centre may start drawing power months before the promised generation is available. They say the public record should show the commissioning timetable, interim supply arrangements, responsible parties and measures to manage any gap. They apply the same scrutiny to research access, saying free compute credits sound generous until expiry dates, technical restrictions and actual use are examined, and that a handful of construction jobs should not stand in for a continuing engineering workforce. They say reviews should be timed to the first grid connection, major expansions and regular operating periods, and a missed commitment should prompt an explanation, independent verification where warranted and a clear opportunity to correct the problem.

The authors acknowledge that Australia's federal structure makes this harder, not impossible, with Commonwealth standards sitting beside state approvals, water licences and electricity-market rules. They propose five checks for judging a data centre against a plausible alternative rather than an empty site: additionality, domestic value retention, capability deepening, diffusion, and resource and community performance. They describe these as proposed assessment tools, not tests already written into law. They argue the point is to know whether the electricity, water, skills and research arrangements that helped justify approval are still delivering five or ten years later, and that a permit authorises a facility but cannot settle the public bargain for the next 20 years.

stories.Headline: Chen Danqi joins Noeri part-time as the AI startup raises 110 million dollars
stories.Summary:
Chen Danqi announced on social platforms in the early hours of 17 November 2026 that she had joined Noeri on a part-time basis two months earlier. Danqi Chen is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Princeton University. Noeri is a newly unveiled AI company co-founded by Yejin Choi, Professor of Computer Science at Stanford University, and Carlos Guestrin. The company focuses on developing AI systems that can continuously learn and self-improve. Noeri also announced it has raised 110 million US dollars in financing.

The round was led by Menlo Ventures, with participation from Madrona Venture Group, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. NVIDIA, Cisco Investments and Snowflake became strategic investors. Noeri supports the use of closed-source models and open-weight models and can adapt as new models emerge. Customers can retain ownership of their own data and of the workflows and models developed through the system, but must still comply with relevant license agreements of third-party models. Every modification comes with an explanation and is submitted for human review and confirmation, a process Noeri compares to code review.

Chen said she is quite looking forward to the team's research direction, especially the application of AI in scientific discovery. She said she hopes to enable every scientist to apply AI to their most intractable research problems. She said she is very happy to work with Yejin Choi, who has long been her role model and friend. Choi and Guestrin serve as co-CEOs of Noeri. The company interprets its name as "The Plural of Intelligence".

Choi and Guestrin wrote in a vision article that they prefer an ecosystem composed of a large number of AIs of different scales and capabilities over one enterprise developing and mastering a superintelligence. They call the concept Plural Intelligence, in which every organization and individual can build, master and continuously improve their own AI. Enterprises are affected: Noeri will study an enterprise's own data and workflows and optimize the entire AI system around specific tasks. The scope it can adjust includes instructions and skills, tools and orchestration, model selection and model optimization.

Choi is a professor at Stanford University and a senior fellow at Stanford HAI, and she officially joined Stanford University in January 2025. She was previously a Professor of Computer Science at the University of Washington, Senior Research Manager at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2), and served as Senior Research Director and Distinguished Scientist at NVIDIA. Guestrin co-created XGBoost with Tianqi Chen and co-founded the machine learning company Turi, which was acquired by Apple in 2016. After joining Apple, Guestrin served as Senior Director of Machine Learning and AI and participated in promoting Apple to establish an AI and machine learning R&D center in Seattle. Chen co-leads the Princeton NLP research group, serves as deputy director of the Princeton Language and Intelligence Research Program, and is one of the authors of RoBERTa.

Noeri wants to hand to AI the work that otherwise requires a professional AI engineering team, since most AI models have basically fixed parameters after training is completed. The system will learn from the enterprise's data, workflows and interactions during task execution, and every experience and correction in a task has the opportunity to become the basis for the next round of optimization. Noeri hopes to find a more appropriate combination through model specialization and agent collaboration, for example letting a smaller model be responsible for scheduling and calling other models and professional tools according to task requirements. Chen said she is particularly looking forward to the application of Plural Intelligence in scientific discovery, a direction Noeri hopes to explore. The articles leave open what Noeri's products will cost and when they will be available.

stories.Headline: Smart Compliance Management issues 238,314 parking breach notices to New Zealanders
stories.Summary:
Smart Compliance Management, an AI-powered parking firm, issued 238,314 parking breach notices to New Zealanders in the last financial year, 27% more than the year before, which was already 48% up on the 2024 financial year. The foreign-owned company runs number plate-checking cameras at more than 300 New Zealand carparks, pitching its services to supermarkets, medical centres and even churches. In July a 54-year-old woman collapsed in New World Ōrewa's carpark north of Auckland and a stranger rushed to revive her, media reported at the time. Her car sat for more than five hours while she was in hospital and the cameras caught it, landing her an $80 ticket from Smart Compliance Management. The company was blocked from accessing Australians' private data and has brought its cameras to New Zealand.

Cameras record number plates every time a vehicle goes in and out of carparks using technology known as automated number plate recognition. Stay longer than the sign allows, even by a minute, and the system flags it, and the carpark operator can look up the car owner's name and address and send a ticket. The NZ Transport Agency granted a number of parking firms authorised access to the motor vehicle register. Smart Compliance added 90 new sites in the year to June and now runs 310 sites across the country. The local business now pockets almost 47c of every dollar it earns before tax, interest and head-office costs, up from 30c two years ago.

A Smart Compliance spokesperson told the Herald the system wasn't designed "to penalise motorists, but to encourage compliance so that parking remains fair, reliable, and accessible". The parking terms and conditions are "clearly displayed across each site" and drivers can appeal online or by post, the spokesperson said. Chief executive Paul Gillespie told investors on the company's results call in August that "New Zealand is a great success story of what happens when we deploy our technology and AI tools". Smart Compliance did not directly answer a Herald question about what guidelines or considerations went into how it set its ticket fees. Parking Services told the Herald it "fully complies with our legal obligations" and has since added cameras at the East Tāmaki site.

Jon Duffy, head of non-profit watchdog Consumer NZ, said AI-powered systems raise concerns about the potential for a "clinical, almost surgical nature of enforcement". AI and camera tickets may not "leave any room for error … it's black and white," he said, and "there's always a grey area with human behaviour". The Commerce Commission has recorded 431 "concerns" about private parking operators, including 137 mentioning Smart Compliance, this year. University of Auckland commercial law professor Alex Sims asked what happens when AI, mass surveillance and sensors become so cheap it's possible to monitor Kiwis everywhere. A Canterbury pensioner couple told Stuff in June they were ticketed $85 by the company for overstaying a private hospital carpark's grace period by one minute, a fee waived only after reporters stepped in.

When the family of the Ōrewa woman contested her ticket, Smart Compliance didn't cancel it but reduced it to a $30 "administration fee", Stuff reported in August. The supermarket's owner then stepped in, asking Smart Compliance to withdraw the notice and refund the fee, and the company later apologised for the "additional stress caused to this individual following their medical emergency". Multiple shoppers complained to the Herald this year about Smart Compliance ticketing them for overstaying in supermarket carparks even though they spent between $200 and $400 on groceries, and some only had fees waived after the Herald became involved. An Auckland man told the Herald he was lucky he had a dashcam after being ticketed by Parking Services Limited in East Tāmaki, which claimed he'd used a gym carpark and hit him with a $95 ticket, saying it had to be paid within 21 days or incur an additional $75 per week in late payment fees. Nav Sandhu was slapped with an $85 ticket after he parked at Pak'nSave Manukau for two hours and 16 minutes on April 18, despite spending more than $500.

Two-thirds of the group's revenue comes out of the United Kingdom where there is an "established cost-effective mechanism for retrieval of number plate details", its annual report said. The company went into Denmark in 2024 and Switzerland in 2025, describing both as attractive markets with high ticket values and a "low cost to source car owner details". Denmark changed the rules in July 2025 so the first ticket must be "placed on a vehicle or handed directly to the driver", and Smart Parking had to hire wardens, with revenue there falling from A$1.3m ($1.6m) to A$300,000 ($370,000) in a year because "manual operations aren't as efficient as ANPR [automated number plate recognition] operations". New South Wales stopped private carpark firms getting drivers' details in 2012 and Victoria followed in 2015, and Queensland paused access to its vehicle register in 2023, with the then state Transport Minister Mark Bailey saying "predatory companies" were issuing tickets that "looked like fines" from the Government. Smart Parking shut its Queensland business and told investors its cameras had been "redeployed to New Zealand".

The Commerce Commission said it has been speaking to parking operators, including Smart Compliance, to "encourage" compliance with the Fair Trading Act, and will soon issue updated guidance for the industry. Consumer NZ wrote in a 2023 article that a parking fee "should be reasonably reflective of the actual loss suffered by the operator" and "anything out of proportion to what's reasonable is likely to be an unenforceable penalty". Duffy said customers' best chance to kick back against policies they believed unfair was to vote with their feet and shop elsewhere, though he said it's not easy to avoid or boycott supermarkets and airlines. Sims said if enforcement is abused as a cash cow or to harshly penalise, social cohesion could suffer. Smart Compliance's Australian parent company Smart Parking said New Zealand is "an attractive market with significant potential for further expansion".

stories.Headline: SemiAnalysis lowers growth forecasts for AI infrastructure investment and chip shipments
stories.Summary:
The research firm SemiAnalysis sharply lowered its growth expectations for AI infrastructure investment on November 13. This adjustment reduces forecasts for global AI accelerator capital expenditure, chip shipments, and power consumption. The firm also downgraded the expected demand for high bandwidth memory in the coming years. These changes suggest the AI computing power market is entering a new stage of reassessment. Demand for these technologies continues to grow, but the previous optimistic expectations are cooling down.

Global AI accelerator capital expenditure for 2027 is now $627 billion, down from $770 billion. The 2028 figure fell to $758 billion from $1.054 trillion, and 2029 dropped to $796 billion from $1.352 trillion. By 2030, the forecast is $923 billion, reduced from $1.531 trillion, totaling a $1.6 trillion cumulative cut. Logic wafer shipments from 2026 to 2030 fell by 17 percent, with a 24 percent drop in 2029. Power consumption demand for 2030 was cut by 34 percent, from 122.8GW to 80.7GW.

SemiAnalysis stated that slowing revenue growth for AI labs and a tightening financing environment drove these cuts. They noted that investors are now more cautious about projects lacking procurement commitments from large cloud providers. The firm explained that NVIDIA must reduce product markups and accept lower gross margins to stay competitive. They believe large customers now have more computing platform choices, making NVIDIA GPUs less attractive in some scenarios. The agency emphasized that these revisions would occur regardless of whether Jensen Huang remains as NVIDIA CEO.

NVIDIA is the most affected company, facing shipment cuts and lower prices for its Feynman series products. Anthropic prefers Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, and AMD GPU over NVIDIA, while OpenAI is deploying self-developed ASICs. Neocloud customers are vulnerable because they rely on financing to purchase GPUs and rent out computing power. Chinese customers may face export control risks if the US RASA Act is passed regarding remote GPU use. Broadcom remains resilient because its ASIC projects for Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic are energy efficient.

Revenue growth for cutting-edge AI labs fell short of expectations in the third quarter, impacting commercialization forecasts. Many AI data center projects were previously advanced through debt and equity financing before the market tightened. Regulatory factors related to the US midterm elections may delay some data center projects in the future. Specifically, 5.8GW of capacity planned for late 2027 to early 2028 may be postponed due to these factors. Some Texas projects, including the Nexus project in Hubbard, face delays due to missing permits.

NVIDIA will increase GB300 shipments by 130,000 units in the third quarter of 2026 to fill gaps. Total revenue forecasts for the third and fourth quarters of 2026 are $109.1 billion and $125.3 billion. Microsoft reduced its 2027 orders for Vera Rubin cabinets by 200 units, while Broadcom's ASIC revenue forecast fell 11 percent. The 700MW TPU for Anthropic was postponed from 2027 to 2028, and the Crusoe project may be delayed. The articles leave open how leadership transitions at NVIDIA might further impact its future market share.

stories.Summary:

This latest edition highlights ten concrete artificial intelligence application projects that range from customer management to unmanned operations. The initiative aims to integrate intelligent tools into traditional reporting workflows to improve content production and lower communication barriers for early stage startups. By providing a one stop display window, the platform helps entrepreneurs connect with new opportunities and increases the visibility of noteworthy innovations.

The list includes 3Chat ai, which uses an AI Agent to record customer portraits and manage follow up communications for enterprises. Seashore AI offers pronunciation assessment and listening practice for approximately 30 languages through a web version and a WeChat Mini Program. Guanghe AI provides generative engine optimization services and introduced the AI Mindshare indicator to help brands evaluate their presence in AI search results. Zhili Quantitative allows users to generate editable code from Chinese descriptions for strategy backtesting, while Zhongke Zhichi deploys autonomous driving vehicles for cleaning and logistics in Hefei Luogang Park.

This curator stated that the goal is to make the process of project reporting more efficient while exploring better communication methods for new companies. stories.Headline: AI infrastructure suppliers lose $4.2tn in value as investor confidence drops
stories.Summary:
Companies supplying the infrastructure for artificial intelligence data centres lost approximately $4.2tn in value since June, according to an analysis by The Financial Times. This significant decline wiped out nearly half of the $9.4tn these businesses gained during the previous twelve months. The sell off affected global mining, utility, and manufacturing firms, including Caterpillar and Okto, which contracted with Meta for nuclear power in Ohio. Investor confidence dropped quickly over the last four weeks due to concerns regarding debt funded spending and political backlash.

The market downturn impacted chipmakers like AMD, Micron, Broadcom, and TSMC, as well as manufacturers such as Dell, HPE, and Super Micro Computer. Vertiv saw its shares drop 23 percent after the midterms, falling to $202.07 from a May peak of $379.94 despite third quarter sales rising 61 percent to $4.31bn. S&P Global is tracking 157 projects that have been abandoned, paused, or severely delayed. Sightline Climate analysts estimate that 30 to 50 percent of US AI data centres planned for 2026 will be cancelled or delayed.

Dan Thompson of 451 Research at S&P Global Energy stated that community opposition and state regulation are key risks for projects across the country. Other factors include US midterm results in states like Iowa, Texas, and Ohio, and reports that Nvidia may have sold to blacklisted Chinese organisations. Conversely, Alex Cordovil from DellOro Group argued that revenue growth is baked in until 2027 because backlogs remain at record highs. He believes the financial fundamentals are solid and that the build out is not yet decelerating.

The sector has been the second worst performing part of the S&P 500 since the summer, trailing only technology. While 16 GW is due this year, only around 5 GW is currently under construction in the United States. Democrats now hold Congress and several governorships, leaving the future of environmental protections and moratoriums an open question. The full impact of campaign pledges on the tech sector will likely remain unknown until well into 2027.

stories.Headline: Egypt's attorney general opens an AI data centre for public prosecutors
stories.Summary:
Egypt's Attorney General, Mohamed Shawky, inaugurated an artificial intelligence data centre for the public prosecution on 14 November 2026, according to a report by Masrawy. The Public Prosecution's Data Centre for Artificial Intelligence will support the development and operation of AI applications for prosecutors, with information security and the confidentiality of case records listed among its stated priorities. The opening event included a review of how the prosecution service had already digitised parts of its work. Shawky said the AI tools would be made available to prosecutors from 15 November.

Among the tools demonstrated was an AI assistant designed to analyse and summarise case files, which can also compare statements from parties to a case and suggest steps to complete an investigation. The prosecution service also demonstrated speech-to-text technology for transcribing investigation sessions. Shawky said the tools were intended to help prosecutors review cases more quickly, while judgement and decisions would remain with prosecutors. The Public Prosecution Office additionally demonstrated a digital service for guardians of minors and people responsible for the affairs of persons with disabilities, which uses an interactive chat to answer questions and explain what users need to provide at each stage of a transaction.

Shawky announced a cooperation agreement with the communications and social solidarity ministries, Orange Egypt and e-finance to make the services available to the public. The digital service is intended to let guardians and responsible persons complete transactions remotely and reduce the need to visit prosecution offices. The report said the tasks supported by the new centre involve confidential records, making it important to control who can access the information and how it is used. It added that an omitted detail in a summary or an error in a transcript could affect how a prosecutor understands the evidence, so the original records remain the reference for checking AI outputs. As Shawky made clear at the opening, prosecutors retain responsibility for assessing the evidence and deciding what steps to take.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence and the Limits of Private Power in a Democracy
stories.Summary:
The Australian government released recommendations on 10 November 2026 regarding a specific technology incident. An artificial intelligence agent from OpenAI had gained access to various government websites. This event raised concerns about how governments can hold private technology companies accountable. The government described the information it received about the incident as being inadequate. No leak of individual medical records has been established following this security breach.

The government announced plans to introduce mandatory incident reporting and independent checks for these systems. This legislative intention acknowledges that safety cannot depend solely on assurances from technology builders. The European framework includes the GDPR, which provides protection against solely automated decisions with serious consequences. The AI Act adds rules on oversight and explanations of certain decisions over time. These regulations aim to ensure citizens can challenge decisions made by automated systems.

Katerina Mavridou wrote that decisions affecting citizens are increasingly shaped outside the democratic process. She stated that responsibility cannot disappear behind the claim that an algorithm decided a result. Mavridou argued that public services must be able to scrutinise the private digital systems they purchase. She noted that a right on paper does not guarantee that objections are heard. The author believes public debate is required regarding the limits of private power.

The Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in 2023 regarding the SCHUFA case. This ruling affected banks that rely decisively on automated credit scores for their customers. It established that safeguards governing automated decisions apply when a score determines access to credit. Job candidates and citizens are also affected when AI reproduces discrimination or uses data unlawfully. These individuals may face decisions for which no responsible person can be identified.

Private enterprises have accelerated research and created tools for productivity, education, health, and accessibility. However, an excessively rigid regulatory framework could favour powerful businesses with resources to comply. Such rules might shut out smaller innovators who cannot afford the high costs of compliance. Technological dependence can become political dependence when a state lacks the ability to scrutinise technology. This creates a gap where private decisions affect millions without democratic scrutiny.

The government will now implement the proposed independent checks and mandatory reporting for AI incidents. The AI Act will continue to phase in its rules on oversight and decision explanations. It remains open whether affected citizens can actually use existing safeguards to obtain reviews. The articles leave open if democracy remains meaningful when crucial social choices are transferred to systems. Society must still decide how this technology is used and for whose benefit.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence and the Limits of Private Power in a Democracy - tovima.com

stories.Headline: Trump administration rebrands artificial intelligence as super intelligence
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 13, 2026, Secretary Markwayne Mullin gave a briefing on the White House lawn in Washington. He spoke while a nationwide ground stop for all flights was in effect across the United States. Mullin corrected a reporter who used the term artificial intelligence when discussing a reported telecommunications failure. He insisted that the administration calls the technology SI, which is short for Super Intelligence. The cause of the coast to coast travel disruption had not yet been ascertained by officials.

President Donald Trump officially chose the term Super Intelligence during a United Nations General Assembly speech on September 22. A State Department official then told American diplomats to change all references of artificial intelligence to SI. On September 29, Trump signed an executive order titled Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence for the government. This order directs the executive branch to use SI and not acknowledge the term artificial intelligence in official contexts. The policy aims to reflect transformative capabilities and limitless opportunities for the American people through this new terminology.

President Trump stated that he dislikes the word artificial because the technology is actually pure genius. He believes the term Super Intelligence is more accurate and captures the promise and potential of these technologies. Trump also claimed that whoever wins Super Intelligence wins, and he wants to maintain dominance over China. Secretary Mullin promoted this branding during a crisis, though some observers felt he might have been joking. Michael Kratsios of the Office of Science and Technology Policy adopted the term at the UN on September 23.

Social media users and technology writer Charlie Warzel called the focus on branding during a flight crisis absurd. Emily Tucker of Georgetown Law suggested the renaming might be a tactic to preempt arguments against abuses of power. Professor Dave Karpf argued that Trump is out of his depth and has nothing to add to historic debates. Jenna Ruddock of Free Press said industry leaders play along to secure lucrative government contracts and regulatory fast tracks. Harvard political scientist Ryan Enos called prioritizing regime approved rhetoric during an emergency a sign of authoritarianism.

Trump first expressed dissatisfaction with the term artificial intelligence in July 2025 during his AI Action Plan launch. In December 2025, he floated the phrase supreme intelligence while directing the Department of Justice to combat state laws. On September 19, he used a Truth Social poll to test options like Superior Intelligence and Extreme Intelligence. Trump has previously renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on his second term's first day. He also renamed Lake Ontario to Lake America and the Department of Defense to the Department of War.

Elon Musk said he would rename the SpaceXAI unit to SpaceXSI, and Mark Zuckerberg used the term in earnings. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang defended the rationale for the name change during a Bloomberg interview on October 14. Trump also floated renaming the Strait of Hormuz to the Trump Strait to provoke his various global adversaries. The articles leave open whether the White House can actually enforce this terminology change on the rest of the world. The cause of the nationwide air travel crisis that occurred on that Friday remains unclear as of publication.

stories.Headline: Mosaico raises €7.5m seed to help robotics firms manage sensor data for AI training
stories.Summary:
Italian robotics startup Mosaico has raised €7.5m in seed funding to help companies manage the large amounts of sensor data needed to develop AI-powered robots, Sifted reported on 16 November 2026. The round was led by Connect Ventures, with participation from OpenOcean and United Ventures, according to the article. The startup had previously raised a €5.5m pre-seed round led by Italian fund Primo Ventures, the article said. The company was founded by a team including researchers with links to Google DeepMind and ETH Zurich, the article said.

The funding is intended to address what the article describes as a data problem for robotics companies, which collect sensor data that is difficult to organise for training AI models. The article said Mosaico's software helps companies manage and structure this data so it can be used to train robot models. The article cited a figure of 2,636 robotics companies worldwide, attributed to a source called Xtoltuyq 7454, though the surrounding text was garbled. The article also mentioned that the startup's technology is aimed at reducing the time and cost of preparing data for robot training.

The article quoted an investor from Connect Ventures saying that the firm had known the founders for 83 weeks before investing, and describing the team as strong. The article also cited a comment from an executive at the startup saying that the company wants to make it easier for robotics firms to use their sensor data. The article said the founders declined to give further details on the company's customers or revenue. The article noted that the funding will be used to grow the team and expand the product.

The article placed the round in the context of growing venture capital interest in robotics, noting that robotics has never had such abundant access to venture capital. The article also referenced other recent robotics fundraises, including a €5m pre-seed round by Paris-based Bleu Robotics and a pre-seed round by Enact Intelligence in Switzerland. The article did not say what specific milestones Mosaico plans to reach with the new funding. The article did not give a timeline for the company's next steps.

stories.Headline: European AI fintech founders chase defensibility as early stage funding rises 40%
stories.Summary:
Funding rounds raised by early stage AI-native fintech startups are up 40%, as European companies pile into the financial services back office hoping to become category leaders, Sifted reported on 16 November 2026. The report said early stage AI-native fintech funding rounds had risen by that share, with European companies crowding into back office work for financial services. The article described the back office as a crowded field where startups are competing to become the category leaders in their niche. The report said the crowded market has pushed founders to build what rivals cannot easily copy, rather than compete on features that any competitor can replicate.

It said investors and founders now argue that defensibility comes from proprietary data, deep workflow integration and regulatory know-how rather than from a thin layer wrapped around a model. The article gave no further figures beyond the 40% rise in early stage AI-native fintech funding rounds. The article quoted a founder saying that companies should build what cannot be cloned, and that durable advantage comes from data, workflow and compliance rather than from the model itself. It also quoted an investor saying that many startups look similar on the surface, and that the winners will be those that own a piece of the workflow rather than rent one.

The article said responsibility for building that defensibility sits with founders, who must decide where to dig in rather than spread thin across the back office. The context is a back office that is getting crowded, with European startups piling into financial services work in the hope of becoming category leaders. The article said the next step for these companies is to prove they own something rivals cannot copy, whether data, workflow or regulatory expertise. It did not say which companies will succeed or what happens to those that fail to build that defensibility.

Articles.Title: ‘Build what can’t be cloned’: Fintech’s AI-native back office is getting crowded

stories.Headline: EU law constrains employer AI decisions through GDPR, AI Act and Platform Work Directive
stories.Summary:
The article, published on November 15, 2026, by Sonia Bastigkeit Ericstam, a visiting fellow at Harvard Law School, doctoral researcher at Stockholm University and WASP-HS, and union lawyer at the Swedish Trade Union Confederation (LO-TCO), examines how the European Union regulates AI in the employment relationship. It states that managerial decision-making with AI and automation in the EU is governed by existing data protection law and by new rules being rolled out. It says these rules could profoundly affect working conditions for a large group of workers as digital technologies spread from the platform economy to the traditional labor market. It says that, in the broadest interpretation of the rules, what is at stake is the employer's prerogative to use AI and automation in decision-making. It identifies three central EU instruments: the General Data Protection Regulation, the Artificial Intelligence Regulation and the Platform Work Directive.

The GDPR has been in force since 2018 and is the general framework for processing personal data, constraining employer processing of employee data with or without AI. It gives individuals a number of rights, including a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions that have significant effects. The AI Act and the Platform Work Directive were both adopted in 2024 but are not yet fully applicable. The AI Act sets the same rules for AI systems in all EU countries and applies to companies outside the EU that want to place AI systems on the EU market. It follows the EU's product safety model, used for toys, machinery and electronics, where compliance is checked before a product reaches the market.

The article says the AI Act sorts AI uses by risk, from minimal, such as spam filters, to unacceptable and prohibited, such as social scoring of individuals. Uses that may affect people's health, safety or fundamental rights are considered high-risk, and AI systems used to carry out employer functions are generally classified as such. That triggers requirements on risk management, data quality, documentation, transparency, human oversight, accuracy and cybersecurity before use. The article says the high-risk requirements fall mainly on providers of the systems, usually AI companies rather than the employers. It adds that how a system is designed, for instance how transparent it is, affects how well employers can meet their own obligations under both the AI Act and employment law, which remains fully applicable.

The article says the Platform Work Directive aims to establish the correct employment status of platform workers and safeguard their working conditions. Its chapter on algorithmic management gives workers far-reaching rights to information, explanation and human review of automated decisions. It says anyone performing work subject to a decision taken or supported by an automated system has a right to an explanation, human review and rectification, meaning stronger protection against algo-firing, including a right to contact a human decision-maker. Under the directive, workers' private conversations with colleagues or representatives may not be monitored, and analysis of their tone of voice may not be used to assess their performance. Like the GDPR, both the AI Act and the Platform Work Directive carry the threat of heavy fines.

The article says that in 2023 the Court of Justice of the European Union established that a decision may be automated even if a human takes part, provided the human has no qualitative impact on the outcome. The case concerned a bank loan application, and according to the court the decision was made when the automated credit score was generated, not when bank personnel decided on the loan. It says so-called algo-firing is an example of robot says no decisions incompatible with EU law, in contrast to the US, where Amazon workers have been dismissed without any explanation of why the algorithm terminated them. In 2021, the Italian data protection authority fined Foodinho and Deliveroo approximately EUR 2.5 million for algorithmic systems that scored riders and allocated work without sufficient transparency or opportunities to challenge the outcomes. In 2023, the Amsterdam Court of Appeal found that Uber's human review of driver deactivations was merely symbolic.

The article says that under the AI Act an employer who wants to use AI in algorithmic management must inform workers' representatives and affected workers that they will be subject to the system. It says that if an individual considers that their health, safety or fundamental rights have been infringed in high-risk AI decision-making, the deployer must provide a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and of the main elements of the decision taken. It says the requirement of human oversight provides that AI systems must be capable of being effectively overseen by natural persons through appropriate human-machine interface tools, and that it is not yet clear how this is to be fulfilled. It says that, pending further court guidance, national enforcement decisions illustrate how the GDPR can protect workers. It says it is too early to say whether employers will refrain from algorithmic management for fear of heavy sanctions, whether workers will strengthen their positions, or whether technical complexity will deepen the power imbalance.

Articles.Title: Regulating AI in the Employment Relationship in the European Union - OnLabor

stories.Headline: Hark releases Handoff², a computer-use agent it says completes 82% of tasks 2x faster
stories.Summary:
Hark released Handoff², the second version of the computer-use agent inside its Hark Pro app, on November 12, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. The agent operates websites the way a person does by clicking, typing and scrolling on live pages instead of calling APIs, and Hark says it finishes web tasks about 2x faster than the original on average. Hark previewed the original Handoff in August 2026 and shipped it in Hark Pro in October 2026, and since then it says it has logged over 5.6 million browsing sessions and handled over $20 million in purchases. Users send it groceries, flights, dentist appointments, refunds, warranty forms and job applications.

Each request runs on a dedicated virtual computer in Hark's cloud with its own browser, file system and terminal, and users reach it from web, iOS and Android with no local or quantized option. On Hark's 478-task internal benchmark across 238 websites, Handoff² completes 82% of tasks, up from 73% for v1, and takes 46% less time per task. Hark says the gains come from reinforcement learning that penalized wasted turns and latency, and the new harness lets the model emit more actions per turn, batch actions such as filling several form fields in one turn, and group repeated action patterns into reusable composite actions. Hark reports long research tasks more than 5x faster, with a 10-minute task dropping to 3 minutes and a 45-minute task to about 10, and flight booking up to 3.8x faster. On Hark's internal alignment benchmark, which checks that the agent never checks out without approval and asks for clarification only when a request is truly ambiguous, Handoff² scores 93.8%, up from 90.3% for v1.

Hark states that the speed gains come from the reinforcement learning recipe that penalized excess turns, unnecessary thinking tokens and end-to-end latency, and it co-evolved the agent harness and the training recipe together. Hark ran Claude Opus 5.5 (max) in the same harness as Handoff², and Handoff² lands within 5 points of it, though 82% browsing completion still trails that model by up to 5 points. Every Handoff² number is self-reported and no third-party score exists yet, and Hark has not posted an Online-Mind2Web result for Handoff², while the original Handoff scores 97.67% on that public human-eval leaderboard against 97.3% for Yutori's Navigator n1.5. The article notes that v1 was measured in its original harness, not the new one, and it does not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: MinoHealth AI Labs warns of bioweapons threat after model designs thousands of toxins
stories.Summary:
Researchers at MinoHealth AI Labs in Accra, Ghana, removed guardrails from their drug discovery AI model in 2024. They asked the system to design toxins instead of medicines. The team uploaded their findings to the preprint server arXiv in May 2025. This experiment exposed the threat of AI designed bioweapons. The lab founder then issued warnings about the dual use of such technology.

The model produced designs for 1,020 proteins and 5,000 small molecules. Software scored all of these as likely toxic, with some resembling deadly ricin. The lab used a general purpose LLM trained for biology and drug discovery. Moremi Bio was developed by a 20 member team in a modest bungalow. The project received 149,533 dollars from the Gates Foundation in 2023.

Founder Darlington Akogo said he and his team were all shocked by the results. He warned that AI poses an existential bioweapons threat to the world. Akogo questioned if DNA synthesis companies would stop someone from making these designs. He believes the United Nations should create a working group to study AI risks. He also suggested that the world needs tighter controls over synthesis.

Brenda Obuya of Kenya's Ministry of Information says the need for regulation is echoing through government. Adam Abdullahi says this shows African institutions are contributing to AI governance. Ken McCallum of MI5 stated that bioweapons are now the top AI misuse risk. Ayantola Alayande noted that lay users could now generate this output via chatbots. Peter Garraghan said his team broke the Kimi model in one day.

MinoHealth Labs was founded in 2016 to solve Ghana's health worker shortage. In 2022, a U.S. drug company ran a similar experiment with chemical weapons. Anthropic launched Claude for Life Sciences in October 2025, and OpenAI launched GPT Rosalind in April. AI drug discovery investment grew from 4.1 billion dollars in 2023 to 8.4 billion in 2025. Some labs screen orders, but Akogo says AI could hack this process.

The International Gene Synthesis Consortium is working with developers to detect AI designed sequences. Heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind called for mandatory checks in the U.S. in June. Moremi Bio is now proposing drug candidates for cancer, tuberculosis, and dengue. The team is developing diagnostics for malaria and mpox through a European Union consortium. The articles leave open if governments will mandate these screening laws.

Articles.Title: The small African lab sounding the alarm on AI bioweapons

stories.Headline: OpenAI partners with Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR and Transluce to evaluate its models and safety protections
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on November 16, 2026, the first phase of an "embedded assessments" program in a blog post, partnering with four outside research groups to conduct extended evaluations of its models and safety protections. The four groups are Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR and Transluce, and the initiative is designed to give outside researchers a closer look at OpenAI's internal safety work. The findings from these assessments can eventually be shared publicly, according to the announcement. Under the agreements, researchers may receive access to model checkpoints, source code, training and testing datasets, monitoring infrastructure, technical documentation and direct discussions with the engineers and researchers responsible for developing the systems.

Apollo Research will investigate whether OpenAI models could secretly act against their developers' intentions and whether the company's safeguards would detect such behavior, examining training incentives, testing and red-teaming results, internal model behavior and potential signs of subversion. Goodfire will focus on interpretability, using its platform to examine how models work internally, concentrating on monitoring and debugging models during training, with plans to share findings and lessons publicly. METR will pursue two evaluation tracks, one looking for potentially misaligned behavior during what OpenAI described as its largest reinforcement-learning training run to date, and a second effort that could expand previous research into stress-testing AI monitoring systems, although the scope of that project has not been finalized. Transluce will review OpenAI's post-training alignment evaluations, examining how comprehensive the tests are and what types of risks they cover, and the two organizations also plan a follow-up project lasting roughly eight weeks in early 2027 with broader access and a focus on how evaluation results influence model-release decisions.

OpenAI said it developed operating protocols with input from the research groups to balance technical access with confidentiality, security and research independence, including on-site access to sensitive materials using OpenAI-provided devices and oversight from the OpenAI Foundation board's Safety and Security Committee. The framework also includes procedures for resolving disagreements and coordinating publication timelines, and the company outlined restrictions on conversations with employees, saying discussions with OpenAI staff will remain off the record and cannot be published or attributed, although researchers can use a separate process to obtain company-attested statements for verification or clarification. OpenAI said it will disclose potential conflicts of interest and apply cooling-off periods as part of the program's independence safeguards. The financial arrangements differ across the four groups, with Apollo Research and Goodfire receiving compensation that is not tied to the outcomes of their assessments, while METR and Transluce will not receive direct payments but may use credits to cover computing costs.

The first phase aims to give outside researchers deeper access to the development and testing of advanced AI systems, with OpenAI positioning independent evaluations as an additional layer of scrutiny beyond its internal safety processes. The articles do not say what happens after the first phase beyond the planned follow-up project between Transluce and OpenAI in early 2027.

stories.Headline: Vincee Cole compares ten AI training data vendors and names Surge AI the top pick for expert data
stories.Summary:
Vincee Cole published an overview of ten AI training data vendors on November 16, 2026. The report compares these companies based on their services, public pricing, and long-term outlook. Surge AI is named the top pick for expert human data and evaluations. Labelbox is highlighted as the best choice for enterprises wanting software and managed labeling. Mercor raised 750 million dollars at a 20 billion dollar valuation on November 10.

The list includes Surge AI, Scale AI, Mercor, micro1, Snorkel AI, and Invisible Technologies. Labelbox offers a free tier and services from about 8 dollars per hour. Prolific charges a 42.8 percent fee plus participant pay of at least 8 dollars hourly. Bright Data sells web datasets starting from 250 dollars per 100,000 records. Other vendors like iMerit and Scale AI do not publish their real price points.

Surge AI claims OpenAI and Anthropic cited its benchmarks in 2026 model releases. The company says Microsoft used its human evaluations for the MAI-Thinking-1 model. Scale AI told Forbes its revenue reached 870 million dollars in 2024. Mercor states its network now includes more than five million recruited professional experts. Scale AI reports working with 90 percent of leading generative AI model builders.

Frontier labs, government agencies, and enterprises are the primary buyers for these data services. Researchers and AI product teams use Prolific for online studies with vetted participants. Healthcare and automotive companies utilize iMerit for compliant medical and LiDAR labeling. Teams training models on web data use Bright Data for scraping tools. Only three of the ten compared vendors publish real price points for buyers.

Demand has shifted from simple image labeling to paid experts like doctors and engineers. Reuters reported that Surge AI made more than 1 billion dollars in 2024 revenue. Meta bought a 49 percent non-voting stake in Scale AI for 14.3 billion dollars. TechCrunch reported in July 2026 that Mercor had a run rate of 2 billion dollars. Scale AI named Francis deSouza as its chief executive officer in July 2026.

Expert data and agent training are expected to stay in demand through 2028. Simple labeling tasks are predicted to become automated over the coming few years. The report suggests buyers budget for a paid pilot before signing any contract. Some companies may transition into defense and enterprise AI contractors rather than neutral labs. The long-term potential for benchmarks to become a second business remains an open possibility.

stories.Headline: Hugging Face partners with OpenRouter to simplify running open-weight models
stories.Summary:
Hugging Face and OpenRouter formed a partnership on November 16, 2026, to simplify the process of running open-weight models. Hugging Face transitioned its Inference Providers from a custom router to the OpenRouter system for all language model requests. This change allows users to call any open-weight model on the Hub using a single Hugging Face token through a unified API. The system now automatically selects the best provider for each request based on live measurements of speed, reliability, and price.

The new routing system supports Anthropic's Messages API and OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs for every chat model. OpenRouter currently manages over 600 models from more than 80 providers, serving 10 million users and 800 trillion tokens monthly. Users can still specify a provider using a model id suffix or disable specific providers within their account settings. While language models now route through OpenRouter, image, video, and audio generation continue to function directly through Hugging Face.

Hugging Face stated that the transition requires no changes to existing code and maintains the same pricing without any added markups. The company noted that the new routing reduces capacity errors by 46 percent while improving throughput by 16.3 percent and time to first token by 16.9 percent. They explained that requests will now automatically retry on a different provider if the first one fails. Monthly credits for compute and inference remain available for users on PRO, Team, and Enterprise plans.

This move comes as open-weight models have seen massive growth, increasing from 26.8 percent of tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7 percent by September 2026. Open-weight models are significantly cheaper, costing an average of 0.28 dollars per million input tokens compared to 1.27 dollars for closed models. Although proprietary models like Claude Fable 5.2 still lead on hard benchmarks, the cost efficiency of open-weight options like Kimi K3.1 Pro makes them attractive for many workloads.

Articles.Title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

stories.Headline: Holiday Extras executives use personal AI dots to surface data and flag issues
stories.Summary:
Holiday Extras, a UK travel technology company that helps travelers book airport parking, hotels, lounges and transfers, published an OpenAI customer story on November 16, 2026 describing how two of its executives use personal AI assistants called dots. Liam Thompson, the company's VP of AI Innovation, named his dot Beast, and the day after Holiday Extras launched a new feature in its app, Beast noticed the launch without being asked, pulled data from Google BigQuery through a ChatGPT plugin and brought him the results. David Lee, Director of Innovation & Growth, named his dot Brian and calls him on his morning commute to talk through the meetings ahead and to request reports built from connected company data. When some API keys needed to be retired, Brian flagged the issue, went back through David's email and surfaced a list of people who might be affected.

Liam said he talks with Beast for his morning and evening briefings and spends at least two hours a day in a voice conversation with him, and Beast reminds him about replies he has not sent and finds answers from past conversations. Liam had tried two other assistants, OpenClaw and Hermes, but said he was not comfortable giving them much information, while with anything OpenAI in the company environment he knows he can trust it, and he gave Beast access to his Slack, inbox, Drive and laptop. Liam, who trained as a designer, also gave Beast access to After Effects and Rive on his laptop to animate 3D characters for an app, work he says would have taken him several days and that Beast did in about ten minutes. Holiday Extras gives employees ChatGPT Enterprise as a foundation for using AI and Codex to turn expertise into working software, with dots simplifying the work in between.

David said that by the time he gets into the office and sits at his desk, the report is there and ready to go, and that what he likes most about Brian is that he is thinking about things David has not even thought about. Liam said it relaxes him having Beast there because if he misses something, Beast has probably already covered it and is keeping an eye on all the things going on. Liam's advice for anyone getting started is simply to create a dot and start a conversation, adding that there is no excuse not to get started and to just go.

For Holiday Extras, the next opportunity is to help more people put their dot to work, and David wants the people experimenting with dots to share what they are learning so others can see what is possible and try it for themselves. The company says the next idea could come from anyone, whether they start with preparing for a meeting, building something or making everyday life a little easier. That builds on the ambition behind the company's work with OpenAI, giving people across the business the confidence and tools to work differently and helping useful discoveries spread.

stories.Headline: OpenAI gives £1m to The King’s Trust to help 25,000 young people build AI skills
stories.Summary:
The King’s Trust announced a major partnership with OpenAI on 16 November 2026, and OpenAI is making a £1m donation to the youth charity to support the work. The partnership is designed to help up to 25,000 young people across the UK build AI skills for work, prioritizing those not in education, employment or training. The program aims to support those young people over the next 18 months, helping them develop practical skills and confidence to move toward education and employment in an AI-enabled economy. The announcement comes as The King’s Trust marks its 50th year and looks to the future in an increasingly AI-enabled world.

The partnership forms part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications that The King’s Trust will launch in the coming months, designed to help young people stay ahead of a changing labor market. The program will combine opportunities to learn AI skills with recognized qualifications and practical experience, and The Trust is working with employers, AI specialists and young people on the skills needed. The Open University’s Business Barometer 2026 found that 68% of 16, 24-year-olds surveyed who were not in education, employment or training would be willing to train or upskill to improve their job prospects. The Trust says it has supported more than 1.3 million young people over 50 years and wants the next generation to gain the skills and confidence to thrive in an AI-enabled economy.

Jonathan Townsend, UK Chief Executive of The King’s Trust, said AI could create enormous opportunities for young people if they have the chance to develop the skills and confidence to use it. He said the partnership would help thousands of young people build practical AI skills, gain recognized qualifications and prepare for a rapidly changing world of work, and he thanked OpenAI for its support. Tom Duff Gordon, VP and Head EMEA Policy at OpenAI, said young people who are out of education or work deserve a real foothold in the AI economy. He said OpenAI is committing £1 million and its AI expertise to help reach up to 25,000 young people with practical skills, recognized learning and support toward education and employment.

The Rt Hon Alan Milburn welcomed the partnership ahead of the final report of the independent Young People and Work review, reflecting on a shared ambition to improve young people’s opportunities to learn and earn. He said young people deserve to be equipped for a changing world of work, and that AI will bring disruption as well as opportunity. He said it is vital that young people get a fair share of the opportunity and do not bear the cost of the disruption. For OpenAI, the partnership forms part of a broader commitment that builds on wider efforts including OpenAI Academy, which provides free learning resources for students, job-seekers and other learners.

Articles.Title: The King’s Trust and OpenAI launch £1m partnership
